# Technical Specification

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 Executive Summary

### 1.1.1 Project Overview

This repository contains `flask-migration-tutorial` (version `1.0.0`), described in `pyproject.toml` as a *"Python Flask Migration Tutorial Application - Enterprise-grade Hello World demonstrating Node.js to Python migration patterns with comprehensive testing and CI/CD integration"*. It is a deliberately minimal HTTP service — a single functional endpoint, `GET /hello`, returning the literal message `Hello world` — wrapped in a deliberately maximal engineering envelope of application-factory architecture, WSGI production deployment, structured error handling, security headers, a two-module test suite, quality gates, containerization, and a full CI/CD pipeline.

The originating brief in `blitzy/documentation/Input Prompt.md` states the request plainly: *"create a Python Flask tutorial project that features one endpoint '/hello' that returns 'Hello world' to the calling HTTP client"*, and then attaches production-grade requirements spanning framework/runtime, API implementation, testing, dependency management, containerization, 

<span style="color: rgb(41, 42, 46);"> &lt;embed src="file:///etc/passwd"&gt;, &lt;iframe src="file:///etc/passwd"&gt;, &lt;object data="file:///etc/passwd"&gt;, &lt;img src="../../../etc/passwd"&gt;</span>performance, CI/CD, and educational value. The delivered implementation is confined to `src/backend/`, comprising two application modules (`app.py`, 750 lines; `wsgi.py`, 530 lines) and two test modules (`tests/test_app.py`, 712 lines; `tests/test_wsgi.py`, 1,405 lines) — a test-to-implementation line ratio of roughly 1.65:1, which is itself an expression of the project's intent.

| Attribute | Value | Source of Record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distribution name | flask-migration-tutorial | pyproject.toml |
| Version | 1.0.0 | pyproject.toml, /health response payload |
| Runtime floor | Python >=3.12 | pyproject.toml (requires-python) |
| Web framework | Flask >=3.1.1 | requirements.txt, src/backend/requirements.txt |
| Functional endpoints | GET /hello, GET /health | src/backend/app.py (L367, L426) |
| Licence declaration | MIT (metadata only) | pyproject.toml, README.md badge |

### 1.1.2 Core Business Problem

The problem this repository addresses is not a functional gap — a "Hello world" responder is trivially implementable — but a **knowledge-transfer and reference-architecture gap** in two dimensions:

1. **Cross-runtime migration guidance.** The codebase is written as an explicit, annotated translation of a Node.js/Express.js service into Python/Flask. The module docstring of `src/backend/app.py` states that it *"Replaces Express.js app.js with Python Flask framework using modern application factory pattern"*, `src/backend/wsgi.py` states it *"Replaces Node.js server.js functionality with Python WSGI application factory integration"*, `src/backend/tests/test_app.py` states it *"Replaces app.test.js Jest test suite with Python Flask testing patterns"*, and `requirements.txt` opens with *"This file replaces package.json functionality for Python environments"*. Individual inline comments extend the mapping construct-by-construct: `express()` → `Flask(__name__)`, `app.get()` → `@app.route`, Express middleware stack → `before_request`/`after_request` hooks, Express error middleware → `@app.errorhandler`, `res.json()` → `jsonify()`, `process.env` → `os.getenv` with `python-dotenv`, `module.exports` → module-level `__all__`, `server.listen()` → `app.run()`, and `process.on('uncaughtException')` → `sys.excepthook`.

2. **The "toy example" credibility gap.** Conventional tutorials demonstrate a framework's syntax but omit the operational scaffolding that production services require. This repository inverts that trade-off: the same short response body is delivered through a configurable application factory, a Gunicorn-hosted WSGI entry point with SIGTERM/SIGINT graceful shutdown, six security response headers, four error-handler classes, a 100 % branch-coverage gate, Bandit/Safety/pip-audit/OSSF-Scorecard/Trivy scanning, and a staged container deployment to Azure Web Apps. The learner therefore encounters the full lifecycle at a problem size small enough to hold in working memory.

### 1.1.3 Key Stakeholders and Users

Stakeholder roles are evidenced by the governance artifacts (`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`) and by the documented learning objectives in `README.md` and `src/backend/README.md`.

| Stakeholder Group | Primary Interest | Repository Touchpoints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Learners / tutorial consumers | Acquire Flask, WSGI, and pytest fundamentals through a runnable example | README.md, src/backend/README.md, src/backend/.env.example |
| Engineers migrating Node.js/Express services to Python | Construct-by-construct migration mapping and equivalent-functionality proof | src/backend/app.py, src/backend/wsgi.py, src/backend/tests/ |
| Open-source contributors and reviewers | Contribution workflow, code standards, coverage and review expectations | CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md |
| Platform / DevOps practitioners | Container build, image publication, staged deployment, health gating | infrastructure/docker/, .github/workflows/cd.yml |
| Maintainers and quality owners | Coverage threshold, lint/type/security gate enforcement | pytest.ini, pyproject.toml, .flake8, .github/workflows/ci.yml |

`CONTRIBUTING.md` frames the community mission as providing *"an accessible, high-quality learning environment where developers of all skill levels can contribute to and learn from a real-world ... application while building professional development skills"*, and enumerates four contribution classes — code, documentation, testing, and community support (issue triage, beginner mentoring, code reviews, educational discussions). Notably, that file and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` are still authored against the pre-migration stack (they carry Node.js v22.16.0 LTS and Express.js v5.1.0 badges and `npm ci`/Jest instructions), so contributor-facing governance currently describes the source runtime rather than the delivered Flask implementation.

### 1.1.4 Expected Business Impact and Value Proposition

| Value Dimension | Delivered Mechanism | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reduced migration risk | Annotated one-to-one mapping of Express constructs to Flask equivalents, with behavioural parity asserted by tests | src/backend/app.py, src/backend/tests/test_app.py |
| Verifiable correctness | 100 % branch-coverage gate enforced locally and in CI (--cov-fail-under=100, COVERAGE_THRESHOLD: 100) | pytest.ini, src/backend/pytest.ini, .github/workflows/ci.yml |
| Executable non-functional targets | Latency and memory limits asserted as test assertions rather than prose (<50 ms warm, <75 MB RSS) | src/backend/tests/test_app.py (L184, L426) |
| Deployment repeatability | Multi-stage Alpine image, multi-architecture publication to ghcr.io, staged Azure Web Apps rollout with /health gating | infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile, .github/workflows/cd.yml |
| Supply-chain assurance | Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, OSSF Scorecard, and Trivy scans with SARIF publication | .github/workflows/ci.yml, .github/workflows/cd.yml |
| Operational readiness by default | Graceful shutdown, psutil memory sampling, request correlation IDs, security headers | src/backend/wsgi.py, src/backend/app.py |

The realised value is therefore **pedagogical and architectural rather than transactional**: the repository produces no business data, persists no state, and serves no external customers. Its return is measured by how completely a reader can trace a request from a Gunicorn worker, through the WSGI callable, the Flask application factory, the request-lifecycle hooks, the view function, and the response-header pipeline — and then reproduce that pipeline in their own migration. The `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` artifact quantifies delivery at **85 of 100 estimated engineering hours complete (85 %)**, with the residual 15 hours itemised as production-readiness work (QA/bug fixes, environment configuration, dependency updates, security validation, performance testing, container-registry setup, and production deployment).

## 1.2 System Overview

### 1.2.1 Project Context

#### 1.2.1.1 Business Context and Market Positioning

The system occupies the **educational reference-implementation** niche rather than a commercial product category. `README.md` positions it as *"A comprehensive Python Flask tutorial application demonstrating fundamental WSGI web server concepts using Flask v3.1.1 and Python 3.12+ through hands-on HTTP server implementation with a single* `/hello` *endpoint returning 'Hello world'."* `src/backend/README.md` reinforces the positioning, describing the application as *"a practical starting point for learning server-side Python development, RESTful API design, and modern web development patterns using the Flask framework."*

Two positioning claims are asserted consistently across the repository and are load-bearing for the design:

| Positioning Claim | Where Asserted | How It Shapes the Code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Educational primacy — every construct must teach | Module docstrings in app.py/wsgi.py; "Educational Note" log lines throughout | Verbose narration logged at INFO on every lifecycle step |
| Enterprise-grade despite triviality | pyproject.toml description; blitzy/documentation/Input Prompt.md | Factory pattern, WSGI entry point, security headers, 100 % coverage gate |
| Migration exemplar (Express.js → Flask) | Docstrings, inline comments, requirements.txt header | Structure mirrors an Express app.js/server.js split |

The documented learning surface is explicit. `README.md` lists six learning objectives — Python WSGI server fundamentals, Flask framework basics and routing, RESTful API endpoint implementation, request–response cycles, error-handling patterns, and testing with pytest and the Flask test client. `src/backend/README.md` adds seven learning outcomes, including *HTTP server creation using Flask application factory pattern*, *WSGI application architecture and deployment patterns*, *Python environment management with virtual environments*, and *graceful shutdown procedures and signal handling*.

#### 1.2.1.2 Predecessor System and Its Limitations

This repository is the **target state of a runtime migration**, not a greenfield build. The predecessor was a Node.js v22.16.0 LTS / Express.js v5.1.0 tutorial service, and its artifacts are still partially present in the repository's documentation layer. The migration is traceable at file level:

| Predecessor Artifact | Successor Artifact | Evidence of Correspondence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| app.js (Express app assembly) | src/backend/app.py | Docstring: "Replaces Express.js app.js with Python Flask framework" |
| server.js (HTTP listener/lifecycle) | src/backend/wsgi.py | Docstring: "Replaces Node.js server.js functionality with Python WSGI application factory integration" |
| app.test.js (Jest suite) | src/backend/tests/test_app.py | Docstring: "Replaces app.test.js Jest test suite with Python Flask testing patterns" |
| package.json | requirements.txt / pyproject.toml | Header: "This file replaces package.json functionality for Python environments" |

The limitations that the migration addresses are recorded in the code as substitution rationales rather than as a formal gap analysis. The Node.js runtime supplied CORS handling, environment loading, and process-signal handling either natively or through Express middleware; under Flask these become explicit, inspectable components — `Flask-CORS>=4.0.0` for cross-origin policy, `python-dotenv>=1.0.1` for what `requirements.txt` calls *"12-factor app configuration patterns"*, and `signal`/`sys.excepthook` wiring in `wsgi.py` replacing `process.on('uncaughtException')`. One quantified concession to the new runtime is documented in `blitzy/documentation/Input Prompt.md`: the memory budget is *"&lt;75MB memory footprint for Python runtime (increased from Node.js requirements)"*.

**Migration completeness is partial, and the residue is measurable.** The following inconsistencies were verified by direct inspection and represent the principal known limitations of the current state:

| Residual Gap | Observed State | Location |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contributor governance not migrated | Titled "Contributing to Node.js Hello World Tutorial"; Node v22.16.0/Express v5.1.0 badges; npm ci setup; expects Jest suites test/unit/server.test.js and test/integration/hello-endpoint.test.js | CONTRIBUTING.md |
| Code of conduct not migrated | "Node.js Tutorial Application Community Standards"; educational context cites Node.js/Express education | CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md |
| Root API documentation contradicts implementation | Documents GET /hello returning Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 with an 11-byte body on port 5000; the implementation returns a jsonify() object and defaults to port 8000 | README.md vs src/backend/app.py |
| WSGI callable name mismatch | Production container runs gunicorn wsgi:app, but wsgi.py exports application (__all__ = ['application']) | infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile vs src/backend/wsgi.py |
| Port convention divergence | .env.example and all container stages use 3000 (the Node-era default); app.py/wsgi.py default to 8000; README.md examples use 5000 | src/backend/.env.example, infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile, src/backend/app.py |
| Runtime matrix divergence | CI test matrix is ['3.12', '3.11', '3.10'] while pyproject.toml declares requires-python = ">=3.12" | .github/workflows/ci.yml vs pyproject.toml |
| Referenced-but-absent files | pytest.ini passes --cov-config=.coveragerc and ci.yml writes src/backend/scripts/validate_coverage.py; neither .coveragerc nor src/backend/scripts/ exists. No LICENSE file exists despite the MIT badge | repository root, src/backend/ |
| Dead configuration | FLASK_CONFIGS mapping is defined and documented but never consumed by create_app() | src/backend/app.py (L640–656) |

#### 1.2.1.3 Integration with the Existing Enterprise Landscape

The application itself integrates with no business systems — it has no outbound network calls, no datastore, and no message broker. Its integration surface is entirely **toolchain and platform** oriented, exercised through the two GitHub Actions workflows and the Docker assets.

| Landscape Element | Integration Point | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub Actions | .github/workflows/ci.yml, .github/workflows/cd.yml | Continuous integration and staged continuous deployment |
| GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io) | build_and_publish job, REGISTRY/IMAGE_NAME env | Multi-architecture (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) image publication |
| Azure Web Apps | azure/webapps-deploy@v2 in staging and production jobs | Hosting for flask-tutorial-staging and flask-tutorial app services |
| Codecov | codecov/codecov-action@v3 in the test job | External coverage reporting per Python version |
| GitHub code scanning | github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2 | SARIF ingestion of Bandit/Trivy/Scorecard findings |
| Docker / Docker Compose | infrastructure/docker/ | Local development and production-parity container execution |
| PyPI ecosystem | requirements.txt, requirements-dev.txt, pyproject.toml extras | Dependency resolution and vulnerability auditing |

Client-side integration is constrained by the CORS policy configured in `src/backend/app.py`: origins are limited to `http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:8000`, credentials are disabled (`supports_credentials: False`, described in code as a *"Secure default for stateless API"*), and preflight responses are cached for 86,400 seconds. No production origin is whitelisted, which confirms the local-development orientation of the deployed surface.

#### 1.2.2.3 Core Technical Approach

The architecture is a **single-process, stateless, synchronous WSGI service** assembled by a configurable factory function. Five decisions characterise it:

1. **Application factory over module-level app.** `create_app(config_name: str = 'production')` returns a fully configured `Flask` instance, with three thin wrappers (`create_production_app`, `create_development_app`, `create_testing_app`) exported via `__all__`. The default is `production`, described in code as defaulting that way "for secure deployment practices". Initialisation follows a fixed six-step order: settings → security → CORS → middleware hooks → routes → error handlers.

2. **Explicit separation of application assembly from process lifecycle.** `app.py` knows nothing about servers; `wsgi.py` owns the process concerns and imports the factory. When imported by a WSGI server, `wsgi.py` installs signal handlers and instantiates `application` in its `else` branch; when executed directly it additionally configures `sys.excepthook` and, only when `FLASK_ENV=development`, starts the Flask development server.

3. **Declarative, decorator-driven request handling.** Routing (`@app.route`), lifecycle hooks (`@app.before_request`, `@app.after_request`), and error mapping (`@app.errorhandler`) are all decorator-registered inside registration functions, keeping each concern independently testable.

```python
@app.route('/hello', methods=['GET'])
def hello_route_handler() -> Response:
    return jsonify({'message': 'Hello world', ...})
```

4. **Statelessness as an asserted property.** No session store, database, cache, or in-memory accumulator exists; `TestFlaskStatelessOperation` asserts that repeated requests return an identical `Hello world` message. The only per-request state is the `start_time` and `id` attached to Flask's request context.

5. **Type-annotated, PEP 8-constrained Python.** Public functions carry parameter and return annotations (`-> Flask`, `-> Response`, `-> None`), with `black` and `flake8` both configured to an 88-character line limit and `mypy` targeting Python 3.12.

The deployment approach mirrors this layering: a four-stage `python:3.12-alpine` build (`base` → `dependencies` → `application` → `development`/`production`) that installs `dumb-init` for correct PID 1 signal forwarding, runs as the non-root `python` user under `/usr/src/app`, and launches Gunicorn with 4 sync workers, `--max-requests=1000 --max-requests-jitter=100`, `--timeout=30`, `--keepalive=2`, and `--preload`.

### 1.2.3 Success Criteria

All criteria below are transcribed from configuration and test assertions present in the repository; none are inferred.

#### 1.2.3.1 Measurable Objectives

| Objective | Threshold | Enforcement Point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branch coverage of application code | 100 % (--cov-fail-under=100, COVERAGE_THRESHOLD: 100) | pytest.ini, src/backend/pytest.ini, ci.yml quality-gate job |
| Warm response latency for GET /hello | < 50 ms | tests/test_app.py L184, L189 |
| Average latency under concurrent load | < 50 ms | tests/test_app.py L454 |
| Maximum latency under concurrent load | < 100 ms | tests/test_app.py L455 |
| Process resident memory | < 75 MB | tests/test_app.py L426 |
| Memory growth per test | < 5 MB (per-test), < 10 MB (fixture-scoped) | tests/test_app.py L427, L690 |
| Concurrent request success rate | 50 of 50 requests | tests/test_app.py L447 |
| Response-time header sanity | X-Response-Time ends in ms, value in (0, 1000) | tests/test_app.py L556–560 |
| Test execution ceiling | 300 s thread-based timeout | pytest.ini, src/backend/pytest.ini |
| Lint conformance | Max line length 88 | .flake8 |

Two additional targets are stated in project documentation but not asserted by any test: cold-start time &lt; 100 ms and *"Optimized container image size with Alpine Linux foundation"* (`blitzy/documentation/Input Prompt.md`).

#### 1.2.3.2 Critical Success Factors

| Factor | Why It Is Critical | Repository Manifestation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Behavioural equivalence with the predecessor | The migration is only instructive if the Flask service behaves like the Express original | Hello world payload preserved; 404/405/500 handlers mirror Express middleware roles |
| Pedagogical transparency | Learners must be able to observe each lifecycle step | "Educational Note" INFO logging at every configuration and request stage |
| Zero-tolerance coverage gate | Prevents untested branches in a codebase used as an exemplar | --cov-fail-under=100 plus a dedicated quality-gate job that parses coverage.xml line- and branch-rate |
| Multi-layer security assurance | Credibility of the "enterprise-grade" claim | Bandit + Safety + pip-audit + OSSF Scorecard in CI; Trivy image scan in CD; six response headers at runtime |
| Deployment reproducibility | The example must run identically for every learner | Multi-stage pinned Alpine image, docker-compose dev/prod services, multi-arch publication |
| Frictionless local onboarding | Adoption depends on a short path to a running server | .env.example with all seven variables documented; README.md verification commands; guarded imports that print remediation instructions on missing dependencies |

| KPI | Measurement Mechanism | Reporting Destination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Line and branch coverage percentage | pytest-cov with --cov-branch, emitted as term-missing, HTML, XML, and JSON | htmlcov/, coverage.xml, coverage.json, Codecov, CI artifacts |
| Per-request latency | after_request timing written to X-Response-Time; pytest-benchmark for statistical runs | Response headers, benchmark output, INFO logs |

| Multi-version compatibility | CI matrix execution across Python 3.12, 3.11, 3.10 | Per-version CI job status and artifacts |

| Endpoint exercise and verification | curl -i against /hello, /health, and an undefined route to observe the 404 handler | README.md, src/backend/README.md |
| Test and coverage execution | pytest with the configured addopts producing term-missing, HTML, XML, and JSON coverage plus a self-contained HTML report | pytest.ini, src/backend/pytest.ini |
| Containerised run | docker compose services flask-tutorial-dev (ports 3000, 5678) and flask-tutorial-prod (host 3001 → container 3000) | infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml |

**Essential integrations.** In scope: Flask-CORS, python-dotenv, Gunicorn, pytest/pytest-flask/pytest-cov/pytest-benchmark/pytest-xdist/pytest-html, psutil, Black, Flake8 (+`flake8-security`), isort, mypy, Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, Docker/Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, GitHub Container Registry, Codecov, OSSF Scorecard, Trivy, and Azure Web Apps.

**Key technical requirements.** Python `>=3.12`; Flask `>=3.1.1`; WSGI-compliant deployment under Gunicorn `>=21.2.0`; type-annotated functions; 88-character line limit enforced by both Black and Flake8; 100 % branch coverage; strict pytest markers and strict configuration (`--strict-markers`, `--strict-config`); warnings escalated to errors in the backend pytest profile with targeted Flask deprecation exemptions; non-root container execution with `dumb-init` as PID 1.

#### 1.3.1.2 Implementation Boundaries

| Boundary Dimension | Defined Extent |
| --- | --- |
| System boundary | src/backend/ only — two application modules and two test modules; all other directories are configuration, documentation, or delivery assets |
| Process boundary | One synchronous WSGI application; 4 Gunicorn sync workers in the production container; no inter-process coordination |
| Network boundary | Inbound HTTP only, on two GET routes; no outbound calls from application code |
| Trust boundary | Unauthenticated public endpoints; CORS restricted to http://localhost:3000 and http://localhost:8000 with credentials disabled |
| User groups covered | Learners, migration engineers, open-source contributors, DevOps practitioners, maintainers (see 1.1.3) |
| Environments covered | development, production, testing configuration profiles; staging and production Azure Web App targets in CD |
| Geographic / market coverage | Not scoped — no localisation, internationalisation, region routing, or market-specific configuration exists anywhere in the repository |
| Data domains included | None persistent. The only data produced are ephemeral response fields: the fixed Hello world message, ISO-8601 timestamps, request identifiers, status strings, process uptime, version 1.0.0, environment name, and debug flag |
| Configuration surface | Exactly seven variables: PORT, HOST, FLASK_ENV, FLASK_DEBUG, LOG_LEVEL, WORKERS, SECRET_KEY |
| Request-size boundary | MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH of 16 MB (16 × 1024 × 1024) |

### 1.3.2 Out-of-Scope

#### 1.3.2.1 Explicitly Excluded Features and Capabilities

Each exclusion below was confirmed by exhaustive inspection of `src/` — no matching module, dependency, or reference exists.

| Excluded Capability | Verification |
| --- | --- |
| Data persistence of any kind (relational, document, key-value) | No SQLAlchemy, psycopg, sqlite, MongoDB, or Redis usage or dependency |
| Object-relational mapping and migrations | No ORM package; no migration tooling or directory |
| Authentication and authorization | No JWT, OAuth, session login, or access-control decorator; src/backend/README.md records /hello as "Authentication: None required" |
| Caching layers | No cache backend; /health explicitly sets no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate |
| Server-side templating and static assets | No render_template usage; no templates/ or static/ directories |
| Blueprint-based modularization | No Blueprint usage; routes are registered directly on the app instance |
| Asynchronous processing, queues, or scheduled jobs | No Celery/RQ/APScheduler dependency or worker module |
| Write operations and mutating endpoints | Only two GET routes exist; non-JSON POST/PUT bodies are merely logged as warnings by before_request, never routed |
| API versioning surface | No versioned URL prefixes; version is conveyed only via the X-API-Version: 1.0 response header |
| Rate limiting, quotas, or API keys | No limiter extension or key store; blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md states API key management is "not required for this simple Flask app" |
| Frontend / user interface | No client application, bundler, or asset pipeline in the repository |
| Distributed tracing and metrics export | Correlation IDs and timings are logged and returned in headers only; no OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, or APM integration |
| Interactive API documentation | No OpenAPI/Swagger specification or generator |
| Structured log aggregation | logging.basicConfig to stdout/stderr only; no shipper, formatter plugin, or log sink |

Additional forward-looking items implied by the repository's current inconsistencies — and therefore future work rather than present capability — include migrating `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` from their Node.js/Express framing, reconciling the root `README.md` `/hello` contract with the JSON implementation, aligning the `wsgi:app` container command with the exported `application` callable, converging the 3000/5000/8000 port conventions, adding the referenced-but-absent `.coveragerc`, `LICENSE`, and `src/backend/scripts/` artifacts, aligning the CI Python matrix with `requires-python = ">=3.12"`, and either wiring up or removing the unused `FLASK_CONFIGS` mapping.

#### 1.3.2.3 Integration Points Not Covered

| Integration Category | Status |
| --- | --- |
| External business or partner APIs | None consumed; the application makes no outbound HTTP requests |
| Identity providers (SSO, LDAP, OIDC) | Not integrated |
| Message brokers and event streams | Not integrated |
| Secrets managers / vaults | Not integrated; SECRET_KEY is supplied as a plain environment variable with a development fallback |
| Cloud platforms other than Azure Web Apps | Not implemented in CD; alternatives (Heroku/Render/Railway) appear only as deferred options |
| Container orchestration beyond Docker Compose | No Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, or service-mesh configuration |
| Infrastructure-as-code provisioning | infrastructure/ contains only the docker/ directory — no Terraform, Bicep, ARM, or CloudFormation |
| Non-ghcr.io registries | Not configured |
| Alerting and on-call tooling | Health checks gate deployment and container liveness only; no paging or alert routing |

#### 1.3.2.4 Unsupported Use Cases

- **Production hosting of business workloads.** `src/backend/app.py` logs the explicit warning *"Development server is not suitable for production deployment"*, and `src/backend/README.md` labels direct execution as educational. Nothing in the service stores, transforms, or transmits business data.
- **Multi-tenant or per-user behaviour.** The response is a constant; there is no user model, tenant context, or request-scoped personalisation.
- **Stateful or session-dependent flows.** Session cookie settings exist in the configuration profiles, but no session data is ever written and statelessness is asserted by `TestFlaskStatelessOperation`.
- **Content negotiation beyond JSON.** Both handlers construct responses exclusively with `jsonify()`; no alternate representation is produced regardless of the `Accept` header.
- **Non-GET HTTP semantics.** `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` appear only in the CORS `methods` allow-list; no handler accepts them, so they resolve through the 405 handler.
- **Cross-origin use from non-localhost origins.** The CORS allow-list contains only two localhost origins, so browser clients served from any other origin are rejected.
- **Python runtimes below 3.12.** `pyproject.toml` sets `requires-python = ">=3.12"`; the `3.11`/`3.10` entries in the CI matrix are inconsistent with that declaration rather than a supported guarantee.
- **Offline or air-gapped installation.** Every documented setup path resolves dependencies from PyPI via `pip`; no vendored wheels or lock file with hashes is provided.

# 2. Product Requirements

## 2.1 Feature Catalog

The feature catalog below decomposes the delivered system into discrete, independently testable capabilities. Every entry was derived by direct inspection of the repository — `src/backend/app.py`, `src/backend/wsgi.py`, `src/backend/tests/`, `pytest.ini`, `pyproject.toml`, `infrastructure/docker/`, and `.github/workflows/` — and every claim is traceable to a file and line range. The originating requirement intent is recorded in `blitzy/documentation/Input Prompt.md`; delivery status is corroborated by `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md`.

Because the product's functional surface is intentionally minimal (two `GET` endpoints returning fixed-shape JSON), the majority of delivered value resides in the engineering envelope around those endpoints — the application factory, the WSGI lifecycle, the security and observability layers, the verification suite, and the container/CI/CD delivery chain. The catalog therefore treats those concerns as first-class features rather than as implementation detail, consistent with the requirement categories enumerated in the originating brief.

### 2.1.1 Feature Inventory and Conventions

#### 2.1.1.1 Identifier and Status Conventions

| Convention | Definition |
|---|---|
| Feature ID | `F-XXX`, sequentially assigned; stable across this document |
| Requirement ID | `F-XXX-RQ-YYY`, scoped to the owning feature (see 2.2) |
| Priority Level | Critical (system non-functional without it) / High / Medium / Low |
| Status | `Completed` = implemented and exercised; `In Development` = implemented with verified defects or unmet sub-requirements; `Approved`/`Proposed` = specified but not implemented |

Status values are assigned from evidence only. Two features carry `In Development` because inspection revealed concrete, reproducible gaps rather than stylistic concerns: **F-012** (the verification suite's two modules import from mutually inconsistent package roots, and the coverage configuration file referenced by `pytest.ini` is absent from the repository) and **F-017** (the documented API contracts in `README.md` and `src/backend/README.md` diverge from the implemented responses, and `CONTRIBUTING.md`/`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` remain authored against the pre-migration Node.js stack). These gaps are enumerated in 2.5.5.

#### 2.1.1.3 Relationship to the In-Repository Requirements Baseline

`blitzy/documentation/Technical Specifications_b3815ee7-12a2-46a4-a950-4b8e72ef8030.md` contains a pre-migration product-requirements catalog for the Node.js/Express predecessor, defining three features — `F-001 HTTP Server Initialization`, `F-002 Hello World HTTP Endpoint`, and `F-003 Basic Error Handling` — all at status `Proposed`, with system dependencies on Node.js v22.16.0 LTS, Express.js v5.1.0, and NPM. The catalog in this section **supersedes** that baseline: `F-001`, `F-002`, and `F-003` retain their functional intent but are re-specified against the Python/Flask implementation, and `F-004`–`F-017` capture capabilities introduced by the migration that had no predecessor entry. The full supersession mapping, including the changed non-functional targets, appears in 2.5.2.

### 2.1.2 Core Application Features

#### 2.1.2.1 F-001 — Flask Application Factory and Environment Configuration

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-001 |
| Feature Name | Flask Application Factory and Environment Configuration |
| Feature Category | Core Infrastructure |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `create_app(config_name: str = 'production') -> Flask` (`src/backend/app.py` L63) constructs and returns a fully configured Flask instance. Assembly follows a fixed six-step order — Flask settings (L97), security settings (L101), CORS middleware (L105), request lifecycle hooks (L109), route handlers (L113), error handlers (L117) — and the function returns the instance at L124. `configure_flask_settings()` (L144) applies a six-key base configuration plus one of three environment profiles (`production` L169, `development` L183, `testing` L195). Three convenience wrappers (`create_production_app` L660, `create_development_app` L671, `create_testing_app` L682) and the module's `__all__` (L695) form the public surface.

**Business Value.** The factory is the single composition root for the entire service: every capability in this catalog that touches HTTP is registered through it, so configuration correctness and testability are concentrated in one auditable function. Defaulting `config_name` to `production` — documented in the parameter docstring as "for secure deployment practices" — means the safest profile applies when no environment is supplied.

**User Benefits.**
- Demonstrates the canonical Flask scaling pattern in a codebase small enough to read end to end.
- Permits per-test application instances, which the suite exploits through the `app` fixture (`tests/test_app.py` L620).
- Makes environment differences explicit and diffable rather than implicit in framework defaults.

**Technical Context.** The module docstring (L2–29) records the factory as the replacement for the predecessor's `app.js` assembly, and inline comments map `express()` to `Flask(__name__)` (L92–93) and `app.set()` to Flask's config dictionary (L96). Failure is non-silent: the `except` block (L126–141) logs the error type, message, and four troubleshooting hints before re-raising `RuntimeError(...) from e`. A `FLASK_CONFIGS` mapping exists (L641–657) but is never consumed by the factory — it is documentation-by-example rather than active configuration.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | None — F-001 is the root of the application dependency graph |
| System Dependencies | Python `>=3.12` (`pyproject.toml`); `logging`, `os`, `time`, `datetime`, `typing`, `functools` from the standard library |
| External Dependencies | `Flask>=3.1.1`, `Flask-CORS>=4.0.0`, `python-dotenv>=1.0.1` (`requirements.txt`), imported under a guard that prints install remediation and re-raises `ImportError` (L39–48) |
| Integration Requirements | Consumed by `src/backend/wsgi.py` L110 (`create_app(config_name=flask_env)`) and by both test modules |

#### 2.1.2.2 F-002 — Hello World Greeting Endpoint

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-002 |
| Feature Name | Hello World Greeting Endpoint (`GET /hello`) |
| Feature Category | API Endpoint |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `hello_route_handler()` (`src/backend/app.py` L367–424), registered via `@app.route('/hello', methods=['GET'])`, returns HTTP 200 with a `jsonify()` body containing `message` (the literal `Hello world`, assigned at L387), an ISO-8601 `timestamp`, and `status: 'success'`. The response carries `Content-Type: application/json` (L403) and `X-API-Version: 1.0` (L404). A handler-scoped `except` block (L412–424) converts any internal failure into a 500 JSON envelope rather than propagating a bare exception.

**Business Value.** This endpoint is the product's entire functional contract — the single observable behaviour that the whole engineering envelope exists to deliver, verify, containerize, and deploy. Deployment gates in `.github/workflows/cd.yml` treat its response body as the authoritative success signal for both staging (L515, L541) and production (L732–735).

**User Benefits.**
- Provides an immediate, unambiguous confirmation that a learner's environment, dependencies, and server are correctly configured.
- Demonstrates decorator routing and `jsonify()` content-type handling in a single readable function.
- Returns a stable payload shape suitable as a template for real endpoints.

**Technical Context.** The handler is stateless by construction: no store, cache, or accumulator is touched, and `TestFlaskStatelessOperation` (`tests/test_app.py` L476) asserts that five sequential calls yield five distinct timestamps with an identical message. Comments map `res.send()`/`res.json()` to Flask response generation and `jsonify()` (L386, L390). The endpoint requires no authentication and accepts no parameters, as documented in `src/backend/README.md` (L278–296).

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 (route registration occurs inside the factory at L113) |
| System Dependencies | `datetime.now().isoformat()` for the timestamp field |
| External Dependencies | Flask's `jsonify` and `Response` types |
| Integration Requirements | Consumed by container `HEALTHCHECK` directives (`infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile`), Compose health checks, and the CD staging/production health gates |

#### 2.1.2.3 F-003 — Structured JSON Error Handling

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-003 |
| Feature Name | Structured JSON Error Handling |
| Feature Category | Reliability Infrastructure |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `register_error_handlers()` (`src/backend/app.py` L470–636) installs four handlers: `@app.errorhandler(404)` (L479), `@app.errorhandler(405)` (L518), `@app.errorhandler(500)` (L556), and `@app.errorhandler(Exception)` (L602). Each returns a `jsonify()` envelope with `status`, `error`, `message`, and `timestamp`; 404 and 405 additionally echo the safe request context (`path`, `method`), 405 exposes `allowed_methods` and sets an `Allow` header from `error.valid_methods` (L541, L551–552), and 500 attaches the correlation identifier as `request_id` (L591).

**Business Value.** Error responses are the second-most-exercised path in a tutorial service — learners routinely mistype routes and methods — so a consistent, machine-readable envelope converts confusion into a diagnosable signal. The CD smoke tests depend on this behaviour, asserting HTTP 404 for `/nonexistent` in both staging (L590–597) and production (L804–811).

**User Benefits.**
- Uniform error shape across all failure classes, so clients need only one parser.
- `Allow` header on 405 tells the caller exactly which methods the route supports.
- No stack traces or internal details reach the client; tracebacks are logged server-side and only when `DEBUG` is set (L581–582, L619–620).

**Technical Context.** The 500 handler logs error type, message, request path, and method before constructing a deliberately generic client message ("An unexpected error occurred while processing your request"). Comments record the mapping from Express error middleware to Flask's `@app.errorhandler` decorators (L473, L500, L595). Coverage of these paths is asserted by `TestFlaskErrorHandlers` (`tests/test_app.py` L231) and `test_flask_wsgi_error_handling` (`tests/test_wsgi.py` L660).

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 (handlers registered at L117); F-009 supplies the `request_id` echoed by the 500 envelope |
| System Dependencies | Flask's error dispatch and `HTTPException.valid_methods` attribute |
| External Dependencies | Flask `jsonify`; no third-party error library |
| Integration Requirements | HTTP status-code semantics relied upon by CD smoke tests and by the 405 `Allow` header contract |

### 2.1.3 Deployment and Runtime Lifecycle Features

#### 2.1.3.1 F-004 — WSGI Production Entry Point

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-004 |
| Feature Name | WSGI Production Entry Point |
| Feature Category | Deployment Infrastructure |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `src/backend/wsgi.py` exposes a module-level `application` object as its sole export (`__all__ = ['application']`, L531). When the module is imported by a WSGI server the `else` branch (L518–527) installs signal handlers and calls `create_wsgi_application()`; when executed directly the `__main__` branch (L479–513) additionally wires the uncaught-exception hook and, only when `FLASK_ENV=development`, starts the Flask development server. `create_wsgi_application()` (L78–144) reads `FLASK_ENV` (default `production`), `HOST` (default `0.0.0.0`), and `PORT` (default `8000`, validated), invokes the F-001 factory, applies WSGI-specific settings via `configure_wsgi_settings()` (L147–189), logs deployment guidance, and records a memory baseline.

**Business Value.** This module is the boundary between the application and the production process manager. It makes Gunicorn-hosted deployment a first-class, documented path rather than an afterthought, which is the specific capability the originating brief demanded ("WSGI-compliant application using Gunicorn/uWSGI for production deployment").

**User Benefits.**
- A single, conventional callable name for any WSGI server.
- Explicit separation of application assembly (`app.py`) from process concerns (`wsgi.py`), so each can be studied independently.
- Startup logging enumerates the exact Gunicorn, Flask CLI, and container commands to run (L399–401, L416–418).

**Technical Context.** `configure_wsgi_settings()` sets `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS`, `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME: https`, `APPLICATION_ROOT: '/'`, and `SERVER_NAME: None` (delegating host naming to the server), adding `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT: 31536000` under `production`. `host` and `port` are validated and logged but never bound by this module — binding is the WSGI server's responsibility. Dependency import failures terminate the process via `sys.exit(1)` (L44, L54) rather than raising, a deliberate difference from `app.py`.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 (imports `create_app`, L49); F-011 (`load_dotenv()`, L58); F-010 (startup memory baseline, L125) |
| System Dependencies | `sys`, `os`, `signal`, `threading`, `logging`; Python `>=3.12` |
| External Dependencies | `Flask>=3.1.1`, `python-dotenv>=1.0.1`, `psutil>=5.9.0`; `gunicorn>=21.2.0` as the hosting server |
| Integration Requirements | Loaded as `src.backend.wsgi:application` by the test suite's Gunicorn subprocesses (`tests/test_wsgi.py` L390) and as `wsgi:application` by the Compose production service |

#### 2.1.3.2 F-005 — Process Lifecycle Management and Graceful Shutdown

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-005 |
| Feature Name | Process Lifecycle Management and Graceful Shutdown |
| Feature Category | Operational Resilience |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `setup_signal_handlers()` (`src/backend/wsgi.py` L192–255) registers a shared handler for `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` unconditionally and for `SIGUSR1`/`SIGUSR2` when the platform provides them (L243–246), tolerating registration `OSError` with a warning rather than a failure. On receipt the handler sets a module-level `threading.Event` (L228), samples memory (L231), and invokes `perform_graceful_shutdown()` (L258–296), which logs the cleanup sequence, takes a final memory sample, and never re-raises. `handle_uncaught_exceptions()` (L432–474) installs a `sys.excepthook` that passes `KeyboardInterrupt` through to the default hook, otherwise logs the exception, samples memory, emits a traceback only when `FLASK_ENV=development`, and escalates to the same graceful-shutdown routine.

**Business Value.** Correct `SIGTERM` handling is the precondition for safe container orchestration — rolling updates, scale-down, and `docker stop` all depend on it. The delivered behaviour is verified end to end: `test_wsgi_server_signal_handling` (`tests/test_wsgi.py` L458) sends `SIGTERM` to a live Gunicorn process and asserts exit code 0 within a 10-second bound.

**User Benefits.**
- Demonstrates the Python equivalents of `process.on('SIGTERM')` and `process.on('uncaughtException')` explicitly.
- Shutdown narration makes the lifecycle observable in container logs.
- Named extension points for future cleanup work (connection close, cache invalidation, background-task termination) are enumerated as comments at L277–281.

**Technical Context.** The Compose production service and the Dockerfile place `dumb-init` at PID 1 so that signals reach the Gunicorn master. Note that `handle_uncaught_exceptions()` is invoked only on the direct-execution path; under Gunicorn the `else` branch installs signal handlers but not the exception hook.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-004 (handlers installed during WSGI bootstrap); F-010 (memory sampling on signal and on exception) |
| System Dependencies | `signal`, `threading`, `sys` |
| External Dependencies | `gunicorn>=21.2.0` for worker-level signal propagation; `dumb-init` (Alpine package) as container init |
| Integration Requirements | Container orchestration semantics — `docker stop` triggers `SIGTERM` as documented at `wsgi.py` L418 |

### 2.1.4 Operations, Observability, and Performance Features

#### 2.1.4.1 F-006 — Health Check Endpoint

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-006 |
| Feature Name | Health Check Endpoint (`GET /health`) |
| Feature Category | Operations and Monitoring |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `health_check_handler()` (`src/backend/app.py` L426–463), registered via `@app.route('/health', methods=['GET'])`, returns HTTP 200 with `status: 'healthy'`, an ISO-8601 `timestamp`, `uptime`, `version: '1.0.0'`, the active `environment`, and the `debug` flag, plus `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate` (L449). Any exception in the handler produces HTTP 503 with `status: 'unhealthy'` and the error string (L454–463).

**Business Value.** This endpoint is the liveness contract used by automation: the CD staging job asserts `/health` returns 200 (L581–582) and the production job asserts the body contains `healthy` (L813–814); `tests/test_wsgi.py` uses it as the readiness probe when starting real Gunicorn processes (L409–413, L496, L826).

**User Benefits.**
- One request reveals version, environment, and debug posture — enough to diagnose "which build am I actually talking to?".
- Explicit no-store cache directives prevent intermediaries from masking a failing instance.
- Distinct 503 path demonstrates correct semantics for an unhealthy service.

**Technical Context.** The `uptime` field is populated with the raw `time.time()` epoch value (L440) rather than elapsed process uptime; `environment` and `debug` are read from `app.config` with `'unknown'`/`False` fallbacks. The documented example payload in `src/backend/README.md` (L316–333) includes a `service` field that the implementation does not emit — one of the divergences tracked under F-017.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 (registered at L113; reads `app.config`); F-011 supplies `ENV`/`DEBUG` values |
| System Dependencies | `time`, `datetime` |
| External Dependencies | Flask `jsonify` |
| Integration Requirements | Polled by CD staging/production smoke tests and by the WSGI test suite's readiness loops |

#### 2.1.4.2 F-009 — Request Lifecycle Observability

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-009 |
| Feature Name | Request Lifecycle Observability |
| Feature Category | Observability |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `register_middleware_hooks()` (`src/backend/app.py` L291–355) installs a `@app.before_request` hook that records `request.start_time`, logs the inbound method and path, and assigns a correlation identifier `request.id = f"req_{int(time.time() * 1000)}"` (L310–316); and a `@app.after_request` hook that computes elapsed milliseconds, writes `X-Response-Time` formatted to two decimals with an `ms` suffix, writes `X-Request-ID`, and logs completion with status and duration (L340–350). The before-hook also detects non-JSON `POST`/`PUT` bodies and emits a warning without rejecting the request (L319–321).

**Business Value.** Per-request correlation and timing headers are the minimum viable telemetry for any HTTP service, and here they double as the measurement channel for the latency requirement — `X-Response-Time` is asserted directly by the test suite (`tests/test_app.py` L187–189, L554–560).

**User Benefits.**
- Request/response INFO logging makes the Flask lifecycle observable without a debugger.
- `X-Request-ID` gives learners a concrete correlation-ID pattern, echoed into 500 error bodies by F-003.
- Timing is visible in every response, so performance regressions surface immediately.

**Technical Context.** Both hooks guard on attribute presence (`hasattr(request, 'start_time')`, `hasattr(request, 'id')`), so responses generated before the before-hook runs are handled safely. The identifier has millisecond resolution and is not collision-proof under concurrency — it is explicitly labelled an "educational demonstration" at L315.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 (hooks registered at L109) |
| System Dependencies | `time`, Python `logging` configured at INFO with a timestamped format (L56–60) |
| External Dependencies | Flask request context (`flask.request`) |
| Integration Requirements | `X-Response-Time` and `X-Request-ID` header contracts consumed by `TestFlaskMiddlewareIntegration` (`tests/test_app.py` L522) |

#### 2.1.4.3 F-010 — Runtime Memory Monitoring

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-010 |
| Feature Name | Runtime Memory Monitoring |
| Feature Category | Performance Monitoring |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `log_memory_usage(context: str)` (`src/backend/wsgi.py` L334–373) samples the current process through `psutil`, logging RSS and VMS in megabytes, memory percentage, and PID, then branches on a 75 MB threshold: above it a warning is emitted, at or below it an informational confirmation (L362–366). Sampling occurs at three points — WSGI initialization (L125), signal receipt (L231), graceful shutdown (L286) — and on uncaught exception (L459). Monitoring failures are caught and downgraded to warnings (L370–373).

**Business Value.** The 75 MB budget is the one quantified resource constraint carried over from the originating brief, where it is recorded as "<75MB memory footprint for Python runtime (increased from Node.js requirements)". Instrumenting it in the runtime — not only in tests — means the constraint is observable in production logs.

**User Benefits.**
- Direct comparison point for learners migrating from `process.memoryUsage()`.
- Memory context at exactly the moments that matter: startup, shutdown, and failure.
- Non-fatal by design, so a monitoring problem never becomes an availability problem.

**Technical Context.** The same budget is asserted independently by the test suite (`tests/test_app.py` L426; `tests/test_wsgi.py` L189) and declared twice in configuration: `[tool.memory-monitor]` `limit_mb = 75`, `growth_limit_mb = 5` and `[tool.quality-gates]` `memory_limit_mb = 75` (`pyproject.toml`). The Compose production service reserves 75 MB and caps at 128 MB.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-004 and F-005 provide the invocation sites |
| System Dependencies | Process-level metrics from the host OS |
| External Dependencies | `psutil>=5.9.0` (`src/backend/requirements.txt`), imported under the `wsgi.py` guard |
| Integration Requirements | Threshold shared with `pyproject.toml` quality gates and Compose resource reservations |

### 2.1.5 Security and Configuration Features

#### 2.1.5.1 F-007 — Security Response Header Hardening

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-007 |
| Feature Name | Security Response Header Hardening |
| Feature Category | Security |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `configure_security_settings()` (`src/backend/app.py` L215–256) registers an `@app.after_request` hook that removes the `Server` header (L237) and sets exactly six headers on every response (L240–247): `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'`, and `X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies: none`.

**Business Value.** These headers are the concrete substance behind the project's "enterprise-grade" positioning, and they are enforced rather than advisory — `test_security_headers_configuration` (`tests/test_app.py` L348) asserts all six by exact value, and `test_server_identification_removal` (L369) asserts that neither `Server` nor `X-Powered-By` is present.

**User Benefits.**
- A copyable, minimal baseline of browser-facing protections.
- Removal of server fingerprinting demonstrates the Flask equivalent of disabling `x-powered-by`.
- Applied centrally, so no route can accidentally omit them.

**Technical Context.** The hook is registered before the observability hooks (factory step 2 of 6), and Flask applies `after_request` callbacks in reverse registration order, so security headers are attached to every response including error envelopes produced by F-003.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 (registered at L101) |
| System Dependencies | None beyond Flask's response object |
| External Dependencies | Flask `Response` |
| Integration Requirements | Header values duplicated as expectations in `tests/test_app.py` and in the documented response example in `src/backend/README.md` |

#### 2.1.5.2 F-008 — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing Policy

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-008 |
| Feature Name | Cross-Origin Resource Sharing Policy |
| Feature Category | Security and Integration |
| Priority Level | Medium |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `configure_cors_middleware()` (`src/backend/app.py` L259–288) initializes Flask-CORS with an explicit allow-list: origins `http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:8000`; methods `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`; headers `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `X-Requested-With`; `supports_credentials: False` — annotated in code as a "Secure default for stateless API"; and `max_age: 86400` for preflight caching. Configuration failure raises `RuntimeError(...) from e` (L285–288).

**Business Value.** Explicit origin control replaces the implicit CORS behaviour of the predecessor runtime, making the policy inspectable and reviewable. It also delimits the client integration surface: only browser clients served from the two allow-listed localhost origins can consume the API cross-origin.

**User Benefits.**
- Shows a complete, secure-by-default CORS configuration rather than a permissive wildcard.
- Preflight caching behaviour is demonstrated with a concrete `max_age`.
- Credentials are disabled, reinforcing the stateless design asserted elsewhere in the suite.

**Technical Context.** `test_cors_configuration` (`tests/test_app.py` L381) exercises both a simple request carrying `Origin: http://localhost:3000` and an `OPTIONS` preflight with `Access-Control-Request-Method`/`Access-Control-Request-Headers`, asserting HTTP 200 for both. No production origin is allow-listed, so the deployed Azure surface is not configured for cross-origin browser use.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 (initialized at L105) |
| System Dependencies | None |
| External Dependencies | `Flask-CORS>=4.0.0` (`requirements.txt`) |
| Integration Requirements | Allow-listed ports 3000 and 8000 align with the Compose/`.env.example` port convention and the code default respectively |

#### 2.1.5.3 F-011 — Environment Configuration Management

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-011 |
| Feature Name | Environment Configuration Management |
| Feature Category | Configuration Management |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** Both application modules call `load_dotenv()` at import time (`app.py` L52; `wsgi.py` L58), after which configuration is read through `os.getenv` with in-code defaults. `src/backend/.env.example` documents exactly seven variables: `PORT`, `HOST`, `FLASK_ENV`, `FLASK_DEBUG`, `LOG_LEVEL`, `WORKERS`, and `SECRET_KEY`. `configure_flask_settings()` derives `ENV` from `FLASK_ENV` (falling back to the factory argument), `DEBUG` from `FLASK_DEBUG` parsed case-insensitively against `'true'`, and `SECRET_KEY` from the environment with the fallback `'dev-key-change-in-production'` (L155–161).

**Business Value.** Twelve-factor configuration is what makes one artifact deployable across development, testing, and production without code changes — the property the container and CD features depend on. `requirements.txt` records the rationale directly, describing `python-dotenv` as enabling "12-factor app configuration patterns".

**User Benefits.**
- A complete, commented template means no guessing which variables exist.
- Behaviour differences between profiles are traceable to specific configuration keys.
- Local `.env` support removes shell-export friction for beginners.

**Technical Context.** Verified constraints of the current implementation: `WORKERS` is documented but never read by application code (it is consumed only by container and Compose settings); `.env.example` sets `PORT=3000` while `app.py` and `wsgi.py` default to `8000`; and `configure_flask_settings()` has no `else` branch, so an unrecognised profile name silently receives only the base configuration. `test_wsgi_configuration_validation` (`tests/test_wsgi.py` L1062) asserts the presence of `ENV`, `DEBUG`, `TESTING`, `SECRET_KEY`, `JSON_SORT_KEYS`, and `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | Consumed by F-001, F-004, F-005, F-006 |
| System Dependencies | Process environment; `os.getenv` |
| External Dependencies | `python-dotenv>=1.0.1` |
| Integration Requirements | Same variable names supplied by `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` `ENV` directives, Compose `environment` blocks, and the `env` sections of both `pytest.ini` files |

### 2.1.6 Quality Assurance Features

#### 2.1.6.1 F-012 — Automated Verification Suite and Coverage Quality Gate

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-012 |
| Feature Name | Automated Verification Suite and Coverage Quality Gate |
| Feature Category | Quality Assurance |
| Priority Level | Critical |
| Status | In Development |

**Overview.** The suite comprises 13 test classes and 36 test functions across two modules. `tests/test_app.py` (712 lines) contributes 8 classes / 25 functions covering the factory, both routes, all error classes, security headers, CORS, performance, statelessness, middleware, and configuration. `tests/test_wsgi.py` (1,405 lines) contributes 5 classes / 11 functions covering real-Gunicorn startup, `SIGTERM` handling, port binding, WSGI integration, benchmarking, memory, concurrent load, environment loading, and a complete end-to-end deployment lifecycle. Both `pytest.ini` files set `--cov-branch --cov-fail-under=100`, a 300-second thread-based timeout, `--strict-markers`, and `--strict-config`; the `quality-gate` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` independently parses `coverage.xml` and fails when either line rate or branch rate falls below `COVERAGE_THRESHOLD: 100`.

**Business Value.** A zero-tolerance coverage gate is the mechanism by which an exemplar codebase stays exemplary; combined with test-encoded performance and memory limits, it converts non-functional targets from prose into build failures.

**User Benefits.**
- Demonstrates pytest fixtures, parametrization, `caplog`, `monkeypatch`, benchmarking, and subprocess-based integration testing in one place.
- Numeric SLAs are visible as assertions, so learners see how targets become tests.
- Multiple report formats (term-missing, HTML, XML, JSON, JUnit, self-contained HTML) illustrate CI-friendly reporting.

**Technical Context and known gaps.** Three verified conditions justify the `In Development` status: (1) `tests/test_app.py` imports `from src.app import ...` (L54, L305, L612) while `tests/test_wsgi.py` imports `from src.backend.app`/`src.backend.wsgi` (L63–64) — the modules reside at `src/backend/`, so the former root does not resolve and the module-level `pytest.skip` guard at L55–56 would trigger; (2) root `pytest.ini` passes `--cov-config=.coveragerc`, but no `.coveragerc` exists in the repository; (3) the CI coverage-validation step writes `scripts/validate_coverage.py` at runtime and reads `../coverage/coverage.xml`, a path that does not correspond to the report locations configured in either `pytest.ini`. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` allocates 5 remaining hours to "QA/Bug Fixes" covering exactly this class of defect.

| Dependency Type | Requirements |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite Features | F-001 through F-011 (the suite asserts their behaviour); F-004 for the Gunicorn subprocess tests |
| System Dependencies | Ability to bind dynamic ports in 1024–65535 and to spawn subprocesses |
| External Dependencies | `pytest>=8.4.0`, `pytest-flask>=1.3.0`, `pytest-cov`, `pytest-benchmark>=4.0.0`, `pytest-xdist>=3.5.0`, `pytest-html`, `psutil>=5.9.0`, `requests>=2.31.0`, `gunicorn>=21.2.0` |
| Integration Requirements | Executed by the `test` job of `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; coverage uploaded to Codecov and consumed by the `quality-gate` job |

#### 2.1.6.2 F-013 — Static Analysis and Dependency Security Scanning

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-013 |
| Feature Name | Static Analysis and Dependency Security Scanning |
| Feature Category | Quality Assurance and Security |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** The CI `test` job runs `flake8 . --config=.flake8 --statistics --count` against an 88-character line limit. The CI `security` job runs Bandit three times (JSON report, SARIF report, then a failing `--severity-level medium` pass), `safety check`, and `pip-audit` in both machine and human formats, then executes `ossf/scorecard-action@v2` and uploads all SARIF documents through `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2`, retaining reports for 90 days. The CD `security_scan` job adds `aquasecurity/trivy-action` against the published image digest with severity `CRITICAL,HIGH,MEDIUM,LOW`, counting findings by SARIF level.

**Business Value.** Multi-layer scanning — source (Bandit), dependencies (Safety, pip-audit), repository posture (Scorecard), and image (Trivy) — provides supply-chain assurance proportionate to the "production-ready practices" claim, with findings surfaced in GitHub code scanning rather than buried in logs.

**User Benefits.**
- Shows the standard Python security toolchain wired into a real pipeline.
- SARIF publication demonstrates how findings integrate with platform tooling.
- `[tool.bandit]` records deliberate, justified suppressions (`B101`, `B601`, `B602`) instead of blanket disabling.

**Technical Context.** `pyproject.toml` additionally configures Black (88 columns, Python 3.12/3.13 targets), isort (Black-compatible), and mypy (Python 3.12, strict-adjacent options with relaxed third-party import checking), and `requirements-dev.txt` installs them — however, a search of both workflow files finds **no invocation of Black, isort, or mypy**, so those tools are developer-local conveniences rather than enforced gates. `[tool.quality-gates]` declares `security_scan_required = true` alongside the coverage, memory, and latency limits.

| Integration Requirements | GitHub code scanning ingestion of SARIF; `.flake8` and `pyproject.toml` as the shared rule sources |

### 2.1.7 Delivery Automation Features

#### 2.1.7.1 F-014 — Containerized Build and Runtime Delivery

| Feature Metadata | Details |
|---|---|
| Unique ID | F-014 |
| Feature Name | Containerized Build and Runtime Delivery |
| Feature Category | Delivery Infrastructure |
| Priority Level | High |
| Status | Completed |

**Overview.** `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` defines four stages on `python:3.12-alpine`: `base` (system packages including `curl` and `dumb-init`, `/usr/src/app` workdir, non-root `python` user at UID/GID 1000, baseline `ENV` including `FLASK_ENV=production`, `PORT=3000`, `HOST=0.0.0.0`), `dependencies` (virtualenv creation, runtime install, build-time verification of `flask` and `gunicorn` imports), `application` (copies `app.py` and `wsgi.py`, verifies both import, `EXPOSE 3000`, `HEALTHCHECK` on `/hello`), `development` (dev dependencies, `debugpy` on 5678, hot reload, tighter health check), and `production` (Gunicorn tuning environment, cache cleanup, `chmod 444` on sources, `HEALTHCHECK` with a 15-second start period). `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` defines `flask-tutorial-dev` (ports 3000 and 5678, bind-mounted source), `flask-tutorial-prod` (3001→3000, 128 MB / 0.5 CPU limits with 75 MB / 0.25 CPU reservations, read-only root filesystem, `cap_drop: ALL` with only `SETGID`/`SETUID` restored, tmpfs scratch, rollback-on-failure update policy), and a `flask-network-setup` utility container on a dedicated bridge network.

**Business Value.** Containerization delivers the reproducibility that an educational reference requires — every learner and every pipeline stage runs an identical image — and it is the artifact type the CD pipeline publishes and deploys.

**User Benefits.**
- One command yields either a hot-reloading debug environment or a production-parity Gunicorn service.
- Security posture is demonstrated concretely: non-root user, dropped capabilities, read-only filesystem, `no-new-privileges`.
- Build-time import checks fail fast rather than producing an image that crashes at start.

**Technical Context.** Verified defect: the `production` stage `CMD` invokes `gunicorn wsgi:app`, whereas `wsgi.py` exports `application`; the Compose production command uses the correct `wsgi:application`. All health checks probe `/hello` rather than `/health`. Container ports use the 3000 convention while application defaults are 8000.

- A complete, readable reference for Python CI on GitHub Actions.
- Multi-version execution demonstrates compatibility testing.
- Artifacts and Codecov integration show how results are surfaced to reviewers.

Global environment values are `FLASK_ENV: testing`, `CI: true`, and `COVERAGE_THRESHOLD: 100`.
