#### 4.1.2.2 API Interaction Contracts

Because the API has no clients inside the repository other than tests and automation, the interaction contract is defined by what the probing systems assert. The table below is the complete inventory of programmatic callers, each with its timeout and retry posture as configured.

| Caller | Target | Assertion | Timing / Retry Configuration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Container `HEALTHCHECK` — `application` stage | `GET /hello` | `curl -f` exit status | 30 s interval, 10 s timeout, 10 s start period, 3 retries |
| Container `HEALTHCHECK` — `development` stage | `GET /hello` | `curl -f` exit status | 15 s interval, 5 s timeout, 5 s start period, 2 retries |
| Container `HEALTHCHECK` — `production` stage | `GET /hello` | `curl -f` exit status | 30 s interval, 10 s timeout, 15 s start period, 3 retries |
| Compose `flask-tutorial-dev` healthcheck | `GET /hello` | `curl -f` exit status | 15 s interval, 5 s timeout, 10 s start period, 3 retries |
| Compose `flask-tutorial-prod` healthcheck | `GET /hello` | `curl -f` exit status | 30 s interval, 10 s timeout, 15 s start period, 3 retries |
| CD staging health gate | `GET /hello` | `curl -f -s` success | 45 s pre-wait, 12 attempts, 15 s per-request timeout, 20 s backoff |
| CD staging smoke tests | `/hello`, `/health`, `/nonexistent` | Body contains `Hello world`; status 200; `application/json`; total time under 3 s (warning only); `/health` 200; `/nonexistent` 404 | Single pass, six checks |
| CD production health gate | `GET /hello` | `curl -f` success **and** body contains `Hello world` | 75 s warm-up, 18 attempts, 20 s per-request timeout, 25 s backoff |
| CD production smoke tests | `/hello`, `/nonexistent`, `/health` | Body match; 10-request average under 1.5 s (warning only); 15-request parallel burst; 404; body contains `healthy` | Single pass, five checks |
| CD production monitoring | `GET /hello` | Rolling failure rate | 12 checks at 30 s intervals over 360 s, 15 s timeout; fails when failure rate exceeds 20 percent |
| Test readiness loop — startup lifecycle | `GET /health` | Status 200 | Up to 10 attempts, 1 s request timeout, 1 s sleep |
| Test readiness loop — end-to-end lifecycle | `GET /health` | Status 200 | Up to 15 attempts, 1 s request timeout, 1 s sleep |
| `wait_for_server_readiness()` helper | `GET /health` | Status 200 | 30 s budget, polled every 0.5 s |
| Test concurrent load | `GET /hello` | Success rate at least 95 percent, average under 50 ms | 100 requests, 10 threads, 5 s per-request timeout |
| Test sustained load (E2E phase 3) | `GET /hello` | Success rate at least 95 percent, average under 100 ms | 10 requests per second for 10 s, 2 s per-request timeout |

Two consistency observations follow directly from this table. All container and Compose liveness probes target `/hello` rather than `/health`, so container liveness is coupled to the business endpoint rather than to the dedicated health endpoint. Conversely, the test suite uses `/health` exclusively as its readiness signal, and the CD gates use `/hello` for liveness while asserting `/health` only inside the smoke-test step.

#### 4.1.2.3 Event Processing Flow — Signals and Uncaught Exceptions

The only event-driven paths in the application are POSIX signal delivery and `sys.excepthook`. Both converge on a single shutdown routine, which is why they are documented as one flow.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Src{"Event source"}
    Src -->|"docker stop or orchestrator scale-down"| Sig1["SIGTERM delivered to dumb-init at PID 1<br/>then forwarded to the Gunicorn master"]
    Src -->|"Ctrl+C in an interactive terminal"| Sig2["SIGINT"]
    Src -->|"operator sends kill -USR1 or -USR2"| Sig3["SIGUSR1 or SIGUSR2<br/>registered only when the platform provides them"]
    Src -->|"exception escapes all handlers"| Exc["sys.excepthook fires — installed only on<br/>the direct-execution path, not under Gunicorn"]

    Sig1 --> H["signal_handler invoked"]
    Sig2 --> H
    Sig3 --> H
    H --> H1["set module-level signal_received to True"]
    H1 --> H2["shutdown_event.set on the threading.Event"]
    H2 --> H3["log_memory_usage with Signal Handler context"]
    H3 --> GS["perform_graceful_shutdown"]

    Exc --> E1{"Is it KeyboardInterrupt?"}
    E1 -->|"Yes"| E2(["Delegate to sys.__excepthook__ and return —<br/>normal interpreter termination"])
    E1 -->|"No"| E3["Log exception type and message"]
    E3 --> E4["log_memory_usage with Uncaught Exception context"]
    E4 --> E5{"FLASK_ENV equals development?"}
    E5 -->|"Yes"| E6["Log the full traceback"]
    E5 -->|"No"| E7["Suppress the traceback"]
    E6 --> GS
    E7 --> GS

    GS --> G1{"Was flask_app instantiated?"}
    G1 -->|"Yes"| G2["Log Flask application context cleanup —<br/>DB close, cache invalidation, task termination<br/>and file-handle closure exist only as comments"]
    G1 -->|"No"| G3["Skip the application cleanup stage"]
    G2 --> G4["log_memory_usage with Graceful Shutdown context"]
    G3 --> G4
    G4 --> G5["Log completion; the routine swallows its own<br/>exceptions, never re-raises, calls no sys.exit,<br/>and enforces no shutdown deadline in code"]
    G5 --> Exit(["Parent process completes termination;<br/>tests bound this at exit code 0 within 10 s"])
```

The absence of a code-level shutdown deadline is compensated externally: `src/backend/tests/test_wsgi.py` asserts `process.wait(timeout=10)` with an exit code of 0 and a duration under 10 seconds, and escalates to `process.kill()` when that bound is exceeded; the Compose production service constrains restarts with `restart_policy` (`delay: 5s`, `max_attempts: 3`, `window: 120s`).

#### 4.1.2.4 Batch Processing Sequence — Continuous Integration

The CI workflow is the repository's principal batch process: a fan-out to two independent jobs followed by a fan-in gate. The `test` job itself fans out three times over the Python version matrix.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Trig{"CI trigger"}
    Trig -->|"push to main or develop,<br/>path-filtered"| Init["Workflow starts; concurrency group per ref<br/>with cancel-in-progress true"]
    Trig -->|"pull_request to main:<br/>opened, synchronize, reopened"| Init
    Trig -->|"schedule cron 0 2 * * 1<br/>weekly Monday 02:00 UTC"| Init
    Trig -->|"workflow_dispatch"| Init
    Init --> Fan["Fan-out to two independent jobs"]

    subgraph JobTest["Job test — 15 min timeout — matrix 3.12, 3.11, 3.10"]
        T1["Checkout with fetch-depth 0"]
        T2["Setup Python and restore pip cache<br/>keyed on requirements file hashes"]
        T3["Install requirements.txt and<br/>requirements-dev.txt"]
        T4{"flake8 clean at 88 columns?"}
        T5{"pytest passes with branch<br/>coverage at 100 percent?"}
        T6["Upload to Codecov<br/>fail_ci_if_error false — non-blocking"]
        T7["Upload coverage and test artifacts<br/>30 day retention, test results if always"]
        TF(["Job fails — no coverage report<br/>because of --no-cov-on-fail"])
    end

    subgraph JobSec["Job security — 10 min timeout — no needs, runs in parallel"]
        S1["Install bandit, safety and pip-audit"]
        S2["Generate JSON and SARIF reports<br/>with || true so reporting never blocks"]
        S3{"bandit at medium severity, safety<br/>and pip-audit all clean?"}
        S4["OSSF Scorecard plus SARIF upload<br/>to code scanning; 90 day retention"]
        SF(["Job fails"])
    end

    subgraph Gate["Job quality-gate — 10 min — needs test and security"]
        Q1["Download coverage-reports-python-3.12<br/>and security-reports artifacts"]
        Q2{"coverage.xml line-rate and branch-rate<br/>both at COVERAGE_THRESHOLD 100?"}
        Q3{"No HIGH bandit findings and no<br/>safety vulnerabilities in the reports?"}
        Q4(["Quality gate passed — summary published"])
        QF(["Quality gate failed"])
    end

    Fan --> T1
    T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4
    T4 -->|"No"| TF
    T4 -->|"Yes"| T5
    T5 -->|"No"| TF
    T5 -->|"Yes"| T6
    T6 --> T7
    Fan --> S1
    S1 --> S2 --> S3
    S3 -->|"No"| SF
    S3 -->|"Yes"| S4
    T7 --> Q1
    S4 --> Q1
    Q1 --> Q2
    Q2 -->|"No"| QF
    Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3
    Q3 -->|"No"| QF
    Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4
```

Two properties of this batch flow are enforced by configuration rather than by convention. The `security` job declares no `needs`, so a security regression is detected in parallel with test failures rather than after them. The `quality-gate` job re-derives coverage from `coverage.xml` independently of `pytest-cov`'s own `--cov-fail-under=100`, giving two separate enforcement points for the same threshold. Conversely, the security-report validation steps are wrapped in `if [ -f ... ]` guards, so a *missing* report skips the check with a warning rather than failing the gate.

#### 4.1.2.5 Batch Processing Sequence — Continuous Deployment

CD is a serialized, five-stage promotion pipeline (`concurrency: cancel-in-progress: false`, so an in-flight deployment is never cancelled). The sequence below shows the staged handoffs, the gate decisions, and the terminal reporting path.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CI as CI Pipeline
    participant CD as CD workflow runner
    participant GH as ghcr.io registry
    participant TR as Trivy scanner
    participant ST as Azure staging
    participant PD as Azure production
    participant RP as Deployment report

    CI-->>CD: workflow_run completed with conclusion success on main
    CD->>CD: build_and_publish — buildx target production for amd64 and arm64
    CD->>GH: push eight tag variants plus provenance and SBOM
    GH-->>CD: immutable image digest
    CD->>TR: scan by digest for CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM and LOW
    TR-->>CD: SARIF findings, exit-code 0 by design
    alt CRITICAL count above zero or safety vulnerabilities present
        CD->>RP: security gate failed — pipeline stops here
    else HIGH above five or bandit issues above three
        CD->>CD: security gate warning — promotion continues
    else counts within limits
        CD->>CD: security gate passed
    end
    CD->>ST: azure/webapps-deploy by digest, 2 Gunicorn workers, PORT 8000
    CD->>CD: sleep 45 s for deployment initialization
    loop up to 12 attempts, 15 s request timeout, 20 s backoff
        CD->>ST: curl -f -s on /hello
        ST-->>CD: success or failure
    end
    CD->>ST: six smoke tests including 404 on /nonexistent
    ST-->>CD: staging validated and ready for production approval
    alt release published on main or manual dispatch to production
        CD->>CD: validate staging status and security scan_result
        CD->>PD: azure/webapps-deploy by digest, 4 Gunicorn workers
        CD->>CD: sleep 75 s warm-up for worker startup
        loop up to 18 attempts, 20 s request timeout, 25 s backoff
            CD->>PD: curl -f on /hello then match Hello world in the body
            PD-->>CD: success or failure
        end
        CD->>PD: five smoke tests then 12 monitoring checks across 360 s
        alt rolling failure rate above 20 percent
            CD->>RP: rollback_required true and the job fails
        else instance stable
            CD->>RP: rollback_required false
        end
    else staging-only run
        CD->>RP: production job skipped — overall status PARTIAL
    end
    CD->>RP: deployment-report.md uploaded, 90 day retention
```

#### 4.1.2.6 Batch Trigger Matrix

| Batch Process | Automatic Triggers | Manual Triggers | Serialization |
|---|---|---|---|
| CI Pipeline | Path-filtered push to `main`/`develop`; pull request to `main`; weekly cron `0 2 * * 1` | `workflow_dispatch` | Per-`workflow`+`ref` group, in-progress runs cancelled |
| CD Pipeline | `workflow_run` on CI completion (branch `main`, conclusion `success`); `release: published` | `workflow_dispatch` with `environment`, `image_tag`, and `skip_tests` inputs | Per-`ref` group `cd-<ref>`, in-progress runs preserved |
| Container image build | Invoked by the CD `build_and_publish` job only | Local `docker compose build` | Not applicable |
| Test suite | Invoked by the CI `test` job across three Python versions | `pytest` locally; `python tests/test_app.py` re-invokes pytest with a 100 percent coverage floor | 300 s thread-based per-test timeout |

The `skip_tests` dispatch input is the pipeline's only sanctioned bypass: setting it to `true` removes the `security_scan` job from the run through its `if` condition, described in the workflow as an allowance for "emergency deployments". Because `deploy_production` validates `needs.security_scan.outputs.scan_result` only against the literal `failed`, a skipped scan does not block promotion.


## 4.2 Flowchart Requirements

This section provides the per-feature detailed process flows required for the system's core capabilities, followed by the validation-rule register and the timing/SLA register that apply across all of them. Each flow is drawn to a uniform standard so that reviewers can locate the same structural elements in every diagram.

### 4.2.1 Flowchart Conventions and Required Elements

| Required Element | Representation in this Section |
|---|---|
| Start and end points | Stadium nodes `([...])` — one start node per flow, one or more terminal nodes including failure terminals |
| Process steps | Rectangles, labelled with the function or workflow step that performs the work |
| Decision diamonds | Rhombus nodes `{...}` with every outgoing edge labelled; the complete register is in 4.1.1.5 |
| System boundaries | `subgraph` swim lanes named for the owning actor, file, or platform |
| User touchpoints | Explicitly named human actions (clone, run, open PR, file issue); flows with no human step say so |
| Error states and recovery paths | Terminal failure nodes plus the retry/loop edges that lead back into the flow |
| Timing and SLA considerations | Annotated on the relevant edge or node, with the full register in 4.2.7 |

Two structural facts constrain all flows: the application has a **single request-scoped transaction boundary** (no database transaction, no distributed transaction, no compensating action), and it has **no user-facing state**, so no flow contains a persistence checkpoint. These are elaborated in 4.3.1.

### 4.2.2 Detailed Process Flow — Application Factory Assembly (F-001, F-007, F-008, F-009)

This flow runs exactly once per process (or once per test fixture). It has no user touchpoint: the caller is either `create_wsgi_application()` or a pytest fixture. Its distinguishing characteristic is that **every stage is inside one `try` block**, so any failure produces a chained `RuntimeError` rather than a partially assembled application.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Entry(["create_app(config_name) invoked —<br/>default value is production"])
    Entry --> L0["Log factory initialization,<br/>environment name and educational note"]
    L0 --> N1["Instantiate Flask(__name__)"]
    N1 --> S1["Step 1 — configure_flask_settings"]
    S1 --> S1a["Read FLASK_ENV with the argument as fallback;<br/>read FLASK_DEBUG and compare to the literal true"]
    S1a --> S1b["Apply base configuration: ENV, SECRET_KEY,<br/>JSON_SORT_KEYS False, JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR True,<br/>MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH 16 MB, APPLICATION_ROOT /"]
    S1b --> S1c{"Which environment profile?"}
    S1c -->|"production"| P1["DEBUG False, PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS True,<br/>https preferred, Secure HttpOnly Lax cookies,<br/>session lifetime 3600 s"]
    S1c -->|"development"| P2["DEBUG taken from FLASK_DEBUG,<br/>EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING True,<br/>session lifetime 86400 s"]
    S1c -->|"testing"| P3["TESTING True, WTF_CSRF_ENABLED False,<br/>cookies not marked secure"]
    S1c -->|"unrecognised name — no else branch exists"| P4["Base configuration only;<br/>DEBUG and TESTING keys never set"]
    P1 --> S2
    P2 --> S2
    P3 --> S2
    P4 --> S2
    S2["Step 2 — configure_security_settings registers<br/>the add_security_headers after_request hook"]
    S2 --> S3{"Step 3 — configure_cors_middleware:<br/>does CORS initialization succeed?"}
    S3 -->|"No"| F1["Log CORS configuration error"]
    S3 -->|"Yes"| S4["Step 4 — register_middleware_hooks installs<br/>the before_request and after_request hooks"]
    S4 --> S5["Step 5 — register_route_handlers installs<br/>GET /hello and GET /health"]
    S5 --> S6["Step 6 — register_error_handlers installs<br/>404, 405, 500 and Exception handlers"]
    S6 --> OK(["Return the configured Flask instance;<br/>log factory completed and ready for WSGI"])
    F1 --> Catch["Factory except block: log error type,<br/>error message and four troubleshooting hints"]
    S1 -.->|"raises"| Catch
    S2 -.->|"raises"| Catch
    S4 -.->|"raises"| Catch
    S5 -.->|"raises"| Catch
    S6 -.->|"raises"| Catch
    Catch --> Abort(["raise RuntimeError chained from the cause —<br/>no partially configured application is returned"])
```

**Recovery path.** There is no in-process recovery: the documented remediation is the four hints emitted before the re-raise (verify dependency versions, check environment variables, confirm Flask-CORS availability, review configuration parameters). When the caller is `create_wsgi_application()`, the `RuntimeError` is re-wrapped as `"WSGI application initialization failed"`, so the operator sees a two-level chained cause identifying both the stage and the module.

**Ordering consequence.** When this flow is invoked from `wsgi.py`, `configure_wsgi_settings()` runs *after* the factory returns and re-applies `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS`, `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME`, `APPLICATION_ROOT`, and `SERVER_NAME`, and in the `development` branch sets `DEBUG: True` unconditionally — overriding whatever `FLASK_DEBUG` produced inside the factory.

### 4.2.3 Detailed Process Flow — Greeting Endpoint (F-002)

This is the system's only functional contract. The flow includes the two-level error containment that distinguishes it: a handler-local `except` block that produces its own 500 envelope, plus the application-level error handlers for everything that escapes routing.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    In(["GET /hello arrives at a Gunicorn sync worker"])
    In --> B1["before_request: record start_time,<br/>assign req_ plus epoch-ms id, log inbound request"]
    B1 --> D1{"URL rule and method match?"}
    D1 -->|"path not registered"| X404["404 handler: JSON with status, error,<br/>message, path, method, timestamp"]
    D1 -->|"path registered, method not GET"| X405["405 handler: adds allowed_methods<br/>and an Allow header when available"]
    D1 -->|"match on GET /hello"| H1["Log Processing GET /hello request"]
    H1 --> H2["Assemble payload: message Hello world,<br/>timestamp from datetime isoformat,<br/>status success"]
    H2 --> H3{"jsonify and header assignment succeed?"}
    H3 -->|"No"| H4["Handler-local except: log the error, return<br/>status error with HTTP 500 — the application<br/>500 handler is bypassed on this path"]
    H3 -->|"Yes"| H5["Set status 200, Content-Type application/json,<br/>X-API-Version 1.0; log 200 OK with the payload"]
    H5 --> Fin["after_request stage 1: X-Response-Time<br/>formatted to two decimals plus X-Request-ID"]
    H4 --> Fin
    X404 --> Fin
    X405 --> Fin
    Fin --> Fin2["after_request stage 2:<br/>Flask-CORS decorates allow-listed origins"]
    Fin2 --> Fin3["after_request stage 3: remove Server,<br/>set the six security headers"]
    Fin3 --> Out(["Response returned; INFO Request completed<br/>with method, path, status and duration in ms"])
    Out --> SLA{"Measured duration under the<br/>50 ms warm-request target?"}
    SLA -->|"Yes"| Pass(["Within the documented budget"])
    SLA -->|"No"| Fail(["No runtime enforcement — the value is only<br/>logged and returned; CI asserts the bound"])
```

**Statelessness invariant.** Nothing in this flow reads or writes shared state. The verification suite encodes that as a behavioural contract: repeated calls must return an identical `message` with distinct `timestamp` values, and no session cookie may be set.

**User touchpoint.** The only human interaction is the invocation itself — `curl http://localhost:PORT/hello`, documented in the startup banner emitted by `log_wsgi_deployment_info()` and in the README verification commands.

### 4.2.4 Detailed Process Flow — Health Probe and Container Liveness (F-006, F-014)

This flow spans two system boundaries: the application handler and the container runtime that polls it. Note that all container probes target `/hello`, not `/health`; `/health` is consumed by the CD smoke tests and by the test suite's readiness loops.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Boot(["Container starts; probe suppressed during the<br/>start period: 15 s production, 5 s development,<br/>10 s in the application stage"])
    Boot --> Probe["HEALTHCHECK executes<br/>curl -f http://localhost:3000/hello"]
    Probe --> App{"Application answers within the timeout:<br/>10 s production, 5 s development?"}
    App -->|"Yes with 2xx"| Healthy(["Container state healthy"])
    App -->|"No, or non-2xx"| Cnt["Increment the consecutive failure counter"]
    Cnt --> Lim{"Failure count reached the retry limit:<br/>3 production, 2 development?"}
    Lim -->|"No"| Wait["Wait one interval:<br/>30 s production, 15 s development"]
    Wait --> Probe
    Lim -->|"Yes"| Unhealthy(["Container state unhealthy"])
    Unhealthy --> Pol{"Which orchestration policy applies?"}
    Pol -->|"Compose production restart always"| R1["Restart with 5 s delay,<br/>at most 3 attempts in a 120 s window"]
    Pol -->|"Compose development restart unless-stopped"| R2["Restart unless the operator stopped it"]
    Pol -->|"Rolling update in progress"| R3["update_config failure_action rollback,<br/>monitored for 60 s with parallelism 1"]
    Pol -->|"Azure Web Apps during a CD gate"| R4["Health gate retries, then the job fails and<br/>rollback_required is surfaced as an output"]
    R1 --> Boot
    R2 --> Boot
    Healthy --> Wait
    subgraph Handler["Application boundary — health_check_handler"]
        HA["Assemble status healthy, timestamp, uptime,<br/>version 1.0.0, environment, debug"]
        HB{"Assembly succeeds?"}
        HC["HTTP 200 with Cache-Control<br/>no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate"]
        HD["HTTP 503 with status unhealthy<br/>and the stringified error"]
        HA --> HB
        HB -->|"Yes"| HC
        HB -->|"No"| HD
    end
    Probe -.->|"CD smoke tests and test readiness loops<br/>call GET /health instead"| HA
```

**Timing consequence.** With production settings, an instance that stops responding is declared unhealthy after roughly `15 s + 3 × 30 s ≈ 105 s` in the worst case. The CD production monitoring window is deliberately longer than one probe cycle: 12 checks at 30-second intervals across 360 seconds, failing the job when the rolling failure rate exceeds 20 percent.

**Known divergence.** `uptime` carries the raw epoch value returned by `time.time()` rather than elapsed process uptime, so it cannot be used to detect a restart without an external baseline.

### 4.2.5 Detailed Process Flow — Verification Suite Execution (F-012)

The verification flow is the gate that every change passes through. It is the only flow in the system that intentionally starts and stops real server processes.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start(["pytest invoked; addopts applied from<br/>the nearest pytest.ini"])
    Start --> Cfg{"strict-config and strict-markers satisfied,<br/>required_plugins installed?"}
    Cfg -->|"No"| Abort(["Collection error — the run aborts<br/>before any test executes"])
    Cfg -->|"Yes"| Env["Inject the test environment: FLASK_ENV testing,<br/>TESTING 1, WTF_CSRF_ENABLED False,<br/>non-production SECRET_KEY, LOG_LEVEL ERROR"]
    Env --> Coll["Collect from tests/ using test_*.py,<br/>Test* classes and test_* functions"]
    Coll --> Imp{"Application modules import from the<br/>configured package root?"}
    Imp -->|"No"| Skip(["Module-level pytest.skip in test_app.py —<br/>the module is skipped, not failed, so the<br/>coverage gate can be reached with no tests run"])
    Imp -->|"Yes"| Auto["autouse fixture sets env vars<br/>and records a start timestamp"]
    Auto --> Grp{"Which test category?"}
    Grp -->|"unit and flask"| U["Factory profiles, both routes,<br/>all four error classes, security headers,<br/>CORS, middleware headers, configuration"]
    Grp -->|"performance and memory"| P["Warm request under 50 ms; RSS under 75 MB;<br/>growth under 5 MB across 20 requests;<br/>50 of 50 concurrent successes"]
    Grp -->|"integration and wsgi"| I["Spawn real Gunicorn on a dynamically<br/>allocated port; poll /health for readiness"]
    Grp -->|"benchmark"| B["pytest-benchmark pedantic run:<br/>10 iterations across 3 rounds<br/>using time.perf_counter"]
    U --> Tear
    P --> Tear
    I --> Sig["Send SIGTERM; assert exit code 0 within 10 s;<br/>assert the endpoint no longer responds;<br/>escalate to kill on timeout"]
    Sig --> Tear
    B --> Tear
    Tear["Teardown: warn when a test exceeds 1 s;<br/>assert fixture-scoped memory growth under 10 MB;<br/>300 s thread-based timeout bounds every test"]
    Tear --> Cov{"Line and branch coverage both<br/>at 100 percent?"}
    Cov -->|"No"| CovF(["Non-zero exit; --no-cov-on-fail<br/>suppresses report generation"])
    Cov -->|"Yes"| Rep["Emit term-missing, htmlcov/, coverage.xml,<br/>coverage.json, junit.xml and a self-contained<br/>HTML report; write tests.log at DEBUG"]
    Rep --> Done(["Suite passed; CI uploads artifacts and<br/>the quality-gate job re-validates coverage.xml"])
```

**Recovery path for infrastructure failures.** Every Gunicorn-based test wraps its process handling in `try`/`finally` with a three-step escalation — `terminate()`, then `wait(timeout=5)`, then `kill()` followed by a blocking `wait()` — so an unresponsive server cannot leak into subsequent tests. The end-to-end lifecycle test additionally kills the process from its `except` block before re-raising.

### 4.2.6 Validation Rules

#### 4.2.6.1 Business Rules at Each Step

| Step | Business Rule | Enforcement Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Factory invocation | The default configuration profile must be the most restrictive one | `config_name: str = 'production'` default, documented in the docstring as "for secure deployment practices" |
| Profile selection | Each named profile must produce a distinct, inspectable configuration set | Three explicit branches in `configure_flask_settings`; asserted by `TestFlaskApplication` and `TestFlaskConfigurationManagement` |
| Response finalization | Security headers must reach every response, including error envelopes | Registration order (security hook first) combined with Flask's reverse `after_request` execution |
| Greeting payload | The `message` value is an invariant literal and must never be derived from input | Hard-coded `'Hello world'`; asserted across `TestFlaskRouteHandlers` and `TestFlaskStatelessOperation` |
| Health payload | Health must be computed per request and never cached | `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate` set by the handler |
| Error envelopes | All four error classes must share one envelope shape; client messages must be generic | Four `@app.errorhandler` registrations with fixed message strings; tracebacks gated on `DEBUG` |
| Statelessness | No request may mutate shared or persistent state | No datastore, session write, or module-level accumulator exists; asserted by `TestFlaskStatelessOperation` |
| Shutdown | Cleanup must never raise and must never leave the process in an indeterminate state | `perform_graceful_shutdown` catches and logs its own exceptions; it never re-raises and never exits |
| Memory budget | Exceeding 75 MB must warn at runtime but fail in verification | `log_memory_usage` warns; the test suite asserts the bound |
| Promotion order | Production may only follow a successful staging deployment | `deploy_production` declares `needs: [build_and_publish, security_scan, deploy_staging]` and re-validates the staging output |
| Quality gate | Coverage must be validated twice, in-process and from the report artifact | `--cov-fail-under=100` plus the independent `quality-gate` parse of `coverage.xml` |
| Emergency bypass | Skipping the security scan must be explicit and recorded | `skip_tests` dispatch input; the resulting `skipped` status is printed in the deployment report |

#### 4.2.6.2 Data Validation Requirements

The inbound data surface is almost empty by design — neither endpoint accepts a path parameter, query parameter, or request body. Validation therefore concentrates on configuration inputs and on response-shape verification.

| Validated Input | Rule | Behaviour on Violation |
|---|---|---|
| Request body size | `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 16 * 1024 * 1024` (16 MB) | Flask rejects oversized bodies before the handler runs; this is the only inbound size control |
| `Content-Type` on `POST`/`PUT` | Warn when a body is present and is not JSON | WARNING logged; **request is not rejected** and processing continues |
| `PORT` | Must parse as an integer within 1–65535; values below 1024 warn | Chained `ValueError` aborting startup; the documented range in `.env.example` is the narrower 1024–65535 |
| `FLASK_ENV` | Documented as one of `development`, `production`, `testing`, case-sensitive | **Not enforced in code** — an unrecognised value falls through to base configuration only |
| `FLASK_DEBUG` | Documented as `true`, `1`, `yes`, or `on` | Code accepts only the lower-cased literal `true`; all other values disable debug silently |
| `SECRET_KEY` | Documented minimum of 32 high-entropy characters | **Not enforced** — the fallback `'dev-key-change-in-production'` is used when unset |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | Documented as one of `error`, `warn`, `info`, `debug` | **Not consumed** by either module; `logging.basicConfig` is hard-coded to INFO |
| `WORKERS` | Documented as an integer 1–8 | **Not read** by application code; only container and Compose settings consume worker counts |
| `HOST` | Documented as a hostname, IP, or `0.0.0.0` | Not validated; binding failures surface from the WSGI server |
| Response shape (verification) | Status 200, JSON media type, and all expected keys present | `validate_wsgi_response_format()` raises `AssertionError` naming the missing key |
| Deployed response body (CD) | Must contain the literal `Hello world` | Health gate retries; the smoke-test step exits non-zero |
| Deployed media type (CD) | `Content-Type` must contain `application/json` | Staging smoke test exits non-zero |
| Coverage report | `line-rate` and `branch-rate` must both be at least 100 | `quality-gate` script exits 1 with both measured values printed |
| Security reports | No `HIGH`-severity Bandit finding and no Safety vulnerability | Job exits 1; a **missing** report skips the check with a warning (fail-open) |
| Container vulnerabilities | Zero `CRITICAL`; `HIGH` above five only warns | `security_gate=failed` with exit 1, or `security_gate=warning` and promotion continues |

#### 4.2.6.3 Authorization Checkpoints

**The application implements no authorization.** Both endpoints are anonymous and unconditional: there is no authentication middleware, no token validation, no role model, and no per-request permission decision anywhere in `src/backend/`. `Authorization` appears only as an allow-listed CORS request-header name, and the session-cookie hardening flags are configured but never exercised because no code writes to the session.

Every authorization checkpoint that does exist belongs to the delivery and runtime-privilege layers:

| Checkpoint | Where Enforced | What It Gates |
|---|---|---|
| Pull-request review | `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` checklist | Human approval before merge; the template's coverage expectation (95 percent minimum, 100 percent target) is weaker than the automated 100 percent gate |
| Branch and path scoping | CI `on:` filters | Which changes are permitted to start a CI run |
| CI success precondition | CD `if:` condition on `workflow_run` conclusion | Whether an image may be built at all |
| Registry authentication | `docker/login-action` with `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` | Permission to push to `ghcr.io` |
| GitHub environment protection | `environment: staging` and `environment: production` declarations | Deployment approval and environment-scoped secret access |
| Publish-profile secrets | `AZURE_WEBAPP_PUBLISH_PROFILE_STAGING` / `_PRODUCTION` | Permission to deploy to each Azure Web App |
| Production trigger restriction | `if:` requiring a release on `main` or an explicit dispatch naming `production` | Which events may reach production |
| Staging prerequisite validation | First step of `deploy_production` | Blocks promotion when the staging status is not `success` or the scan result is `failed` |
| Container privilege reduction | `USER python` (UID/GID 1000), `cap_drop: ALL` with only `SETGID`/`SETUID` restored, `no-new-privileges:true`, `read_only: true`, `chmod 444` on sources | What the running process is permitted to do inside the container |

#### 4.2.6.4 Regulatory Compliance Checks

**No regulatory compliance controls are implemented, and none are required by the system's data flows.** The service processes no personal data, no payment data, and no health data: the only values it emits are a fixed greeting string, timestamps, a version literal, an environment name, a debug flag, and process-level metrics. Logs record method, path, status code, and duration — never bodies, headers, or credentials — so no data-subject or retention obligation is triggered by the log stream.

What the repository does implement, and what a compliance reviewer would find in place of regulatory checks:

| Control Present | Implementation | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| Transport preference | `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME: 'https'` in the production profile and the WSGI settings | Configuration signal only; TLS termination is external |
| Browser-facing hardening | Six response security headers plus `Server` removal | Enforced on every response and asserted by exact value in tests |
| Cross-origin restriction | Literal origin allow-list with credentials disabled | No wildcard and no production origin configured |
| Information-disclosure control | Generic client-facing error messages; tracebacks gated on `DEBUG`; `FLASK_DEBUG` documented as "NEVER enable in production" | Enforced in code and reinforced in the configuration template |
| Supply-chain assurance | Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, OSSF Scorecard, Trivy; SBOM and provenance attestations on published images | Pipeline gates with SARIF publication to GitHub code scanning |
| Artifact auditability | Digest-addressed images, 30/90-day artifact retention, `deployment-report.md` audit trail | Traceability rather than certification |
| Community standards | `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, issue and PR templates | Governance, not regulation |

One documentation gap is relevant to license compliance: `pyproject.toml` declares the MIT license and `README.md` displays an MIT badge, but **no `LICENSE` file exists in the repository**.

### 4.2.7 Timing and SLA Considerations

Every value below is transcribed from the repository. Values are labelled by their enforcement strength: **asserted** (a test failure), **gating** (a pipeline or probe failure), **advisory** (logged or warned only), or **documented** (stated in prose with no mechanism).

| Constraint | Value | Source and Enforcement |
|---|---|---|
| Warm `GET /hello` latency | Under 50 ms | `tests/test_app.py` measured duration and `X-Response-Time` — asserted |
| Concurrent average latency | Under 50 ms across 50 requests / 10 threads | `tests/test_app.py` — asserted |
| Concurrent maximum latency | Under 100 ms | `tests/test_app.py` — asserted |
| WSGI concurrent average latency | Under 50 ms across 100 requests, 2 workers | `tests/test_wsgi.py` — asserted |
| Sustained-load average latency | Under 100 ms at 10 req/s for 10 s | `tests/test_wsgi.py` end-to-end phase 3 — asserted |
| Concurrent success rate | 50 of 50 (test client); at least 95 percent (real server) | `tests/test_app.py`, `tests/test_wsgi.py` — asserted |
| Cold start / startup measurement | Under 100 ms threshold `cold_start_ms` | `performance_baseline` fixture — asserted |
| Gunicorn readiness window | 10 attempts (lifecycle test), 15 attempts (end-to-end), 30 s budget in `wait_for_server_readiness` | `tests/test_wsgi.py` — asserted |
| Graceful shutdown | Exit code 0 within 10 s | `tests/test_wsgi.py` SIGTERM test — asserted |
| Full deployment-lifecycle test | Total under 60 s | `tests/test_wsgi.py` — asserted |
| Per-test timeout | 300 s, thread-based | both `pytest.ini` files — gating |
| Per-test duration warning | 1 s | autouse fixture in `tests/test_app.py` — advisory |
| Fixture setup/teardown timeout | 30 s each | `src/backend/pytest.ini` — gating |
| Flask test client timeout | 10 s | `src/backend/pytest.ini` — gating |
| Resident memory ceiling | 75 MB | `wsgi.py` warning (advisory) and test assertions (asserted) |
| Memory growth bounds | 5 MB per test, 10 MB per fixture | `tests/test_app.py` — asserted |
| Environment-loading budget | Under 0.2 s, under 2 KB overhead | `src/backend/.env.example` — documented |
| Gunicorn request timeout | 30 s | Dockerfile `GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS`, Compose command, CD `GUNICORN_TIMEOUT` — gating |
| Gunicorn keep-alive | 2 s | Dockerfile and Compose — gating |
| Worker recycling | 1000 requests with 100 jitter | Dockerfile and Compose — gating |
| Container probe cadence (production) | 30 s interval, 10 s timeout, 15 s start period, 3 retries | Dockerfile / Compose `HEALTHCHECK` — gating |
| Container probe cadence (development) | 15 s interval, 5 s timeout, 5 s start period, 2 retries | Dockerfile — gating |
| Restart policy | 5 s delay, 3 attempts, 120 s window; rolling update monitored 60 s with 10 s delay | Compose `restart_policy` and `update_config` — gating |
| CI job timeouts | `test` 15 min, `security` 10 min, `quality-gate` 10 min | `ci.yml` — gating |
| CD job timeouts | build 20 min, scan 15 min, staging 12 min, production 18 min, notification 5 min | `cd.yml` — gating |
| Staging initialization wait | 45 s fixed | `cd.yml` — gating |
| Staging health gate | 12 attempts, 15 s request timeout, 20 s backoff (worst case ≈ 465 s including the pre-wait) | `cd.yml` — gating |
| Staging response-time smoke check | Under 3 s | `cd.yml` — advisory (warning only) |
| Production warm-up wait | 75 s fixed | `cd.yml` — gating |
| Production health gate | 18 attempts, 20 s request timeout, 25 s backoff (worst case ≈ 885 s including warm-up) | `cd.yml` — gating |
| Production performance smoke check | 10-request average under 1.5 s | `cd.yml` — advisory (warning only) |
| Production monitoring window | 360 s total, 12 checks at 30 s, 15 s per-request timeout | `cd.yml` — gating |
| Rollback trigger | Rolling failure rate above 20 percent | `cd.yml` monitoring step — gating (sets `rollback_required=true` and fails the job) |
| Session lifetime | 3600 s production, 86400 s development | `app.py` profiles — configured but unused (no session is written) |
| CORS preflight cache | 86400 s | `app.py` `max_age` — gating for browser clients |
| Static-asset cache age | 31536000 s (1 year) | `wsgi.py` production profile — inert (no static assets exist) |
| Scheduled CI run | Weekly, Monday 02:00 UTC | `ci.yml` cron — gating |
| Artifact retention | 30 days (coverage, test results, CD security scans); 90 days (CI security reports, deployment report) | `ci.yml`, `cd.yml` — gating |

There is **no formally published SLA** in the repository: these values are engineering budgets encoded in tests, probes, and pipeline steps. The gap between the two strictest layers is worth noting for operators — CI asserts a 50 ms warm response against the in-process test client, while the deployed smoke tests tolerate 3 s (staging) and 1.5 s (production) as warnings only, because those measurements include public internet round-trip and Azure Web Apps cold-start effects.


## 4.3 Technical Implementation

This section documents how the workflows in 4.1 and 4.2 are realised technically: where state lives and how it transitions, and how failures are detected, contained, reported, and recovered from.

### 4.3.1 State Management

#### 4.3.1.1 State Inventory

The system holds state in exactly four places, none of which survives the process that created it.

| State Location | Contents | Scope and Lifetime | Mutability |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flask `app.config` | Environment profile keys written by `configure_flask_settings()` and then by `configure_wsgi_settings()` | Process lifetime, established during assembly | Written only during startup; read-only thereafter |
| Flask request context | `request.start_time` (float) and `request.id` (`req_` + epoch milliseconds) | One HTTP request | Written once by `before_request`, read by `after_request` and by the 500 handler |
| `wsgi.py` module globals | `flask_app: Optional[Flask]`, `shutdown_event: threading.Event`, `signal_received: bool` | Process lifetime | `flask_app` set once during initialization; the other two set once on signal receipt |
| Container filesystem | Virtual environment and two 10 MB tmpfs mounts in production; bind-mounted source in development | Container lifetime | Production root filesystem is read-only with `*.py` at mode 444 |

There is **no** session store, database connection pool, cache client, in-memory accumulator, counter, or module-level mutable collection in `src/backend/app.py`. The absence is asserted behaviourally rather than merely documented: `TestFlaskStatelessOperation` requires repeated requests to return an identical `message` and forbids a session cookie.

#### 4.3.1.2 Process Lifecycle State Transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Module import of wsgi.py" as ModuleImport
    state "Guarded dependency validation" as DepCheck
    state "Environment loaded by load_dotenv" as EnvLoaded
    state "Signal handlers registered" as SignalsReady
    state "PORT validated" as PortValid
    state "Flask app assembled by create_app" as AppBuilt
    state "WSGI settings applied over app config" as WsgiConfigured
    state "application callable exported" as Ready
    state "Serving requests" as Serving
    state "Graceful shutdown in progress" as ShuttingDown
    state "Startup aborted" as Aborted
    state "Terminated by parent process" as Terminated

    [*] --> ModuleImport
    ModuleImport --> DepCheck
    DepCheck --> Aborted : ImportError, then process exit code 1
    DepCheck --> EnvLoaded : flask, dotenv, psutil and app all resolved
    EnvLoaded --> SignalsReady : setup_signal_handlers
    SignalsReady --> PortValid : validate_port_number
    PortValid --> Aborted : ValueError outside the 1 to 65535 range
    PortValid --> AppBuilt : create_app with FLASK_ENV
    AppBuilt --> Aborted : chained RuntimeError from any factory stage
    AppBuilt --> WsgiConfigured : configure_wsgi_settings
    WsgiConfigured --> Ready : startup memory baseline sampled
    Ready --> Serving : WSGI server begins dispatching
    Serving --> Serving : request handled with no state retained
    Serving --> ShuttingDown : SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGUSR1 or SIGUSR2
    Serving --> ShuttingDown : uncaught exception on the direct-execution path
    ShuttingDown --> Terminated : cleanup logged and final memory sample taken
    Aborted --> [*]
    Terminated --> [*]
```

Two properties of this machine are unusual and deliberate. The `Serving → Serving` self-transition is the whole point of the design: because no request mutates process state, every request begins from an identical starting condition, which is what permits horizontal scaling without sticky sessions. And the transition out of `ShuttingDown` is performed by the *parent* — `perform_graceful_shutdown()` returns normally and leaves termination to Gunicorn under `dumb-init`, so the state machine has no self-terminating edge.

#### 4.3.1.3 Request-Scoped State Transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "No request context" as NoCtx
    state "Context created by Flask" as CtxNew
    state "Instrumented with start_time and id" as Instrumented
    state "Route handler executing" as InHandler
    state "Error handler executing" as InError
    state "Response finalizing" as Finalizing
    state "Context torn down" as TornDown

    [*] --> NoCtx
    NoCtx --> CtxNew : worker receives the WSGI environ
    CtxNew --> Instrumented : before_request hook runs
    Instrumented --> InHandler : URL rule and method matched
    Instrumented --> InError : no rule matched or method not allowed
    InHandler --> InError : exception escapes the handler
    InHandler --> Finalizing : response object returned
    InError --> Finalizing : JSON error envelope returned
    Finalizing --> TornDown : headers written and completion logged
    TornDown --> [*] : all request-scoped state discarded
```

The `Finalizing` state is where the three after-request stages run in reverse registration order — timing and correlation headers, then Flask-CORS decoration, then `Server` removal plus the six security headers. Both instrumentation reads are attribute-guarded (`hasattr`), so a response produced before `before_request` completed still finalizes cleanly with the corresponding header simply absent.

#### 4.3.1.4 Deployment Artifact State Transitions

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Image built for the production target" as Built
    state "Published to ghcr.io by digest" as Published
    state "Scanned by Trivy" as Scanned
    state "Deployed to staging" as Staging
    state "Staging validated" as StagingOk
    state "Deployed to production" as Production
    state "Under monitoring for 360 seconds" as Monitored
    state "Stable" as Stable
    state "Rollback required" as RollbackFlag
    state "Pipeline failed" as PipelineFailed

    [*] --> Built : CI success on main, published release, or manual dispatch
    Built --> Published : buildx push for amd64 and arm64 with provenance and SBOM
    Published --> Scanned : scan the immutable digest
    Scanned --> PipelineFailed : critical findings, security gate failed
    Scanned --> Staging : gate passed or gate warning
    Staging --> PipelineFailed : health gate exhausted after 12 attempts
    Staging --> StagingOk : six smoke tests passed
    StagingOk --> Production : release on main or dispatch naming production
    StagingOk --> [*] : staging-only run reported as PARTIAL
    Production --> PipelineFailed : health gate exhausted after 18 attempts
    Production --> Monitored : five smoke tests passed
    Monitored --> RollbackFlag : rolling failure rate above 20 percent
    Monitored --> Stable : all 12 monitoring checks completed
    Stable --> [*] : report SUCCESS
    RollbackFlag --> [*] : job fails, remediation is manual
    PipelineFailed --> [*] : report FAILED or WARNING
```

#### 4.3.1.5 Data Persistence Points

There are no application data persistence points. Every value the system emits is synthesised at request time and discarded when the response is written. What the repository does persist is verification and delivery output:

| Persisted Artifact | Written By | Durability |
|---|---|---|
| `htmlcov/`, `coverage.xml`, `coverage.json` | `pytest-cov` | Working tree; uploaded as a CI artifact for 30 days |
| `junit.xml`, `pytest_report.html` | pytest reporters | Working tree; uploaded for 30 days (with `if: always()`) |
| `tests.log` / `logs/pytest.log` | pytest `log_file` at DEBUG | Working tree |
| Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, Scorecard, Trivy reports (JSON and SARIF) | CI `security` and CD `security_scan` jobs | Artifacts for 90 days (CI) and 30 days (CD), plus GitHub code scanning |
| `deployment-report.md` | CD `deployment_notification` job | Artifact for 90 days |
| Container image layers | `docker/build-push-action` | `ghcr.io`, digest-addressed and immutable |
| Named volumes `venv_cache_dev/prod`, `pip_cache_dev/prod` | Docker Compose | Host-local caches; recreated on `down --volumes` |
| Application log stream | `logging.StreamHandler` on stdout and stderr | Not persisted by the application; collection is the host platform's responsibility |

Two artifacts warrant an explicit note. The Compose file declares a `flask-tutorial-shared` volume labelled for educational persistence, but **no service mounts it** — there is no code path that persists application state. And in `wsgi.py`, `logging.basicConfig` installs handlers for *both* stdout and stderr, so each log record is emitted twice; any downstream log store will see duplicates.

#### 4.3.1.6 Caching Requirements

There is no cache server and no cache client library. Caching exists only as HTTP directives and as build-time acceleration.

| Cache Layer | Directive or Mechanism | Effect and Status |
|---|---|---|
| Health-probe responses | `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate` | **Anti-caching requirement** — probes must always reflect current state |
| CORS preflight | `max_age: 86400` (24 h) | Reduces `OPTIONS` traffic; allow-list changes propagate to browsers only after expiry |
| Static assets | `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT: 31536000` in the WSGI production profile | Configured but **inert** — the application serves no static files |
| Greeting responses | None set | No `Cache-Control` on `/hello`; intermediaries may apply their own defaults |
| pip downloads | `actions/setup-python` with `cache: 'pip'` plus `actions/cache@v3` on `~/.cache/pip`, keyed on OS + Python version + requirements hashes, with `restore-keys` fallbacks | CI acceleration |
| Docker layers | `cache-from: type=gha`, `cache-to: type=gha,mode=max` | CD build acceleration |
| Local build layers | Compose `cache_from` on the base and per-target cache tags | Local iteration speed |
| Virtual environment and pip volumes | Named volumes, mounted read-only in the production service | Container start acceleration |

#### 4.3.1.7 Transaction Boundaries

The system has exactly one transaction boundary, and it is the HTTP request itself.

| Boundary | Span | Atomicity Guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Request/response cycle | `before_request` → handler or error handler → three `after_request` stages | Response construction is the only unit of work; either a response object is produced or an error handler produces one. Nothing external is mutated, so there is nothing to roll back |
| Application assembly | Single `try` block wrapping all six factory steps | All-or-nothing: a failure raises before any application object is returned, so a partially configured app can never serve traffic |
| Process startup | `create_wsgi_application()` | Port validation precedes app construction; a configuration error aborts before the WSGI callable exists |
| Graceful shutdown | `perform_graceful_shutdown()` | Best-effort, not transactional: it catches its own exceptions, has no deadline in code, and completes even when the cleanup stage is skipped |
| Deployment promotion | Each CD job, gated by `needs` and `if` | Compensation is external — the pipeline sets `rollback_required` and fails; it performs no automated redeploy |
| Container rolling update | Compose `update_config` with `parallelism: 1`, `delay: 10s`, `monitor: 60s` | `failure_action: rollback` is the only automated compensating action anywhere in the repository |

Because there is no database, the usual concerns — isolation level, deadlock handling, two-phase commit, idempotency keys — do not arise. The one concurrency-visible artifact is the correlation identifier: `req_<epoch-ms>` has millisecond resolution and is explicitly labelled an educational demonstration in the source, so two requests handled within the same millisecond can share an identifier.

### 4.3.2 Error Handling

#### 4.3.2.1 Error Taxonomy and Handling Layers

Errors are handled at six distinct layers, each with its own containment rule. Understanding which layer catches a given failure explains why some failures are fatal and others are silent.

| Layer | Scope | Containment Rule |
|---|---|---|
| L1 — Import guards | Module load of `app.py` and `wsgi.py` | Print actionable remediation, then fail fast: `raise ImportError` in `app.py`, `sys.exit(1)` in `wsgi.py` |
| L2 — Configuration validation | `validate_port_number()` | Log three diagnostic lines, then raise a chained `ValueError` |
| L3 — Factory assembly | One `try` around all six `create_app` steps | Log type, message, and four troubleshooting hints, then raise a chained `RuntimeError` |
| L4 — Handler-local | Inside `hello_route_handler` and `health_check_handler` | Return a self-built envelope (500 for greeting, 503 for health) without consulting the application error handlers |
| L5 — Application error handlers | `@app.errorhandler` for 404, 405, 500, and `Exception` | Log server-side detail, return a uniform generic envelope, gate tracebacks on `DEBUG` |
| L6 — Process-level | `sys.excepthook` and signal handlers | Log, sample memory, dev-only traceback, then escalate to graceful shutdown |

Advisory layers sit alongside these: memory-sampling failures and signal-registration `OSError`s are downgraded to warnings and never affect request handling.

#### 4.3.2.2 Runtime Error-Handling Flowchart

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Err{"Where did the failure originate?"}
    Err -->|"Missing third-party dependency at import"| L1["Print the exact pip install command;<br/>app.py re-raises ImportError,<br/>wsgi.py exits with code 1"]
    Err -->|"Invalid PORT value"| L2["Log three diagnostic lines;<br/>raise a chained ValueError"]
    Err -->|"CORS initialization failure"| L4["Log the CORS error and raise RuntimeError<br/>into the enclosing factory except block"]
    Err -->|"Any other factory stage"| L3["Log error type, message and<br/>four troubleshooting hints"]
    L4 --> L3
    Err -->|"Exception inside a route handler"| L5["Handler-local except: log, then return a<br/>self-built envelope — 500 for the greeting,<br/>503 unhealthy for the health endpoint"]
    Err -->|"Path not registered"| L6["404 handler: WARNING log;<br/>echo only the caller path and method"]
    Err -->|"Method not allowed for the rule"| L7["405 handler: WARNING log; add<br/>allowed_methods and the Allow header"]
    Err -->|"Exception escapes to Flask dispatch"| L8{"Which handler matches?"}
    L8 -->|"HTTP 500"| L9["500 handler: ERROR log with type,<br/>message, request path and method"]
    L8 -->|"Any other exception type"| L10["Exception handler: ERROR log<br/>with type and message"]
    L9 --> Dbg{"Is app.config DEBUG set?"}
    L10 --> Dbg
    Dbg -->|"Yes"| Trace["Log the full traceback with exc_info"]
    Dbg -->|"No"| NoTrace["Suppress the traceback entirely"]
    Trace --> Client["Return the generic JSON envelope;<br/>500 bodies carry request_id"]
    NoTrace --> Client
    L5 --> Client
    L6 --> Client
    L7 --> Client
    Client --> Hdr["after_request applies timing, correlation,<br/>CORS and the six security headers"]
    Hdr --> Done(["Client receives a uniform JSON error"])
    Err -->|"psutil sampling failure"| L11(["WARNING only — monitoring never<br/>affects request handling"])
    Err -->|"Signal registration OSError"| L12(["WARNING only — the process continues<br/>with reduced signal coverage"])
    Err -->|"Exception during graceful shutdown"| L13(["Logged and swallowed; never re-raised"])
    Err -->|"Uncaught exception in-process"| L14["Log type and message, sample memory,<br/>emit a traceback only in development"]
    L1 --> Fatal(["Process never begins serving"])
    L2 --> Fatal
    L3 --> Fatal
    L14 --> Shut(["Graceful shutdown, then termination"])
```

#### 4.3.2.3 Retry Mechanisms

**The application performs no retries.** Every request is a single attempt, and because there are no outbound calls there is nothing to retry. All retry behaviour lives in the probing, orchestration, and pipeline layers, and every one uses a *fixed* interval — no exponential backoff or jitter appears anywhere in the repository except Gunicorn's request-count jitter.

| Retry Mechanism | Attempts and Interval | Escalation on Exhaustion |
|---|---|---|
| Container `HEALTHCHECK` (production / application stage) | 3 retries, 30 s interval, 10 s timeout | Container marked unhealthy |
| Container `HEALTHCHECK` (development stage) | 2 retries, 15 s interval, 5 s timeout | Container marked unhealthy |
| Compose service restart policy (production) | 3 attempts, 5 s delay, 120 s window, `condition: any` | Service remains stopped |
| Compose rolling update | `parallelism: 1`, 10 s delay, 60 s monitor | `failure_action: rollback` |
| CD staging health gate | 12 attempts, 20 s backoff, 15 s per-request timeout, after a 45 s pre-wait | `health_status=unhealthy` and job failure |
| CD production health gate | 18 attempts, 25 s backoff, 20 s per-request timeout, after a 75 s warm-up | `health_status=unhealthy` and job failure |
| CD production monitoring | 12 checks at 30 s (sampling loop, not a retry) | `rollback_required=true` when the rolling failure rate exceeds 20 percent |
| Test startup readiness loop | 10 attempts, 1 s timeout, 1 s sleep | `pytest.fail` naming the 10-second bound |
| Test end-to-end readiness loop | 15 attempts, 1 s timeout, 1 s sleep | Assertion failure on `server_ready` |
| `wait_for_server_readiness()` helper | Polls every 0.5 s within a 30 s budget | Returns `False` |
| Test process termination ladder | `terminate()` → `wait(timeout=5)` → `kill()` → blocking `wait()` | Guarantees no orphaned server process |
| Gunicorn worker recycling | `--max-requests 1000 --max-requests-jitter 100` | Proactive worker replacement rather than reactive retry |
| Gunicorn request timeout | `--timeout 30` | Worker killed and replaced by the master |
| pip cache restoration | `restore-keys` hierarchy from exact key to OS-only prefix | Falls through to a clean install |

#### 4.3.2.4 Fallback Processes

Fallbacks are pervasive and deliberate; they are the reason a partial failure rarely becomes a total failure. The pattern is consistent — a safe default plus a log line.

| Fallback | Applies When | Substituted Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `getattr(request, 'id', 'unknown')` | The 500 handler runs before `before_request` set an id | `request_id` reported as `unknown` |
| `getattr(error, 'valid_methods', [])` | The 405 error object exposes no method list | `allowed_methods` is `[]` and the `Allow` header is omitted |
| `app.config.get('ENV', 'unknown')` / `get('DEBUG', False)` | The health handler runs under an unrecognised profile | Health payload reports `unknown` / `False` |
| `hasattr` guards in `after_request` | Instrumentation attributes absent | The corresponding header is simply not written |
| `os.getenv` defaults | Any variable unset | `FLASK_ENV` production, `HOST` `0.0.0.0` (or `localhost` in `app.py`), `PORT` 8000, `SECRET_KEY` a development literal |
| Handler-local `except` | `jsonify` or header assignment fails inside a route | Self-built 500 (greeting) or 503 (health) envelope |
| Memory-monitoring `except` | psutil unavailable or sampling fails | WARNING logged; the caller proceeds unchanged |
| Signal-registration `except OSError` | Platform rejects a signal | WARNING logged; the process runs with the signals it did obtain |
| Shutdown `except` | Cleanup raises | Logged and swallowed so termination still completes |
| Scanner report generation with `\|\| true` | Bandit, Safety, or pip-audit report writing fails | Reporting continues; only the subsequent evaluating invocation can fail the job |
| `fail_ci_if_error: false` | Codecov upload fails | CI continues; coverage remains enforced locally and in the gate job |
| `if [ -f ... ]` guards in `quality-gate` | A security report artifact is missing | Check skipped with a warning — **fail-open** |
| Trivy `exit-code: '0'` | Vulnerabilities found | Scanner never fails the step; the separate summary step applies the gate logic |
| `if: always()` steps | An upstream step failed | Test results, SARIF uploads, security artifacts, and the deployment report are still produced |
| Module-level `pytest.skip` | Application modules are not importable | Test module is skipped rather than failed |
| CD version extraction fallback | `grep '^Flask=='` finds nothing in `requirements.txt` (which pins with `>=`) | Hard-coded `3.1.1` is used |

#### 4.3.2.5 Error Notification Flow

There is **no automated alerting integration in the repository** — no Slack, email, webhook, PagerDuty, or on-call step appears in either workflow. Notification is therefore pull-based (logs, job pages, artifacts, code scanning) with human follow-up through the issue templates.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources["Failure signal sources"]
        N1["Application logs on stdout and stderr<br/>with WARNING and ERROR records"]
        N2["HTTP error responses carrying request_id"]
        N3["Container and orchestrator health state"]
        N4["CI job and gate failures"]
        N5["CD health-gate and monitoring failures"]
        N6["Scanner findings from Bandit, Safety,<br/>pip-audit, Scorecard and Trivy"]
    end

    subgraph Channels["Notification channels present in the repository"]
        C1["GitHub Actions job logs<br/>and printed step summaries"]
        C2["Uploaded artifacts: coverage, junit,<br/>security reports, deployment-report.md"]
        C3["GitHub code scanning via SARIF upload"]
        C4["Codecov coverage reporting per version"]
        C5["Container health status exposed<br/>to the orchestrator"]
        C6["Host platform log collection<br/>on Azure Web Apps"]
    end

    subgraph Human["Human follow-up paths"]
        H1["Issue filed with bug_report.md,<br/>auto-labelled bug and needs-triage"]
        H2["Pull request review checklist"]
        H3["Manual rollback, redeploy or restart"]
    end

    N1 --> C6
    N1 --> C1
    N2 --> H1
    N3 --> C5
    N4 --> C1
    N4 --> C2
    N4 --> C4
    N5 --> C2
    N6 --> C3
    C1 --> H1
    C2 --> H3
    C3 --> H2
    C4 --> H2
    C5 --> H3
    C6 --> H1
```

The `deployment_notification` job is the closest thing to a broadcast mechanism: it runs with `if: always()`, derives a four-way overall status (`SUCCESS`, `PARTIAL`, `WARNING`, `FAILED`) from the four upstream job results, and writes a Markdown report containing pipeline results, artifact identifiers, environment URLs with status markers, and security counts. That report is an uploaded artifact, not a push notification — someone must open it.

#### 4.3.2.6 Recovery Procedures

| Failure Scenario | Recovery Procedure | Automation Level |
|---|---|---|
| Missing dependency at startup | Follow the printed `pip install` command; re-run | Manual, guided by the error output |
| Invalid `PORT` or unbindable port | Change `PORT` in `.env`; the six documented troubleshooting items in `.env.example` and the three startup hints name this case first | Manual, guided |
| Factory or CORS misconfiguration | Read the four troubleshooting hints (dependency versions, environment variables, Flask-CORS availability, configuration validity) and correct the input | Manual, guided |
| Container fails its liveness probe | `restart: always` (production) or `unless-stopped` (development) restarts it with a 5 s delay, up to 3 attempts in a 120 s window | Automatic |
| Container fails during a rolling update | `update_config.failure_action: rollback` reverts after a 60 s monitor window | Automatic |
| Worker becomes slow or leaks | `--timeout 30` kills the worker; `--max-requests 1000` with 100 jitter recycles workers proactively | Automatic |
| Staging health gate exhausted | Job fails before production is touched; promotion is blocked by `needs` and by the staging prerequisite check | Automatic prevention, manual repair |
| Production health gate exhausted | Job fails with `health_status=unhealthy`; the previous revision remains as deployed by Azure | Automatic detection, manual remediation |
| Production monitoring detects instability | `rollback_required=true` is emitted and the job fails; **no rollback job or step exists** — an operator must redeploy a previous digest | Detection automatic, remediation manual |
| Coverage or security gate failure | Fix the code or dependency and re-run CI; artifacts and SARIF entries identify the exact deficit | Manual, evidence-rich |
| Local environment corruption | `docker-compose down --volumes --remove-orphans` documented in the Compose file, followed by a rebuild | Manual, documented |
| Unexplained runtime defect | File a bug report; the template supplies Flask-specific troubleshooting for application-factory problems, route handlers, WSGI configuration, Flask-CORS, pytest/test-client issues, and virtual environments | Manual, templated |
| Graceful shutdown stalls | No in-code deadline exists; external bounds apply — tests escalate `terminate()` to `kill()` after 5 s, and the container runtime applies its own stop timeout | Partially automatic |

The recovery posture is consistent with the system's nature: automated recovery is confined to the container and worker layers, where restart is genuinely safe because the process is stateless; everything above that layer is designed to *stop* and report rather than to self-heal.


## 4.4 Workflow Traceability and Coverage

This sub-section closes the loop between the process flows documented above and the feature catalog and functional requirements defined in Section 2, and records the workflow elements that are deliberately absent or known to be defective so that no reader mistakes a documented flow for a capability the repository does not have.

### 4.4.1 Workflow-to-Requirement Traceability

| Workflow | Features Exercised | Governing Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| W-1 First-run onboarding to first response | F-011, F-017, F-002 | F-011-RQ-001…004, F-017-RQ-001, F-017-RQ-004, F-002-RQ-001 |
| W-2 Process bootstrap and WSGI initialization | F-001, F-004, F-010, F-011 | F-001-RQ-001…004, F-004-RQ-001…005, F-010-RQ-001, F-011-RQ-001…003 |
| W-3 Greeting request-response cycle | F-002, F-007, F-008, F-009 | F-002-RQ-001…005, F-007-RQ-001/002, F-008-RQ-001/002, F-009-RQ-001…003 |
| W-4 Health probe cycle | F-006, F-014 | F-006-RQ-001…004, F-014-RQ-003 |
| W-5 Error dispatch and response shaping | F-003, F-007, F-009 | F-003-RQ-001…004, F-007-RQ-001, F-009-RQ-001 |
| W-6 Graceful shutdown | F-005, F-010, F-014 | F-005-RQ-001…003, F-010-RQ-001…003, F-014-RQ-002 |
| W-7 Continuous integration batch | F-012, F-013, F-015 | F-012-RQ-001…005, F-013-RQ-001…004, F-015-RQ-001…004 |

Two requirements are validated by workflows other than those of their owning feature, which is worth noting for change impact analysis. `F-002-RQ-001` (greeting payload) is asserted not only by the unit suite in W-7 but also by the staging and production smoke tests in W-8, so a payload change breaks the deployment pipeline as well as the tests. Similarly, `F-006-RQ-004` (health as a readiness signal) is exercised by W-4, W-7, and W-8 simultaneously.

### 4.4.3 Workflow Elements Deliberately Absent

The following process-flow constructs are commonly expected in a technical specification of this kind and are **not present in this repository**. They are listed so that their absence is recorded as a finding rather than inferred as an omission in this document.

| Absent Element | Confirmation |
|---|---|
| Data persistence step in any workflow | No database, ORM, migration tool, or object-storage SDK is declared or imported; `.env.example` marks its database and Redis blocks "not used in tutorial" |
| Message queue or event bus | No broker client is declared; `CELERY_BROKER_URL` appears only as a commented example |
| Batch job inside the application | No scheduler, cron entry, or worker loop exists in `src/backend/`; the only scheduled trigger is the weekly CI cron |
| Authentication or authorization checkpoint in any request flow | No auth code exists; `Authorization` is only a CORS-allowed header name; see 4.2.6.3 |
| Regulatory compliance check | No regulated data is processed; see 4.2.6.4 |
| Multi-actor business transaction | The two endpoints are anonymous, parameterless, and independent |
| Automated rollback execution | `rollback_required` is an output flag only — no rollback job or step exists in `cd.yml`; the only automated compensating action anywhere is Compose `update_config.failure_action: rollback` |
| Automated alerting or paging | No Slack, email, webhook, or PagerDuty integration in either workflow; notification is pull-based (see 4.3.2.5) |
| Exponential backoff or jitter in retries | Every retry interval in the repository is a fixed constant; the only jitter is Gunicorn's `--max-requests-jitter` |
| Circuit breaker, bulkhead, or rate limiter | No such middleware or configuration exists |
| Distributed tracing | Correlation is a single per-request header; there is no trace context propagation and no tracing backend |
| Formal published SLA | The timing values in 4.2.7 are engineering budgets encoded in tests, probes, and pipeline steps |

### 4.4.4 Known Defects Affecting the Documented Flows

These defects were verified by direct inspection and change how the corresponding flow behaves in practice. They are recorded here because a reader tracing a flow against the code will otherwise encounter an unexplained discrepancy.

| Flow Affected | Defect | Effect on the Flow |
|---|---|---|
| W-2 bootstrap, production container | The `production` stage `CMD` in the Dockerfile launches `gunicorn wsgi:app`, but `wsgi.py` exports `application` (`__all__ = ['application']`) | The container command as written cannot resolve the callable; the Compose production service uses the correct `wsgi:application` |
| W-7 verification | `tests/test_app.py` imports from `src.app` while the module lives at `src/backend/app.py`; the failure is caught by a module-level `pytest.skip` | The entire module is skipped rather than failed, so the coverage gate can be reached with the application tests not executed |
| W-7 verification | Root `pytest.ini` passes `--cov-config=.coveragerc`, but no `.coveragerc` exists | Coverage settings resolve from `pyproject.toml` or defaults instead of the referenced file |
| W-7 quality gate | The gate step writes `scripts/validate_coverage.py` via heredoc **before** running `mkdir -p scripts`, and reads `../coverage/coverage.xml` | The script write can fail on a clean checkout, and the report path does not match either `pytest.ini` output location |
| W-7 test matrix | CI tests Python 3.12, 3.11, and 3.10 while `pyproject.toml` declares `requires-python = ">=3.12"` | Two matrix legs run against interpreters the project does not claim to support |
| W-7 dependency install | CI steps set `working-directory: src/backend` while installing `requirements.txt` and `requirements-dev.txt`, which reside at the repository root | The install step depends on the backend-local `requirements.txt` resolving equivalently |
| W-8 deployment | `deploy_production` targets app name `flask-tutorial-production` while its environment URL is `flask-tutorial.azurewebsites.net` | The deployment target and the health-gate target are named inconsistently |
| W-8 version stamping | The version-extraction step greps `^Flask==` from `requirements.txt`, which pins with `>=` | The hard-coded `3.1.1` fallback is always used |
| W-8 security gate | A skipped `security_scan` (via `skip_tests`) leaves `scan_result` empty, and the production prerequisite check compares only against the literal `failed` | A bypassed scan does not block promotion |
| W-3 / W-1 port convention | `.env.example` and all container ports use 3000; `app.py` and `wsgi.py` default to 8000; `README.md` examples use 5000 | The URL a learner should call differs by which document they follow |
| W-6 shutdown under Gunicorn | `handle_uncaught_exceptions()` is called only on the `__main__` path, not in the `else` branch used by WSGI servers | Under Gunicorn the custom excepthook is not installed, so the uncaught-exception branch of 4.1.2.3 does not apply |
| W-4 health semantics | `uptime` carries the raw `time.time()` epoch value rather than elapsed process uptime | A restart cannot be detected from the health payload alone |
| All flows, observability | `wsgi.py` configures `logging.basicConfig` with handlers on both stdout and stderr | Every `wsgi.py` log record is emitted twice |
| W-2 dependency contract | `wsgi.py` imports `psutil`, which is not declared in the root `requirements.txt` runtime set | A runtime install from the production manifest alone would fail the L1 import guard and exit with code 1 |

# 5. System Architecture

## 5.1 High-Level Architecture

### 5.1.1 System Overview

#### 5.1.1.1 Architecture Style and Rationale

The system is a **single-process, stateless, synchronous WSGI web service** whose entire runtime consists of two Python modules — `src/backend/app.py` (application assembly) and `src/backend/wsgi.py` (process lifecycle and WSGI exposure) — served by Gunicorn inside one container image. There is no service mesh, no message broker, no database, and no second deployable unit; `infrastructure/` contains only `docker/`.

The style is best characterised as a **function-composed modular monolith**: rather than packages or classes, the application is decomposed into six single-purpose registration functions that a factory invokes in a fixed order. `create_app()` (`app.py` L63) calls, in sequence, `configure_flask_settings` → `configure_security_settings` → `configure_cors_middleware` → `register_middleware_hooks` → `register_route_handlers` → `register_error_handlers` (L97–L117). Each function owns exactly one cross-cutting concern and mutates only the `Flask` instance passed to it, which makes every concern independently readable and independently testable while keeping the deployable surface to a single process.

The rationale is legible in the repository itself and is dominated by two forces that normally pull in opposite directions:

| Force | Evidence in the Repository | Architectural Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Minimal functional scope — one greeting endpoint | `blitzy/documentation/Input Prompt.md` requests "one endpoint `/hello` that returns 'Hello world'"; `register_route_handlers` defines exactly two routes | No layering beyond assembly/lifecycle; no domain, repository, or service tier exists |
| Production-shaped scaffolding for teaching | `pyproject.toml` description ("Enterprise-grade Hello World"); `Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable` classifier | Factory pattern, WSGI entry point, signal handling, security headers, containerisation, and a 100 % coverage gate are all present despite trivial functionality |
| Migration exemplarity (Express.js → Flask) | Module docstrings: `app.py` "Replaces Express.js app.js"; `wsgi.py` "Replaces Node.js server.js functionality" | The two-module split deliberately mirrors the Express `app.js` / `server.js` division rather than a Python-idiomatic package layout |

The consequence of the third force is structural: the boundary between *what the application is* and *how the process runs* is a hard boundary. `app.py` imports nothing about servers, ports, signals, or process identity; `wsgi.py` imports `create_app` and owns everything else.

#### 5.1.1.2 Key Architectural Principles

| Principle | Implementation | Verified Location |
|---|---|---|
| Deferred, parameterised instantiation | `create_app(config_name: str = 'production')` returns a fresh configured instance; three thin wrappers (`create_production_app`, `create_development_app`, `create_testing_app`) are the only exported factories | `app.py` L63, L660–L690, `__all__` L695 |
| Separation of assembly from lifecycle | Application construction lives in `app.py`; signal handling, port validation, memory sampling, and the WSGI callable live in `wsgi.py` | `app.py`, `wsgi.py` L78–L474 |
| Configuration through environment only | `load_dotenv()` at import time in both modules; every tunable read through `os.getenv` with an in-code default | `app.py` L52, L155–L156, L161; `wsgi.py` L58, L104–L106 |
| Statelessness by construction | No datastore, no session writes, no module-level mutable accumulators in `app.py`; per-request data attached to the request context only | `app.py` L310, L316; asserted by `TestFlaskStatelessOperation` |
| Fail fast, explain loudly | Guarded imports print remediation instructions then `raise ImportError` (`app.py`) or `sys.exit(1)` (`wsgi.py`); factory failures re-raise as chained `RuntimeError` | `app.py` L39–L48, L141; `wsgi.py` L35–L54, L144 |
| Secure-by-default response contract | Six security headers plus `Server` removal applied to *every* response, independent of route | `app.py` L223–L253 |
| Uniform machine-readable error surface | Four `@app.errorhandler` registrations return the same JSON envelope shape; internals suppressed unless `DEBUG` | `app.py` L479–L632 |
| Immutable, least-privilege runtime | Non-root uid/gid 1000, `chmod -R 444 *.py`, `read_only: true` root filesystem, `cap_drop: ALL` | `Dockerfile` L41–L43, L213; `docker-compose.yml` L319–L333 |
| Verification as a gate, not a report | `--cov-fail-under=100` with `--cov-branch` in both pytest configs and a dedicated `quality-gate` CI job | `pytest.ini`, `src/backend/pytest.ini`, `ci.yml` L208–L340 |

The recurring pattern vocabulary is explicit rather than implied:

- **Application Factory** — `create_app` builds and returns the `Flask` object; no module-level app instance exists in `app.py`.
- **Front Controller / single WSGI callable** — `wsgi.py` exposes exactly one entry point, `application` (`__all__ = ['application']`, L531), created at import time in the module's `else` branch (L518–L527).
- **Interceptor chain via decorators** — `@app.before_request` and `@app.after_request` replace an Express-style middleware stack (`app.py` L299, L326).
- **Centralised exception mapping** — an error-handler registry rather than per-route `try`/`except` (with the two route handlers additionally wrapping their own bodies defensively).
- **Health-check endpoint** — `GET /health` exists purely as an operational affordance (`app.py` L426).
- **Graceful-shutdown handler** — `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` (plus optional `SIGUSR1`/`SIGUSR2`) drive a coordinated shutdown sequence with a `threading.Event` (`wsgi.py` L192–L296).
- **Immutable infrastructure** — images are built once and deployed by digest, never mutated in place (`cd.yml` L213–L240, L484–L492).

#### 5.1.1.3 System Boundaries and Major Interfaces

Five boundaries are observable in the repository, each with exactly one crossing mechanism:

| Boundary | What Crosses It | Mechanism and Location |
|---|---|---|
| Client ↔ service | HTTP/1.1 requests to `/hello`, `/health`; JSON responses; six security headers, `X-Request-ID`, `X-Response-Time`, `X-API-Version` | Gunicorn socket bind `0.0.0.0:3000` (`Dockerfile` L216–L220) or `0.0.0.0:8000` (documented in `wsgi.py` L399) |
| Server ↔ application | One WSGI call per request against the `application` object | `gunicorn wsgi:application` (`docker-compose.yml` L263); PEP 3333 WSGI contract |
| Application ↔ configuration | Seven environment variables plus an optional `.env` file | `python-dotenv` `load_dotenv()`; `src/backend/.env.example` |
| Container ↔ orchestrator | `HEALTHCHECK` probe of `/hello`; `SIGTERM` on stop; resource limits | `Dockerfile` L209–L210; `docker-compose.yml` L267–L299 |
| Repository ↔ delivery platform | Source → image → registry → Azure Web App, gated by tests, scans, and health probes | `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.github/workflows/cd.yml` |

Notably, there is **no outbound boundary**: neither runtime module opens a socket, calls an API, or reads a credential store, so the service has no upstream dependency to degrade against.

```mermaid

    Caller["HTTP client<br/>curl, browser, requests"]

    subgraph Platform["Delivery and hosting platform"]
```
