```mermaid
    end

    subgraph Container["Container instance - python:3.12-alpine"]
```

### 5.1.2 Core Components

The runtime component inventory is small and precisely bounded. The first table states responsibility and dependencies; the second states integration points and the considerations that matter when changing each component.

| Component | Primary Responsibility | Key Dependencies |
|---|---|---|
| WSGI entry point (`wsgi.py`) | Create and expose the `application` callable; own process-level concerns | `flask`, `python-dotenv`, `psutil`, `app.create_app` |
| Application factory (`create_app`, `app.py` L63) | Build a fully configured `Flask` instance in a deterministic six-step order | `flask`, the five configuration/registration helpers |
| Configuration subsystem (`configure_flask_settings` L144 + `configure_wsgi_settings` `wsgi.py` L147) | Resolve environment into a Flask config dict; apply per-profile production/development/testing settings | `os.environ`, `python-dotenv`, `src/backend/.env.example` |
| Security header middleware (`configure_security_settings` L215) | Strip `Server`; set six hardening headers on every response | Flask `after_request` hook |
| CORS policy component (`configure_cors_middleware` L259) | Enforce origin, method, and header allow-lists; cache preflight for 86 400 s | `Flask-CORS>=4.0.0` |
| Request lifecycle middleware (`register_middleware_hooks` L291) | Assign request ID, time the request, emit correlation/timing headers and access logs | Flask `before_request`/`after_request`, `time`, `logging` |
| Route handlers (`register_route_handlers` L358) | Serve `GET /hello` (greeting) and `GET /health` (status) as JSON | `flask.jsonify`, `datetime`, `time`, `app.config` |
| Error handler registry (`register_error_handlers` L470) | Map 404, 405, 500, and unhandled `Exception` to a uniform JSON envelope | Flask `errorhandler`, `logging` |
| Process lifecycle manager (`wsgi.py` L192–L296, L432–L474) | Register signal handlers, coordinate graceful shutdown, install `sys.excepthook` | `signal`, `threading.Event`, `sys` |
| Resource monitor (`log_memory_usage`, `wsgi.py` L334) | Sample RSS/VMS/percent and warn above a 75 MB threshold | `psutil>=5.9.0` |
| Serving tier (Gunicorn, configured in `Dockerfile` L216–L220 / `docker-compose.yml` L263) | Accept sockets, fork and recycle workers, enforce request timeout | `gunicorn>=21.2.0`, `dumb-init` |
| Container image (`infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile`) | Reproducible five-stage build producing `development` and `production` leaves | `python:3.12-alpine`, `requirements*.txt` |
| Verification suite (`src/backend/tests/`) | Behavioural, security, performance, statelessness, and lifecycle assertions | `pytest`, `pytest-flask`, `pytest-cov`, `pytest-benchmark`, `psutil` |
| Delivery pipelines (`.github/workflows/`) | Quality gating, image publication, scanning, staged deployment, post-deploy monitoring | GitHub Actions, GHCR, Trivy, Azure Web Apps |

| Component | Integration Points | Critical Considerations |
|---|---|---|
| WSGI entry point | Imported by Gunicorn as `wsgi:application`; imported by `test_wsgi.py` | Module import has side effects — handlers are installed and the app is built at import time (L518–L527); the production `Dockerfile` CMD references `wsgi:app`, which does not match the exported name |
| Application factory | Called by `wsgi.py` and by the pytest `app` fixture | Ordering is load-bearing: because Flask runs `after_request` callbacks in reverse registration order, the security-header callback registered first is applied last |
| Configuration subsystem | Reads `FLASK_ENV`, `FLASK_DEBUG`, `SECRET_KEY`, `HOST`, `PORT`; re-applied post-factory by `configure_wsgi_settings` | `configure_wsgi_settings` overrides factory values (e.g. forces `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS`, `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME='https'`); `SECRET_KEY` silently falls back to `'dev-key-change-in-production'`; `LOG_LEVEL` and `WORKERS` from `.env.example` are read by no code path |
| Security header middleware | Applies to all routes and all error responses | `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'` is fixed in code; there is no per-route override mechanism |
| CORS policy component | Browser preflight `OPTIONS` and cross-origin `GET` | Allow-list contains only `http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:8000` — no deployed origin is permitted; `supports_credentials=False` |
| Request lifecycle middleware | Every request; consumed by clients via headers and by operators via logs | `request.id` is `req_<epoch-ms>`, so concurrent requests within the same millisecond can collide; no inbound `X-Request-ID` is honoured |
| Route handlers | Client traffic; container `HEALTHCHECK`; CD health/smoke gates | `/health` reports `uptime` as a raw `time.time()` epoch value, not elapsed seconds; it performs no dependency checks because the service has none |
| Error handler registry | Werkzeug routing failures and any handler exception | An `Exception` handler is registered alongside the 500 handler, so unhandled exceptions are converted to JSON rather than propagating despite `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS=True` |
| Process lifecycle manager | Container stop (`SIGTERM`), interactive interrupt, uncaught exceptions | Handlers are installed at import time; the repository does not address precedence against Gunicorn's own arbiter/worker signal handling, and shutdown work is limited to logging plus a `threading.Event` |
| Resource monitor | Startup baseline, signal receipt, uncaught exception | `psutil` is imported unconditionally but is absent from the root `requirements.txt` installed by the image's `dependencies` stage |
| Serving tier | Socket ingress; worker recycling; stdout/stderr log streams | Worker count, timeout, keepalive, and bind address are hardcoded in the image CMD, so `WORKERS`/`GUNICORN_WORKERS` environment values do not retune a running container |
| Container image | Compose services and Azure Web Apps | `EXPOSE 3000` and `--bind=0.0.0.0:3000` conflict with the `PORT=8000` declared on the CD deploy steps |
| Verification suite | CI `test` job across Python 3.12/3.11/3.10 | Enforces a 100 % branch-coverage floor; `test_wsgi.py` starts real WSGI processes on dynamic ports |
| Delivery pipelines | GHCR, Codecov, GitHub code scanning, Azure Web Apps | Azure app names and URLs are literals; no IaC exists, so target infrastructure is assumed pre-provisioned |

### 5.1.3 Data Flow Description

#### 5.1.3.1 Primary Request/Response Flow

All traffic follows one path, and that path is uniform for both endpoints. A client opens an HTTP/1.1 connection to Gunicorn, which converts the request into a WSGI `environ` dictionary and invokes the `application` callable exported by `wsgi.py`. Flask then executes the interceptor chain: `before_request_middleware` stamps `request.start_time` from `time.time()`, logs the method and path at INFO, assigns `request.id = f"req_{int(time.time() * 1000)}"`, and — for `POST`/`PUT` bodies that are not JSON — emits a warning without rejecting the request (`app.py` L299–L324). Werkzeug then matches the URL rule and invokes the view function.

`hello_route_handler` builds an in-memory dictionary `{message, timestamp, status}` where `message` is the literal `'Hello world'` and `timestamp` is `datetime.now().isoformat()`, serialises it with `jsonify()`, sets HTTP 200, and attaches `Content-Type: application/json` and `X-API-Version: 1.0` (L367–L410). `health_check_handler` builds `{status, timestamp, uptime, version, environment, debug}` — reading `ENV` and `DEBUG` back out of `app.config` — and adds `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate` (L426–L452).

On the way out, the response passes through the `after_request` callbacks in reverse registration order: `after_request_middleware` first (computing `(time.time() - request.start_time) * 1000` into `X-Response-Time` and logging completion with status and duration, L326–L352), then the Flask-CORS callback, then `add_security_headers`, which removes `Server` and sets the six hardening headers last (L223–L253). Gunicorn writes the serialised body and headers back to the socket, and the request context — the only place per-request state ever lived — is discarded.

#### 5.1.3.2 Error and Exception Flow

Failures re-enter the same response pipeline rather than bypassing it. Unmatched paths and disallowed methods raise Werkzeug HTTP exceptions that Flask routes to `not_found_handler` (404) and `method_not_allowed_handler` (405); the latter reads `error.valid_methods` to populate both an `allowed_methods` field and the `Allow` header (L541, L551–L552). Explicit 500s reach `internal_server_error_handler`, and any other exception reaches the registered `Exception` handler. Both 500-class handlers log the failure server-side with type, message, path, and method, attach a traceback via `exc_info=True` **only** when `app.config['DEBUG']` is set, and return a generic client payload that carries no internals — the 500 envelope additionally echoes `request_id` for correlation (L556–L632). Because these handlers return responses, error responses still traverse the `after_request` chain and therefore still carry the security headers, `X-Response-Time`, and `X-Request-ID`.

#### 5.1.3.3 Configuration and Startup Flow

Configuration flows once, at process start, and is never re-read. `load_dotenv()` merges an optional `.env` file into `os.environ` at import time in both modules. `create_wsgi_application` then resolves `FLASK_ENV` (default `production`), `HOST` (default `0.0.0.0`), and `PORT` (default `'8000'`), passing the port through `validate_port_number`, which converts the string to `int`, rejects values outside 1–65535 with a chained `ValueError`, and warns for privileged ports below 1024 (`wsgi.py` L104–L106, L299–L331). `create_app(config_name=flask_env)` builds the instance; `configure_wsgi_settings` then applies a second layer of settings — `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS=True`, `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME='https'`, `APPLICATION_ROOT='/'`, `SERVER_NAME=None` for all profiles, plus `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT=31536000` for production (L147–L189). Startup completes with a deployment banner and a psutil RSS baseline sample.

#### 5.1.3.4 Observability and Delivery Flows

Telemetry is a one-way stream: `logging.basicConfig` formats records as `%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s` at INFO, and `wsgi.py` attaches handlers for **both** stdout and stderr (L62–L69), so container logs are the sole sink — there is no shipper, aggregator, or trace exporter anywhere in the repository. The delivery flow is equally linear: source changes trigger `ci.yml` (lint → tests with coverage → security scans → quality gate), a successful CI run triggers `cd.yml`, which builds a multi-architecture image with provenance and SBOM attestations, pushes it to `ghcr.io`, scans it with Trivy, and deploys it by immutable digest to staging and then production Azure Web Apps, each gated by retry-based `/hello` health loops and smoke assertions.

#### 5.1.3.5 Data Transformation Points

| Transformation | From → To | Location |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP bytes → WSGI `environ` → Flask `Request` | Wire format → Python objects | Gunicorn + Werkzeug (framework boundary) |
| Python `dict` → JSON body + `Content-Type` | Structured data → serialised response | `jsonify()` in both route handlers and all error handlers |
| Environment string → typed config value | `str` → `int`/`bool`/config entry | `validate_port_number` (`wsgi.py` L299); `FLASK_DEBUG` lower-case comparison (`app.py` L156) |
| Monotonic timing → header string | `float` seconds → `"<n.nn>ms"` | `after_request_middleware` (`app.py` L342) |
| Epoch milliseconds → correlation ID | `int` → `req_<epoch-ms>` | `before_request_middleware` (`app.py` L316) |
| psutil byte counts → human-readable MB | `int` bytes → `float` MB with 75 MB comparison | `log_memory_usage` (`wsgi.py` L350–L366) |
| Werkzeug exception → JSON envelope | Exception object → `{status, error, message, ...}` | `register_error_handlers` (`app.py` L470–L632) |
| Coverage XML → pass/fail verdict | `coverage.xml` line/branch rates → gate decision | Embedded validator in `ci.yml` `quality-gate` (L242–L294) |

#### 5.1.3.6 Data Stores and Caches

**There is no data store.** No ORM, database driver, cache client, object-storage SDK, migration tool, or schema artifact exists in the repository; `.env.example` contains commented `DATABASE_URL`/`REDIS_URL` blocks explicitly labelled as unused examples, and no code path reads them. All response data is synthesised per request from literals and clock reads, then discarded. The only inbound-size control is `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 16 * 1024 * 1024` (`app.py` L164).

Caching exists only in two non-runtime-state forms:

- **HTTP cache semantics** — `/health` is explicitly uncacheable (`no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate`); CORS preflight results are cacheable for 86 400 s (`max_age`); `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT` is set to one year in the WSGI production profile but is inert because the application serves no static assets.
- **Build/dependency caches** — GitHub Actions pip caching and `cache-from/cache-to: type=gha` Docker layer caching in CD, plus the Compose named volumes `venv_cache_dev`/`venv_cache_prod` and `pip_cache_dev`/`pip_cache_prod`.

The architectural payoff is that horizontal scaling requires no shared store, no sticky sessions, and no cache-coherency protocol; the architectural limit is that nothing survives a restart, including the request IDs used for correlation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client["HTTP client"]

    subgraph Ingress["Ingress and serving"]
        Sock["Gunicorn socket<br/>bind 0.0.0.0:3000"]
        WsgiEnv["WSGI environ dict"]
    end

    subgraph Pipeline["Flask request pipeline"]
        Before["before_request<br/>start_time, request.id,<br/>access log"]
        Match["URL rule matching<br/>/hello or /health"]
```

### 5.1.4 External Integration Points

No integration is invoked by application code at runtime; every entry below is a platform or toolchain integration exercised by the container assets and the two GitHub Actions workflows.

| System Name | Integration Type | Data Exchange Pattern | Protocol / Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP clients (`curl`, browsers, `requests`) | Inbound API consumer | Synchronous request/response, stateless, no auth | HTTP/1.1; JSON bodies; custom `X-*` headers |
| Container orchestrator / Docker engine | Runtime supervision | Periodic liveness probe plus signal-based stop | `HEALTHCHECK` shell `curl -f /hello`; `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` |
| GitHub Actions | CI/CD execution | Event-triggered pipeline runs on `ubuntu-latest` | YAML workflow definitions; job outputs and artifacts |
| GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`) | Artifact publication | Push on build; pull by digest at deploy | OCI registry API; multi-arch image + provenance/SBOM attestations |
| Azure Web Apps | Deployment target | Push-based container deployment via `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` | Publish-profile credential; image reference by digest |
| Codecov | Coverage telemetry | One upload per matrix Python version | `coverage.xml` over HTTPS |
| GitHub code scanning | Security finding sink | SARIF upload from CI and CD scan jobs | SARIF 2.1 JSON |
| Trivy / Bandit / Safety / pip-audit / OSSF Scorecard | Static and image scanning | Scan-and-report inside pipeline jobs | JSON and SARIF reports |
| PyPI | Dependency source | Resolution at build/install time | `requirements*.txt` lower-bound specifiers over HTTPS |
| Docker Hub | Base-image source | Pull at image build | `python:3.12-alpine`, `alpine:3.19` |

**Service-level expectations.** The repository contains no contractual SLA, uptime target, or error-budget document. What it does contain are enforceable thresholds encoded in configuration and test assertions; these — and only these — should be treated as the system's operational commitments:

| Integration Surface | Encoded Expectation | Where Defined |
|---|---|---|
| Container liveness (`/hello`) | Production: 30 s interval, 10 s timeout, 3 retries, 15 s start period. Development: 15 s interval, 5 s timeout, 2 retries | `Dockerfile` L174–L175, L209–L210 |
| Request completion | Gunicorn `--timeout=30`, `--keepalive=2`, worker recycling at 1000 requests ±100 jitter | `Dockerfile` L216–L220; `docker-compose.yml` L263 |
| Warm latency for `GET /hello` | `< 50 ms` (and `< 50 ms` average, `< 100 ms` maximum under 50 concurrent requests) | `tests/test_app.py` L184, L454–L455 |
| Process memory | RSS `< 75 MB`, with a runtime warning emitted above the threshold | `tests/test_app.py` L426; `wsgi.py` L362 |
| Graceful shutdown | `< 10 s` from signal to completion | `tests/test_wsgi.py` L511 |
| Staging deploy gate | 12 health attempts, 20 s back-off, `--max-time 15`; single-request latency warning above 3.0 s | `cd.yml` L501–L532, L570–L577 |
| Production deploy gate | 18 health attempts, 25 s back-off, `--max-time 20`; 10-request average latency warning above 1.5 s | `cd.yml` L717–L756, L774–L791 |
| Post-deploy stability | 6-minute window, 30 s checks; `rollback_required=true` when failure rate exceeds 20 % | `cd.yml` L825–L864 |
| Container restart policy | `condition: any`, 5 s delay, 3 attempts, 120 s window; rolling update with `failure_action: rollback` | `docker-compose.yml` L290–L299 |
| Quality gate | 100 % line **and** branch coverage | `pytest.ini`, `src/backend/pytest.ini`, `ci.yml` L242–L294 |


## 5.2 Component Details

This sub-section details each major component using a uniform template — purpose and responsibilities, technologies, key interfaces, data persistence, and scaling considerations. Only components that exist in the repository are described; where a template field has no counterpart in the code (persistence being the common case) that is stated rather than filled with plausible-sounding text.

### 5.2.1 Component Interaction Overview

Interaction is almost entirely intra-process and synchronous. Four interaction edges carry all runtime coupling: the WSGI server invoking the application callable, the factory invoking its six registration helpers at build time, Flask invoking hooks and views per request, and the signal subsystem invoking shutdown coordination out of band. Every component writes to one shared sink — the process log streams.

### 5.2.2 WSGI Entry Point and Process Lifecycle Manager

**Purpose and responsibilities.** `src/backend/wsgi.py` is the deployment boundary. It resolves environment configuration, constructs the application through the factory, applies WSGI-specific overrides, exposes the single `application` callable, installs process signal handling, coordinates graceful shutdown, samples process memory, and installs a last-resort exception hook. It contains no request-handling logic.

**Technologies and frameworks.** Standard library `os`, `sys`, `signal`, `logging`, `threading`, `time`, `datetime`, `typing`; `flask` (type only), `python-dotenv` for `.env` loading, `psutil>=5.9.0` for process metrics. It is designed for Gunicorn (`gunicorn>=21.2.0`) but depends on no server API — only on PEP 3333 semantics.

**Key interfaces.**

| Interface | Signature / Contract | Consumer |
|---|---|---|
| `application` | Module-level WSGI callable, sole member of `__all__` (L531) | Gunicorn (`wsgi:application`), `test_wsgi.py` |
| `create_wsgi_application()` | `() -> Flask`; raises chained `RuntimeError` on any failure (L78–L144) | Module import branches, tests |
| `configure_wsgi_settings(app, environment)` | `(Flask, str) -> None`; applies four global plus per-profile settings (L147–L189) | `create_wsgi_application` |
| `setup_signal_handlers()` | `() -> None`; registers SIGTERM/SIGINT unconditionally, SIGUSR1/SIGUSR2 when available; downgrades `OSError` to a warning (L192–L256) | Both import branches |
| `perform_graceful_shutdown(signal_name)` | `(str) -> None`; logs, samples memory, never raises (L258–L296) | Signal handler, `sys.excepthook` |
| `validate_port_number(port)` | `(str) -> int`; enforces 1–65535, warns below 1024 (L299–L331) | `create_wsgi_application`, tests |
| `log_memory_usage(context)` | `(str) -> None`; RSS/VMS/percent with 75 MB warning; failures downgraded to warnings (L334–L373) | Startup, signals, exception hook |

**Dual entry semantics** are the component's defining behaviour. When the module is *imported* (the Gunicorn path), the `else` branch installs signal handlers and immediately builds `application` (L518–L527) — import therefore has deliberate side effects. When it is *executed* (`python wsgi.py`), the `__main__` branch additionally installs `sys.excepthook` and, only when `FLASK_ENV=development`, starts the Flask development server with `use_reloader=False` (L479–L513).

**Data persistence requirements.** None. Three module-level globals hold ephemeral coordination state — `flask_app` (the built instance), `shutdown_event` (a `threading.Event`), and `signal_received` (a flag) — all process-local and lost on exit. `perform_graceful_shutdown` carries commented placeholders for database cleanup, cache invalidation, background-task termination, and file-handle closure (L277–L281), confirming that no such resources exist to release.

**Scaling considerations.** The module is import-safe for pre-fork multiprocessing: with Gunicorn's `--preload`, the arbiter imports the module once and forks workers, so configuration resolution, factory execution, and the memory baseline occur a single time. Because no state is shared between requests, additional workers or additional container replicas require no coordination. Two constraints are inherent: the memory baseline is captured only in the process that performed the import, and the repository does not address how the handlers registered here interact with the WSGI server's own arbiter and worker signal handling.

**State transitions.** The process moves through a small, explicit state machine driven by import mode, configuration validity, and signals.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ModuleImport : python -m gunicorn wsgi:application
    ModuleImport --> DependencyCheck : guarded imports of flask, dotenv, psutil
    DependencyCheck --> Terminated : ImportError, print guidance, sys.exit(1)
    DependencyCheck --> FactoryImport : dependencies satisfied
    FactoryImport --> Terminated : cannot import create_app, sys.exit(1)
    FactoryImport --> SignalsInstalled : setup_signal_handlers
    SignalsInstalled --> ConfigResolution : read FLASK_ENV, HOST, PORT
    ConfigResolution --> StartupFailed : invalid port or factory error
    StartupFailed --> [*] : chained RuntimeError propagates to server
    ConfigResolution --> AppConstructed : create_app then configure_wsgi_settings
    AppConstructed --> Ready : deployment banner and memory baseline logged
    Ready --> Serving : first WSGI invocation
    Serving --> Serving : subsequent requests, no retained state
    Serving --> ShutdownRequested : SIGTERM or SIGINT received
    Ready --> ShutdownRequested : SIGTERM or SIGINT received
    Serving --> ExceptionEscalated : uncaught exception reaches sys.excepthook
    ExceptionEscalated --> ShutdownRequested : perform_graceful_shutdown invoked
    ShutdownRequested --> Draining : shutdown_event set, memory sampled
    Draining --> Terminated : cleanup logged, process exits
    Terminated --> [*]
```

**Graceful shutdown sequence.** Container stop is the normal termination path, and the chain from orchestrator to Python handler is explicit in the assets.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Orchestrator as Docker / Azure
    participant Init as dumb-init PID 1
    participant Arbiter as Gunicorn arbiter
    participant Wsgi as wsgi.py handler
    participant Log as stdout / stderr

    Orchestrator->>Init: SIGTERM on container stop
    Init->>Arbiter: forward SIGTERM
    Arbiter->>Wsgi: signal delivered to process
    Wsgi->>Log: log signal name, educational note
    Wsgi->>Wsgi: shutdown_event.set()
    Wsgi->>Log: log_memory_usage "Signal Handler"
    Wsgi->>Wsgi: perform_graceful_shutdown
    Wsgi->>Log: Flask context cleanup logged
    Wsgi->>Log: log_memory_usage "Graceful Shutdown"
    Wsgi-->>Arbiter: handler returns
    Arbiter-->>Orchestrator: process exits
    Note over Wsgi,Log: Test suite asserts the sequence completes in under 10 seconds
```

### 5.2.3 Application Factory and Configuration Subsystem

**Purpose and responsibilities.** `create_app` is the single construction point for the application graph. `configure_flask_settings` translates environment into a Flask config dictionary and selects one of three profiles; the factory then delegates to the four concern-specific registrars. Three convenience wrappers express intent at call sites, and the factory's default argument is `'production'` — the safe default.

**Technologies and frameworks.** Flask 3.1.1+ (`Flask`, `request`, `jsonify`, `Response`), Flask-CORS 4.0.0+, python-dotenv 1.0.1+, standard-library `logging`, `time`, `datetime`, `typing`, and `functools`.

**Key interfaces and the configuration contract.**

| Configuration Input | Consumed By | Default and Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `FLASK_ENV` | `configure_flask_settings` (L155); `create_wsgi_application` (L104) | Falls back to the `config_name` argument; selects the profile |
| `FLASK_DEBUG` | `configure_flask_settings` (L156) | `'false'`; only affects the development profile's `DEBUG` value |
| `SECRET_KEY` | `configure_flask_settings` (L161) | Falls back to `'dev-key-change-in-production'` with no warning |
| `HOST` | `create_wsgi_application` (L105); `app.py` `__main__` (L721) | `0.0.0.0` for WSGI, `localhost` for the direct development server |
| `PORT` | `validate_port_number` (L106); `app.py` `__main__` (L722) | `8000` in both modules, while container stages and `.env.example` use `3000` |
| `LOG_LEVEL`, `WORKERS` | Declared in `.env.example` only | Read by no code path; logging is fixed at INFO and worker count is set in container CMDs |

Profile differences are narrow and security-oriented rather than functional:

| Setting | production | development | testing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DEBUG` / `TESTING` | `False` / `False` | from `FLASK_DEBUG` / `False` | `False` / `True` |
| Exception propagation | `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS: True` | not set by the factory | not set by the factory |
| URL scheme | `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME: https` | default | default |
| Session cookies | secure, HTTP-only, `SameSite=Lax`, 3600 s | non-secure, HTTP-only, 86 400 s | non-secure, non-HTTP-only |
| Extras | — | `EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING: True` | `WTF_CSRF_ENABLED: False` |

Shared settings applied to all profiles are `JSON_SORT_KEYS: False`, `JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR: True`, `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH: 16 MB`, and `APPLICATION_ROOT: '/'` (L159–L166). Cookie policy is configured defensively even though no code path writes to `session`.

**Data persistence requirements.** None. The configuration dictionary lives in `app.config` for the process lifetime and is never persisted, exported, or reloaded. A `FLASK_CONFIGS` mapping (L641–L657) is defined and documented but never consumed — dead configuration that should not be mistaken for an active code path.

**Scaling considerations.** Because construction is a pure function of environment plus argument, every worker, test, and container builds an identical graph, which is what makes replica scaling and 100 % reproducibility possible. The cost of the factory is paid once per process, and `--preload` reduces that to once per container. One caveat is ordering: `configure_wsgi_settings` runs *after* the factory and overrides profile values, so the effective configuration of a Gunicorn-served process is the union of both layers with WSGI settings winning.

### 5.2.4 Request Lifecycle Middleware Chain

**Purpose and responsibilities.** `register_middleware_hooks` provides observability and light request validation without touching business logic: correlation-ID assignment, request timing, access logging, and a non-blocking content-type advisory. `configure_security_settings` and Flask-CORS contribute two further response-stage callbacks.

**Technologies.** Flask's `before_request`/`after_request` decorators, `time.time()` for timing, the module `logging` logger, and Flask-CORS for the cross-origin callback.

**Key interfaces.**

| Stage | Callback | Effect on the Exchange |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-dispatch | `before_request_middleware` (L299) | Sets `request.start_time` and `request.id`; logs `method path`; warns on non-JSON `POST`/`PUT` bodies; returns `None` to continue |
| Post-dispatch (first) | `after_request_middleware` (L326) | Adds `X-Response-Time: <n.nn>ms` and `X-Request-ID`; logs status and duration |
| Post-dispatch (second) | Flask-CORS callback | Applies allow-list headers and 86 400 s preflight cache |
| Post-dispatch (last) | `add_security_headers` (L223) | Removes `Server`; sets the six hardening headers |

Because Flask invokes `after_request` callbacks in reverse registration order, and the factory registers security headers (step 2) before CORS (step 3) and the timing hook (step 4), the effective response-stage order is timing → CORS → security headers. That ordering is favourable: header hardening cannot be clobbered by an earlier-registered callback.

**Data persistence requirements.** None. `start_time` and `id` are attributes on Flask's request-scoped object and vanish with the request context. Correlation IDs are therefore usable only within a single log stream and a single response, not across restarts or aggregated stores.

**Scaling considerations.** The chain is O(1) per request and allocates only small strings, which is consistent with the sub-50 ms assertions in the test suite. Two limits are structural: `req_<epoch-ms>` collides for requests that begin in the same millisecond across workers, and no inbound correlation header is honoured, so distributed tracing cannot be stitched from upstream identifiers.

### 5.2.5 API Surface — Route Handlers

**Purpose and responsibilities.** Two GET endpoints constitute the entire public API. `GET /hello` delivers the tutorial's functional payload; `GET /health` exposes runtime status for probes and deployment gates. Both are read-only, side-effect-free, and require no authentication.

**Technologies.** Flask routing decorators, `flask.jsonify` for serialisation and content typing, `datetime.now().isoformat()` for timestamps, `time.time()` for the uptime field, and `app.config` reads for environment reporting.

**Key interfaces.**

| Endpoint | Success Contract | Failure Contract |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /hello` | 200; body `{message: "Hello world", timestamp, status: "success"}`; headers `Content-Type: application/json`, `X-API-Version: 1.0` | Handler-local `except` returns 500 with `{status: "error", message, timestamp}` |
| `GET /health` | 200; body `{status: "healthy", timestamp, uptime, version: "1.0.0", environment, debug}`; `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate` | Handler-local `except` returns 503 with `{status: "unhealthy", error, timestamp}` |

Two properties deserve emphasis. First, `/health` is a **liveness** probe, not a dependency-aware readiness probe — it cannot be otherwise, because the service has no dependencies to interrogate. Second, its `uptime` field is the raw epoch value returned by `time.time()`, not elapsed seconds since start; consumers should not treat it as a duration.

**Data persistence requirements.** None; every field is a literal or a clock read.

**Scaling considerations.** Both handlers are pure functions of the clock and configuration, so they scale linearly with worker and replica count and never contend on shared resources. The measured envelope from the test suite is 50 of 50 concurrent requests succeeding with average latency under 50 ms and maximum under 100 ms.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as HTTP client
    participant Gunicorn as Gunicorn worker
    participant Flask as Flask application
    participant Before as before_request
    participant View as hello_route_handler
    participant After as after_request chain
    participant Log as Log stream

    Client->>Gunicorn: GET /hello HTTP/1.1
    Gunicorn->>Flask: WSGI environ
    Flask->>Before: dispatch pre-hooks
    Before->>Before: set start_time and request.id
    Before->>Log: INFO incoming request GET /hello
    Before-->>Flask: return None, continue
    Flask->>View: URL rule matched
    View->>View: build message, timestamp, status
    View->>View: jsonify then status_code 200
    View->>Log: INFO 200 OK response sent
    View-->>Flask: Response object
    Flask->>After: timing hook
    After->>After: X-Response-Time and X-Request-ID
    After->>Log: INFO request completed with duration
    Flask->>After: CORS callback then security headers
    After->>After: remove Server, set six headers
    After-->>Gunicorn: finalized response
    Gunicorn-->>Client: 200 application/json
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Probe as HEALTHCHECK / CD gate
    participant Server as Gunicorn
    participant Health as health_check_handler
    participant Config as app.config
    participant Log as Log stream

    Probe->>Server: curl -f /hello or /health
    Server->>Health: WSGI invocation for /health
    Health->>Config: read ENV and DEBUG
    Config-->>Health: environment and debug values
    Health->>Health: assemble status, timestamp, uptime, version
    alt assembly succeeds
        Health->>Log: INFO health check completed
        Health-->>Server: 200 healthy with no-store headers
        Server-->>Probe: healthy, container stays in service
    else assembly raises
        Health->>Log: ERROR health check error
        Health-->>Server: 503 unhealthy with error text
        Server-->>Probe: failure counted toward retries
    end
    Note over Probe,Server: Container probes target /hello#59; CD gates check both /hello and /health
```

### 5.2.6 Error Handling Registry

**Purpose and responsibilities.** `register_error_handlers` centralises the translation of routing failures and exceptions into a uniform JSON envelope, ensuring clients never receive HTML error pages or stack traces. It also concentrates the security decision about what may cross the boundary.

**Technologies.** Flask `errorhandler` registrations for the integer codes 404, 405, and 500 plus the `Exception` class; `logging` for server-side detail; `jsonify` for the response.

**Key interfaces.** All four handlers return a JSON object keyed `status`, `error`, `message`, and `timestamp`. The 404 and 405 handlers add safe request context (`path`, `method`); 405 additionally exposes `allowed_methods` and sets the `Allow` header from `error.valid_methods`; the 500 handler echoes `request_id`. Detailed diagnostics — including `exc_info=True` tracebacks — are written to logs and gated on `app.config['DEBUG']`, never to the response.

**Data persistence requirements.** None; errors are logged to the process streams only, with no error store, dead-letter queue, or incident record.

**Scaling considerations.** Handler cost is equivalent to a normal response, so error storms are bounded by the same worker concurrency as success traffic. Because the registry includes a handler for `Exception`, unhandled errors are converted into 500 JSON responses rather than propagating to the WSGI server, even though `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` is `True` — a deliberate trade of debugger fidelity for a consistent client contract.

### 5.2.7 Serving Tier and Container Runtime

**Purpose and responsibilities.** Gunicorn provides the HTTP/socket layer, pre-fork worker management, request timeouts, and worker recycling. The image built by `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` provides a reproducible, least-privilege filesystem for that process. `dumb-init` occupies PID 1 so signals reach Gunicorn correctly.

**Technologies.** `python:3.12-alpine` base with `curl`, `dumb-init`, `build-base`, `libffi-dev`, `openssl-dev`; a virtual environment at `/usr/src/app/.venv`; `gunicorn>=21.2.0`; Docker Compose 3.8 for local orchestration.

**Key interfaces and effective runtime configuration.**

| Aspect | Configured Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Image stages | `base` → `dependencies` → `application` → `development` \| `production` (five `FROM` directives) | `Dockerfile` L9, L64, L101, L137, L184 |
| Process identity | uid/gid 1000 (`python`), `WORKDIR /usr/src/app`, `USER python` | `Dockerfile` L41–L43, L59 |
| Runtime env | `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`, `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, `FLASK_ENV=production`, `FLASK_APP=app.py`, `PORT=3000`, `HOST=0.0.0.0` | `Dockerfile` L46–L55 |
| Serving command | `gunicorn ... --workers=4 --worker-class=sync --max-requests=1000 --max-requests-jitter=100 --timeout=30 --keepalive=2 --preload --access-logfile=- --error-logfile=-` | `Dockerfile` L216–L220; `docker-compose.yml` L263 |
| Liveness | `HEALTHCHECK` `curl -f http://localhost:3000/hello` — 30 s/10 s/3 retries/15 s start (production) | `Dockerfile` L209–L210 |
| Hardening | `read_only: true`, `tmpfs` `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, `cap_drop: ALL` plus `SETGID`/`SETUID`, `no-new-privileges`, `chmod -R 444 *.py` | `docker-compose.yml` L314–L333; `Dockerfile` L213 |
| Resource envelope | limits 128 M / 0.5 CPU; reservations 75 M / 0.25 CPU; `replicas: 1` | `docker-compose.yml` L279–L289 |

**Data persistence requirements.** No application data volume is mounted. The development service bind-mounts source for hot reload and both services mount virtual-environment and pip cache volumes — build acceleration, not state. Production mounts those volumes read-only.

**Scaling considerations.** With the `sync` worker class, effective in-process concurrency equals the worker count — four concurrent requests per container — while `--worker-connections=1000` pertains to the asynchronous worker classes and therefore does not raise that ceiling. `--max-requests=1000` with 100-request jitter recycles workers to bound memory drift, complementing the 75 MB RSS warning in `log_memory_usage`. Three tensions are worth recording: the 128 M container limit is modest for four workers when a single process is budgeted at 75 MB; the worker count, bind address, and timeout are baked into the image CMD, so `WORKERS`/`GUNICORN_WORKERS` values supplied by Compose or the CD deploy steps cannot retune a running container; and horizontal scaling beyond `replicas: 1` has no configuration in the repository — statelessness makes it safe, but no autoscaling rule, load balancer, or multi-replica manifest exists.

### 5.2.8 Verification and Delivery Components

**Purpose and responsibilities.** `src/backend/tests/` is the executable specification: `test_app.py` covers factory construction, both endpoints, all error handlers, security headers, CORS, statelessness, middleware behaviour, and performance envelopes; `test_wsgi.py` covers real process lifecycle, signal handling, port validation, factory/WSGI integration, environment loading, and end-to-end deployment timing. The two workflows in `.github/workflows/` convert those assertions into merge and release gates.

**Technologies.** pytest with `pytest-flask`, `pytest-cov` (branch mode), `pytest-benchmark`, `pytest-xdist`, `pytest-html`, `pytest-mock`, and `psutil`; flake8, black, mypy, bandit, safety, and pip-audit for static assurance; GitHub Actions, Docker Buildx, GHCR, Trivy, and `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` for delivery.

**Key interfaces.** Tests consume the application exclusively through published interfaces — the `create_app` factory, the Flask test client, and the `application` object — never through private helpers. The pipelines consume the repository through path-filtered triggers and publish machine-readable artifacts: `coverage.xml`/`coverage.json`/`htmlcov`, `junit.xml`, `pytest_report.html`, and SARIF security reports.

**Data persistence requirements.** Only reproducible artifacts: coverage and test reports (30-day CI retention), security reports (90-day retention), and digest-addressed container images in GHCR with provenance and SBOM attestations.

**Scaling considerations.** The `test` job fans out across Python 3.12, 3.11, and 3.10 — broader than the `requires-python = ">=3.12"` declaration in `pyproject.toml` — and `pytest-xdist` is available for parallel execution. The CD pipeline is serialised by design: `concurrency: cd-${{ github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: false` prevents overlapping deployments, and production is additionally gated on a successful staging deployment plus a non-failed security scan.

## 5.3 Technical Decisions

Every decision recorded here is reconstructed from artifacts in the repository — code, configuration, manifests, and the original brief in `blitzy/documentation/Input Prompt.md`. Where a rationale is stated in the source it is reported as such; where only the outcome is observable, the tradeoff is described in terms of its verifiable consequences rather than attributed intent.

### 5.3.1 Architecture Style Decisions and Tradeoffs

| Decision | Observable Alternative | Rationale Evidenced in Repository | Tradeoff Accepted |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-process modular monolith | Split into services, or a package with blueprints | One endpoint of scope; `register_route_handlers` defines both routes in one function | No blueprint boundary exists, so route growth pressures a single module |
| Two-module split (`app.py` / `wsgi.py`) | One module exposing both app and server bootstrap | Docstrings state the modules replace Express `app.js` and `server.js` | Import-time side effects concentrate in `wsgi.py`; the WSGI callable cannot be built without also installing signal handlers |
| Function-composed assembly | Class-based configuration objects, or Flask `Config` subclasses | Six registration helpers invoked in fixed order (`app.py` L97–L117) | Configuration is imperative; the declarative `FLASK_CONFIGS` map was written and left unused |
| Application factory over module-level app | `app = Flask(__name__)` at import | Factory returns a fresh instance per call; the pytest `app` fixture depends on it | Callers must know which factory wrapper to use; the effective config is the union of factory plus WSGI layers |
| Synchronous WSGI over ASGI/async | `asyncio`, Quart, or an async worker class | `--worker-class=sync`; no `async def` anywhere; PEP 3333 contract only | In-process concurrency is capped at the worker count |
| Stateless request handling | Session store, in-memory counters, or a database | No datastore dependency declared; `TestFlaskStatelessOperation` asserts payload identity across requests | Nothing survives a restart — including correlation IDs |
| Container-first packaging | Bare-metal or platform-buildpack deployment | Five-stage `Dockerfile`; Compose dev/prod services; CD builds and deploys images by digest | Local runs depend on Docker for parity; image CMD hardcodes serving parameters |

The dominant style tension in this repository is between *pedagogical explicitness* and *operational configurability*. The code consistently resolves it toward explicitness: serving parameters are literals in the image CMD rather than environment-derived, logging is fixed at INFO in `logging.basicConfig`, and the CORS allow-list is a literal list in `configure_cors_middleware`. The result is a system that is easy to read end-to-end and hard to retune without a rebuild — an acceptable trade for a reference implementation, and the first thing to change if the pattern is reused for a production service.

The runtime resolves its own execution mode and configuration profile through a small decision tree that is entirely determined by import mode and two environment variables.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start{{"How is the code entered?"}}
    Start -->|"imported as wsgi:application"| ImportBranch["else branch, wsgi.py L518<br/>install signals, build application"]
    Start -->|"python wsgi.py"| MainBranch["__main__ branch, wsgi.py L479<br/>install sys.excepthook and signals"]
    Start -->|"python app.py"| AppMain["app.py __main__ L705<br/>create_development_app"]

    ImportBranch --> EnvCheck{{"FLASK_ENV value?"}}
    MainBranch --> DevCheck{{"FLASK_ENV equals development?"}}
    DevCheck -->|"yes"| DevServer["application.run debug=True<br/>use_reloader=False"]
    DevCheck -->|"no"| GuidanceOnly["log Gunicorn start guidance<br/>no server started"]

    EnvCheck -->|"production, the default"| ProdProfile["DEBUG False, PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS True<br/>secure cookies, https URL scheme"]
    EnvCheck -->|"development"| DevProfile["DEBUG from FLASK_DEBUG<br/>template loading diagnostics"]
    EnvCheck -->|"testing"| TestProfile["TESTING True, CSRF disabled<br/>non-secure cookies"]

    ProdProfile --> WsgiOverride["configure_wsgi_settings applies<br/>1-year static cache, no debug"]
    DevProfile --> WsgiOverride
    TestProfile --> WsgiOverride
    WsgiOverride --> PortGate{{"PORT parses to 1-65535?"}}
    PortGate -->|"no"| Abort["ValueError chained,<br/>startup fails fast"]
    PortGate -->|"yes, below 1024"| WarnPriv["warn privileged range,<br/>continue"]
    PortGate -->|"yes"| Ready["application ready,<br/>memory baseline logged"]
    WarnPriv --> Ready
    AppMain --> Ready
    DevServer --> Ready
```

### 5.3.2 Communication Pattern Choices

| Concern | Chosen Mechanism | Where Configured | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Client interaction | Synchronous HTTP/1.1 request–response with JSON bodies | `@app.route` handlers; `jsonify` | Simple, cacheable-by-directive, no client SDK needed; no streaming or push capability |
| Intra-application calls | Direct Python function invocation inside one process | `create_app` calling its six registrars | Zero serialisation cost and no partial-failure modes; no independent deployability |
| Cross-origin browser access | Preflight-based CORS with explicit allow-lists | `configure_cors_middleware`; `max_age: 86400` | Predictable policy; changes propagate to browsers only after preflight cache expiry, and no deployed origin is currently allowed |
| Correlation between client and logs | Response headers `X-Request-ID` and `X-Response-Time` | `after_request_middleware` | Human-traceable request pairing; not a distributed trace and not derived from inbound headers |
| Orchestrator ↔ container control | Liveness probe over loopback HTTP plus POSIX signals | `HEALTHCHECK`; `setup_signal_handlers` | Works identically under Docker, Compose, and Azure Web Apps; probe targets `/hello` rather than the purpose-built `/health` |
| Asynchronous work | **None** — no broker, queue, scheduler, or background thread pool | — | No eventual-consistency or retry semantics to reason about; also no capacity for long-running work |
| Pipeline stage coordination | Job dependencies plus step outputs (`needs`, `outputs`) | `ci.yml` `quality-gate`; `cd.yml` staging → production gate | Deterministic promotion path; gate decisions live in shell logic inside YAML rather than in a policy engine |

The consistent choice is *synchronous and observable*. Nothing in the runtime defers work, retries, or fans out, which is why the error model can be a simple envelope and the scaling model can be pure replication.

### 5.3.3 Data Storage and Caching Rationale

**Storage.** The decision is to have no persistence tier at all, and the repository is internally consistent about it: no driver, ORM, migration tool, object-storage SDK, or schema artifact exists, and the database/Redis blocks in `src/backend/.env.example` are commented and explicitly labelled as unused examples. The justification visible in the code is that neither endpoint has any data to persist — `/hello` returns a literal and `/health` returns clock and configuration reads. The consequences are favourable for this system and important to state plainly:

- Horizontal scaling requires no shared store, no sticky sessions, and no cache invalidation protocol.
- There is no backup, restore, or migration procedure to design — and correspondingly nothing to recover.
- Restart is always safe and always total: no warm state, no queued work, no in-flight transactions.
- The single storage-adjacent control is `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 16 MB`, which bounds inbound request size.

**Caching.** No cache server was introduced; caching decisions were pushed to HTTP semantics and to the build system.

| Cache Decision | Value | Rationale / Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `/health` explicitly uncacheable | `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate` | Probes and deployment gates must observe current state, never a cached verdict |
| CORS preflight cached | `max_age: 86400` (24 h) | Removes repeated `OPTIONS` round trips; delays propagation of allow-list changes by up to a day |
| Static asset max-age | `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT: 31536000` in the WSGI production profile | Configured for completeness; inert because the application serves no static files |
| Response caching for `/hello` | Not set | The payload carries a per-request timestamp, so caching it would be semantically wrong |
| Build-layer caching | `cache-from/cache-to: type=gha`; Compose `cache_from`; pip caches; `venv_cache_*` volumes | Shortens CI and local rebuild time without affecting runtime behaviour |

Because no in-process cache exists, memory behaviour is dominated by the interpreter and framework rather than by application data — which is what makes the flat 75 MB RSS expectation and `--max-requests` recycling a coherent pair.

### 5.3.4 Security Mechanism Selection

| Mechanism | Selected Implementation | Rationale and Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Response hardening | Six headers plus `Server` removal applied by an `after_request` callback to all responses | Chosen over a reverse proxy or WAF because the application is the only component in the request path; a fixed `default-src 'self'` policy is adequate for a JSON-only API |
| Cross-origin control | Flask-CORS with explicit origin/method/header allow-lists and `supports_credentials=False` | Described in code as a "Secure default for stateless API"; allow-list is localhost-only, so cross-origin browser access from a deployed origin is denied by default |
| Authentication and authorization | **Not implemented** | No identity provider, token library, or session login exists; `src/backend/README.md` documents `/hello` as "Authentication: None required". The only credential material is Flask's `SECRET_KEY`, read from the environment with a development fallback |
| Error information disclosure | Generic client messages with detail confined to logs; tracebacks gated on `DEBUG` | Prevents internal path/stack leakage while preserving debuggability in development |
| Request size limiting | `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 16 MB` | Bounds memory consumption from oversized bodies at the framework layer |
| Container least privilege | Non-root uid/gid 1000, read-only root filesystem, `cap_drop: ALL` with only `SETGID`/`SETUID`, `no-new-privileges`, `chmod -R 444 *.py`, tmpfs for writable paths | Reduces blast radius of a compromised process; `apparmor:unconfined` is retained in Compose and is a known relaxation |
| Supply-chain assurance | Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, and OSSF Scorecard in CI; Trivy image scan in CD; provenance and SBOM attestations on published images | Multi-tool defence in depth; all dependency specifiers are lower bounds with no lockfile, so resolved versions can drift between builds |
| Secret handling | GitHub Actions secrets for GHCR and the two Azure publish profiles; environment protection on `staging` and `production` | No secrets manager integration; a missing `SECRET_KEY` silently falls back to a well-known development value |
| Transport security | `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME='https'` and secure session cookies in the production profile; TLS terminated by the hosting platform | The container itself serves plain HTTP on its bind port; HTTPS is a property of the Azure Web App front end |

### 5.3.5 Architecture Decision Records

The following ADRs are reconstructed from repository artifacts. Status reflects what is actually implemented, including two decisions whose implementation contains a verified defect.

#### 5.3.5.1 ADR-001 — Application Factory as the Sole Construction Path

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (`app.py` L63–L141).
- **Context:** The application must be constructible in three environments — production WSGI, local development, and pytest — with different configuration and without duplicated wiring.
- **Decision:** Expose `create_app(config_name='production')` plus three intent-revealing wrappers, and export only those four names in `__all__`. No module-level `Flask` instance exists in `app.py`.
- **Consequences:** Tests build isolated instances per fixture; production defaults to the hardened profile even if the caller passes nothing. The cost is that effective configuration must be traced through two layers once `configure_wsgi_settings` runs, and the unused `FLASK_CONFIGS` map remains as misleading dead code.

#### 5.3.5.2 ADR-002 — Separate the WSGI Entry Point from Application Assembly

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (`wsgi.py`).
- **Context:** Process concerns (ports, signals, memory, exception hooks) must not contaminate application logic, mirroring the predecessor's `app.js`/`server.js` split.
- **Decision:** `wsgi.py` owns environment resolution, port validation, signal handling, graceful shutdown, memory sampling, and the exported `application` object; `app.py` owns nothing about servers.
- **Consequences:** Either module can be reasoned about alone, and the app is trivially embeddable in tests. The cost is import-time side effects: importing `wsgi` installs signal handlers and constructs the application.

#### 5.3.5.3 ADR-003 — Synchronous Pre-Fork Serving with Gunicorn

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (`Dockerfile` L216–L220; `docker-compose.yml` L263).
- **Context:** The workload is CPU-trivial, I/O-free, and must demonstrate production-grade WSGI serving.
- **Decision:** Gunicorn with four `sync` workers, `--timeout=30`, `--keepalive=2`, `--max-requests=1000 --max-requests-jitter=100`, and `--preload`, fronted by `dumb-init` as PID 1.
- **Consequences:** Concurrency equals worker count, which the test suite's 50-request concurrency assertions comfortably tolerate for this payload; worker recycling bounds memory drift; `--preload` shortens boot and shares the imported module across workers. The declared `--worker-connections=1000` has no effect under the sync class, and because all parameters are literals in the image CMD, environment variables named `WORKERS`/`GUNICORN_WORKERS` cannot retune a running container.

#### 5.3.5.4 ADR-004 — No Persistence Tier

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (verified absence across all manifests and code).
- **Context:** Neither endpoint has durable data; adding a store would add operational surface without pedagogical or functional return.
- **Decision:** Keep the service stateless; document database and cache configuration only as commented examples in `.env.example`.
- **Consequences:** Scaling, restart, and rollback all become trivial; there is no backup or migration story to maintain. Conversely, nothing persists across restarts, and any future feature needing state will require a new architectural layer rather than an extension.

#### 5.3.5.5 ADR-005 — Uniform JSON Error Envelope via a Handler Registry

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (`app.py` L470–L632).
- **Context:** Clients of a JSON API should never receive HTML error pages or stack traces, and error responses must remain useful for support.
- **Decision:** Register handlers for 404, 405, 500, and `Exception`; return a consistent envelope; log full detail server-side; include tracebacks only when `DEBUG` is set; echo `request_id` on 500.
- **Consequences:** Error responses are machine-parseable and carry the same security headers as success responses. Registering an `Exception` handler means unhandled exceptions become 500 JSON responses rather than propagating to the server despite `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS=True` — chosen contract consistency over debugger fidelity.

#### 5.3.5.6 ADR-006 — Twelve-Factor Environment Configuration with In-Code Defaults

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (`load_dotenv` plus `os.getenv` throughout; `src/backend/.env.example`).
- **Context:** The same image must run in development, testing, staging, and production without code changes.
- **Decision:** Read all tunables from the environment with `python-dotenv` support for a local `.env`, and give every variable an in-code default.
- **Consequences:** Zero-configuration startup is possible and the twelve-factor pattern is demonstrated. The costs are real: `SECRET_KEY` silently falls back to `'dev-key-change-in-production'`; `LOG_LEVEL` and `WORKERS` are documented in the template but read by no code; and the `PORT` default differs between the modules (8000) and the container/template (3000).

#### 5.3.5.7 ADR-007 — Application-Layer Security Headers Instead of Edge Middleware

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (`app.py` L223–L253).
- **Context:** There is no proxy, gateway, or WAF in the architecture, so hardening must originate in the application.
- **Decision:** Apply six headers and strip `Server` in an `after_request` callback registered first, so Flask's reverse-order execution applies it last.
- **Consequences:** Every response — including error responses — is hardened, with no bypass path. The policy is fixed in code with no per-route override, and header values cannot be tuned without a code change.

#### 5.3.5.8 ADR-008 — Omit Authentication and Authorization

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (verified absence of any auth mechanism).
- **Context:** The endpoint returns a public constant; the brief specifies no identity requirement.
- **Decision:** Serve both endpoints anonymously; keep JWT/session examples commented in `.env.example`.
- **Consequences:** Radically simpler request path and test surface. Any deployment of this pattern to a non-public payload must add an authentication layer, a decision this architecture explicitly defers.

#### 5.3.5.9 ADR-009 — Multi-Stage Alpine Image with an Immutable Production Leaf

- **Status:** Accepted with a known defect (`Dockerfile`).
- **Context:** The image must be small, reproducible, hardened, and able to serve both development and production from one definition.
- **Decision:** Five stages — `base`, `dependencies`, `application`, and the `development`/`production` leaves — on `python:3.12-alpine`, installing into a virtual environment, running as uid 1000, verifying imports at build time, and making sources read-only in production.
- **Consequences:** Development and production share dependency resolution while diverging only at the leaf; build-time import verification catches packaging errors early. Two defects are verified: the production CMD invokes `gunicorn wsgi:app` although the module exports `application`, and the `dependencies` stage installs only the root `requirements.txt`, which omits `psutil` — a package `wsgi.py` imports unconditionally and whose absence triggers `sys.exit(1)`.

#### 5.3.5.10 ADR-010 — Quality Gates as Hard Merge Criteria

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (`pytest.ini`, `src/backend/pytest.ini`, `ci.yml`).
- **Context:** A reference implementation is only credible if its own standards are enforced.
- **Decision:** Require 100 % line and branch coverage (`--cov-fail-under=100`), run flake8, and add a dedicated `quality-gate` job that re-parses `coverage.xml` and rejects high-severity Bandit findings or any Safety vulnerability.
- **Consequences:** Untested branches cannot merge, and security findings block promotion. The gate also raises the cost of every change, and the CI matrix intentionally exceeds the declared support floor by testing Python 3.11 and 3.10 alongside 3.12.

#### 5.3.5.11 ADR-011 — Digest-Pinned, Progressively Gated Deployment

- **Status:** Accepted and implemented (`cd.yml`).
- **Context:** Deployments must be reproducible and reversible without an orchestration platform of their own.
- **Decision:** Build a multi-architecture image with provenance and SBOM attestations, publish to GHCR, scan with Trivy, then deploy the same digest to staging and — after staging success plus a clean scan — to production, each behind retry-based health loops and smoke assertions, with a 6-minute post-deploy monitor that raises `rollback_required` above a 20 % failure rate.
- **Consequences:** Staging and production run byte-identical artifacts, and promotion is evidence-based. The gap is that `rollback_required` is surfaced as an output and job failure rather than executing an automated redeploy of the previous digest, and no IaC defines the Azure targets.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ADR004["ADR-004<br/>No persistence tier"]
    ADR003["ADR-003<br/>Sync pre-fork Gunicorn"]
    ADR001["ADR-001<br/>Application factory"]
    ADR002["ADR-002<br/>Separate WSGI entry point"]
    ADR006["ADR-006<br/>Env configuration"]
    ADR005["ADR-005<br/>JSON error envelope"]
    ADR007["ADR-007<br/>App-layer security headers"]
```

## 5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns

### 5.4.1 Monitoring and Observability Approach

Observability is deliberately self-contained: the process emits signals that a human or a probe can read directly, and nothing exports telemetry to an external system. There is no `/metrics` endpoint, no Prometheus client, no OpenTelemetry SDK, no APM agent, and no alerting configuration anywhere in the repository.

| Signal | Mechanism | Emission Points | Consumer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liveness | `HEALTHCHECK curl -f /hello` | Every 30 s in production (10 s timeout, 3 retries, 15 s start period); every 15 s in development | Docker/Compose health status |
| Application status | `GET /health` returning `status`, `timestamp`, `uptime`, `version`, `environment`, `debug` | On demand | CD smoke tests; operators |
| Request timing | `X-Response-Time` header plus a matching INFO log line | Every response | Clients, log readers |
| Request correlation | `X-Request-ID` header (`req_<epoch-ms>`) | Every response | Clients, log readers |
| Process memory | `psutil` RSS/VMS/percent sampling with a 75 MB warning threshold | Three event points only — startup, signal receipt, uncaught exception | Log readers, tests |
| Deployment health | Retry loops of `curl` against `/hello` plus body assertions | Staging: 12 attempts / 20 s back-off; production: 18 attempts / 25 s back-off | CD job outcome |
| Post-deploy stability | 6-minute, 30-second-interval poll computing a failure rate | Production deploy only | `rollback_required` output |
| Coverage and scan telemetry | Codecov upload; SARIF to GitHub code scanning; retained artifacts | Per CI run | Reviewers, code scanning dashboard |

Three properties of this approach shape what operators can and cannot see. Memory sampling is **event-driven, not periodic**, so a slow leak between startup and shutdown produces no telemetry — worker recycling at 1000 requests is the mitigation rather than the alarm. The container probe targets `/hello` rather than `/health`, so the richer status document is exercised only by the CD smoke tests. And because health results feed only container restart policy and deployment gates, there is no notification path: a failing probe restarts a container or fails a pipeline, and nothing pages anyone.

### 5.4.2 Logging and Tracing Strategy

Logging is the primary observability channel and is configured identically in both runtime modules: `logging.basicConfig` at `INFO` with the format `%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s`. `wsgi.py` additionally attaches **two** stream handlers — one for `stdout` and one for `stderr` — which means records emitted under the WSGI entry point are written to both streams. Gunicorn contributes a second producer through `--access-logfile=- --error-logfile=- --log-level=info`. Together these give container logs an application narrative plus a conventional access log, with no shipper, aggregator, index, or retention policy defined anywhere in the repository.

| Log Category | Level | Representative Content | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lifecycle narration | INFO | Factory initialisation, per-step configuration confirmation, deployment banner with Python version, PID, platform, and endpoint list | `app.py`, `wsgi.py` L376–L429 |
| Access log | INFO | Inbound `method path`; completion with status code and duration in ms | `before_request_middleware`, `after_request_middleware` |
| Client-error log | WARNING | 404 with method and path; 405 with method and path; non-JSON `POST`/`PUT` advisory | `app.py` L496, L531, L321 |
| Server-error log | ERROR | Exception type, message, request path and method; `exc_info` traceback only when `DEBUG` | `app.py` L573–L582, L615–L620 |
| Resource log | INFO / WARNING | RSS, VMS, memory percent, PID; warning when RSS exceeds 75 MB | `wsgi.py` L354–L366 |
| Shutdown log | INFO | Signal name, cleanup steps, final memory sample, completion | `wsgi.py` L224–L291 |
| Startup failure log | ERROR | Error type and message plus four explicit troubleshooting suggestions | `app.py` L128–L138, `wsgi.py` L131–L141 |
| Test log | INFO to console, DEBUG to file | Live CLI logging plus `logs/pytest.log` with function and line number | `src/backend/pytest.ini` |

**Tracing.** There is no distributed tracing. The `X-Request-ID` value is generated locally from epoch milliseconds, is not read from any inbound header, is not propagated anywhere (the service makes no outbound calls), and is not persisted. It supports single-service log correlation only, and two requests entering in the same millisecond receive the same identifier. `LOG_LEVEL` appears in `.env.example` and in container environment blocks but is not consumed by the logging configuration, so verbosity is effectively fixed at INFO for the application logger.

### 5.4.3 Error Handling Patterns

Four patterns are used consistently, and each maps to a different failure class:

1. **Guarded import with remediation guidance.** Missing third-party packages are caught at import time; the process prints the exact `pip install` command and then either raises a chained `ImportError` (`app.py` L39–L48) or exits with status 1 (`wsgi.py` L35–L54). Dependency problems therefore fail before any socket is bound.
2. **Fail-fast startup with exception chaining.** Factory and WSGI initialisation wrap their bodies in `try`/`except`, log the error type, message, and four troubleshooting hints, then re-raise as `RuntimeError(...) from e`. A misconfigured process never enters a half-initialised serving state.
3. **Centralised request-error mapping.** The handler registry converts 404, 405, 500, and any `Exception` into a uniform JSON envelope, logging full detail server-side and disclosing internals only when `DEBUG` is set. Route handlers additionally wrap their own bodies, returning 500 for `/hello` and 503 for `/health` before the registry is consulted.
4. **Non-fatal degradation for auxiliary functions.** Failures in observability and shutdown paths are downgraded to warnings so they cannot cascade: `log_memory_usage` swallows any exception, `setup_signal_handlers` downgrades `OSError` from unavailable signals to a warning, and `perform_graceful_shutdown` catches and logs its own errors rather than raising during termination.

A fifth mechanism is the last-resort `sys.excepthook` installed by `handle_uncaught_exceptions`, which logs the exception, samples memory, prints a traceback only when `FLASK_ENV=development`, and then invokes the graceful-shutdown sequence — while explicitly delegating `KeyboardInterrupt` to the default hook so interactive interruption behaves normally.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Incoming["Inbound HTTP request"] --> PreHook["before_request: assign id, start timer, log"]
    PreHook --> Match{{"Does a URL rule match the path?"}}
    Match -->|"no"| H404["errorhandler 404<br/>WARNING log, JSON with path and method"]
    Match -->|"yes, method not allowed"| H405["errorhandler 405<br/>WARNING log, allowed_methods and Allow header"]
    Match -->|"yes"| Invoke["Invoke view function"]

    Invoke --> ViewGuard{{"Did the handler body raise?"}}
    ViewGuard -->|"no"| Success["200 JSON payload"]
    ViewGuard -->|"yes, /hello"| LocalHello["Local except: 500 JSON<br/>error status and timestamp"]
    ViewGuard -->|"yes, /health"| LocalHealth["Local except: 503 JSON<br/>unhealthy with error text"]
    ViewGuard -->|"yes, escapes handler"| Registry{{"Which registry entry applies?"}}

    Registry -->|"HTTP 500 raised"| H500["errorhandler 500<br/>ERROR log with path and method<br/>generic message plus request_id"]
    Registry -->|"any other exception"| HExc["errorhandler Exception<br/>ERROR log with type and message<br/>generic Unexpected Error payload"]

    H500 --> DebugGate{{"Is DEBUG enabled?"}}
    HExc --> DebugGate
    DebugGate -->|"yes"| Trace["Log exc_info traceback<br/>server-side only"]
    DebugGate -->|"no"| NoTrace["Suppress traceback entirely"]

    Success --> PostChain["after_request chain:<br/>timing, CORS, security headers"]
    LocalHello --> PostChain
    LocalHealth --> PostChain
    H404 --> PostChain
    H405 --> PostChain
    Trace --> PostChain
    NoTrace --> PostChain
    PostChain --> Emit["Response returned to client<br/>hardened headers on every path"]
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Boot["Process start: import wsgi module"] --> DepGate{{"Are flask, dotenv and psutil importable?"}}
    DepGate -->|"no"| DepFail["Print pip install guidance<br/>sys.exit(1)"]
    DepGate -->|"yes"| FactoryGate{{"Can create_app be imported from app?"}}
    FactoryGate -->|"no"| FactoryFail["Print module guidance<br/>sys.exit(1)"]
    FactoryGate -->|"yes"| PortGate{{"Does PORT validate to 1-65535?"}}
    PortGate -->|"no"| PortFail["Log invalid port<br/>raise chained ValueError"]
    PortGate -->|"yes"| BuildGate{{"Did create_app and CORS setup succeed?"}}
    BuildGate -->|"no"| BuildFail["Log error type, message,<br/>four troubleshooting hints<br/>raise chained RuntimeError"]
    BuildGate -->|"yes"| Serving["Serving: application ready"]

    DepFail --> Restart{{"Container restart policy applies?"}}
    FactoryFail --> Restart
    PortFail --> Restart
    BuildFail --> Restart
    Restart -->|"prod: condition any, 5s delay, 3 attempts, 120s window"| Boot
    Restart -->|"attempts exhausted"| Unhealthy["Container reported unhealthy<br/>deployment gate fails"]

    Serving --> Runtime{{"Runtime disruption type?"}}
    Runtime -->|"uncaught exception outside request"| Hook["sys.excepthook: log, sample memory,<br/>traceback only in development"]
    Runtime -->|"SIGTERM or SIGINT"| Signal["Signal handler: set shutdown_event,<br/>sample memory"]
    Hook --> Drain["perform_graceful_shutdown<br/>errors logged, never raised"]
    Signal --> Drain
    Drain --> Exit["Process exits, target under 10 seconds"]
```

### 5.4.4 Authentication and Authorization Framework

**No authentication or authorization framework exists in this system, and that is an explicit design position rather than an oversight.** Both endpoints are anonymous: there is no identity provider integration, no OAuth/OIDC client, no JWT or token library, no session login, no API-key check, and no role or permission model. `src/backend/README.md` documents `GET /hello` as "Authentication: None required", and `.env.example` carries a commented `JWT_SECRET_KEY` block labelled as an unused example.

What does exist is a set of adjacent controls that are frequently mistaken for an authorization layer, so they are enumerated precisely:

| Control | What It Actually Enforces | What It Does Not Do |
|---|---|---|
| Flask-CORS allow-list | Which browser origins may read cross-origin responses (`localhost:3000`, `localhost:8000`), with `supports_credentials=False` | Does not restrict non-browser clients; `curl` and server-side callers are unaffected |
| Security response headers | Client-side rendering and sniffing constraints on every response | Does not authenticate or authorize any caller |
| `SECRET_KEY` | Flask's signing key, read from the environment with a `'dev-key-change-in-production'` fallback | Signs nothing in practice — no code writes to `session` or issues signed tokens |
| Session cookie policy | Secure/HTTP-only/`SameSite=Lax` attributes and lifetimes per profile | No session is ever created |
| Container least privilege | Non-root execution, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities | Process-level isolation, not request-level authorization |
| GitHub Actions secrets and environment protection | Who and what may publish images and deploy to `staging`/`production` | Applies to the delivery pipeline only, never to application traffic |

Two consequences follow for anyone reusing this architecture. First, the trust boundary is the network: any caller that can reach the bound port has full access to both endpoints. Second, `GET /health` publicly discloses the resolved `environment` name and `debug` flag, which is benign for a tutorial payload but would be an information-disclosure finding on a service that adopts this health handler unchanged. Adding authentication would require a new component — a `before_request` guard or an extension — because no seam for it exists today.

### 5.4.5 Performance Requirements and Service Expectations

The repository contains no contractual SLA, uptime commitment, or error budget. It does contain enforceable thresholds in three distinct enforcement layers, and only these should be treated as requirements.

| Requirement | Threshold | Enforcement Layer |
|---|---|---|
| Warm latency, `GET /hello` | `< 50 ms` | Test assertion (`test_app.py` L184) |
| Average latency under 50 concurrent requests | `< 50 ms` | Test assertion (`test_app.py` L454) |
| Maximum latency under 50 concurrent requests | `< 100 ms` | Test assertion (`test_app.py` L455) |
| Concurrent success rate | 50 of 50 requests | Test assertion (`test_app.py` L447) |
| WSGI benchmark mean latency | `< 50 ms` | Test assertion (`test_wsgi.py` L768) |
| Process resident memory | `< 75 MB`, with a runtime WARNING above the threshold | Test assertion (`test_app.py` L426) and `log_memory_usage` |
| Memory growth bounds | `< 5 MB` per test, `< 10 MB` fixture-scoped, `< 20 MB` in WSGI load tests | Test assertions |
| Graceful shutdown duration | `< 10 s` | Test assertion (`test_wsgi.py` L511) |
| End-to-end lifecycle duration | `< 60 s` | Test assertion (`test_wsgi.py` L1309) |
| Request timeout | 30 s Gunicorn worker timeout | Runtime configuration |
| Worker recycling | 1000 requests ± 100 jitter | Runtime configuration |
| Container resource envelope | Limit 128 M / 0.5 CPU; reservation 75 M / 0.25 CPU | Compose `deploy.resources` |
| Inbound request size | 16 MB (`MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`) | Runtime configuration |
| Staging smoke latency | Warning above 3.0 s for a single request | CD gate (non-blocking) |
| Production smoke latency | Warning above 1.5 s averaged over 10 requests | CD gate (non-blocking) |
| Post-deploy failure rate | `rollback_required` above 20 % over a 6-minute window | CD gate (blocking) |
| Test execution ceiling | 300 s thread-based timeout | pytest configuration |

Three interpretation notes matter. The `<50 ms` and `<75 MB` figures are measured against the **Flask test client and single-process runs**, not against a deployed Azure endpoint — the deployed gates use second-scale thresholds, and the CD pipeline allows 45 s (staging) and 75 s (production) of warm-up before probing, which reflects platform provisioning rather than application initialisation. The `<100 ms` cold-start target stated in `blitzy/documentation/Input Prompt.md` is not asserted by any test. Finally, capacity is bounded by the sync worker model: four workers per container means four concurrent requests, so throughput scales with workers and replicas rather than with per-worker concurrency.

### 5.4.6 Availability, Recovery, and Disaster Recovery Procedures

Statelessness collapses most of the disaster-recovery problem space: with no datastore, cache, queue, or session store, there is no data to lose and therefore no backup, restore, or point-in-time recovery procedure to define. Recovery is always the same operation — restart the process or redeploy an image digest.

| Scenario | Configured Response | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Process crash or failed startup | Compose `restart: always` (production) / `unless-stopped` (development); `restart_policy` `condition: any`, 5 s delay, 3 attempts, 120 s window | `docker-compose.yml` L252, L295–L299 |
| Unhealthy container | `HEALTHCHECK` failure after 3 retries marks the container unhealthy for the orchestrator | `Dockerfile` L209–L210 |
| Graceful stop / rescheduling | `dumb-init` forwards `SIGTERM`; handler sets `shutdown_event`, samples memory, logs cleanup; asserted under 10 s | `Dockerfile` L132/L220, `wsgi.py` L192–L296 |
| Bad rolling update | `update_config` `parallelism: 1`, `delay: 10s`, `failure_action: rollback`, `monitor: 60s` | `docker-compose.yml` L290–L294 |
| Failed staging validation | Health loop exits non-zero after 12 attempts; production job is blocked by the `deployment_status == 'success'` prerequisite | `cd.yml` L501–L532, L652–L671 |
| Failed production validation | Health loop exits non-zero after 18 attempts, failing the deployment job | `cd.yml` L717–L756 |
| Post-deploy instability | Monitoring step sets `rollback_required=true` and exits non-zero when the failure rate exceeds 20 % | `cd.yml` L825–L864 |
| Reverting a bad release | Every deployment references an immutable digest, so redeploying a prior digest reproduces the previous runtime exactly | `cd.yml` L213–L240, L484–L492 |
| Corrupted or vulnerable image | Trivy scan gates promotion; provenance and SBOM attestations support forensic review | `cd.yml` L346–L436 |
| Loss of local environment | Full rebuild from `Dockerfile` plus `requirements*.txt`; `.env.example` documents every variable | `infrastructure/docker/`, `src/backend/.env.example` |

Recovery objectives, expressed in the terms this architecture actually supports: **RPO is not applicable** — no state is retained, so no data can be lost; **RTO is bounded by process start plus probe convergence** — the production container allows a 15 s start period before probing, while the CD pipeline budgets 75 s of warm-up before its first production health check.

Four gaps should be recorded rather than papered over. `rollback_required` is surfaced as a job output and a failed job, not as an automated redeploy of the previous digest — reversion is a manual action. No infrastructure-as-code defines the Azure Web Apps targets, so the hosting environment itself is not reproducible from this repository. There is no multi-region, multi-replica, or load-balancer configuration (`replicas: 1`), so availability is bounded by a single instance per environment. And there is no alerting, on-call routing, or incident runbook: health signals gate deployments and trigger restarts, but nothing notifies a human. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` corroborates that container-registry credentials and production deployment remain open human tasks, so the recovery path described here is structurally complete but not yet exercised end to end.
