## 6.2 Database Design

### 6.2.1 Applicability Determination

**Database Design is not applicable to this system.** The repository contains no database, no persistence tier, no object-relational mapping layer, no migration tooling, no cache server, and no application code path that writes durable state of any kind. There are therefore no entities to relate, no tables or collections to model, no indexes or constraints to declare, no partitions to plan, no replicas to configure, and no backups to schedule.

This sub-section records that determination and the evidence establishing it. Sub-sections 6.2.2 through 6.2.5 then walk each topic the section prompt enumerates — schema design, data management, compliance, and performance optimisation — and state for each whether an observable analogue exists elsewhere in the stack or whether the concern is genuinely vacuous. Nothing in this section describes a capability the repository does not contain.

Related sections: `3.5 Databases & Storage` establishes the same verdict from the technology-stack perspective and owns the container storage topology and generated-artifact inventory; `1.3 Scope` lists persistence, ORM/migrations, and caching layers among the explicit exclusions; `5.3 Technical Decisions` records the governing decision (ADR-004, no persistence tier); `6.1 Core Services Architecture` owns the redundancy, failover, and recovery-objective analysis referenced here rather than repeated.

#### 6.2.1.1 Why the Verdict Follows from the System's Purpose

The system is an educational Flask service whose entire externally observable behaviour is two anonymous `GET` endpoints that synthesise their responses from literals and clock reads. `src/backend/app.py` L367 registers `GET /hello`, which returns the constant string `Hello world` alongside a timestamp and a status literal; L426 registers `GET /health`, which returns a status literal, a timestamp, `time.time()` as uptime, the version `1.0.0`, and two values read back out of `app.config`. Neither handler accepts a request body, neither consults an external system, and no third route exists.

Because every response field is either a compile-time constant, a clock read, or a configuration read, there is no input to record and no derived state to keep. Statelessness is not merely a by-product of the small feature set — it is an asserted property. `src/backend/tests/test_app.py` L476 defines `TestFlaskStatelessOperation`; its `test_stateless_operation_multiple_requests` (L482) issues five sequential requests and asserts that all five timestamps are distinct while all five messages are identical, and `test_no_session_persistence` (L507) asserts that no response carries a `Set-Cookie` header containing `session`. A store would have to be introduced *against* these tests, not alongside them.

#### 6.2.1.2 Evidence of Absence — Dependency Manifests

Two manifests define everything the application may import. Neither declares a database driver, ORM, migration tool, cache client, or object-storage SDK.

| Manifest | Declared Packages | Persistence-Related Declarations |
|---|---|---|
| `requirements.txt` (production runtime) | `Flask>=3.1.1`, `python-dotenv>=1.0.1`, `Flask-CORS>=4.0.0`, `gunicorn>=21.2.0`, `wheel>=0.42.0` | None |
| `src/backend/requirements.txt` (combined runtime + tooling) | 42 declarations spanning Flask, pytest, coverage, benchmarking, linting, typing, and security scanners | None |
| `requirements-dev.txt` | 44 tooling declarations; the words "security database" and "OSV database" appear only as descriptions of the vulnerability corpora consulted by `safety` and `pip-audit` | None |
| `pyproject.toml` `[project.dependencies]` and extras | Mirrors the runtime set plus `dev`, `security`, `docs`, and `performance` extras | None |

A per-technology-class search across every `*.py`, `*.txt`, `*.toml`, `*.ini`, `*.yml`, `*.cfg`, `*.example`, and the `Dockerfile` returns zero matches for `flask_sqlalchemy`, `psycopg`, `asyncpg`, `mysqlclient`, `PyMySQL`, `sqlite3`, `pymongo`, `motor`, `pymemcache`, `Flask-Caching`, `alembic`, `Flask-Migrate`, `boto3`, `azure-storage-blob`, `google-cloud-storage`, `minio`, `cassandra`, `influxdb`, `duckdb`, `peewee`, `tortoise`, and `pony`.

#### 6.2.1.3 Evidence of Absence — Code and Filesystem

| Evidence Class | Observation |
|---|---|
| Complete application import set | `src/backend/app.py` L31-L42 imports only `os`, `logging`, `time`, `datetime`, `typing`, `functools.wraps`, `flask` (`Flask`, `request`, `jsonify`, `Response`), `flask_cors.CORS`, and `dotenv.load_dotenv`; `src/backend/wsgi.py` L25-L49 adds only `sys`, `signal`, `threading`, `psutil`, and `app.create_app`. No client library of any kind is importable. |
| Session and application-context globals | `flask.session` and `flask.g` are never imported, so no server-side session or context store can be engaged. The only session-related lines in the repository are the `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME` values at `app.py` L178 (3600 s) and L190 (86400 s), which configure a cookie policy that no code exercises. |
| Application file I/O | No `open(...)`, `pathlib.Path`, `tempfile`, `shelve`, `pickle`, `json.dump`, or `os.makedirs` call exists in either runtime module. The only `with open(...)` occurrences in the repository are `.github/workflows/ci.yml` L303 and L321, which read security-scan JSON reports inside an inline CI script. |
| Schema and data artifacts | The repository contains no `.sql`, `.ddl`, `.db`, `.sqlite`, `.csv`, `.parquet`, or `.ndjson` file. The complete file census is 10 Markdown, 4 Python, 3 YAML, 3 text, 2 INI, 1 TOML, 1 Dockerfile, 1 `.dockerignore`, 1 `.env.example`, 2 `.gitignore`, and 1 `.flake8`. |
| Persistence-shaped directories | `migrations/`, `models/`, `db/`, `data/`, `config/`, and Flask's `instance/` folder do not exist at the repository root or under `src/backend`. The entire `src/` tree is `src/backend/` plus `src/backend/tests/`. |
| Container mount points | `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` contains no `VOLUME` instruction, so the image declares no persistent mount point. The production stage instead sets sources to mode 444 (L213) and the Compose production service mounts a read-only root filesystem (`docker-compose.yml` L325). |
| Orchestration services | `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` defines exactly three services — `flask-tutorial-dev` (L34), `flask-tutorial-prod` (L175), and the `alpine:3.19` helper `flask-network-setup` (L346). No database, cache, or broker container is defined. |
| CI/CD data steps | Neither `.github/workflows/ci.yml` nor `cd.yml` declares a `services:` block instantiating a datastore, and neither contains a migration, seed, fixture-load, or schema-validation step. |

#### 6.2.1.4 Non-Implementation References That Superficially Resemble Database Configuration

Six locations mention database vocabulary. Every one is illustrative, anticipatory, or unrelated; none is read by any code path or acted on by any tool. Recording them here prevents a future reader from mistaking them for evidence of a persistence tier.

| Location | Content | Why It Is Not Persistence |
|---|---|---|
| `src/backend/.env.example` L172-L176 | Commented block headed "Database Configuration Example (not used in tutorial)" containing `DATABASE_URL`, `DATABASE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=10`, `DATABASE_SSL_MODE=prefer`, and `SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI` | Entirely commented out; the surrounding "Educational Configuration Examples" preamble states these patterns are "not required for the basic tutorial application". No code reads any of these names. |
| `src/backend/.env.example` L190-L194 | Commented block headed "Redis Configuration Example (not used in tutorial)" containing `REDIS_URL`, `REDIS_PASSWORD`, `REDIS_DB=0`, and `CELERY_BROKER_URL` | Same commented, explicitly-disclaimed block. No cache or broker client is installed. |
| `src/backend/wsgi.py` L277-L281 | Comment list inside `perform_graceful_shutdown` naming "Database connection cleanup", "Cache invalidation", "Background task termination", and "File handle closure" as procedures that "can be added here" | These are the four cleanup actions that *would* be required if such resources existed. Their presence as comments is direct evidence that the shutdown path drains nothing, because there is nothing to drain. |
| `.flake8` L63, L155-L157 | `migrations` listed in `exclude`; per-file ignore rules for `migrations/*.py` and `alembic/*.py` | Anticipatory lint configuration for directories that do not exist. The same block also excludes `instance` and `.instance`, which likewise do not exist. |
| `infrastructure/docker/.dockerignore` L481-L485 | Excludes `database.yml`, `config/database.yml`, `config/application.yml`, `config/production.py`, `config/staging.py` under a "defence-in-depth" secret-hygiene heading | Generic build-context hygiene patterns copied from broader conventions; none of the named files exists in the repository. |
| `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` L439-L449 | Named volume `flask_shared_data` (Docker name `flask-tutorial-shared`, label `tutorial.purpose=educational-persistence`, bind device `${PWD}/data`) | Declared in the `volumes:` block and referenced by **no service** — the identifier occurs exactly once in the file. Its bind target `${PWD}/data` does not exist. It is an inert declaration, not a data volume in use. |
| `src/backend/README.md` L596, L847-L871, L937 | "Database fixtures (if implemented in future)"; a "Next Steps → Adding Database Integration" learning path; Flask-Migrate and Flask-Caching in an "Advanced Flask Concepts" list | Forward-looking curriculum prose. The `tests/conftest.py` that L596 describes does not exist — `src/backend/tests/` contains only `test_app.py` and `test_wsgi.py`. |

#### 6.2.1.5 What Holds State Instead

Three tiers of state exist, and none of them is durable. The first lives for one request, the second for the life of the process, and the third — the persistent domain — is empty.

| State Tier | Contents | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| Request-scoped | `request.start_time` (`app.py` L310) and `request.id` = `req_<epoch-ms>` (L316); the response `dict` built inside the handler | Destroyed at request teardown; the response `dict` becomes unreachable once `jsonify` has serialised it |
| Process-lifetime, non-business | `app.config` populated once by `create_app`; `wsgi.py` L74-L76 globals `flask_app`, `shutdown_event` (a `threading.Event`), and `signal_received`; the module-level `logger`; the unused `FLASK_CONFIGS` mapping (`app.py` L641-L658) | Discarded when the worker process exits; never serialised or shared between workers |
| Persistent | Nothing. No table, collection, key space, file, or volume receives application data | Not applicable |

**Diagram 6.2.1-A — Persistence-domain map: the two live state tiers, the write paths that do not exist, and the point at which every data object becomes unreachable.**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Req["Inbound HTTP request<br/>GET /hello or GET /health"]

    subgraph Transient["Request-scoped state - one request only"]
        Ctx["request.start_time and request.id<br/>app.py L310 and L316"]
        Payload["Response dict built in the handler<br/>message, timestamp, status"]
        Ser["jsonify serialises the dict<br/>reference then dropped"]
    end

    subgraph Process["Process-lifetime state - no business data"]
        Cfg["app.config, populated once by create_app"]
        Glob["wsgi.py globals: flask_app,<br/>shutdown_event, signal_received"]
        Logs["logging handlers to stdout and stderr"]
    end

    subgraph Absent["Persistent domain - empty"]
        NoRel["No relational store<br/>no driver, no ORM, no DDL"]
        NoDoc["No document or key-value store<br/>no cache server, no session store"]
        NoFile["No application file writes<br/>no open call in app.py or wsgi.py"]
    end

    Resp["HTTP response written to the client"]
    Reclaim["Objects unreachable after the response<br/>reclaimed by the interpreter"]

    Req --> Ctx --> Payload --> Ser --> Resp
    Ser --> Reclaim
    Cfg -.->|"read only"| Payload
    Glob -.->|"lifecycle control only"| Ser
    Ctx --> Logs
    Payload -.->|"no write path exists"| NoRel
    Payload -.->|"no write path exists"| NoDoc
    Payload -.->|"no write path exists"| NoFile
```

#### 6.2.1.6 Conditions That Would Change This Determination

The verdict is a property of the current codebase rather than a permanent judgement. Introducing any of the following would create genuine database-design concerns: a relational or document store (entities, keys, indexes, migrations, connection pooling, and a readiness dependency for `/health`); a cache server (coherency across replicas and an invalidation policy); a mutating endpoint (write paths, transactions, and idempotency); or persisted request logs or audit records (retention, archival, and privacy obligations). `6.1 Core Services Architecture` records the same trigger set from the services perspective, noting that a persistence or cache tier "would create readiness dependencies for `/health` and cache-coherency concerns across replicas".

`src/backend/README.md` documents the intended progression explicitly, which is the closest the repository comes to a target-state data architecture. It is curriculum guidance, not a commitment, and no artifact in the repository implements any row of it.

| Documented Next Step (README.md L849-L857) | Technology Named | Design Concern It Would Introduce |
|---|---|---|
| Relational integration | SQLAlchemy with PostgreSQL | Entity modelling, DDL, indexes, constraints, transactions |
| Flask-native ORM binding | Flask-SQLAlchemy | Application-factory wiring, per-request session scope, connection pooling |
| Document store integration | MongoDB with PyMongo | Collection and document modelling, sharding, secondary indexes |
| Cache tier | Redis | Cache keys, TTLs, invalidation, and session storage |
| Schema evolution | Alembic (and Flask-Migrate, README L937) | Versioned migrations, forward/backward compatibility, deployment ordering |

The illustrative snippet at `src/backend/README.md` L860-L871 shows the shape such a change would take — an extension object instantiated at module scope and bound to the application inside the factory:

```python
db = SQLAlchemy()
app.config['SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI'] = 'postgresql://user:pass@localhost/db'
db.init_app(app)
```

Adopting it would require adding the driver and ORM to both `requirements.txt` manifests, creating the absent `migrations/` directory that `.flake8` already anticipates, wiring a connection lifecycle into `create_app`, and implementing the "Database connection cleanup" step that `wsgi.py` L278 currently carries only as a comment.


### 6.2.2 Schema Design

**No schema exists.** There is no DDL, no ORM model class, no document schema, no key-space convention, and no schema artifact of any kind in the repository. This sub-section therefore documents, for each schema-design topic the section prompt enumerates, the verified absence and — where one exists — the structure or mechanism that occupies the position a schema element would otherwise hold.

#### 6.2.2.1 Entity Relationships

**Not applicable — there are no entities.** An entity model requires identity, attributes, and lifecycle; nothing in this system has any of the three. The closest analogue to a data model is the set of JSON response contracts constructed inline by the route and error handlers, and those contracts have four properties that disqualify them from being entities:

| Property of a Persisted Entity | Status in This System |
|---|---|
| Stable identity (primary key or document `_id`) | Absent. No handler produces or consumes an identifier for a business object. `request.id` (`app.py` L316) identifies a *request*, is derived from `int(time.time() * 1000)`, and is never stored or referenced again after the response headers are written. |
| Referential association to another entity | Absent. No payload field points at another payload, and the six response structures share no field that could act as a join key. |
| Independent lifecycle (create, read, update, delete) | Absent. Every structure is created at handler entry and unreachable after `jsonify` returns. Only two `GET` routes exist, so no create, update, or delete operation is expressible. |
| Cardinality | Absent. Exactly one instance of one structure exists per in-flight request; there is no collection, set, or sequence anywhere in the code. |

#### 6.2.2.2 Data Models and Structures

Six response structures exist in total. Each is a Python `dict` literal built inside a function body and handed directly to `jsonify()`. The tables below are the complete field-level inventory of every data structure the system produces.

**Success payloads.**

| Structure and Location | Field | Type and Derivation |
|---|---|---|
| `/hello` 200 — `app.py` L391-L395 | `message` | `str`, the literal `Hello world` assigned at L389 |
| | `timestamp` | `str`, `datetime.now().isoformat()` |
| | `status` | `str`, the literal `success` |
| `/health` 200 — `app.py` L437-L444 | `status` | `str`, the literal `healthy` |
| | `timestamp` | `str`, `datetime.now().isoformat()` |
| | `uptime` | `float`, the raw `time.time()` epoch value (not an elapsed interval) |
| | `version` | `str`, the hard-coded literal `1.0.0` |
| | `environment` | `str`, `app.config.get('ENV', 'unknown')` |
| | `debug` | `bool`, `app.config.get('DEBUG', False)` |

**Error payloads.** All four share a `status`/`error`/`message`/`timestamp` core; the variable fields are listed per handler.

| Handler and Location | Additional Fields | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 404 — `app.py` L501-L508 | `path`, `method` | Echoes the requested path and method; `status` is the integer `404` |
| 405 — `app.py` L535-L543 | `path`, `method`, `allowed_methods` | `allowed_methods` is `getattr(error, 'valid_methods', [])`; the same list populates the `Allow` header |
| 500 — `app.py` L586-L592 | `request_id` | `getattr(request, 'id', 'unknown')`; the exception text is logged server-side but never placed in the payload |
| Generic `Exception` — `app.py` L623-L628 | None | Fixed `Unexpected Error` / `An unexpected error occurred` envelope |
| Route-local guards — `app.py` L418-L423, L457-L462 | `error` (503 branch only) | `/hello` returns a 500 `status: error` envelope; `/health` returns a 503 `status: unhealthy` envelope carrying `str(e)` |

Two structural properties are worth recording because they would matter to any future schema. First, `JSON_SORT_KEYS` is set to `False` in the base configuration (`app.py` L159-L166), so serialisation preserves the insertion order of each literal — field order is a stable part of the response contract rather than alphabetical. Second, `status` is a `str` in the two success payloads and the two route-local guards, but an `int` in the four registered error handlers, so the field is not type-uniform across the response surface.

**Diagram 6.2.2-A — Entity-relationship diagram of the logical data structures. These are transient JSON contracts, not persisted entities: no box corresponds to a table or collection, no attribute is a key, and there are deliberately no relationship lines because no association exists between any two structures.**

```mermaid
erDiagram
    HELLO_RESPONSE {
        string message "literal Hello world"
        string timestamp "ISO-8601, per request"
        string status "literal success"
    }
    HEALTH_RESPONSE {
        string status "literal healthy"
        string timestamp "ISO-8601, per request"
        float uptime "raw time.time epoch value"
        string version "literal 1.0.0"
        string environment "read from app.config ENV"
        boolean debug "read from app.config DEBUG"
    }
    ERROR_ENVELOPE_404 {
        int status "404"
        string error "Not Found"
        string message "static text"
        string path "echoed request path"
        string method "echoed request method"
        string timestamp "ISO-8601, per request"
    }
    ERROR_ENVELOPE_405 {
        int status "405"
        string error "Method Not Allowed"
        string path "echoed request path"
        string method "echoed request method"
        string allowed_methods "list from error.valid_methods"
        string timestamp "ISO-8601, per request"
    }
    ERROR_ENVELOPE_500 {
        int status "500"
        string error "Internal Server Error"
        string message "generic, internals suppressed"
        string request_id "req_ plus epoch milliseconds"
        string timestamp "ISO-8601, per request"
    }
    REQUEST_CONTEXT {
        float start_time "set by before_request"
        string id "req_ plus epoch milliseconds"
    }
```

`REQUEST_CONTEXT` is included because it is the only structure with a lifetime longer than a single function call — it is attached to Flask's request proxy at `app.py` L310 and L316 and consumed by `after_request` at L339-L350 to emit `X-Response-Time` and `X-Request-ID`. It is destroyed at request teardown and never leaves the process except as those two header values.

#### 6.2.2.3 Indexes and Constraints

**No database indexes, primary keys, unique keys, foreign keys, check constraints, or not-null constraints exist**, because no schema exists to carry them. The table below is the complete constraint inventory of the system as implemented — every one is an application-layer or process-layer guard rather than a storage constraint.

| Constraint | Enforcement Point | Behaviour on Violation |
|---|---|---|
| Request body ≤ 16 MB (`MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 16 * 1024 * 1024`) | `app.py` L159-L166, applied by Werkzeug | Request rejected before reaching a handler; the only storage-adjacent resource limit in the application |
| Method allow-list per route (`methods=['GET']`) | `app.py` L367, L426 | Routed to the 405 handler, which returns the `allowed_methods` list and an `Allow` header |
| Path must match a registered rule | Flask URL map — only two rules exist | Routed to the 404 handler, which echoes `path` and `method` |
| JSON content type on `POST`/`PUT` with a body | `app.py` L318-L321 | **Advisory only** — a warning is logged and processing continues; the request is not rejected |
| `PORT` must parse as an integer in 1-65535 | `wsgi.py` L299-L331 | `ValueError` chained and re-raised, aborting startup; ports below 1024 log a privileged-range warning |
| Field order preserved in serialisation | `JSON_SORT_KEYS: False`, `app.py` L159-L166 | Not a validation rule; guarantees deterministic field ordering in every response |
| CORS origin allow-list | `app.py` L259-L288 — `http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:8000`, `supports_credentials: False` | Browser-enforced rejection for any other origin |

An index exists to accelerate selective retrieval from a large collection. Both endpoints return a fixed structure in constant time with no lookup, filter, sort, join, or scan of any kind, so there is no access pattern an index could serve and no cardinality to reason about. The same reasoning voids every index-adjacent concern: no covering indexes, no composite keys, no partial or expression indexes, no full-text or vector indexes, and no statistics or query-plan artifacts.

#### 6.2.2.4 Partitioning Approach

**Not applicable.** Partitioning distributes rows or documents across physical units according to a partition key; there is no dataset, no row count, no growth curve, and no key. The repository contains no partition, shard, or bucket declaration, and no configuration surface where one could be expressed — the seven documented environment variables (`PORT`, `HOST`, `FLASK_ENV`, `FLASK_DEBUG`, `LOG_LEVEL`, `WORKERS`, `SECRET_KEY`) contain no data-placement setting.

The only division of work in the system is at the process level: `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` L216 configures four Gunicorn `sync` workers, and the kernel distributes accepted connections among them from a single listening socket. That is request-level parallelism over identical, stateless workers — every worker can serve every request because none owns any data — and it is documented in `6.1 Core Services Architecture` rather than repeated here.

#### 6.2.2.5 Replication Configuration

**No data replication exists**, and none is possible: replication copies state between nodes, and this system holds no state to copy. There is no primary/replica topology, no streaming or logical replication slot, no read replica, no quorum or consensus configuration, and no conflict-resolution policy anywhere in the repository. `6.1 Core Services Architecture` records the corresponding search result — probes for backup and replication tooling such as `pg_dump`, snapshot scripts, and any `replica` declaration beyond `replicas: 1` return nothing operational.

Two forms of copying *do* exist, and neither is data replication. They are recorded here so the distinction is unambiguous.

| Copying Mechanism | What Is Copied | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| Runtime instance count | Nothing — one container instance per environment | `docker-compose.yml` L289 declares `replicas: 1`, the only replication keyword in the repository |
| Worker fan-out within an instance | The preloaded interpreter image, shared copy-on-write across 4 forked workers | `Dockerfile` L216 (`--workers=4 --preload`) |
| Container image distribution | The immutable, digest-addressed image, built for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` multi-architecture build and push to `ghcr.io` |
| Dependency cache volumes | Virtualenv and pip content only; the production service mounts both `read_only: true` | `docker-compose.yml` L234-L245 |

Statelessness is what makes the single-instance model safe to multiply if it ever needs to be: because no worker or instance owns data, adding a second instance would require no replication, no cache-coherency protocol, and no sticky routing. `6.1 Core Services Architecture` documents that horizontal scaling is architecturally unobstructed but operationally unconfigured, and notes the one caveat that would matter — `request.id` is millisecond-derived with no instance discriminator, so correlation identifiers are not unique across concurrent workers or replicas.

**Diagram 6.2.2-B — Replication architecture: the artifact-level and process-level copying that exists, contrasted with the data-replication topology that does not.**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Source["Git repository<br/>two runtime modules plus manifests"]

    subgraph Build["Artifact replication - the only durable copying"]
        Img["Container image built once<br/>linux/amd64 and linux/arm64"]
        Reg["ghcr.io registry<br/>digest-addressed and immutable"]
        Attest["Provenance and SBOM attestations<br/>published with the image"]
    end

    subgraph Runtime["Runtime fan-out - identical stateless copies"]
        Inst["One container instance per environment<br/>docker-compose.yml replicas: 1"]
        Arb["Gunicorn arbiter, preload<br/>single listening socket"]
        W1["sync worker 1"]
        W2["sync worker 2"]
        W3["sync worker 3"]
        W4["sync worker 4"]
    end

    subgraph NoData["Data replication topology - does not exist"]
        NoPrimary["No primary node<br/>no write-ahead log, no replication slot"]
        NoReplica["No read replica<br/>no standby, no follower"]
        NoQuorum["No quorum, consensus<br/>or conflict resolution policy"]
    end

    Source --> Img --> Reg --> Attest
    Reg -->|"deployed by digest"| Inst
    Inst --> Arb
    Arb -->|"copy-on-write fork"| W1
    Arb --> W2
    Arb --> W3
    Arb --> W4
    W1 -.->|"no state to replicate"| NoPrimary
    W2 -.->|"no state to replicate"| NoReplica
    W3 -.->|"no state to replicate"| NoQuorum
```

#### 6.2.2.6 Backup Architecture

**No data backup exists or is required.** There is no dump, snapshot, export, point-in-time-recovery, or restore procedure in the repository, because there is no data whose loss would be meaningful. `6.1 Core Services Architecture` states the consequence in recovery terms: **RPO is not applicable — no state is retained, so no data can be lost** — and notes that nothing application-generated is written to a volume, so no volume is a backup candidate.

What is durable, and therefore recoverable, is the *artifact* set rather than any dataset.

| Recoverable Asset | Durability Mechanism | Restore Operation |
|---|---|---|
| Application source | Git history; the entire runtime is two Python modules | Checkout a commit |
| Runtime image | Digest-addressed, immutable images in `ghcr.io`, with provenance and SBOM attestations | Redeploy a prior digest |
| Dependency set | `requirements.txt`, `src/backend/requirements.txt`, `requirements-dev.txt`, and the `pyproject.toml` extras | Rebuild the virtualenv or image |
| Runtime configuration | `src/backend/.env.example` documents all seven variables with defaults and validation notes; every tunable also has an in-code default | Recreate `.env` from the template |
| Local topology | `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` and `Dockerfile` | `docker compose up` |
| Verification and audit reports | Coverage, test, benchmark, and security-scan artifacts uploaded by CI/CD with 30-day and 90-day retention | Download the workflow artifact |

The production runtime is deliberately non-durable, which is the design property that makes the absence of backups coherent rather than negligent: `docker-compose.yml` L325-L329 mounts a read-only root filesystem whose only writable space is two 10 MB `tmpfs` mounts at `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, and `Dockerfile` L213 sets the production sources to mode 444. A container cannot accumulate state that would need backing up. The complete inventory of files the system does write — coverage, test, benchmark, log, and security-scan outputs, all reproducible and all git-ignored — is catalogued in `3.5 Databases & Storage` and is not repeated here.


### 6.2.3 Data Management

Data management in the conventional sense — moving a schema forward, versioning stored records, ageing data into an archive tier, and mediating reads and writes through a data-access layer — has no subject in this system. What follows documents each topic against what the repository actually implements, and records the mechanisms that occupy the equivalent position where one exists.

#### 6.2.3.1 Migration Procedures

**No migration procedure exists**, because there is no schema to migrate. The verified absences are: no `alembic` or `Flask-Migrate` declaration in any manifest; no `migrations/` or `alembic/` directory; no `alembic.ini`, revision script, or version table; and no migration, seed, or fixture step in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` or `cd.yml`.

`.flake8` anticipates a migration layer that was never built — L63 lists `migrations` in the `exclude` set and L155-L157 define per-file ignore rules for `migrations/*.py` and `alembic/*.py`. Both targets are absent, so these rules never match a file. `src/backend/README.md` L857 names "Database Migration Strategies: Alembic for schema management and version control" as a future learning step, and L937 lists Flask-Migrate under advanced extensions.

Change management that *does* operate in this repository targets code, configuration, and images rather than data:

| Change Class | Propagation Mechanism | Ordering Guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Application code | Commit → CI quality gate → image build → digest-pinned deployment to staging, then production | Production deploys only after staging reports success |
| Dependency set | Edit `requirements.txt` / `src/backend/requirements.txt`; the image rebuild resolves them | Rebuild is the only propagation path; no runtime dependency injection |
| Runtime configuration | Environment variables documented in `src/backend/.env.example`; every tunable has an in-code default | Read once at process start by `load_dotenv()` and `os.getenv` |
| Container runtime | Rebuild from `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile`; new digest published to `ghcr.io` | Immutable digests make any prior runtime redeployable |

Because no deployment step mutates persistent state, there is no forward/backward compatibility window, no expand-contract sequencing, no online-migration concern, and no rollback-safety analysis to perform. This is the direct operational benefit of the absent persistence tier, and it is why the rollback primitive documented in `6.1 Core Services Architecture` — redeploying a prior image digest — is unconditionally safe.

#### 6.2.3.2 Versioning Strategy

**No data or schema versioning exists.** No payload carries a schema version, no field records a record version or revision, no optimistic-concurrency token (`etag`, `version`, `updated_at`) is produced, and there is no `Last-Modified` or `ETag` header on either endpoint. Four version identifiers do exist, all of them describing the *software*:

| Version Identifier | Value and Location | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Package version | `1.0.0` in `pyproject.toml` `[project]` | Distribution metadata |
| API version header | `X-API-Version: 1.0`, set on `/hello` responses (`app.py` L404) | Static header; no versioned URL prefix exists |
| Reported service version | `version: '1.0.0'` in the `/health` payload (`app.py` L441) | Hard-coded literal, independent of the package metadata |
| Image identity | Digest-addressed, immutable tags in `ghcr.io` published by `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | The only version identifier that is cryptographically bound to content |

Two consequences follow. First, because the API version is a static header rather than a URL segment, a breaking change to either response contract would be invisible to clients that do not inspect headers — there is no negotiation mechanism, and `1.3 Scope` records the absence of an API versioning surface as an explicit exclusion. Second, the package version and the `/health` literal are maintained independently, so they can drift; only the image digest is guaranteed to identify exactly what is running.

#### 6.2.3.3 Archival Policies

**No archival policy exists for application data**, because no application data is retained past the response that produced it. There is no cold-storage tier, no time-based rollover, no tiered-storage configuration, and no export job.

Retention policy in this repository applies exclusively to CI/CD verification artifacts:

| Artifact Class | Retention | Declaration |
|---|---|---|
| Coverage and test-result reports | 30 days | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` L114, L124 |
| Security scan reports (Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, Scorecard SARIF) | 90 days | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` L206 |
| CD scan results and deployment artifacts | 30 days and 90 days | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L429, L1002 |
| Documented default | `artifact_retention_days = 30` | `pyproject.toml` L475 |
| Container images | No expiry policy declared in the repository | `ghcr.io` registry defaults apply |

Application log output is written to stdout and stderr only; no log file, rotation policy, shipper, or sink is configured anywhere in the repository, so log retention is entirely a property of whatever collects the container's streams — and no such collector is configured here. The complete inventory of generated files and their retention is catalogued in `3.5 Databases & Storage`.

#### 6.2.3.4 Data Storage and Retrieval Mechanisms

There is no storage mechanism and no retrieval mechanism. Every response is *constructed*, never *fetched*. The complete data path for a request is four in-process steps with no I/O other than the socket write and the log write:

| Step | Operation | Location |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Context attachment | `before_request` sets `request.start_time` and `request.id` on the request proxy | `app.py` L310, L316 |
| 2. Construction | The handler builds a `dict` from literals, `datetime.now()`, `time.time()`, and `app.config` reads | `app.py` L391-L395, L437-L444 |
| 3. Serialisation | `jsonify()` converts the `dict` to a JSON body with insertion order preserved | `app.py` L397, L446 |
| 4. Header decoration and discard | `after_request` computes elapsed time, sets `X-Response-Time` and `X-Request-ID`; the security hook adds six headers and removes `Server`; all objects then become unreachable | `app.py` L326-L352, L215-L256 |

There is consequently no data-access layer to document: no repository, DAO, mapper, query builder, unit of work, or connection abstraction exists in either runtime module. No read is ever served from a store, and no write is ever attempted — which is why the absence of transactions, isolation levels, locking, and idempotency keys is a non-issue rather than a gap.

**Diagram 6.2.3-A — Data flow for a single request, showing every point at which data is created, transformed, exposed, and discarded, and the three write paths that do not exist.**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Client["HTTP client"]
    Arrive["Request arrives at a Gunicorn sync worker<br/>one request per worker at a time"]

    subgraph Create["Data creation - in-process, per request"]
        Hook["before_request<br/>start_time and req id assigned"]
        Sources["Value sources: string literals,<br/>datetime.now, time.time, app.config reads"]
        Dict["Response dict assembled in the handler"]
    end

    subgraph Transform["Transformation and exposure"]
        Json["jsonify serialises the dict<br/>key order preserved"]
        Timing["after_request adds X-Response-Time<br/>and X-Request-ID"]
        SecHdr["Security hook adds six headers<br/>and removes Server"]
    end

    subgraph Sinks["Where data actually goes"]
        Wire["HTTP response body and headers<br/>to the client"]
        Stdout["Log lines to stdout and stderr<br/>method, path, status, elapsed ms"]
    end

    subgraph NoWrite["Write paths that do not exist"]
        NoDB["No insert, update or delete<br/>no driver, no ORM, no connection"]
        NoCache["No cache write<br/>no Redis, no Flask-Caching"]
        NoDisk["No file or volume write<br/>read-only root filesystem in production"]
    end

    Gone["Request context torn down<br/>dict unreachable, memory reclaimed"]

    Client --> Arrive --> Hook
    Sources --> Dict
    Hook --> Dict --> Json --> Timing --> SecHdr --> Wire --> Client
    Hook --> Stdout
    Timing --> Stdout
    Dict -.->|"no code path"| NoDB
    Dict -.->|"no code path"| NoCache
    Dict -.->|"no code path"| NoDisk
    Wire --> Gone
```

#### 6.2.3.5 Caching Policies

**There is no cache tier.** No cache server, client library, or Flask caching extension is installed, and no memoisation, `lru_cache`, or module-level result store exists in either runtime module. `1.3 Scope` lists caching layers among the explicit exclusions.

Three cache-related *policies* are nevertheless expressed, all at the HTTP layer, and each has a consequence worth stating:

| Policy | Declaration | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `/health` must never be cached | `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate` set at `app.py` L449 | Probes and deployment gates always observe current process state; the response cannot be served stale by an intermediary |
| CORS preflight results may be cached for 24 hours | `max_age: 86400` in the Flask-CORS configuration (`app.py` L275) | Reduces `OPTIONS` traffic, but a change to the origin allow-list can take up to a day to propagate to a browser that has cached the preflight |
| Static files may be cached for one year | `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT: 31536000` in the production WSGI profile (`wsgi.py` L171) | **Inert** — the repository contains no `static/` directory and no `send_file` call, so no response is ever governed by this setting |

Notably, `/hello` sets no `Cache-Control` header at all, so its cacheability is left to intermediary defaults even though its payload contains a per-request `timestamp` that makes every response byte-different. Because the handler is a constant-time construction with no lookup behind it, a cache would save no work — which is why the absence of a cache tier is a correct design choice here rather than an omission. The build-time and dependency caches that do exist (pip, Docker layer, virtualenv volumes) accelerate the toolchain, never a request, and are catalogued in `3.5 Databases & Storage`.


### 6.2.4 Compliance Considerations

Data-compliance obligations attach to stored data. Because this system stores nothing, the compliance posture is determined by what it *never collects* rather than by controls applied to a repository of records. This sub-section documents each compliance topic against verified behaviour, including the controls that do exist at the container and process layers and the gaps that would become material the moment data were introduced.

#### 6.2.4.1 Data Retention Rules

**No data-retention rule exists for application data, and none is needed.** Every value the system produces is discarded when the response is written; the retention period for application data is therefore the duration of a single request. A repository-wide scan of `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `pyproject.toml`, `pytest.ini`, and both `README.md` files for retention, archival, or data-governance policy language returns exactly one hit — `pyproject.toml` L475 `artifact_retention_days = 30` — which governs CI artifacts, not data.

| Retained Item | Retention Period | Governing Declaration |
|---|---|---|
| Application data | None — no data is retained beyond the response | No storage mechanism exists |
| Coverage and test artifacts | 30 days | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` L114, L124 |
| Security scan reports | 90 days | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` L206; `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L1002 |
| CD deployment artifacts | 30 days | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L429 |
| Container logs | Undefined in-repository — streams go to stdout/stderr with no rotation, shipper, or sink configured | `app.py` L56-L61 (`logging.basicConfig`) |
| Container images | No expiry policy declared; registry defaults apply | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` publishes to `ghcr.io` |

#### 6.2.4.2 Backup and Fault Tolerance Policies

**No backup policy exists because there is no recoverable dataset**, and the fault-tolerance posture is replace-and-restart rather than restore-from-backup. `6.1 Core Services Architecture` establishes the recovery framing this section inherits: RPO is not applicable since no state is retained, RTO is process start plus probe convergence, and no volume is a backup candidate because nothing application-generated is written to one.

| Policy Dimension | Implemented Position | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Data backup | None — no dump, snapshot, export, or PITR capability | No storage tier exists |
| Recovery point objective | Not applicable — no data can be lost | Stateless by construction; `TestFlaskStatelessOperation` asserts it |
| State loss on restart | Total and inconsequential — only `request.*` context, `app.config`, and the `wsgi.py` lifecycle globals are lost, all rebuilt at startup | `wsgi.py` L74-L76; `app.py` L144-L211 |
| Shutdown integrity | `perform_graceful_shutdown` logs cleanup narration and samples memory; it flushes, checkpoints, and drains nothing, because there is nothing to flush | `wsgi.py` L258-L296; the four cleanup actions remain comments at L277-L281 |
| Immutability of the running instance | Read-only root filesystem with only two 10 MB `tmpfs` mounts; production sources at mode 444 | `docker-compose.yml` L325-L329; `Dockerfile` L213 |
| Instance redundancy | None — `replicas: 1`; no standby, slot, or multi-region target | `docker-compose.yml` L289 |
| Artifact durability | Digest-addressed immutable images with provenance and SBOM attestations; full source in Git | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` |

#### 6.2.4.3 Privacy Controls

The strongest privacy control in this system is structural: **no personal data is ever collected, so none can be stored, exposed, or subject-accessed.** This is verifiable rather than aspirational. A search of both runtime modules for `request.remote_addr`, `request.user_agent`, `request.headers`, `request.args`, `request.form`, `request.get_json`, `request.data`, and any `X-Forwarded` handling returns **zero matches** — the application never reads the client's IP address, user agent, headers, query string, form fields, or body.

| Privacy Dimension | Verified Position |
|---|---|
| Personal data collected | None. The only request-derived values the system ever touches are `request.method` and `request.path`, used in two log lines and echoed in the 404/405 payloads. |
| Personal data stored | None. No store exists, and no session is ever written — `flask.session` is not imported. |
| Personal data transmitted | None. Both payloads consist of literals, a timestamp, a clock read, and configuration values. |
| Identifiers generated | `request.id` = `req_<epoch-ms>` (`app.py` L316) — derived solely from the clock, containing no client-derived component, and never persisted. |
| Cross-origin credential exposure | Prevented: Flask-CORS is configured with `supports_credentials: False`, annotated in code as the "Secure default for stateless API" (`app.py` L275 block). |
| Data-subject rights machinery | Not applicable and absent — no export, deletion, rectification, or consent mechanism exists, because no subject data exists. |
| Encryption at rest | Not applicable — nothing is written to disk by the application. |
| Encryption in transit | Not terminated by the service: the container serves plain HTTP on port 3000 and `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME` is set to `https` (`app.py` production profile, `wsgi.py` L157-L160) for URL generation only. TLS is a property of the hosting front end. |

Information-disclosure controls limit what internal detail can reach a client even in failure. The 500 handler and the generic `Exception` handler log full tracebacks only when `DEBUG` is enabled (`app.py` L581-L582, L619-L620) and always return a generic message to the caller. Six security headers are applied to every response and the `Server` header is removed (`app.py` L223-L253): `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'`, and `X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies: none`. One exception to the suppression discipline is worth recording precisely: the `/health` failure branch places `str(e)` directly into the response body (`app.py` L459), making it the only path by which internal exception text can reach a client regardless of `DEBUG`.

#### 6.2.4.4 Audit Mechanisms

**There is no audit trail in the data-governance sense** — no audit table, append-only log store, change-data-capture stream, immutable ledger, or actor attribution exists. Attribution is impossible in any case, because the endpoints are anonymous and no client identity is captured.

The mechanisms that produce audit-adjacent evidence are these:

| Mechanism | Evidence Produced | Location |
|---|---|---|
| Request correlation | `request.id` assigned per request, returned as `X-Request-ID`, and embedded in the 500 payload as `request_id` | `app.py` L316, L348-L350, L590 |
| Request/response logging | One INFO line on arrival (`method`, `path`) and one on completion (`method`, `path`, status, elapsed ms) | `app.py` L313, L344-L346 |
| Error logging | WARNING for 404/405 with method and path; ERROR for 500 and unhandled exceptions, with type and message | `app.py` L479-L632 |
| Lifecycle logging | Startup deployment details, memory samples at startup/signal/uncaught-exception, and shutdown narration | `wsgi.py` L192-L296, L334-L373 |
| Security posture evidence | Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, OSSF Scorecard, and Trivy reports retained 30-90 days and surfaced through GitHub code scanning | `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `cd.yml` |
| Supply-chain provenance | Digest-addressed images with provenance and SBOM attestations; Git history for every source change | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` |

Three limitations should be read alongside that table, all consistent with `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns`. Logs are written to stdout and stderr with no aggregation, shipping, or tamper-evident storage, so nothing is durable once a container is replaced. `request.id` is millisecond-derived with no worker or instance discriminator, so two requests handled in the same millisecond by different workers receive the same identifier — the correlation key is not a reliable audit key. And because no client identity is recorded, the logs establish *what happened* but never *who did it*.

#### 6.2.4.5 Access Controls

**No data access controls exist because there is no data store to control.** There are no database users, roles, grants, schemas, row-level security policies, connection credentials, or credential rotation procedures, and no secret in the repository refers to a datastore. The commented `DATABASE_URL` and `REDIS_PASSWORD` examples in `src/backend/.env.example` L173 and L191 are the only credential-shaped strings related to persistence, and both are inert illustrations.

Access control that does exist operates at three layers, none of which is data-scoped:

| Layer | Control | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Application | **None.** Both endpoints are anonymous; `1.3 Scope` records `/hello` as "Authentication: None required", and no JWT, OAuth, session login, or authorisation decorator exists | `app.py` L367, L426 |
| Browser origin | CORS allow-list restricted to `http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:8000`, methods GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/OPTIONS, headers Content-Type/Authorization/X-Requested-With, credentials disabled | `app.py` L259-L288 |
| Process identity | Container runs as non-root `USER python` in the image and `user: "1000:1000"` in Compose | `Dockerfile` L59; `docker-compose.yml` L318 |
| Kernel capabilities | `cap_drop: ALL` with only `SETGID`/`SETUID` restored, plus `no-new-privileges:true` | `docker-compose.yml` L314-L336 |
| Filesystem | Read-only root filesystem; production sources at mode 444; dependency cache volumes mounted `read_only: true`; writable space limited to two 10 MB `tmpfs` mounts | `docker-compose.yml` L237-L245, L325-L329; `Dockerfile` L213 |
| Secret handling | `SECRET_KEY` supplied as a plain environment variable; `.env` files are git-ignored and `.env.example` ships only example values | `.gitignore` L16-L22; `src/backend/.env.example` |

One control weakness is material enough to state plainly even though no data is at risk today: when `SECRET_KEY` is unset the application silently falls back to the literal `'dev-key-change-in-production'` (`app.py` L159-L166) rather than refusing to start, and the shipped template value is `dev-secret-key-change-in-production-environments` (`src/backend/.env.example` L162). No secrets manager or vault is integrated. Nothing currently depends on that key — no session or signed token is ever produced — but it would become a genuine access-control defect the moment session-backed or token-backed data access were added.


### 6.2.5 Performance Optimization

Database performance optimisation has no subject here: there is no query to plan, no pool to size, no replica to read from, and no batch to schedule. What follows documents each optimisation topic against verified behaviour, records the mechanisms that occupy the analogous position at the HTTP and process layers, and names the one counter-optimisation present in the code.

#### 6.2.5.1 Query Optimization Patterns

**No queries exist.** Neither endpoint performs a lookup, filter, sort, aggregation, join, or scan. The `/hello` handler assembles a three-field `dict` from a string literal and a timestamp (`app.py` L391-L395); the `/health` handler assembles a six-field `dict` from literals, `time.time()`, and two `app.config` reads (`app.py` L437-L444). Both are constant-time constructions with no I/O behind them, so the classic optimisation levers — index selection, predicate pushdown, projection pruning, plan caching, N+1 elimination, and prepared statements — have nothing to act on.

The response-path optimisations that do exist are serialisation-level and process-level:

| Optimisation | Effect | Location |
|---|---|---|
| `JSON_SORT_KEYS: False` | Skips key sorting on every serialisation; also makes field order a stable contract | `app.py` L159-L166 |
| No template engine and no static assets | Response construction is a `dict` → `jsonify` call with zero filesystem access per request | `app.py` L391-L400, L437-L446 |
| `--preload` before fork | Application imported once in the arbiter; the four workers share interpreter and framework pages copy-on-write | `Dockerfile` L216; `docker-compose.yml` L263 |
| `sync` worker class | No async machinery in the request path for a CPU-trivial payload | `Dockerfile` L216 |

One counter-optimisation is present and is recorded here because it directly affects every response: `JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR` is set to `True` in the **base** configuration that applies to all three profiles, with the in-code comment "Pretty-print JSON in development" (`app.py` L159-L166). Production responses are therefore pretty-printed, adding serialisation work and response bytes on every request. `6.1 Core Services Architecture` records the same finding among its performance observations.

#### 6.2.5.2 Caching Strategy

**No cache tier exists and none would help.** The caching policies that are declared — `/health` marked `no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate`, the 24-hour CORS preflight `max_age`, and the inert one-year `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT` — are documented in 6.2.3.5, and the toolchain caches (pip, Docker layer, virtualenv volumes) are catalogued in `3.5 Databases & Storage`.

The reason a cache is not merely absent but unnecessary is worth stating explicitly: a cache trades memory for avoided work, and there is no work to avoid. The `/hello` payload is a literal plus a timestamp, and caching it would be actively counterproductive because the `timestamp` field must differ per request — an invariant asserted by `test_stateless_operation_multiple_requests` (`src/backend/tests/test_app.py` L482), which requires five sequential requests to produce five distinct timestamps. A cache in front of `/hello` would break that contract.

#### 6.2.5.3 Connection Pooling

**No database connection pool exists**, because no connection is ever opened. There is no pool object, no minimum/maximum size, no acquisition timeout, no idle-eviction policy, no pre-ping or liveness check, and no leak detection anywhere in the codebase. `src/backend/.env.example` L174 carries `DATABASE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=10` inside the commented "not used in tutorial" block — the only pool-sizing value in the repository, and it is read by nothing.

The pooling analogue in this system is inbound HTTP connection and worker-slot management, configured entirely in the container layer:

| Control | Value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Worker slots | `--workers=4 --worker-class=sync` | Four concurrent requests per instance; each worker handles one request at a time |
| Idle connection retention | `--keepalive=2` | Bounds how long an idle client connection occupies resources |
| Request occupancy cap | `--timeout=30` | A worker exceeding the budget is killed and replaced, so one slow request cannot hold a slot indefinitely |
| Slot recycling | `--max-requests=1000 --max-requests-jitter=100` | Retires each worker after roughly 900-1100 requests, bounding memory drift and staggering restarts |

All four are declared in `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` L216 and mirrored in the Compose production command (`docker-compose.yml` L263). Two caveats apply, both established in `6.1 Core Services Architecture`: `--worker-connections=1000` is declared but **inert** under the `sync` worker class, and no async worker library (`gevent`, `eventlet`) is installed, so in-node concurrency equals the worker count exactly. Because the arguments are literals in the start command, the `WORKERS` variable documented in `src/backend/.env.example` and the `GUNICORN_WORKERS` value injected by the CD deploy steps cannot retune a running container.

#### 6.2.5.4 Read/Write Splitting

**Not applicable — the system performs no writes at all**, so there is nothing to split. The complete route surface is two `GET` endpoints (`app.py` L367, L426); `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` appear only in the CORS `methods` allow-list and resolve through the 405 handler. `1.3 Scope` records "Write operations and mutating endpoints" among the explicit exclusions.

| Splitting Prerequisite | Status |
|---|---|
| A write path to route away from replicas | Absent — no handler mutates anything, in memory or otherwise |
| A read replica to route toward | Absent — no replica of any kind; `replicas: 1` is the only replication declaration |
| A router, proxy, or driver-level read preference | Absent — no reverse proxy, no `ProxyFix`, no driver at all |
| A replication-lag tolerance to reason about | Absent — no replication, therefore no lag |

Both endpoints are pure reads of *computed* values rather than stored ones, so every request is trivially safe to serve from any worker or any future instance without routing logic, read-your-write concerns, or consistency-level selection.

#### 6.2.5.5 Batch Processing Approach

**No batch processing exists.** There is no bulk insert or update path, no ETL job, no scheduled task, no background worker, and no queue. Verified absences include any Celery, RQ, or APScheduler dependency, any `threading`-based worker pool in the request path (`wsgi.py` imports `threading` solely for the `shutdown_event` primitive at L75), and any batching or chunking construct in either runtime module. The commented `CELERY_BROKER_URL` at `src/backend/.env.example` L194 is the only reference to asynchronous work anywhere, and it is inert.

Three mechanisms have batch-like shapes but process no data:

| Mechanism | What It Batches | Location |
|---|---|---|
| Worker recycling | Requests per worker lifetime — roughly 900-1100 before the worker is retired | `Dockerfile` L216 |
| Header application loop | Iterates the six-entry security-header dictionary once per response | `app.py` L249-L252 |
| CI test execution | The full pytest suite per run, with `pytest-xdist` available for multi-core distribution | `pytest.ini`; `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| Scheduled workflow | The weekly CI cron — the only scheduled job in the repository, and it runs tests and scans rather than processing data | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |

The measured performance envelope for the request path — warm-response, concurrency, and memory thresholds asserted by the test suite — belongs to `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns` and the capacity-planning discussion in `6.1 Core Services Architecture`, and is deliberately not restated here. The only data-adjacent figure that belongs to this section is the 16 MB `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` ceiling (`app.py` L159-L166), which bounds inbound payload size and is the sole storage-adjacent resource control in the application.


### 6.2.6 References

#### 6.2.6.1 Files Examined

- `src/backend/app.py` — Established the complete set of data structures in the system: the six response payloads (`/hello` L391-L395, `/health` L437-L444, and the 404/405/500/generic envelopes at L501-L508, L535-L543, L586-L592, L623-L628, plus the route-local guards at L418-L423 and L457-L462); the request-scoped context attributes `start_time` and `id` (L310, L316); the configuration matrix including `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`, `JSON_SORT_KEYS: False`, `JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR: True`, and the `SECRET_KEY` fallback (L159-L166); the session-cookie policy that no code exercises (L178, L190); the six security headers and `Server` removal (L223-L253); the CORS configuration with `supports_credentials: False` and `max_age: 86400` (L259-L288); the `/health` `no-cache` directive (L449); the `DEBUG`-gated traceback suppression (L581-L582, L619-L620); the unused `FLASK_CONFIGS` mapping (L641-L658); and the complete import set (L31-L42) proving no persistence client is importable and that `flask.session` and `flask.g` are never imported.
