## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Applicability Determination and Security Baseline

**Detailed Security Architecture is not applicable for this system.** The repository implements an educational Flask service whose entire externally reachable surface is two anonymous `GET` endpoints that synthesise their responses from string literals, clock reads, and configuration values. There is no user, no account, no credential, no session, no token, no role, no permission, no persisted record, and no personal data anywhere in the codebase. Consequently there is no identity to authenticate, no privilege to authorise, and no stored asset to encrypt — the three pillars on which a detailed security architecture would rest.

What the repository *does* contain is an unusually deliberate application of **standard security practices** for a service of this shape: defence-in-depth response hardening, an explicit cross-origin allow-list, environment-externalised secrets with git-hygiene enforcement, least-privilege container execution, and a multi-tool supply-chain scanning pipeline with blocking gates. This section documents those practices exhaustively, walks each area the section prompt enumerates (authentication, authorisation, data protection) to record precisely what exists and what is verifiably absent, and defines the security zones and control matrices that describe the system as built. Nothing in this section describes a capability the repository does not contain.

#### 6.4.1.1 Basis of the Determination

The determination rests on direct verification rather than inference. A repository-wide search across every `*.py` file for nineteen authentication, authorisation, and cryptography terms returns exactly **two** matches, and neither is a security control:

| Search Term Class | Terms Probed | Matches in `src/**/*.py` |
|---|---|---|
| Authentication | `auth`, `login`, `jwt`, `oauth`, `oidc`, `saml`, `mfa`, `flask_login`, `itsdangerous` | 1 — the string `'Authorization'` inside the CORS `allow_headers` list (`src/backend/app.py` L273) |
| Credentials | `password`, `passwd`, `credential`, `bcrypt`, `api_key` | 1 — the key `'supports_credentials': False` in the CORS configuration (`src/backend/app.py` L274) |
| Authorisation | `authz`, `rbac`, `role`, `permission`, `principal`, `current_user`, `login_required` | 0 |
| Tokens and crypto | `token`, `totp`, `hashlib`, `hmac`, `secrets.`, `cryptography`, `werkzeug.security` | 0 |

The `Authorization` request header is therefore *permitted by the CORS preflight policy but never read by any code path*, and `supports_credentials: False` explicitly disables cookie and credential propagation on cross-origin requests. Three further verifications complete the picture:

| Verification | Result |
|---|---|
| Dependency manifests | `requirements.txt` declares five runtime packages — `Flask>=3.1.1`, `python-dotenv>=1.0.1`, `Flask-CORS>=4.0.0`, `gunicorn>=21.2.0`, `wheel>=0.42.0`. No authentication extension, identity SDK, cryptography library, or secrets-manager client appears in any manifest. |
| Route surface | `src/backend/app.py` registers exactly two rules — `GET /hello` (L367) and `GET /health` (L426). Neither accepts a body, neither inspects a header, and no third route, blueprint, or `before_request` guard performs an access decision. |
| Documented posture | `src/backend/README.md` L282 records the `/hello` contract as **"Authentication: None required"**. `src/backend/.env.example` L178-L182 carries a commented block headed "Authentication Configuration Example (not used in tutorial)" containing `JWT_SECRET_KEY`, `JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRES=3600`, `SESSION_PERMANENT`, and `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME` — inert illustrations read by nothing. |

`1.3 Scope` records the same conclusion as an explicit exclusion — "Authentication and authorization … No JWT, OAuth, session login, or access-control decorator" — alongside the related exclusions of rate limiting, quotas, API keys, identity providers (SSO/LDAP/OIDC), and secrets managers. `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns` states the position in one sentence: no authentication or authorisation framework exists, **and that is an explicit design position rather than an oversight**.

#### 6.4.1.2 Standard Security Practices Followed Instead

Fourteen distinct practices are implemented and evidenced. Each row names the practice, the mechanism that implements it, and the artifact that proves it.

| Standard Practice | Implementing Mechanism | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Secure-by-default configuration profile | `create_app()` defaults to `config_name='production'`, annotated "for secure deployment practices" | `src/backend/app.py` L63, L75 |
| Response hardening headers | Six headers applied to every response by an `after_request` hook | `src/backend/app.py` L223-L253 |
| Framework fingerprint suppression | `response.headers.pop('Server', None)` on every response; tests also assert `X-Powered-By` absence | `src/backend/app.py` L237; `tests/test_app.py` L368-L378 |
| Cross-origin allow-listing | Flask-CORS restricted to two explicit origins with credentials disabled | `src/backend/app.py` L259-L288 |
| Request-size ceiling | `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 16 * 1024 * 1024`, enforced by Werkzeug before any handler runs | `src/backend/app.py` L164 |
| Environment-externalised configuration | `python-dotenv` `load_dotenv()` plus `os.getenv` for all seven variables; no secret literal in application logic other than the documented fallback | `src/backend/app.py` L52; `src/backend/.env.example` |
| Secret git-hygiene | `.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.crt`, `*.csr`, `secrets/`, `.credentials`, `apikeys.json` excluded from version control and from the Docker build context | `.gitignore` L16-L43; `src/backend/.gitignore`; `infrastructure/docker/.dockerignore` L111-L157 |
| Information-disclosure suppression | 404/405/500 and generic handlers return fixed envelopes; tracebacks logged only when `DEBUG` is set | `src/backend/app.py` L470-L632, L581-L582, L619-L620 |
| Fail-fast startup | Guarded imports plus chained `RuntimeError`/`ValueError` prevent a half-initialised process from serving | `src/backend/app.py` L39-L48, L126-L141; `src/backend/wsgi.py` L129-L144 |
| Input validation on configuration | `validate_port_number` enforces 1-65535 and warns below 1024 before binding | `src/backend/wsgi.py` L299-L331 |
| Least-privilege container execution | Non-root UID/GID 1000, `no-new-privileges:true`, `cap_drop: ALL`, read-only root filesystem | `Dockerfile` L41-L59; `docker-compose.yml` L314-L336 |
| Immutable runtime artifacts | Production sources set to mode `444`; images deployed by digest | `Dockerfile` L213; `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L346-L357 |
| Static and dependency security scanning | Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, OSSF Scorecard in CI; Bandit, Safety, Trivy in CD with a blocking gate | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` L126-L206; `cd.yml` L264-L436 |
| Build provenance | `provenance: true` and `sbom: true` on the image build | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L236-L238 |

Two configuration-hygiene settings reinforce the same posture at the interpreter level: `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` prevents `.pyc` artifacts inside the read-only image, and `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` guarantees that log records reach the container's streams immediately rather than sitting in a buffer that a crash would discard (`Dockerfile` L46-L57). Graceful termination is a fifteenth practice: `dumb-init` runs as PID 1 (`Dockerfile` L132, L220) and forwards `SIGTERM` to the handlers registered in `src/backend/wsgi.py` L192-L296.

#### 6.4.1.3 Attack Surface and Trust Boundary

The system's reachable surface is deliberately minimal, which is itself the dominant security property. Enumerated exhaustively:

| Surface | Exposure | Controls Applied |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /hello` on the bound port | Anonymous, unauthenticated, no parameters accepted | Method allow-list, six response headers, 16 MB body ceiling, CORS policy for browser callers |
| `GET /health` on the bound port | Anonymous; discloses resolved `environment` name and `debug` flag | `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate`; same header set; 503 branch echoes `str(e)` |
| Any other path or method | Resolves through the 404/405 handlers, which echo `path` and `method` | Fixed JSON envelope; `Allow` header on 405; no internal detail beyond the caller's own input |
| Debug adapter port 5678 | Present **only** in the `development` container target and the `flask-tutorial-dev` Compose service | Not built into the `production` target; `FLASK_DEBUG=0` in the production stage |
| Delivery pipeline | GitHub Actions workflows with registry and cloud credentials | Encrypted repository secrets, GitHub `environment` protection, digest-pinned promotion |

The trust boundary is therefore **the network**: any client that can reach the bound TCP port has complete access to both endpoints. `1.3 Scope` states the same boundary as "Unauthenticated public endpoints; CORS restricted to `http://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:8000` with credentials disabled". Two implications follow and are carried through the rest of this section. First, no request-level control distinguishes one caller from another, so all mitigation is either network-perimeter (outside the repository) or response-shaping (inside it). Second, the CORS allow-list is a browser-enforced control only — `curl`, server-side clients, and any non-browser agent are entirely unaffected by it, so it must never be read as an access-control mechanism.

#### 6.4.1.4 Section Ownership and Cross-References

This section is the authoritative security reference. To avoid duplication, the following adjacent analyses are owned elsewhere and referenced rather than restated:

| Topic | Owning Section |
|---|---|
| Observability signals, log categories, tracing limitations, error-handling patterns | `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns` |
| Summary statement of the absent authentication/authorisation framework and the adjacent-controls distinction | `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns` |
| Data retention, privacy controls, audit mechanisms, and data-access controls for the (empty) persistence domain | `6.2 Database Design` |
| Authoritative in-scope/out-of-scope declarations, including every security-adjacent exclusion | `1.3 Scope` |
| Dependency inventory and version policy | `3.3 Open Source Dependencies` |
| Container topology, worker model, and deployment pipeline mechanics | `6.1 Core Services Architecture` |


### 6.4.2 Authentication Framework

**No authentication framework exists on the request plane.** Both endpoints are anonymous by design: no credential is accepted, no challenge is issued, no `401` or `403` response can be produced by any code path, and no `WWW-Authenticate` header is ever emitted. The complete set of `HTTPStatus` values the application can return is 200, 404, 405, 500, and 503 — the two authentication-related status codes are structurally unreachable.

Authentication does, however, exist on the **delivery plane**, where the CI/CD pipeline authenticates to a container registry and a cloud host. That surface is real, credentialled, and worth documenting precisely, so it is treated in 6.4.2.6. The distinction matters: nothing in the delivery plane authenticates application traffic, and nothing in the request plane consumes a pipeline credential.

#### 6.4.2.1 Identity Management

No identity store, directory, user model, or registration path exists. There is no `User` class, no account table (there is no database at all — see `6.2 Database Design`), no identity-provider client, and no federation configuration. `1.3 Scope` records identity providers (SSO, LDAP, OIDC) as "Not integrated".

Three identities nevertheless govern the running system, and confusing any of them with a *caller* identity would be a category error:

| Identity | Established By | What It Governs |
|---|---|---|
| Process identity — `python`, UID 1000 / GID 1000 | `addgroup -g 1000 python && adduser -D -u 1000 -G python python` then `USER python` (`Dockerfile` L41-L59); re-asserted as `user: "1000:1000"` in both Compose services | Filesystem and kernel privilege of the running interpreter — the only identity the operating system evaluates at runtime |
| Container/network identity | `container_name` and `hostname` per service; membership of the `flask-tutorial-network` bridge with IPAM subnet `172.21.0.0/16` (`docker-compose.yml`) | Which containers can address the service on the private bridge |
| Pipeline identity | `${{ github.actor }}` and `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` for registry operations; Azure publish-profile secrets for deployment (`.github/workflows/cd.yml` L127, L171, L357, L480, L692) | Who may publish an image and who may deploy to `staging` or `production` |

The application itself never resolves an identity of any kind. `src/backend/app.py` reads exactly two attributes off the inbound request — `request.method` and `request.path` — and reads neither headers, query string, form fields, body, nor `remote_addr`; `6.2 Database Design` records the corresponding zero-match verification across `request.remote_addr`, `request.user_agent`, `request.headers`, `request.args`, `request.form`, `request.get_json`, `request.data`, and any `X-Forwarded` handling.

#### 6.4.2.2 Multi-Factor Authentication

**Not applicable and entirely absent.** There is no first factor to augment. No TOTP, HOTP, WebAuthn, FIDO2, SMS, push-notification, backup-code, or recovery-flow implementation exists; no MFA library appears in any manifest; and no configuration variable relates to step-up authentication. The seven-variable configuration surface (`PORT`, `HOST`, `FLASK_ENV`, `FLASK_DEBUG`, `LOG_LEVEL`, `WORKERS`, `SECRET_KEY`) contains no authentication setting at all.

The nearest MFA-adjacent control is external to the repository: the GitHub organisation account policy that protects the `staging` and `production` deployment environments and the encrypted secrets they consume. That policy is not expressed in any file here, so it is recorded as an environmental dependency rather than an implemented control. `src/backend/README.md` L883 lists "Multi-Factor Authentication: Enhanced security with 2FA/TOTP" under a forward-looking enhancement section, confirming it as unimplemented curriculum guidance.

#### 6.4.2.3 Session Management

**No session is ever created.** `flask.session` is never imported by either runtime module, no code writes to a session object, and no response sets a session cookie. `src/backend/tests/test_app.py` asserts this as an invariant: `test_no_session_persistence` (L507) requires that no response carry a `Set-Cookie` header containing `session`, and `test_stateless_operation_multiple_requests` (L482) requires five sequential requests to be mutually independent.

A complete session-cookie *policy* is nevertheless configured per environment profile. It is dormant — Flask applies these attributes only when a session cookie is actually written — but it is the correct policy for each profile and would take effect unchanged the moment a session were introduced:

| Setting | `production` | `development` | `testing` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE` | `True` | `False` (HTTP permitted locally) | `False` |
| `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY` | `True` | `True` | `False` |
| `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` | `'Lax'` | Not set (Flask default) | Not set |
| `PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME` | `3600` s (1 hour) | `86400` s (24 hours) | Not set |
| `WTF_CSRF_ENABLED` | Not set (no Flask-WTF installed) | Not set | `False` (explicitly disabled) |

Source: `src/backend/app.py` L170-L202. Two observations matter for anyone extending this service. `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` is set only in the production profile, so a development session cookie would inherit Flask's default rather than an explicit policy; and `WTF_CSRF_ENABLED: False` in the testing profile (mirrored by `WTF_CSRF_ENABLED = False` in the `env` blocks of both `pytest.ini` files) is inert today because Flask-WTF is not a declared dependency — no CSRF machinery exists to disable. `src/backend/tests/test_app.py` L96-L97 asserts the two production hardening flags (`SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is True`, `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY is True`), so the dormant policy is at least regression-protected.

The only genuine per-request state is transient and non-authenticating: `request.start_time` and `request.id` are attached by `before_request` (`src/backend/app.py` L310, L316) and destroyed at request teardown.

#### 6.4.2.4 Token Handling

**No token is issued, validated, refreshed, or revoked.** There is no JWT, PASETO, opaque bearer token, API key, or signed-cookie payload anywhere in the system. Four token-shaped artifacts exist, and each is precisely characterised below so none is mistaken for a credential:

| Artifact | What It Actually Is | Security Weight |
|---|---|---|
| `SECRET_KEY` | Flask's signing key, read via `os.getenv('SECRET_KEY', 'dev-key-change-in-production')` (`src/backend/app.py` L161) | Configured but **unused** — no code signs a cookie, session, or token, so the key currently protects nothing |
| `X-Request-ID` (`req_<epoch-ms>`) | Correlation identifier generated locally at `src/backend/app.py` L316 and echoed at L350 | Not a security token: never validated, never read from an inbound header, not unpredictable, and collision-prone within the same millisecond (see `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns`) |
| `Authorization` request header | Listed in the CORS `allow_headers` set (`src/backend/app.py` L273) | Permitted by preflight policy only; no handler reads it, so any value sent is silently ignored |
| `itsdangerous>=2.1.2` | Transitive Flask dependency pinned in `src/backend/requirements.txt` L160 with the comment "Cryptographic signing for Flask sessions" | Available in the environment but never imported by application code |

Because `SECRET_KEY` has a hard-coded fallback rather than a startup assertion, a deployment that forgets to set it starts successfully using the literal `'dev-key-change-in-production'`. That is inconsequential today — nothing is signed — but it is the single most consequential latent defect in the authentication area, and it is carried into the residual-risk register in 6.4.5. `6.2 Database Design` records the same fallback in its access-control discussion.

The delivery plane does handle real tokens: `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` authenticates registry login and the Trivy scanner's registry pull, and Azure publish profiles authenticate deployment. These are enumerated in 6.4.2.6.

#### 6.4.2.5 Password and Credential Strength Policies

**No password policy exists because no password exists** — there is no password field, no hashing routine (`werkzeug.security`, `bcrypt`, `argon2`, and `hashlib` are all absent), no complexity validator, no expiry or history rule, and no lockout or back-off mechanism. Rate limiting, which would be the natural companion control, is likewise absent and is recorded as out of scope in `1.3 Scope`.

The repository does define one credential-strength policy, and it applies to `SECRET_KEY`. It is documentation-only — no code enforces any clause — but it is explicit and complete, and it is reproduced here because it is the closest analogue to a password policy in the system:

| Policy Clause | Stated Requirement | Enforcement Status |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum length | At least 32 characters | Documented twice (`src/backend/.env.example` L151, L268); not validated at startup |
| Generation method | Cryptographically secure random generation; mixed case, numbers, and symbols | Documented (L150-L152); no generator shipped |
| Hard-coding prohibition | "Never hardcode in production applications" | Documented (L153); contradicted by the in-code fallback at `app.py` L161 |
| Per-environment uniqueness | Unique key per environment; different keys for staging and production | Documented (L156, L159); no mechanism distributes or verifies this |
| Storage | "Store in secure environment variable management" | Documented (L157); supplied as a plain environment variable — `1.3 Scope` records that no secrets manager or vault is integrated |
| Rotation | "Rotate keys periodically for security" | Documented (L158); no rotation automation, versioning, or dual-key overlap exists |

Two related documentation controls reinforce the same discipline: `src/backend/.env.example` L14 states the template "contains only example values, no actual secrets", and L90-L96 warn that `FLASK_DEBUG` must never be enabled in production because debug mode "can expose sensitive information and security vulnerabilities". The shipped template values are deliberately self-identifying placeholders — `SECRET_KEY=dev-secret-key-change-in-production-environments` (L162) and `SECRET_KEY = testing-secret-key-not-for-production` in the root `pytest.ini` `env` block — so a leaked value is recognisable as non-production.

#### 6.4.2.6 Delivery-Plane Authentication

The pipeline is the only place where real credentials are presented. Every one is supplied through GitHub's encrypted-secrets mechanism; no plaintext credential exists in any file in the repository.

| Credential | Purpose | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` | Repository checkout for the version step, `ghcr.io` registry login for image push, and registry authentication for the Trivy image pull | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L127, L171, L357 |
| `secrets.AZURE_WEBAPP_PUBLISH_PROFILE_STAGING` | Authenticates the staging deployment to Azure Web Apps | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L480 |
| `secrets.AZURE_WEBAPP_PUBLISH_PROFILE_PRODUCTION` | Authenticates the production deployment to Azure Web Apps | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L692 |

Two structural properties strengthen this surface, and one weakens it. Strengthening: deployments target GitHub `environment:` objects (`staging` at L444-L446, `production` at L636-L638), which is the hook through which platform-side approval and reviewer rules apply; and promotion is digest-pinned, so the artifact that passed the security gate is byte-identical to the artifact deployed. Weakening: **neither workflow declares a `permissions:` block** at workflow or job level, so the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` permission set applies rather than an explicitly least-privileged scope. Additionally, `workflow_dispatch` exposes a `skip_tests` boolean documented as "Skip security scanning for emergency deployments" (`cd.yml` L54), which is an intentional human-operated bypass of the scanning gate.

Notably, the pipeline injects only `FLASK_ENV: production` into the deployed application settings (`cd.yml` L484, L696). **`SECRET_KEY` is not supplied by the pipeline**, so a deployment performed exactly as configured runs on the in-code fallback value.

#### 6.4.2.7 Authentication Flow

The diagram below traces an inbound request end to end. Every decision node reflects a check that the code actually performs; the dashed zone records the authentication stages that do not exist and names the exact insertion point a future implementation would use.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Client["HTTP client - browser, curl,<br/>probe or any network peer"]
    Arrive["Request reaches the bound port<br/>0.0.0.0:3000 in the container"]

    Client --> Arrive --> SizeGate{{"Body within MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH<br/>16 MB?"}}
    SizeGate -->|"no"| Reject413["Werkzeug rejects before any<br/>application code executes"]
    SizeGate -->|"yes"| Pre["before_request:<br/>attach start_time and req id,<br/>log method and path"]

    Pre --> NoCred{{"Is any credential extracted<br/>from the request?"}}
    NoCred -->|"never - no header, cookie,<br/>query or body is read"| Anon["Caller treated as anonymous<br/>no principal is created"]

    subgraph Absent["Authentication stages that do not exist"]
        direction TB
        NoChallenge["No 401 challenge<br/>no WWW-Authenticate header"]
        NoVerify["No credential verification<br/>no password hash, no token signature"]
        NoMFA["No second factor<br/>no TOTP, WebAuthn or push"]
        NoSession["No session establishment<br/>flask.session never imported"]
        NoChallenge --> NoVerify --> NoMFA --> NoSession
    end

    Anon -.->|"insertion point for a future<br/>before_request guard"| NoChallenge

    Anon --> Route{{"Does a URL rule match<br/>the path and method?"}}
    Route -->|"no path match"| E404["404 handler:<br/>fixed JSON envelope<br/>echoes path and method"]
    Route -->|"path matches, method does not"| E405["405 handler:<br/>allowed_methods plus Allow header"]
    Route -->|"match"| Handler["Invoke /hello or /health handler<br/>response built from literals,<br/>clock and app.config"]

    Handler --> Post["after_request chain:<br/>timing headers, CORS headers,<br/>six security headers, Server removed"]
    E404 --> Post
    E405 --> Post
    Post --> Out["Response returned<br/>no authentication state carried"]
    Out --> Client
```

The corresponding delivery-plane flow is materially different, because it does authenticate:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as "Committer"
    participant GA as "GitHub Actions runner"
    participant GHCR as "ghcr.io registry"
    participant Scan as "Trivy / Bandit / Safety"
    participant Azure as "Azure Web Apps"

    Dev->>GA: Push to main, publish release,<br/>or manual dispatch
    GA->>GA: Resolve encrypted secrets<br/>GITHUB_TOKEN, publish profiles
    GA->>GHCR: docker login with github.actor<br/>and GITHUB_TOKEN
    GHCR-->>GA: Session established for push
    GA->>GHCR: Push image with provenance<br/>and SBOM attestations
    GA->>Scan: Scan image by digest<br/>plus source and dependency scans
    Scan-->>GA: Counts by severity
    GA->>GA: Gate - fail on CRITICAL > 0<br/>or Safety vulnerabilities > 0
    GA->>Azure: Deploy to environment staging<br/>with publish-profile credential
    Azure-->>GA: Deployment status
    GA->>Azure: Deploy to environment production<br/>only after staging success
    Azure-->>GA: Deployment status and URL
```


### 6.4.3 Authorization System

**No authorization system exists on the request plane.** Because no caller identity is ever established (6.4.2.1), no authorisation decision is possible even in principle. The effective policy is a universal grant: every reachable client is permitted to invoke both endpoints, and the only "denials" the system can produce are routing outcomes — a path that matches no rule yields 404, and a method that no rule accepts yields 405. Neither is an access-control decision; both are dispatch results.

Authorisation controls that genuinely exist operate at two layers below and beside the application: the **operating-system/kernel layer**, which constrains what the process may do, and the **delivery pipeline**, which constrains who may publish and deploy. Both are documented here because they are the system's real authorisation surfaces.

#### 6.4.3.1 Role-Based Access Control

**No RBAC exists in the application.** There is no role, group, scope, claim, ACL, or capability model; no `@roles_required`-style decorator; no policy file, rule engine, or ABAC attribute evaluation; and no administrative interface. A repository-wide grep across `src/**/*.py` for `role`, `permission`, `rbac`, `principal`, `current_user`, and `login_required` returns zero matches.

Role-like separation exists only in the delivery pipeline and in the container runtime, and it is coarse:

| Role-Like Boundary | Subject | What It Gates |
|---|---|---|
| Repository contributor | `${{ github.actor }}` on a push or pull request | Triggers CI (`push` to `main`/`develop` with path filters, `pull_request` to `main`); CI cannot deploy |
| Release authority | Whoever publishes a GitHub release, or dispatches the workflow with `environment: production` | The only paths that can reach `deploy_production` (`cd.yml` L631-L634) |
| Deployment environment approver | Platform-side rules attached to the `staging` and `production` GitHub environments | Whether a deployment job may proceed; the rules themselves live in GitHub, not in this repository |
| Runtime process role | `USER python` (UID/GID 1000) in the image, `user: "1000:1000"` in Compose | Every filesystem and syscall the interpreter attempts |

Note the ordering constraint that gives this structure teeth: `deploy_production` declares `needs: [build_and_publish, security_scan, deploy_staging]`, so production promotion is impossible unless the security scan and the staging deployment both succeeded.

#### 6.4.3.2 Permission Management

The permission model that is actually enforced at runtime is the kernel's, and it is configured restrictively. Each control below is declarative and verifiable in the repository:

| Permission Control | Configured Value | Effect | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process user | UID 1000 / GID 1000 (`python`) | No root privilege at any point after image build | `Dockerfile` L41-L59; `docker-compose.yml` L156, L319 |
| Privilege escalation | `no-new-privileges:true` on both services | `setuid`/`setgid` binaries cannot raise privilege | `docker-compose.yml` L152-L153, L314-L315 |
| Linux capabilities | `cap_drop: ALL`, then `cap_add: SETGID, SETUID` | All capabilities removed; only the two needed for Gunicorn's worker user handling are restored | `docker-compose.yml` L331-L336 |
| Root filesystem | `read_only: true` | No write anywhere in the container filesystem except the declared exceptions | `docker-compose.yml` L325 |
| Writable exceptions | `tmpfs` at `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, `rw,size=10M,mode=1777` | Bounded scratch space, 10 MB each, non-persistent | `docker-compose.yml` L326-L329 |
| Application source mode | `chmod -R 444 *.py` in the production stage | Sources are read-only even to the owning user — the image cannot self-modify | `Dockerfile` L213 |
| Virtualenv mode | `chmod -R 755 /usr/src/app/.venv` | Standard read/execute permissions for dependencies | `Dockerfile` L96 |
| File ownership | `COPY --chown=python:python` on every copy instruction | No root-owned file in the application tree | `Dockerfile` L71-L72, L108-L109, L158-L159 |
| Dependency cache mounts | `read_only` on both production volume mounts | Cached packages cannot be mutated at runtime | `docker-compose.yml` L237-L245 |
| Resource ceiling | Limits 128 M / 0.5 CPU; reservations 75 M / 0.25 CPU | Bounds the blast radius of runaway consumption | `docker-compose.yml` L283-L286 |

One deviation is explicit and self-documented: `security_opt` includes `apparmor:unconfined` on the production service with the inline comment "Educational: would be configured properly in real production" (`docker-compose.yml` L316). This disables AppArmor mediation and is the single deliberate relaxation in an otherwise tight profile; it is carried into the residual-risk register in 6.4.5.

#### 6.4.3.3 Resource Authorization

Four allow-lists constitute the entirety of resource gating. Each is a positive allow-list — anything not enumerated is refused or ignored — which is the correct default-deny shape, but note that only the first two apply to non-browser callers:

| Allow-List | Enumerated Values | Applies To |
|---|---|---|
| URL rules | `/hello`, `/health` — exactly two rules in the Flask URL map | All callers; anything else → 404 |
| Methods per rule | `GET` only, declared as `methods=['GET']` on both routes | All callers; anything else → 405 with `Allow` header |
| CORS origins | `http://localhost:3000`, `http://localhost:8000` | Browser callers only (`supports_credentials: False`) |
| CORS methods and headers | Methods `GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS`; headers `Content-Type, Authorization, X-Requested-With`; `max_age: 86400` | Browser preflight only |

Two mismatches inside this table are worth stating plainly because they are easy to misread. The CORS `methods` list advertises five methods while the application implements only `GET`, so a browser that is granted `POST` by preflight will still receive a 405 from the route layer — the CORS policy is broader than the route policy. And the 24-hour preflight cache means a change to the origin allow-list can take up to a day to propagate to a browser that has already cached the preflight response.

One further resource control is enforced before any application code executes: `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH = 16 * 1024 * 1024` (`src/backend/app.py` L164) caps inbound body size at the Werkzeug layer. By contrast, the JSON content-type check in `before_request` (`src/backend/app.py` L318-L321) is **advisory only** — a non-JSON `POST`/`PUT` body with a content length logs a warning and processing continues; nothing is rejected.

#### 6.4.3.4 Policy Enforcement Points

Enforcement is distributed across three planes. The table below is the complete inventory of points at which a request, a process action, or a release can be refused.

| Enforcement Point | Plane | What It Refuses or Constrains |
|---|---|---|
| Werkzeug body-size check | Request | Bodies exceeding 16 MB, before any handler runs |
| Flask URL map | Request | Every path other than `/hello` and `/health` → 404 envelope |
| Flask method matching | Request | Every method other than `GET` on a matched rule → 405 envelope with `Allow` |
| `before_request` content-type check | Request | Nothing — advisory warning only (`app.py` L318-L321) |
| Flask-CORS `after_request` | Request (browser) | Cross-origin reads from any origin outside the two-entry allow-list; credentialled cross-origin requests |
| Security-header `after_request` | Request | Constrains client-side behaviour: sniffing, framing, cross-domain policy files, referrer leakage, and non-self resource loading |
| Error-handler registry | Request | Internal detail — generic messages to the client, full detail to logs, tracebacks only under `DEBUG` |
| `validate_port_number` | Process startup | A `PORT` outside 1-65535 aborts startup with a chained `ValueError` |
| Guarded imports | Process startup | A missing dependency terminates before any socket is bound (`app.py` L39-L48; `wsgi.py` guarded imports with `sys.exit(1)`) |
| Kernel capability set and `no-new-privileges` | Runtime | Every privileged syscall outside `SETGID`/`SETUID`; all privilege escalation |
| Read-only filesystem and mode-444 sources | Runtime | Every write outside the two `tmpfs` mounts; any modification of application code |
| Gunicorn `--timeout=30`, `--max-requests=1000` | Runtime | A request occupying a worker beyond 30 s; unbounded worker lifetime |
| Container `HEALTHCHECK` | Runtime | An unresponsive container is marked unhealthy after three retries, triggering the restart policy |
| CI `quality-gate` job | Delivery | A merge candidate whose coverage or scan validation fails (`needs: [test, security]`) |
| CD security gate | Delivery | Promotion when Trivy reports `CRITICAL > 0` or Safety reports any vulnerability (`cd.yml` L393-L398, `exit 1`) |
| GitHub `environment` protection | Delivery | Deployment to `staging`/`production` without satisfying platform-side rules |
| `deploy_production` `needs` chain | Delivery | Production deployment when the security scan or staging deployment did not succeed |

Two enforcement defects in the CI chain are recorded here because they are verifiable from the workflow definition and they weaken the gate they appear to implement:

| Defect | Evidence | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Bandit target does not resolve | The `security` job sets `working-directory: src/backend` and then runs `bandit -r src/` (`ci.yml` L158-L161); `src/backend/src` does not exist — the modules are `src/backend/app.py` and `src/backend/wsgi.py` | The CI Bandit invocation does not scan the application modules. The CD job's `bandit -r src/backend/` (`cd.yml` L311-L312) runs from the repository root and does resolve correctly. |
| Gate reads a non-existent report path | `quality-gate` downloads the `security-reports` artifact to workspace-root `security/`, then from `working-directory: src/backend` reads `../security/bandit-report.json` and `../security/safety-report.json` (`ci.yml` L299, L317) | The relative path resolves under `src/`, not the workspace root; both checks are wrapped in `if [ -f ... ]` with an `else` branch that prints "Bandit report not found, skipping security validation", so the HIGH-severity gate degrades to a skip rather than a failure. |

#### 6.4.3.5 Audit Logging

There is no audit trail in the compliance sense — no append-only store, no tamper-evident log, no actor attribution, and no retention policy for application logs. What exists is operational logging that doubles as audit-adjacent evidence. `6.2 Database Design` owns the data-governance framing; the security-relevant record inventory is:

| Record | Fields Emitted | Level |
|---|---|---|
| Request arrival | `method`, `path` | INFO (`app.py` L313) |
| Request completion | `method`, `path`, status code, elapsed milliseconds | INFO (`app.py` L345-L346) |
| Not-found attempt | `method`, `path`, "Route not matched" | WARNING (`app.py` L496) |
| Method-not-allowed attempt | `method`, `path` | WARNING (`app.py` L531) |
| Non-JSON body advisory | Received `content_type` | WARNING (`app.py` L321) |
| Server error | Exception type, message, `path`, `method`; `exc_info` traceback only when `DEBUG` | ERROR (`app.py` L573-L582) |
| Unhandled exception | Exception type and message; `exc_info` only when `DEBUG` | ERROR (`app.py` L615-L620) |
| Startup fingerprint | Python version, PID, platform, host, port, endpoint list | INFO (`wsgi.py` L376-L429) |
| Signal receipt and shutdown | Signal name, cleanup narration, memory sample | INFO (`wsgi.py` L224-L291) |
| Uncaught exception at process level | Exception detail; traceback only when `FLASK_ENV == 'development'` | ERROR (`wsgi.py` `handle_uncaught_exceptions`) |

Correlation is provided by `X-Request-ID` / the `request_id` field in the 500 envelope, and every record reaches stdout (plus stderr under the WSGI entry point, which attaches handlers for both streams). Gunicorn adds a conventional access log via `--access-logfile=- --error-logfile=-`.

Five limitations bound what these records can be used for, and all five follow directly from the architecture:

| Limitation | Cause |
|---|---|
| No actor attribution | No identity is captured; the logs establish *what* happened, never *who* did it |
| No client provenance | `request.remote_addr`, `request.headers`, and `X-Forwarded-*` are never read, so the source IP is absent from application records |
| Correlation IDs are not unique | `req_<epoch-ms>` carries no worker or instance discriminator, so two requests in the same millisecond collide (see `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns`) |
| No durable or tamper-evident sink | Streams only — no shipper, aggregator, index, rotation, or retention configuration exists anywhere in the repository; records vanish when a container is replaced |
| Verbosity is effectively fixed | `LOG_LEVEL` is documented in `.env.example` and set in container environments but is not consumed by `logging.basicConfig`, so the application logger stays at INFO |

Security-posture evidence *is* retained durably, but in the pipeline rather than the runtime: Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, OSSF Scorecard, and Trivy reports are uploaded as artifacts (90-day retention for the CI security reports) and their SARIF forms are pushed to GitHub code scanning via `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2`.

#### 6.4.3.6 Authorization Flow

The diagram traces the decision sequence for one request, marking each gate with what it actually evaluates. The dashed zone records the authorisation stages that do not exist.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    In["Inbound request on the bound port"]
    In --> G1{{"Body size within 16 MB?"}}
    G1 -->|"no"| D1["Refused by Werkzeug<br/>no handler executes"]
    G1 -->|"yes"| G2{{"Path matches a rule in the<br/>two-entry URL map?"}}
    G2 -->|"no"| D2["404 envelope<br/>WARNING log with method and path"]
    G2 -->|"yes"| G3{{"Method allowed on that rule?<br/>GET only"}}
    G3 -->|"no"| D3["405 envelope plus Allow header<br/>WARNING log"]
    G3 -->|"yes"| G4{{"Browser cross-origin request?"}}
    G4 -->|"yes, origin not allow-listed"| D4["CORS headers withheld<br/>browser blocks the read"]
    G4 -->|"yes, origin allow-listed"| Grant["Universal grant:<br/>no principal, no role,<br/>no resource-level check"]
    G4 -->|"no, non-browser caller"| Grant

    subgraph NoAuthz["Authorization stages that do not exist"]
        direction TB
        NoPrincipal["No principal or subject resolved"]
        NoPolicy["No policy lookup<br/>no role, scope, claim or ACL"]
        NoDecision["No permit/deny decision<br/>403 is unreachable"]
        NoPrincipal --> NoPolicy --> NoDecision
    end

    Grant -.->|"insertion point for a future<br/>policy enforcement point"| NoPrincipal

    Grant --> Exec["Handler executes:<br/>response built from literals,<br/>clock and app.config"]
    Exec --> Shape["Response shaping as enforcement:<br/>six security headers,<br/>Server header removed,<br/>generic error envelopes"]
    D2 --> Shape
    D3 --> Shape
    Shape --> Log["Audit-adjacent record:<br/>method, path, status, elapsed ms,<br/>X-Request-ID"]
    Log --> Out["Response to client"]
```

The runtime and delivery planes enforce their own policies in parallel with every request:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Runtime["Runtime enforcement - kernel and container"]
        direction TB
        Uid["Process runs as UID/GID 1000<br/>no root privilege"]
        Caps["cap_drop ALL, cap_add SETGID and SETUID<br/>no-new-privileges true"]
        Fs["Read-only root filesystem<br/>sources at mode 444<br/>tmpfs 10M at /tmp and /var/tmp"]
        Res["Limits 128M and 0.5 CPU<br/>Gunicorn timeout 30s, recycle at 1000 requests"]
        Uid --> Caps --> Fs --> Res
    end

    subgraph Delivery["Delivery enforcement - pipeline gates"]
        direction TB
        CIGate["CI quality-gate<br/>needs test and security jobs"]
        ScanGate["CD security gate<br/>fail if CRITICAL over 0<br/>or Safety findings over 0"]
        EnvGate["GitHub environment protection<br/>staging then production"]
        DigestGate["Digest-pinned promotion<br/>scanned artifact equals deployed artifact"]
        CIGate --> ScanGate --> EnvGate --> DigestGate
    end

    Res -->|"constrains the process<br/>serving every request"| Delivery
```


### 6.4.4 Data Protection

Data protection in this system is governed by what the service **never handles**. The complete data inventory is six response structures assembled from string literals, `datetime.now()`, `time.time()`, and `app.config` reads, plus two transient request attributes. No personal data, credential, payment instrument, health record, or business record is ever received, derived, stored, or transmitted. `6.2 Database Design` establishes the corresponding verification: `flask.session` and `flask.g` are never imported, no `open()` call exists in either runtime module, and the application reads only `request.method` and `request.path` from the inbound request.

Protection therefore reduces to three concerns that *are* live: keeping the one configured secret out of source control and out of images, preventing internal detail from leaking through responses and headers, and constraining the transport and cross-origin surface. Each is addressed below.

#### 6.4.4.1 Encryption Standards

**No cryptographic operation is performed by application code.** There is no encryption, decryption, signing, verification, hashing, key derivation, or random-token generation anywhere in `src/backend/app.py` or `src/backend/wsgi.py` — `hashlib`, `hmac`, `secrets`, `cryptography`, `bcrypt`, and `werkzeug.security` are all absent from the import graph. Consequently no cipher suite, key length, mode of operation, or algorithm agility policy is expressed in the repository, and none can be invented here.

| Encryption Domain | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Data at rest | **Not applicable** — the application writes nothing. Production runs on a read-only root filesystem whose only writable space is two non-persistent 10 MB `tmpfs` mounts, and no `VOLUME` instruction exists in the image | `docker-compose.yml` L325-L329; `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` |
| Data in transit, inbound | **Plain HTTP at the container boundary.** Gunicorn binds `0.0.0.0:3000`; the `HEALTHCHECK` probes `http://localhost:3000/hello`. TLS is not terminated by the service | `Dockerfile` L209-L220 |
| Data in transit, upstream | Every external endpoint referenced by the delivery pipeline is `https://` (`flask-tutorial.azurewebsites.net`, `flask-tutorial-staging.azurewebsites.net`), so TLS is a property of the Azure Web Apps front end rather than of this codebase | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` L446, L638 |
| URL scheme preference | `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME: 'https'` is set in the production profile and in the WSGI settings — this affects **external URL generation only** and does not encrypt, redirect, or upgrade any connection | `src/backend/app.py` L174; `src/backend/wsgi.py` L159 |
| Application-level field encryption | Absent — no field is encrypted, tokenised, or hashed before it enters a response or a log | Verified by import-graph inspection |
| TLS libraries present in the image | `openssl-dev=3.*` is installed in the base stage and `certifi>=2023.11.17` is pinned with the comment "Certificate bundle for HTTPS requests"; both support outbound TLS capability that no application code exercises | `Dockerfile` L24-L33; `src/backend/requirements.txt` L169 |

Two absences are material enough to state explicitly. **No `Strict-Transport-Security` header is set anywhere in the repository** — a repository-wide search for `strict-transport` and `hsts` returns zero matches — so even when the service is fronted by TLS, no HSTS policy is asserted to browsers. And there is no HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, no `ProxyFix` middleware, and no `X-Forwarded-Proto` handling, so the application has no awareness of whether a given request arrived over TLS. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` L34 lists "validate HTTPS readiness for Gunicorn production" as outstanding High-priority work, which corroborates that transport security is deliberately deferred to the hosting platform.

#### 6.4.4.2 Key Management

Exactly one application secret exists — `SECRET_KEY` — and its full lifecycle is:

| Lifecycle Stage | Implemented Behaviour | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Documented as "Secret key for Flask session management and security features"; purpose stated as session encryption, CSRF protection, and security-token generation | `src/backend/.env.example` L144-L147 |
| Generation | Policy only: cryptographically secure random generation, ≥32 characters, mixed case, numbers, and symbols. No generator, script, or startup validator is provided | `src/backend/.env.example` L149-L153, L267-L270 |
| Distribution | Supplied as a plain process environment variable, optionally via a git-ignored `.env` file loaded by `load_dotenv()` | `src/backend/app.py` L52, L161 |
| Loading | `os.getenv('SECRET_KEY', 'dev-key-change-in-production')` — a missing value silently yields the hard-coded fallback rather than aborting startup | `src/backend/app.py` L161 |
| Storage at rest | Not stored by the application; no vault, KMS, or secrets-manager client is integrated (`1.3 Scope` records secrets managers as "Not integrated") | Verified by manifest inspection |
| Rotation | Policy only: "Rotate keys periodically" and "Different keys for staging and production". No rotation automation, key versioning, or dual-key overlap exists | `src/backend/.env.example` L156-L159 |
| Revocation / destruction | No mechanism — there is nothing signed with the key that could be invalidated | Verified: no signing operation exists |
| Actual consumption | **None.** No code writes to `session` or issues a signed token, so the key protects nothing at present | Verified by import-graph inspection |

Leakage prevention is the one key-management dimension that is genuinely enforced, and it is enforced in three independent places:

| Exclusion Layer | Patterns Excluded | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Version control (root) | `.env`, `.env.*`, `.env.local`, `.env.development.local`, `.env.test.local`, `.env.production.local`, `*.env`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `config/secrets.*`, `secrets/`, `.secrets/`, `*.secret*`, `.credentials`, `apikeys.json` | `.gitignore` L16-L43, annotated "SECURITY: .env*, *.key, secrets/ - Prevents credential exposure" at L389 |
| Version control (backend) | A dedicated "Security Critical Files" block: `*.key`, `*.pem`, `config/secrets.py`, `secrets.py`, `*.crt`, `*.csr`, plus the `.env` family | `src/backend/.gitignore` |
| Docker build context | A section headed "ENVIRONMENT AND SECRETS (LOCALIZED SECURITY PATTERNS)" marking env-file inclusion as "Security Risk: CRITICAL", excluding `.env*`, `.flaskenv`, `config/secrets.py`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.crt`, `*.cer`, `*.der`, `id_rsa*`, `id_dsa*`, `id_ecdsa*`, `id_ed25519*`, `secrets/`, `auth.json`, `credentials.json`; a second "SECURITY AND COMPLIANCE EXCLUSIONS" section adds `.ssh/`, `known_hosts`, `.gnupg/`, `*.gpg`, `*.asc`, `database.yml`, `config/production.py`, `.security/`, `security-audit.json`, `vulnerability-report.*` | `infrastructure/docker/.dockerignore` L111-L157, L462-L490 |

Pipeline secrets are managed by the platform rather than by this repository: all three (`GITHUB_TOKEN` and the two Azure publish profiles) are referenced only through the `secrets.` context, so no credential value appears in any file. The one gap already noted in 6.4.2.6 belongs here too — the CD workflow injects only `FLASK_ENV: production` into application settings, so `SECRET_KEY` is never provisioned to the deployed instance and the fallback value would be in force.

#### 6.4.4.3 Data Masking Rules

There is no personal or sensitive data to mask, so masking in this system means **suppression of internal detail in outbound responses**. Four mechanisms implement it, and the suppression matrix below states precisely what each status code discloses:

| Response | Disclosed to Client | Withheld from Client |
|---|---|---|
| 200 `/hello` | Fixed message, ISO timestamp, `status: success`, `X-API-Version: 1.0` | Everything else — no server, framework, version, or environment detail |
| 200 `/health` | `status`, timestamp, raw `time.time()` uptime, version `1.0.0`, resolved `environment` name, `debug` flag | Process, host, and dependency detail |
| 404 | Fixed message plus the caller's own `path` and `method` | Route table, framework identity, internal paths |
| 405 | Fixed message, caller's `path`/`method`, `allowed_methods` list, `Allow` header | Handler names, internal routing detail |
| 500 | Generic "An unexpected error occurred while processing your request", timestamp, `request_id` | Exception type, exception message, stack trace, file paths — all logged server-side only |
| Generic `Exception` | Generic "An unexpected Error"/"An unexpected error occurred" envelope | Exception type and message, traceback, `request_id` (not included on this path) |
| 503 `/health` failure | **`str(e)` — the raw exception text** plus `status: unhealthy` and a timestamp | Traceback only |

The supporting controls are: removal of the `Server` header on every response (`src/backend/app.py` L237), which suppresses framework and server fingerprinting; `DEBUG`-gated traceback logging in both the 500 and generic handlers (L581-L582, L619-L620), so tracebacks never reach a client and reach the log only when debug is enabled; and a `FLASK_ENV == 'development'` gate on the process-level `sys.excepthook` traceback in `src/backend/wsgi.py`. `src/backend/tests/test_app.py` L368-L378 asserts the absence of both `Server` and `X-Powered-By` on `/hello` responses.

Two deviations are recorded rather than smoothed over. The `/health` 503 branch (`src/backend/app.py` L457-L462) places `str(e)` directly in the response body and is therefore the **only** path by which internal exception text can reach a client irrespective of `DEBUG` — `6.2 Database Design` records the same finding from the privacy perspective. And the `/health` 200 payload discloses the resolved `environment` name and `debug` flag to any anonymous caller; benign for a fixed tutorial payload, this would be an information-disclosure finding on any service that adopts the handler unchanged.

Logs are subject to the inverse rule: they deliberately carry the detail that responses withhold. Because the application never reads client IP, user agent, headers, query strings, or bodies, log records cannot contain caller-supplied sensitive data — the only caller-derived values ever logged are `request.method` and `request.path`. The startup banner does log environment fingerprint data (Python version, PID, platform, host, port) to the container streams, which is appropriate for an operator-visible channel and never exposed over HTTP.

#### 6.4.4.4 Secure Communication

Six response headers are applied to **every** response — success and error alike — by the `after_request` hook registered in `configure_security_settings` (`src/backend/app.py` L223-L253). All six are asserted by value in `src/backend/tests/test_app.py` L348-L366:

| Header | Value | Protection Provided |
|---|---|---|
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` | Prevents MIME-type sniffing of the JSON payload |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` | Blocks all framing, mitigating clickjacking |
| `X-XSS-Protection` | `1; mode=block` | Legacy browser XSS filter activation |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` | Limits referrer leakage on cross-origin navigation |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `default-src 'self'` | Restricts all resource loading to same origin |
| `X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies` | `none` | Denies Adobe cross-domain policy-file access |

The cross-origin policy is configured once, in `configure_cors_middleware` (`src/backend/app.py` L259-L288), and applies to browser callers only:

| CORS Parameter | Configured Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `origins` | `http://localhost:3000`, `http://localhost:8000` | Development origins only; both are plain HTTP |
| `methods` | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS` | Broader than the implemented route surface (`GET` only) |
| `allow_headers` | `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `X-Requested-With` | `Authorization` is permitted but never read |
| `supports_credentials` | `False` | Annotated "Secure default for stateless API" — blocks cookie/credential propagation |
| `max_age` | `86400` s | 24-hour preflight cache; delays allow-list changes reaching browsers |

Transport and network posture, stated exactly as configured:

| Dimension | Configuration | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Application bind address | `HOST` defaults to `0.0.0.0` under WSGI, `localhost` in the `__main__` development path and in `.env.example` | `wsgi.py` L105; `app.py` L721; `.env.example` L52 |
| Container listener | Gunicorn `--bind=0.0.0.0:3000`, plain HTTP | `Dockerfile` L216-L220 |
| Published ports | Development `3000:3000` and debugpy `5678:5678`; production `3001:3000` | `docker-compose.yml` L86-L87, L231 |
| Network isolation | Dedicated bridge `flask-tutorial-network` (bridge `flask-br0`), IPAM subnet `172.21.0.0/16`, gateway `172.21.0.1`, range `172.21.240.0/20`; inter-container communication enabled | `docker-compose.yml` L368-L390 |
| Host binding of the bridge | `com.docker.network.bridge.host_binding_ipv4: "0.0.0.0"` | `docker-compose.yml` L368-L378 |
| TLS termination | Not performed by the service; upstream Azure Web Apps endpoints are `https://` | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` |
| `SERVER_NAME` | Explicitly `None`, delegating host handling to the WSGI server | `wsgi.py` L161 |

Two consequences follow. Because the container serves plain HTTP and no HSTS or redirect exists, transport confidentiality depends entirely on a correctly configured front end — an environmental dependency, not a repository control. And because `0.0.0.0` is the WSGI default bind address, the process listens on all interfaces inside its network namespace; isolation is provided by the container network and the published-port mapping rather than by the bind address.

#### 6.4.4.5 Compliance Controls

**No regulatory or certification regime is named anywhere in the code or configuration.** A repository-wide search for `GDPR`, `HIPAA`, `PCI-DSS`, `SOC 2`, `ISO 27001`, `CCPA`, `FedRAMP`, `NIST`, and `CIS Benchmark` returns no matches in `src/`, `infrastructure/`, `.github/`, or any root manifest; the only `OWASP` references in the repository sit in the legacy pre-migration specification under `blitzy/documentation/`, which describes the Node.js system rather than this one. The controls below are therefore engineering-quality and supply-chain controls that the repository actually enforces, not attestations of compliance with any external framework.

**Supply-chain and code-security controls.**

| Control | Tool and Invocation | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|
| Python static analysis | Bandit (`bandit[toml]`), JSON + SARIF + `--severity-level medium` in CI; `bandit -r src/backend/` in CD | CI target path does not resolve (see 6.4.3.4); CD invocation resolves and feeds the gate |
| Dependency vulnerability scan | Safety (`safety check --json`, `--short-report`) in both CI and CD | Any Safety finding fails the CD security gate |
| Dependency audit | pip-audit (JSON + SARIF + plain) in CI | Reported and uploaded; not independently gated |
| Container image scan | Trivy (`aquasecurity/trivy-action`) against the published **digest**, severities `CRITICAL,HIGH,MEDIUM,LOW`, `exit-code: 0` | Evaluated by the summary gate: `CRITICAL > 0` fails; `HIGH > 5` or Bandit findings `> 3` warns |
| Supply-chain posture score | OSSF Scorecard (`ossf/scorecard-action@v2`, `publish_results: true`) | Reported as SARIF; not gated |
| Security lint in development | `flake8-security` with `S` in both `select` and `enable-extensions`; complexity ceilings `max-complexity = 10`, `max-annotations-complexity = 4`, `max-expression-complexity = 7` | Local and CI lint; `S101`/`S311` relaxed for tests, `S602`/`S603`/`S607` for `scripts/` and `deploy/` |
| Bandit policy | `[tool.bandit]` excludes `tests`, `venv`, `.venv`, `build`, `dist`, `.pytest_cache`, `htmlcov`; skips `B101` (assert), `B601` (paramiko), `B602` (shell=True) | `pyproject.toml` L378-L396 |
| Build attestation | `provenance: true` and `sbom: true` on `docker/build-push-action@v5`; multi-arch `linux/amd64,linux/arm64` | Published alongside the image for forensic review |
| Findings surfacing | `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2` publishes Bandit, pip-audit, Scorecard, and Trivy SARIF to GitHub code scanning | Runs with `if: always()` |
| Declared quality gate | `[tool.quality-gates]`: `coverage_threshold = 100`, `memory_limit_mb = 75`, `response_time_limit_ms = 50`, `security_scan_required = true` | `pyproject.toml` L479-L484 |
| Security test category | Dedicated pytest `security` marker in both `pytest.ini` files, plus `security_markers = security`, `security_scan_timeout = 30`, `security_report_format = json` | `pytest.ini` L97; `src/backend/pytest.ini` L39, L126, L241-L243 |

**Governance and process controls.**

| Control | Definition | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Vulnerability disclosure | A responsible-disclosure process with a named security contact and a structured report template | `CONTRIBUTING.md` L1503+ (written in the pre-migration Node.js framing) |
| Disclosure response timeline | Acknowledgment within 24 hours; investigation 3-5 days; resolution 1-2 weeks; coordinated public advisory | `CONTRIBUTING.md` security-response table |
| Security policy location | `"Security Policy"` project URL pointing at the GitHub security policy page | `pyproject.toml` L148 |
| Merge-time requirements | Contribution checklist items requiring no critical or high-severity vulnerabilities, plus a required `CI Pipeline / Security Scan` status check | `CONTRIBUTING.md` L1014-L1020, L1084 |
| Scheduled re-verification | Weekly CI cron (`'0 2 * * 1'`) described as dependency and security validation | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` L16-L18 |
| Evidence retention | Security scan reports retained 90 days; coverage/test and CD artifacts 30 days; documented default `artifact_retention_days = 30` | `ci.yml` L206; `cd.yml` L429; `pyproject.toml` L475 |
| Transitive dependency hygiene | Security-motivated lower bounds with explicit rationale comments: `Werkzeug>=3.0.1` ("security fixes"), `Jinja2>=3.1.2` ("security patches"), `MarkupSafe>=2.1.3`, `itsdangerous>=2.1.2`, `certifi>=2023.11.17`, `urllib3>=2.1.0` ("security updates") | `src/backend/requirements.txt` L157-L171 |
| Declared security tooling extra | `security = ["bandit>=1.7.5", "safety>=3.0.1", "pip-audit>=2.6.1"]` | `pyproject.toml` L124-L128 |

**Privacy compliance posture.** The strongest privacy control is structural rather than procedural: no personal data is collected, so none can be stored, exposed, or subject to an access request. `6.2 Database Design` records the supporting verification and the consequent inapplicability of data-subject-rights machinery, retention scheduling, and at-rest encryption.

**Outstanding compliance work** is explicitly scheduled rather than implied. `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` lists three High-priority security items as remaining engineering effort: dependency remediation via pip-audit and Safety (2 h), security validation covering header verification, Bandit result review, error-message disclosure checks, and Gunicorn HTTPS readiness (2 h), and production environment configuration (2 h); plus one Medium item — documenting API-key management practices for potential future integrations (1 h), noted as "not required for this simple Flask app". `1.3 Scope` reproduces the same schedule.


### 6.4.5 Security Zones, Control Matrix, and Residual Risk

Because the system has no request-level identity, its security posture is expressed almost entirely through zone boundaries and the controls that sit on them. This sub-section defines those zones, consolidates every control into a single traceable matrix, and records the residual risks that the current design accepts.

#### 6.4.5.1 Security Zone Model

Six zones are observable in the repository. Trust levels are relative descriptions of what each zone is permitted to do, derived from the configuration rather than from any classification scheme in the codebase.

| Zone | Trust Level | Boundary Control Into the Zone |
|---|---|---|
| Public client zone | Untrusted | None — any network peer that can reach the published port is admitted; no credential is requested |
| Host / published-port zone | Untrusted ingress | Docker port publication: `3000:3000` and `5678:5678` (development), `3001:3000` (production); the bridge binds `0.0.0.0` |
| Container network zone | Semi-trusted | Dedicated bridge `flask-tutorial-network` (`flask-br0`), IPAM `172.21.0.0/16`, inter-container communication enabled; only declared services are attached |
| Application runtime zone | Constrained execution | Non-root UID/GID 1000, `no-new-privileges:true`, `cap_drop: ALL` (+`SETGID`/`SETUID`), read-only root filesystem, sources at mode 444, 128 M / 0.5 CPU ceiling |
| Build and delivery zone | Privileged | GitHub Actions with encrypted secrets, `environment` protection for `staging`/`production`, blocking security gate, digest-pinned promotion |
| Developer workstation zone | Trusted-by-convention | `.gitignore` and `.dockerignore` secret exclusions, `flake8-security`/Bandit/Safety/pip-audit tooling, `.env.example` template carrying no real secret |

Two properties of this model deserve emphasis. The **only** boundary crossing that involves no authentication or authorisation whatsoever is the one that carries production traffic (public client → application runtime); every other crossing is credentialled or capability-constrained. And the debug-adapter port (5678) exists only on the development boundary — the `production` image target does not expose it and sets `FLASK_DEBUG=0`.

The diagram below shows the zones, the controls on each boundary, and the two crossings that require credentials.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Z1["Zone 1 - Public client zone - untrusted"]
        direction TB
        Browser["Browser client<br/>subject to CORS and CSP"]
        Tool["curl, probe, script or any peer<br/>CORS does not apply"]
    end

    subgraph Z2["Zone 2 - Host and published ports - untrusted ingress"]
        direction TB
        PortProd["Production mapping 3001 to 3000"]
        PortDev["Development mapping 3000 to 3000<br/>plus debugpy 5678"]
    end

    subgraph Z3["Zone 3 - Container network - semi-trusted"]
        direction TB
        Bridge["Bridge flask-tutorial-network / flask-br0<br/>subnet 172.21.0.0/16, gateway 172.21.0.1"]
        Helper["alpine 3.19 network-setup helper<br/>no application privilege"]
    end

    subgraph Z4["Zone 4 - Application runtime - constrained execution"]
        direction TB
        Init["dumb-init as PID 1<br/>forwards SIGTERM and SIGINT"]
        Gun["Gunicorn arbiter, 4 sync workers<br/>timeout 30s, recycle at 1000 requests"]
        App["Flask app: two GET rules<br/>six security headers, Server removed,<br/>16 MB body ceiling"]
        Least["UID/GID 1000, cap_drop ALL,<br/>no-new-privileges, read-only rootfs,<br/>sources mode 444, tmpfs 10M"]
    end

    subgraph Z5["Zone 5 - Build and delivery - privileged"]
        direction TB
        CI["CI: tests, Bandit, Safety, pip-audit,<br/>OSSF Scorecard, quality gate"]
        Reg["ghcr.io image with provenance and SBOM"]
        Gate["CD gate: Trivy by digest<br/>fail on CRITICAL over 0"]
        Env["GitHub environment protection<br/>staging then production"]
    end

    subgraph Z6["Zone 6 - Developer workstation - trusted by convention"]
        direction TB
        Env2[".env from .env.example<br/>git-ignored, never in build context"]
        Lint["flake8-security, Bandit, Safety, pip-audit<br/>run locally before commit"]
    end

    Browser -->|"plain HTTP, no credential requested"| PortProd
    Tool -->|"plain HTTP, no credential requested"| PortProd
    Browser --> PortDev
    PortProd --> Bridge
    PortDev --> Bridge
    Bridge --> Init --> Gun --> App
    Least -.->|"constrains every syscall<br/>and every write"| App

    Z6 -->|"commit"| CI
    CI --> Reg --> Gate --> Env
    Env ==>|"credentialled crossing:<br/>Azure publish profile"| Z4
    Reg ==>|"credentialled crossing:<br/>GITHUB_TOKEN registry login"| Gate
```

Data-flow sensitivity across these boundaries is uniformly low, which is what makes the untrusted ingress acceptable:

| Boundary Crossing | Data Carried | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| Client → application | `method` and `path` only; body ignored, headers unread | None — nothing caller-supplied is retained |
| Application → client | Literals, timestamps, uptime, version, `environment`, `debug`, generic error text | Low; `environment`/`debug` and the 503 `str(e)` are the only internal details exposed |
| Application → container streams | Method, path, status, latency, exception detail, startup fingerprint | Operator-visible; never reachable over HTTP |
| Pipeline → registry / cloud | Image layers, attestations, deployment payload | Credentialled; secrets never materialise in the repository |

#### 6.4.5.3 Residual Risk Register

Each entry is a risk the current design accepts, stated with its evidence and the condition under which it becomes material. Nothing here is speculative — every row is grounded in an observed configuration.

| Residual Risk | Evidence | When It Becomes Material |
|---|---|---|
| `SECRET_KEY` falls back to a hard-coded literal instead of failing startup, and the CD pipeline never provisions it | `app.py` L161; `cd.yml` L484, L696 inject only `FLASK_ENV` | The moment any session, signed cookie, CSRF token, or signed URL is introduced |
| No authentication or authorisation on either endpoint; the trust boundary is the network | 6.4.2, 6.4.3; `1.3 Scope` | As soon as any non-public data or mutating operation is added |
| No TLS in the application and no HSTS header anywhere | Plain `0.0.0.0:3000` bind; zero matches for `strict-transport`/`hsts` | Any deployment not fronted by a correctly configured TLS terminator |
| `apparmor:unconfined` on the production service | `docker-compose.yml` L316, with the inline "Educational" caveat | Any real production use of the Compose profile |
| `/health` discloses `environment` and `debug` to anonymous callers; the 503 branch echoes `str(e)` | `app.py` L437-L444, L457-L462 | Reuse of the handler in a service where internals are sensitive |
| 404/405 envelopes echo the caller's `path` and `method` | `app.py` L505-L506, L539-L541 | Only if the reflected value were rendered by a client without escaping |
| CI Bandit target does not resolve, and the quality gate reads a non-existent report path, degrading to a skip | `ci.yml` L158-L161, L299, L317 | Immediately — the CI security gate provides less assurance than it appears to |
| Neither workflow declares a `permissions:` block, so default `GITHUB_TOKEN` scope applies | Zero matches for `permissions:` in `ci.yml`/`cd.yml` | Any compromise of a workflow step or third-party action |
| `skip_tests` dispatch input can bypass security scanning | `cd.yml` L54 | Whenever an emergency deployment is performed |
| CORS `methods` advertises five methods against a `GET`-only route surface | `app.py` L272 | If write routes are added without revisiting the CORS policy |
| 24-hour CORS `max_age` delays allow-list changes reaching browsers | `app.py` L275 | During incident response requiring a rapid origin revocation |
| No rate limiting, quota, or throttling of any kind | `1.3 Scope`; no limiter dependency | Any internet exposure — the 30 s worker timeout and 4-worker pool are the only backpressure |
| Logs have no durable, aggregated, or tamper-evident sink | `logging.basicConfig` to streams only | Any need for post-incident forensics or audit evidence |
| `request.id` collides within the same millisecond and carries no worker/instance discriminator | `app.py` L316; corroborated in `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns` | Any attempt to use correlation IDs as audit keys |
| `LOG_LEVEL` is documented and set in container environments but never consumed | `.env.example` L116; `docker-compose.yml` environment blocks | Any attempt to reduce log verbosity to suppress sensitive output |
| Runtime dependencies are declared with lower bounds (`>=`) and no lock file or hashes | `requirements.txt`; `1.3 Scope` records no hash-pinned lock file | A malicious or broken upstream release could enter a fresh build |
| Development container exposes a debug adapter on 5678 with `--wait-for-client` | `Dockerfile` L171-L179; `docker-compose.yml` L87 | If a development Compose profile were ever run on a reachable host |

#### 6.4.5.4 Conditions That Would Make a Detailed Security Architecture Applicable

The determination in 6.4.1 is a property of the current codebase, not a permanent judgement. Each trigger below would convert one of the "not applicable" findings in this section into a genuine architectural requirement:

| Trigger | Security Architecture It Would Require |
|---|---|
| Any non-public endpoint or per-user response | Identity management, credential verification or federation, session or token lifecycle, and a `before_request` policy enforcement point — `5.4 Cross-Cutting Concerns` notes that no seam for this exists today |
| Any mutating endpoint (`POST`/`PUT`/`DELETE`) | CSRF defence (Flask-WTF is not installed), request-body validation beyond the advisory content-type warning, idempotency handling, and authorisation on the write path |
| Any persistence tier | At-rest encryption decisions, database credentials and rotation, least-privilege grants, and an audit trail with retention — `6.2 Database Design` enumerates the same trigger set |
| Any personal data collection | Lawful-basis and consent handling, data-subject-rights machinery, retention scheduling, masking in logs, and a named regulatory framework where none exists today |
| Internet exposure without an upstream terminator | Application-terminated or platform-terminated TLS with HSTS, a redirect policy, `X-Forwarded-Proto` awareness, and rate limiting |
| Multi-instance or multi-region operation | Instance-discriminating correlation IDs, a durable log sink, and shared-secret distribution across instances |
| Third-party outbound integration | Outbound credential storage, egress allow-listing, certificate validation policy, and secret rotation — `1.3 Scope` records that the application currently makes no outbound calls |
