# 7. User Interface Design

## 7.1 User Interface Assessment

**No user interface required.**

This repository implements a headless HTTP service. Its entire runtime consists of two Python modules — `src/backend/app.py` (Flask application assembly) and `src/backend/wsgi.py` (process lifecycle and WSGI exposure) — exposing exactly two `GET` routes that return `application/json` payloads. No presentation layer of any kind is delivered: there is no browser client, no server-rendered markup, no static asset pipeline, no command-line or terminal interface, and no mobile or desktop client. Consequently the design topics normally documented in this section (screen inventories, component hierarchies, view-model schemas, interaction patterns, and visual design systems) have no corresponding implementation to describe.

The remainder of this section records the evidence establishing that determination, documents the client consumption model that exists in place of a user interface, and captures the interface-adjacent provisioning already present in the codebase that would govern any client added in the future.

### 7.1.1 Determination and Evidence Basis

The determination was reached by exhaustive census of the repository — 31 non-`.git` files in total — rather than by sampling. Every category below was verified directly.

| Verification Category | What Was Checked | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Asset census | All file extensions present in the repository | Only `.md`, `.py`, `.yml`, `.txt`, `.ini`, `.toml`, `.pyc`, `.gitignore`, `.flake8`, `.example`, `.dockerignore`, and one extension-less `Dockerfile`. Zero `.html`, `.css`/`.scss`/`.less`, `.js`/`.jsx`/`.ts`/`.tsx`, `.vue`/`.svelte`, `.jinja`/`.j2`/`.hbs`/`.ejs`/`.pug`, `.svg`/`.png`/`.ico`/`.woff*`, `.dart`/`.swift`/`.kt`/`.xaml` files, and no `package.json` or `node_modules` |
| Directory census | Conventional client directories | `templates/`, `static/`, `public/`, `assets/`, `frontend/`, `web/`, `client/`, and `ui/` do not exist anywhere. The only directories beneath `src/` are `src/backend/` and `src/backend/tests/` |
| Rendering-symbol census | Template and static-file APIs across all Python, TOML, INI, and YAML sources | Zero occurrences of `render_template`, `render_template_string`, `send_from_directory`, `send_file`, or `url_for(`; zero occurrences of `<html` or `<!DOCTYPE` |
| Dependency manifests | `requirements.txt`, `requirements-dev.txt`, `src/backend/requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml` | No frontend framework or bundler (React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, Next, Vite, webpack, Babel, Tailwind, Bootstrap, jQuery, htmx); no dashboard toolkit (Streamlit, Gradio, Dash, Panel, Bokeh, Plotly); no interactive API-documentation UI (Flasgger, Flask-RESTX, apispec, Swagger UI, ReDoc, Connexion); no terminal-UI library (Rich, Textual, curses, urwid, blessed, Typer, prompt_toolkit); no desktop toolkit (Tkinter, PyQt, PySide, Kivy, wxPython, Eel, pywebview); no notebook stack |
| Delivery pipelines | `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | Zero references to `npm`, `yarn`, `node-version`, webpack, Vite, Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, Puppeteer, Lighthouse, axe, Storybook, Percy, or any browser runner — neither pipeline contains a UI build, UI lint, or browser-test stage |
| Container assets | `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml` | Five build stages (`base` L9, `dependencies` L64, `application` L101, `development` L137, `production` L184) are all Python-only; no Node/asset-build stage, no nginx or static file server, no `dist/` copy. Compose defines `flask-tutorial-dev`, `flask-tutorial-prod`, and an `alpine:3.19` network helper — no frontend service |
| Test suite | `src/backend/tests/test_app.py`, `src/backend/tests/test_wsgi.py` | Zero browser, DOM, or HTML-parsing assertions. Every endpoint is exercised through the programmatic `flask.testing.FlaskClient` (`test_app.py` L47), e.g. `client.get('/hello')` L117, `client.get('/health')` L196, `client.get('/nonexistent-route')` L243 |

Three findings deserve explicit clarification because they could otherwise be mistaken for UI evidence:

- **Jinja2 is present only as a transitive Flask dependency.** `src/backend/requirements.txt` L158–L159 pins `Jinja2>=3.1.2` (annotated "Flask templating engine with security patches") and `MarkupSafe>=2.1.3`, and L161 pins `click>=8.1.7` ("Command line interface library used by Flask"). None of these packages is imported or exercised by application code; no template file exists for Jinja to render.
- **Flask's default template and static conventions are unused.** `src/backend/app.py` L93 constructs the application with `app = Flask(__name__)`, which nominally establishes `templates/` and `static/` lookup paths, but neither directory is ever created or populated. The related configuration keys are inert: `EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING` is set in the development profiles (`app.py` L187, `wsgi.py` L181) and `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT = 31536000` is set in the WSGI production profile (`wsgi.py` L170–L171), yet no template is loaded and no static file is served.
- **The only HTML in the system is generated developer reporting, and it is not committed.** `pytest.ini` L49 configures `--cov-report=html:htmlcov` and L69 requires `pytest-html`; `src/backend/pytest.ini` L22/L26/L27 add `--html=pytest_report.html --self-contained-html` and L161–L163 title it "Flask Migration Tutorial - Test Results". `.gitignore` L143 states that "Test results and coverage reports are generated artifacts, not source code" and ignores the resulting outputs (L147, L150–L153). These artifacts are a test-tooling by-product consumed by engineers and CI, not an interface of the application under specification.

This determination is consistent with the already-documented system boundary. Section 1.3.2.1 lists "Frontend / user interface" as an explicit exclusion ("No client application, bundler, or asset pipeline in the repository"), alongside "Server-side templating and static assets" and "Interactive API documentation". Section 5.1.1.3 defines the single client boundary as "HTTP/1.1 requests to `/hello`, `/health`; JSON responses", and Section 5.1.4 classifies the counterparty as an "Inbound API consumer".

### 7.1.2 Client Consumption Model in Place of a User Interface

Because no interface is shipped, the human-facing surface is whatever the operator's own tool renders from the JSON response. Two endpoints and four error classes constitute the complete externally observable contract, and all six produce `application/json`.

| Surface | Location | Response Content Type | Payload Fields |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /hello` | `src/backend/app.py` L367 | `application/json` (set explicitly at L403) | `message` (literal `Hello world`), `timestamp` (ISO-8601), `status` (`success`) |
| `GET /health` | `src/backend/app.py` L426 | `application/json` | `status`, `timestamp`, `uptime`, `version`, `environment`, `debug` |
| 404 handler | `src/backend/app.py` L479 | `application/json` | `status`, `error`, `message`, `path`, `method`, `timestamp` |
| 405 handler | `src/backend/app.py` L518 | `application/json` | `status`, `error`, `message`, `allowed_methods` (plus `Allow` header) |
| 500 handler | `src/backend/app.py` L556 | `application/json` | `status`, `error`, `message`, `timestamp`, `request_id` |
| Unhandled `Exception` handler | `src/backend/app.py` L602 | `application/json` | `status`, `error`, `message`, `timestamp` |

Response construction is uniformly serialisation, never rendering:

```python
response = jsonify(response_data)                        # src/backend/app.py L399
response.headers['Content-Type'] = 'application/json'    # src/backend/app.py L403
response.headers['X-API-Version'] = '1.0'                # src/backend/app.py L404
```

The documented ways a person or program reaches these surfaces are all client-side tooling that the repository does not itself contain:

| Access Path | How It Is Documented | Nature of the "Display" |
|---|---|---|
| `curl` command matrix | `README.md` L217–L230 (basic request, `-i` with headers, an undefined route to exercise the 404 handler, `Accept: application/json`); `src/backend/README.md` L223–L225, L245, L263, L268, L385–L386, and verbose troubleshooting at L843–L844 | Raw JSON and headers printed to the terminal by cURL |
| Browser address bar | `README.md` L207–L215 ("Browser Access: Open: http://localhost:5000/hello"); `src/backend/README.md` L220–L221 instructs the reader to navigate to `/hello` "in any web browser to see the JSON 'Hello world' response" | The browser's built-in JSON/plain-text viewer. The application contributes no markup, styling, or script to this view |
| Startup banner | `README.md` L191–L209 shows the console banner listing the listening URL, available endpoints, testing commands, and browser access hint | Text written to stdout by the process, not an interactive interface |
| Python `requests` snippet | `README.md` L317–L322 | Illustrative consumer code in documentation only; no such module exists in the repository |
| JavaScript `fetch` snippet | `README.md` L325–L329 | Illustrative consumer code in documentation only; it is the sole JavaScript in the repository and it lives inside a Markdown fence |
| Programmatic test client | `src/backend/tests/test_app.py` (`FlaskClient`, L47 and subsequent `client.get(...)` calls) | Assertions against response objects; no rendering occurs |
| Container liveness probe | `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` `HEALTHCHECK` invoking `curl -f` against `/hello` | Machine-only consumption; exit status, not display |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Consumers["Documented consumers - none implemented in this repository"]
        Curl["curl and curl -i<br/>README.md and backend README.md"]
        Browser["Web browser address bar<br/>native JSON viewer only"]
        Requests["Python requests snippet<br/>documentation example"]
        Fetch["JavaScript fetch snippet<br/>documentation example"]
        TestClient["flask.testing.FlaskClient<br/>src/backend/tests"]
        Probe["Container HEALTHCHECK<br/>curl -f /hello"]
    end

    subgraph Service["Flask WSGI service - src/backend"]
        Hello["GET /hello<br/>app.py L367"]
        Health["GET /health<br/>app.py L426"]
        Errors["404, 405, 500, Exception<br/>app.py L470 to L632"]
    end

    Payload["application/json only<br/>no HTML, CSS, JS, templates or static assets"]

    Curl --> Hello
    Browser --> Hello
    Requests --> Hello
    Fetch --> Hello
    TestClient --> Hello
    TestClient --> Health
    Curl --> Health
    Probe --> Hello
    Curl --> Errors
    Hello --> Payload
    Health --> Payload
    Errors --> Payload
```

One documentation inconsistency is relevant to any future client author: the root `README.md` "API Documentation" block (L283–L330) presents `GET /hello` as returning `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8` with an 11-byte `Hello world` body, and its `fetch` example correspondingly calls `response.text()`. The implementation at `src/backend/app.py` L399–L403 returns a JSON object. `src/backend/README.md` L216–L232 documents the JSON contract and therefore matches the code. Client code should be written against the JSON contract.

### 7.1.3 Applicability of the User Interface Design Topics

Each topic that this section would ordinarily document is recorded below with its applicability and the supporting evidence, so that the absence is explicit rather than implied.

| Topic | Applicability | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Core UI technologies | Not applicable | No UI framework, bundler, styling system, state-management library, template engine consumer, or component library appears in any manifest (`requirements.txt`, `requirements-dev.txt`, `src/backend/requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`) |
| UI use cases | Not applicable | The only documented user workflows are command invocations — running the server (`python wsgi.py`, `flask run`, `gunicorn wsgi:application`), exercising endpoints with `curl -i`, running `pytest`, and starting Compose services. None involves a graphical or interactive interface |
| UI / backend interaction boundaries | Not applicable as a UI boundary; the equivalent boundary is HTTP/JSON | The service boundary is a stateless, unauthenticated HTTP/1.1 request-response exchange over two `GET` routes, described in 7.1.2 and corroborated by Section 5.1.1.3. No client-side data-fetching layer, API client module, or generated SDK exists in the repository |
| UI schemas | Not applicable | There are no component props, view models, form definitions, or client-side validation schemas. The only schemas in the system are the flat JSON response bodies enumerated in 7.1.2, constructed inline as Python dictionaries; no JSON Schema, OpenAPI document, or serialiser class defines them |
| Screens required | None exist | No screen, page, view, layout, or route-to-view mapping is defined anywhere. Werkzeug URL rules resolve only to two JSON-emitting view functions (`hello_route_handler` L368, `health_check_handler` L427) |
| User interactions | Not applicable | No event handlers, forms, inputs, navigation, keyboard handling, focus management, or client-side feedback mechanisms exist. All interaction is a single HTTP `GET`; `POST`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` appear only in the CORS method allow-list and resolve through the 405 handler |
| Visual design considerations | Not applicable | No stylesheet, design token, theme, colour palette, typography definition, icon, image, font, or responsive breakpoint exists in the repository. Section 1.3.1.2 additionally records that no localisation or internationalisation is scoped, so no text-direction or locale-formatting concerns arise |
| Accessibility considerations | Not applicable | With no rendered markup there is no semantic structure, ARIA surface, contrast ratio, or focus order to specify, and no accessibility linting or auditing tool is configured in either pipeline |

The nearest thing the codebase offers to "presentation" is the emoji-prefixed structured log line emitted to stdout and stderr for operator visibility — for example the request-received and request-completed entries produced by the `before_request`/`after_request` hooks (`src/backend/app.py` L299–L352). These are diagnostic log records consumed via container logs, not an interface, and Section 5.1.3.4 documents container logs as the sole telemetry sink.

### 7.1.4 Interface Provisioning Available to a Future Client

Although no interface exists, the service already carries browser-directed configuration. These are the constraints a future front-end would inherit, and they are documented here so that adding a client does not require rediscovering them.

| Provision | Configured Value | Location | Consequence for a Future Client |
|---|---|---|---|
| CORS origin allow-list | `http://localhost:3000`, `http://localhost:8000` (annotated "Development origins") | `src/backend/app.py` L270–L276, applied at L279 | A browser client served from any other origin — including the deployed Azure Web App hostnames — is rejected until the allow-list is extended |
| CORS methods / headers | `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`; `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `X-Requested-With` | `src/backend/app.py` L271–L273 | Preflight succeeds for methods that no route actually implements; only `GET` resolves to a handler |
| Credentialed requests | `supports_credentials: False` (annotated "Secure default for stateless API") | `src/backend/app.py` L274 | Cookie- or credential-bearing cross-origin requests are unsupported by design |
| Preflight cache | `max_age: 86400` | `src/backend/app.py` L275 | Browsers may cache the preflight result for 24 hours |
| Framing policy | `X-Frame-Options: DENY` | `src/backend/app.py` L241 | The service's responses cannot be embedded in a frame or iframe by any host page |
| Content policy | `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'` | `src/backend/app.py` L245 | A fixed, code-level policy with no per-route override mechanism; any future asset origins would require changing this default |
| MIME and referrer policy | `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies: none`; `Server` header removed | `src/backend/app.py` L237, L240–L247 | Applied to every response, including error responses, independent of route |
| Client-visible observability | `X-Request-ID` and `X-Response-Time` on every response; `X-API-Version: 1.0` on `/hello` | `src/backend/app.py` L342, L350, L404 | A client can surface correlation IDs and server-side timing without additional endpoints |
| Static-asset serving | Not enabled in practice; `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT = 31536000` present but inert | `src/backend/wsgi.py` L171 | Serving bundled assets from this process would work through Flask's default `static/` convention, but no such directory or route exists today |
| Host/port conventions | Application defaults `HOST=0.0.0.0`, `PORT=8000` (`wsgi.py`); container `EXPOSE 3000` and Gunicorn `--bind=0.0.0.0:3000`; Compose publishes `3000:3000` (dev) and `3001:3000` (prod); documentation variously cites 5000, 3000, and 8000 | `src/backend/wsgi.py`; `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` L120, L220; `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` L86, L231; `README.md`, `src/backend/README.md` | A client's base URL must be configurable; the repository has no single canonical port, and the CORS allow-list matches only ports 3000 and 8000 |

## 7.2 References

### 7.2.1 Repository Files Examined

# 8. Infrastructure

## 8.1 Deployment Environment

Detailed Infrastructure Architecture **is applicable** for this system. Although the delivered application is a single-endpoint educational Flask service, the repository carries a substantive, non-trivial deployment-infrastructure layer expressed entirely as code:

| Infrastructure Asset | Size | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` | 291 lines, 5 stages | Image build definition (dev + prod variants) |
| `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` | 562 lines, 3 services | Single-host service composition and hardening |
| `infrastructure/docker/.dockerignore` | 762 lines | Build-context reduction and secret exclusion |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | 340 lines, 3 jobs | Validation and quality gates |
| `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | 1,082 lines, 5 jobs | Image publish, scan, and two-environment deploy |

One qualification governs every statement in this section and is repeated where it materially changes an assessment: **the infrastructure is defined-as-code but has never been provisioned or executed against live cloud resources.** `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` records the project at 85 of 100 estimated hours and lists, among the outstanding "Human Inputs Needed", both *Docker Registry Setup* ("Configure container registry credentials for Python containers, push Docker images to registry") at Medium priority / 1 hour and *Production Deployment* ("Deploy Flask app to chosen platform, configure production Gunicorn environment variables") at High priority / 0.5 hours. Only three distinct secrets are referenced across both workflows, and none are set in the repository. Section 3.4 reaches the same conclusion from the service-integration angle: the CD pipeline is structurally complete but not operable as committed. Consequently this section documents the **designed** environment faithfully and marks each capability as *implemented*, *declared-but-inert*, or *absent*.

### 8.1.1 Target Environment Assessment

#### 8.1.1.1 Environment Type

The target environment is **hybrid multi-provider by role, not by redundancy**. Three distinct execution surfaces plus one artifact plane are defined, and each provider performs a single non-overlapping function — there is no failover relationship between them.

| Surface | Provider / Platform | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Local development & prod simulation | Developer-owned Docker Engine | `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` |
| Build / test / deploy control plane | GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners | `ci.yml`, `cd.yml` (`runs-on`) |
| Container artifact plane | GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`) | `cd.yml` L79 `REGISTRY: ghcr.io` |
| Application runtime | Azure App Service (Linux, container) | `cd.yml` L477, L689 `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` |

No on-premises hosts, virtual machines, or IaaS resources appear anywhere in the repository. There is no AWS or GCP service reference in any executable file — the strings `aws`, `gcp`, `k8s`, `terraform`, and `helm` occur only as *exclusion patterns* inside `infrastructure/docker/.dockerignore` and as advisory prose in `src/backend/README.md`. The candidate platforms named in documentation (Heroku, Render, Railway, DigitalOcean App Platform in `README.md`; Heroku/Render/Railway again in `Project Guide.md`) are **not** the platform the pipeline actually targets; the deployment target of record is Azure App Service.

A second, mutually inconsistent Azure path exists in documentation only. `README.md` (Deployment section, L474-L664) describes a *code/buildpack* deployment — `az webapp create --runtime "PYTHON|3.12"` with a Startup Command of `gunicorn wsgi:app` and `az webapp deployment source config-local-git` — whereas `cd.yml` implements a *container* deployment that supplies an `images:` reference pinned to a registry digest. These are alternative, non-composable delivery models for the same service; only the container path is automated.

    subgraph Workstation["Developer Workstation - Docker Engine and Compose"]
        NetSetup["flask-network-setup<br/>alpine:3.19 utility"]
        DevSvc["flask-tutorial-dev<br/>target development<br/>ports 3000 and 5678"]
        ProdSvc["flask-tutorial-prod<br/>target production<br/>host 3001 to container 3000"]

#### 8.1.1.2 Geographic Distribution Requirements

**No geographic distribution requirement is declared or configured anywhere in the repository.** This is a verified absence, not an omission in the documentation:

- No Azure region, resource group, App Service plan, or SKU appears in any file. A repository-wide search for `sku`, `location`, `region`, `resource-group`, and `az webapp` across `.github/workflows/` returns zero matches — the deploy action supplies only an app name and a publish profile.
- The two runtime endpoints use default platform hostnames (`flask-tutorial-staging.azurewebsites.net`, `flask-tutorial.azurewebsites.net`), so the serving region is implicitly whatever region the pre-existing App Service plan occupies.
- There is no CDN, Front Door, Traffic Manager, custom DNS, load balancer, or any multi-region construct. Section 3.4 independently confirms the absence of CDN, DNS, and load-balancing services.
- The local surface is explicitly single-host: the Compose bridge sets `host_binding_ipv4: "0.0.0.0"` and a single private subnet (`docker-compose.yml` L368-L394).

The one deliberate portability decision is at the **image** level rather than the geographic level: `cd.yml` L215-L239 builds for `linux/amd64,linux/arm64`, so the same digest can run on either processor architecture.

#### 8.1.1.3 Resource Requirements and Sizing Guidelines

Three independent sizing statements exist in the repository and they agree on a ~75 MB working-set target.

**Host baseline** — the only explicit host sizing table, `README.md` L66-L74:

| Component | Minimum | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.12.0 | Latest 3.12.x |
| pip | 23.0.0 | Latest |
| Memory | 75 MB | 150 MB |
| Disk | 100 MB | 200 MB |
| Docker | Optional | Latest stable |

**Container runtime envelope** — `docker-compose.yml` L279-L299, applied to `flask-tutorial-prod` only:

| Control | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Memory limit | 128 M | Hard ceiling |
| CPU limit | 0.5 cores | Hard ceiling |
| Memory reservation | 75 M | Scheduling floor |
| CPU reservation | 0.25 cores | Scheduling floor |

The development service declares **no** `deploy.resources` block at all, so `flask-tutorial-dev` runs unbounded on the host — a deliberate asymmetry given that the dev service additionally installs `requirements-dev.txt` at container start (`docker-compose.yml` L115-L127). The runtime is corroborated by `pyproject.toml` L461-L465 `[tool.memory-monitor]` (`limit_mb = 75`, `growth_limit_mb = 5`) and by `src/backend/README.md` L952-L958, which states startup under 2 seconds, memory under 75 MB, and response time under 50 ms.

**Storage footprint** — all figures are author-documented in the artifacts themselves:

| Item | Documented size | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Development image | ~200-250 MB | `Dockerfile` educational notes L222-L291 |
| Production image | ~100-120 MB | `Dockerfile` educational notes L222-L291 |
| Build context after exclusions | < 25 MB (from ~500 MB) | `.dockerignore` L751-L756 |
| Named cache volumes | 4 (venv + pip, per environment) | `docker-compose.yml` L401-L440 |

**Compute/concurrency sizing.** The production stage fixes concurrency at build time: `Dockerfile` L216 sets `GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS` with `--workers=4 --worker-class=sync --worker-connections=1000`, and the Compose production command (L255-L264) independently passes `--workers 4`. Because the worker class is `sync`, four workers means **four concurrent in-flight requests**, regardless of the `--worker-connections=1000` value, which is meaningful only for async worker classes. The `src/backend/README.md` claim of "Concurrent Requests: 100+" (L952-L958) therefore describes queued throughput on a trivial handler rather than parallelism.

`src/backend/.env.example` L128-L138 provides the only explicit worker-sizing guidance in the repository:

| Workload profile | Recommended workers | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| CPU-bound | = CPU cores | Documented guidance |
| I/O-bound | 2 × cores + 1 | Documented guidance |
| Memory-constrained | Reduce to fit RAM | Documented guidance |
| Single-core host | 1-2 maximum | Documented guidance |

The same file notes that containers should account for CPU limits and that Azure Web Apps workers should be adjusted to the pricing tier's CPU allocation. The declared `WORKERS` variable is validated in documentation to the range 1-8 (`.env.example` L141), but is **not read by `app.py` or `wsgi.py`** — actual worker count comes from the Gunicorn command line, so this variable is documentation-only.

**Network and port surface.** Four different port conventions coexist across the repository; this is a genuine configuration drift that any deployment must reconcile:

| Port | Where it applies | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 3000 | Container `EXPOSE`, dev/prod container listen port | `Dockerfile` L120; `.env.example` L38 |
| 5678 | `debugpy` remote-debug listener (dev only) | `Dockerfile` L171; Compose L87 |
| 3001 | Host binding for the local prod simulation | Compose L230-L231 |
| 8000 | Value injected by the Azure deploy steps | `cd.yml` L484, L697 |

The 8000/3000 divergence is the operationally significant one: the image declares and listens on 3000 while the CD deploy steps set `PORT: 8000`. Two further defects compound it — the `env:` blocks on the `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` steps set variables in the **runner** process, not App Service application settings, so they never reach the container; and `README.md` L640-L650 documents a `PORT` default of 5000, matching neither. Section 1.3 also records this three-way port divergence.

#### 8.1.1.4 Compliance and Regulatory Requirements

**No regulatory or compliance regime is declared anywhere in this repository.** An exhaustive search for GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001, FedRAMP, and CCPA returns zero matches across all file types. Every occurrence of the word "compliance" in the repository refers to code style or packaging standards — PEP 8 conformance in `ci.yml` L85 and `README.md` L889, and PEP 518/621 packaging conformance in `pyproject.toml` L491-L502.

The de-facto compliance posture follows from the system's shape rather than from a stated obligation:

| Factor | Observed state | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Persistent data | None — no datastore configured | No data-residency or retention obligation |
| Personal data | None — single static JSON response | No subject-rights or consent surface |
| Authentication | None — no authn/authz implemented | No credential-handling obligation |
| Secrets at rest | Excluded from images and git | Reduces disclosure exposure |

`src/backend/.env.example` L164-L194 confirms the first three points explicitly: `DATABASE_URL`, `SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI`, `JWT_SECRET_KEY`, `API_KEY`, `REDIS_URL`, and `CELERY_BROKER_URL` are all present but commented out and annotated as not used in the tutorial. Secret exclusion is enforced in two independent layers — `.gitignore` L15-L38 (`.env*`, `secrets/`, `*.secret*`, `config/secrets.*`) and `.dockerignore` L110-L157 (`.env*`, `*.key`, `*.pem`, `*.p12`, `*.crt`, `id_rsa*`, `credentials.json`, with the stated principle at L119 that environment variables are provided at container runtime, not build time).

Attestation and audit primitives that *do* exist, and which would support a future compliance claim, are: `provenance: true` and `sbom: true` on the image build (`cd.yml` L215-L239); SARIF upload to GitHub code scanning from both workflows; `ossf/scorecard-action@v2` with `publish_results: true` (`ci.yml` L179); 90-day retention on security and deployment-report artifacts; and a declared security-policy URL in `pyproject.toml` L142-L148. Counterweights that would fail a real audit are equally clear: `security_opt: apparmor:unconfined` on the production Compose service (L314-L316, self-annotated as educational), no `permissions:` block in either workflow, no TLS or certificate configuration of any kind, and no `SECURITY.md` despite the declared policy URL.

### 8.1.2 Environment Management

#### 8.1.2.1 Infrastructure as Code Approach

**There is no infrastructure-as-code layer in this repository.** This is established by exhaustive negative evidence: a repository-wide search for `*.tf`, `*.tfvars`, `*.bicep`, ARM/CloudFormation JSON templates, `Chart.yaml`, Kubernetes manifests, Ansible playbooks, `Vagrantfile`, `Makefile`, shell scripts, `Procfile`, and systemd units returns **exactly three YAML files in the entire repository** — `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.github/workflows/cd.yml`, and `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml`. The `infrastructure/` directory contains exactly one child directory, `infrastructure/docker/`, and no first-order files. Section 3.6 records the same finding from the toolchain perspective.

The practical consequences are precise:

| Concern | Status | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Azure resource creation | Manual / out-of-band | App Service, plan, region, SKU must pre-exist |
| Networking and TLS | Manual | No VNet, no cert automation, platform defaults only |
| Registry configuration | Manual | Package visibility and access set in GitHub UI |
| Secret provisioning | Manual | 3 secrets entered by an operator |

`docker-compose.yml` is correctly classified as **host-level service composition**, not infrastructure provisioning: it declares containers, one bridge network, and five named volumes on a machine that already exists. Similarly, the use of `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` with a publish profile is a *deployment* mechanism that presupposes a provisioned Web App — the action cannot create one. `Project Guide.md` reflects this division of labour by crediting 15 hours to "Docker containerization" and 15 hours to "CI/CD pipelines" as complete, while leaving registry setup and production deployment as human tasks.

#### 8.1.2.2 Configuration Management Strategy

Configuration follows a twelve-factor environment-variable model with **four independent layers**, applied in increasing order of precedence:

| Layer | Mechanism | Location |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Image defaults | `ENV` instructions | `Dockerfile` L46-L55, L141-L143, L190-L198 |
| 2. Compose overrides | `environment:` maps | `docker-compose.yml` L55-L84, L196-L227 |
| 3. Local developer file | `.env` loaded by `python-dotenv` | documented by `src/backend/.env.example` |
| 4. Platform injection | App Service application settings | intended by `cd.yml` L481-L490, L695-L705 |

Layer 1 establishes the production-safe baseline in the `base` stage (`FLASK_ENV=production`, `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`, `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, `PORT=3000`, `HOST=0.0.0.0`) and is then specialised per stage — the `development` stage sets `FLASK_ENV=development`, `FLASK_DEBUG=1`, `LOG_LEVEL=debug` and re-enables bytecode writing, while the `production` stage sets `FLASK_DEBUG=0`, `LOG_LEVEL=info`, and the eight Gunicorn tuning variables.

`src/backend/.env.example` is the authoritative configuration contract, documenting seven active variables with defaults, validation rules, and usage:

| Variable | Documented default | Validation |
|---|---|---|
| `PORT` | 3000 | Integer 1024-65535 |
| `HOST` | localhost | Hostname, IP, or 0.0.0.0 |
| `FLASK_ENV` | production | development / production / testing |
| `FLASK_DEBUG` | False | Truthy: true, 1, yes, on |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | info | error / warn / info / debug |
| `WORKERS` | 1 | 1-8 (documentation-only) |
| `SECRET_KEY` | — | ≥ 32 chars, high entropy |

The file also carries per-platform recipes (L196-L231) for Heroku (`PORT=5000`), Render (`PORT=10000`), Railway (`PORT=3333`), Azure Web Apps (`PORT=8000`, `WORKERS=2`, `HOST=0.0.0.0`), and Docker (`PORT=3000`, `WORKERS=2`), each noting that the platform supplies `PORT` automatically. Its `SECRET_KEY` guidance is the repository's only secret-management policy: cryptographically secure generation, never hardcoded, unique per environment, stored in secure environment-variable management, rotated periodically, and different between staging and production.

**Layer 4 is defective as committed.** The `env:` blocks attached to the two `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` steps set variables inside the GitHub runner process; they are not translated into App Service application settings and therefore never reach the deployed container. Nothing else in the pipeline configures app settings — there is no `az webapp config appsettings set` call and no `az` CLI usage at all. In its committed form the container would run entirely on its baked-in `ENV` defaults, listening on 3000 rather than the intended 8000.

#### 8.1.2.3 Environment Promotion Strategy

Four promotion stages are defined, but only two of them are *managed* environments. GitHub deployment environments exist for `staging` and `production` only (`cd.yml` L444-L446, L635-L637); there is no dev, QA, or UAT environment — pre-merge work happens entirely on the developer's Docker host.

| Stage | Trigger | Approval surface |
|---|---|---|
| Local development | `docker compose up flask-tutorial-dev` | None |
| Local prod simulation | `docker compose up flask-tutorial-prod` | None |
| Staging | Automatic on CI success (branch `main`) | `environment: staging` |
| Production | Manual `workflow_dispatch` only | `environment: production` |

Two promotion characteristics deserve emphasis. First, the local prod-simulation service is a genuine pre-merge gate: it builds the same `production` target, publishes on host port 3001, and applies the full hardening set (read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, resource ceilings), so a developer can validate the production image locally before pushing. Second, production is reachable **only** by manual dispatch. The `deploy_production` job's condition (`cd.yml` L631-L633) requires either `github.event_name == 'release' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` or a dispatch with `environment == 'production'`; for a `release: published` event `github.ref` is `refs/tags/<tag>`, so the release branch of that condition can never be satisfied.

A related gap sits upstream of promotion: `ci.yml` path filters (L3-L20) limit push-triggered runs to `src/backend/**`, `tests/**`, `requirements*.txt`, `pytest.ini`, and `pyproject.toml`. Changes confined to `infrastructure/**` or `.github/workflows/**` therefore do **not** trigger CI, and because `cd.yml` is gated on a successful CI `workflow_run`, an infrastructure-only change does not reach staging either. The declared `tests/**` filter matches no existing path — the tests live under `src/backend/tests/`.

#### 8.1.2.4 Backup and Disaster Recovery

**No backup or disaster-recovery capability exists in this repository.** A search across all Markdown, YAML, TOML, text, and example files for `backup`, `disaster`, `restore`, `failover`, `RPO`, and `RTO` produces a single match — `restore-keys` in the `actions/cache` step of `ci.yml` L70, which is pip cache resolution, not data restoration. There is no RPO, RTO, backup schedule, snapshot policy, restore runbook, or failover target defined anywhere.

For this system that absence is architecturally coherent rather than negligent, because there is no state to protect:

| Asset | Durability model | Recovery action |
|---|---|---|
| Application code | Git history on GitHub | Re-clone |
| Container image | `ghcr.io`, immutable digest tags | Re-deploy prior digest |
| Runtime state | None — stateless request handler | Not applicable |
| Named volumes | Caches only (pip, venv) | Rebuilt on next start |

The four named volumes (`venv_cache_dev`, `venv_cache_prod`, `pip_cache_dev`, `pip_cache_prod`, `docker-compose.yml` L401-L440) hold only reconstructible dependency caches, and both production cache volumes are additionally mounted `read_only: true` (L234-L245). A fifth volume, `flask_shared_data`, is declared with a bind device of `${PWD}/data` but is **never mounted by any service**, and that host directory does not exist — it is inert.

The one genuine recovery asset the pipeline does provide is **digest pinning**: both deploy steps reference the image as `${REGISTRY}/${IMAGE_NAME}@${{ needs.build_and_publish.outputs.image_digest }}` rather than a mutable tag, so re-running an earlier successful workflow — or dispatching a deploy against a previously published digest — reproduces a byte-identical runtime. This is undermined at the *build* layer, however, because no dependency lockfile exists anywhere in the repository: all five entries in `requirements.txt` use `>=` constraints, so rebuilding from source does not reproduce a prior image even though redeploying a prior digest does.

#### 8.1.2.5 Maintenance Procedures

Maintenance is defined at three levels, all of them repository-resident:

| Procedure | Mechanism | Cadence |
|---|---|---|
| Dependency/vulnerability sweep | `ci.yml` `schedule: '0 2 * * 1'` | Weekly, Monday 02:00 UTC |
| OS package refresh | `apk update && apk upgrade` in base stage | Every image rebuild |
| Python dependency refresh | Unpinned `>=` constraints resolved at build | Every image rebuild |
| Local operations runbook | `docker-compose.yml` L451-L562 | On demand |

The weekly cron is the only automated maintenance trigger; it re-runs the full CI matrix including Bandit, Safety, and pip-audit, so newly disclosed advisories surface without a code change. Because the base stage upgrades Alpine packages and the dependencies stage resolves `>=` constraints on every build, patch adoption is automatic but non-deterministic — the same commit built on two dates yields different dependency sets.

`docker-compose.yml` L451-L562 embeds a 110-line operations runbook covering service inspection (`docker-compose ps`, `logs -f`, `exec sh`), scaling experiments (`up --scale flask-tutorial-dev=2`), network and volume inspection, live resource observation (`docker stats $(docker-compose ps -q)`), teardown (`down --volumes --remove-orphans`), and six container-security verification commands including capability inspection via `/proc/self/status` and a read-only filesystem probe. Two of its documented procedures cannot be executed as written: the load-generation step uses `ab` (Apache Bench), which is not installed in any image or declared in any manifest, and the referenced `safety check` runs only if development dependencies are present.

There is no automated dependency-update mechanism: `.github/` contains `ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, and `workflows/` — no `dependabot.yml`, no `renovate.json`, and no `CODEOWNERS`.


## 8.2 Cloud Services

Cloud services **are applicable** to this system. Two cloud providers are referenced from executable pipeline code, each in a single, non-overlapping role: GitHub supplies the build, artifact, and security-reporting plane, and Microsoft Azure App Service supplies the application runtime. Section 3.4 catalogues these as service integrations with their credential requirements; this sub-section documents them as an infrastructure architecture — selection, service inventory, availability design, cost, and cloud-layer security.

### 8.2.1 Cloud Provider Selection and Justification

No architecture decision record, RFC, or trade-off document exists anywhere in the repository, so provider selection is documented here **as observed**, with the rationale that is inferable from the artifacts themselves rather than asserted.

| Provider | Role | Inferable rationale from artifacts |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub | Source, CI/CD, registry, scanning | Zero-additional-credential path — same identity as source |
| Azure App Service | Container runtime (staging + prod) | Only cloud runtime with an executable deploy step |

The GitHub choice is self-reinforcing and visible in the code: `pyproject.toml` L142-L148 declares the project home, repository, and CI/CD-pipeline URLs on `github.com`; `cd.yml` L79 sets `IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}` so the image namespace is derived from the repository itself; and the registry login at L167-L174 authenticates with `github.actor` and `secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` — the automatically provisioned workflow token — meaning no separate registry account, PAT, or key management is introduced. `cd.yml` L79 fixes `REGISTRY: ghcr.io`; no alternative registry is parameterised.

The Azure choice is the pipeline's, not the documentation's, and the repository is internally inconsistent about it:

| Source | Platform named | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | Azure App Service | Executable — `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` |
| `README.md` L474-L664 | Heroku, Azure, Railway, DigitalOcean | Documentation only |
| `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` | Heroku / Render / Railway | Outstanding human task |
| `src/backend/README.md` L908-L930 | AWS, Google Cloud, Azure | Advisory prose |

Only the Azure path is automated, and only in container form. The `README.md` Azure instructions describe the *code/buildpack* model (`az webapp create --runtime "PYTHON|3.12"` with a Gunicorn startup command), which is a different and non-composable delivery mechanism from the digest-pinned container the pipeline actually deploys. Neither Heroku nor Render nor Railway nor DigitalOcean appears in any executable file — the required Heroku support files (`Procfile`, `runtime.txt`) named in `README.md` do not exist in the repository.

There is no cross-provider redundancy: GitHub is a single point of failure for build and image distribution, and Azure is a single point of failure for serving.

### 8.2.2 Core Services Required with Versions

**Managed cloud services.** All version pins below are the literal values in the workflows.

| Service | Version / pin | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub-hosted runner | `ubuntu-latest` (floating) | All 8 jobs across both workflows |
| GitHub Container Registry | `ghcr.io` (no version) | Multi-arch image + attestation storage |
| GitHub code scanning | `codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2` | SARIF ingestion from CI and CD |
| Azure App Service | `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` | Container runtime, 2 apps |

**Build and delivery actions consumed from the GitHub marketplace:**

| Action | Version | Function |
|---|---|---|
| `docker/setup-buildx-action` | `@v3` | BuildKit builder, `network=host`, multi-platform |
| `docker/login-action` | `@v3` | `ghcr.io` authentication |
| `docker/metadata-action` | `@v5` | 7 tag rules + 12 OCI labels |
| `docker/build-push-action` | `@v5` | Build, push, provenance, SBOM |
| `aquasecurity/trivy-action` | `@master` (unpinned) | Image vulnerability scan |
| `ossf/scorecard-action` | `@v2` | Supply-chain posture, `publish_results: true` |
| `codecov/codecov-action` | `@v3` | Coverage upload, `fail_ci_if_error: false` |
| `actions/checkout` | `@v4` | 8 call sites |
| `actions/setup-python` | `@v4` (CI) / `@v5` (CD) | Version skew between workflows |
| `actions/cache`, `actions/upload-artifact`, `actions/download-artifact` | `@v3` | Superseded majors |

**Base images and runtime components pulled at build time:**

| Component | Declared version | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `python:3.12-alpine` | tag-pinned, not digest-pinned | `Dockerfile` L9 |
| `alpine:3.19` | tag-pinned | `docker-compose.yml` L347 |
| Flask | `>=3.1.1` | `requirements.txt` |
| Gunicorn | `>=21.2.0` | `requirements.txt` |

Three version-hygiene observations follow directly from the tables. First, `aquasecurity/trivy-action@master` is the only floating third-party action reference in either workflow — every other third-party action is major-pinned. Second, `ubuntu-latest` and the tag-pinned base images mean the build environment and base layer can change without a repository commit. Third, no image is referenced by digest at *build* input; digest pinning is applied only downstream, to the *output* image consumed by the deploy steps.

### 8.2.3 High Availability Design

**No high-availability design is implemented.** Each environment is a single application instance with no redundancy construct of any kind:

| HA construct | State | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple instances | Absent | One `app-name` per environment; `replicas: 1` |
| Deployment slots / swap | Absent | No slot parameter, no swap step in `cd.yml` |
| Load balancer / traffic manager | Absent | No such service referenced anywhere |
| Multi-region / geo-failover | Absent | No region declared (see 8.1.1.2) |
| Auto-scaling | Absent | No scale rule; see 8.4 |
| App Service health-check path | Not configured | No health-check setting in any file |

The single-instance posture has a hard concurrency consequence: the production image fixes `--workers=4 --worker-class=sync` (`Dockerfile` L216), so the serving tier processes at most four requests in parallel and additional load queues at the listener backlog.

The resilience mechanisms that *do* exist operate at the process and container level, not the infrastructure level:

| Mechanism | Configuration | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Worker recycling | `--max-requests 1000 --max-requests-jitter 100` | Bounds per-worker leak exposure |
| Preload | `--preload` | Faster worker respawn, shared memory |
| PID-1 signal handling | `dumb-init` entrypoint | Clean SIGTERM to workers |
| Container health probe | `HEALTHCHECK` per stage on `/hello` | Docker/Compose only |

The `HEALTHCHECK` directives (`Dockerfile` L124-L125 application, L174-L175 development, L209-L210 production) and the Compose `healthcheck:` blocks are consumed by the local Docker/Compose runtime; nothing in the repository configures an equivalent platform health probe on App Service, so on the cloud surface these probes are inert. Likewise the Compose `restart: always` (L252) and `restart_policy` (L293-L299) govern only the local host. Section 6.5 documents the resulting detection windows and the fact that the probes target `/hello` rather than the purpose-built `/health` endpoint.

**Critical availability risk.** The image the CD pipeline attempts to build cannot currently be produced. `src/backend/wsgi.py` L34-L43 imports `psutil` inside a `try/except` that calls `sys.exit(1)` on failure; `psutil` is declared in `requirements-dev.txt`, `src/backend/requirements.txt`, and the `pyproject.toml` dev/performance extras, but **not** in the root `requirements.txt` that the Dockerfile `dependencies` stage installs (L88-L93). The `application` stage then runs `python -c "import wsgi"` as a build-time verification (L112-L116). A `--target production` build — exactly what `cd.yml` L215-L239 requests — therefore fails at that layer. The `development` target escapes only because it additionally installs `requirements-dev.txt`. This is the highest-severity infrastructure defect in the repository and it blocks every downstream cloud service.

### 8.2.4 Cost Optimization Strategy

#### 8.2.4.1 Cost-Control Mechanisms Already Implemented

Eight distinct cost-reducing techniques are present in the committed configuration:

| Mechanism | Configuration | Cost effect |
|---|---|---|
| Alpine base image | `python:3.12-alpine` | Smaller pulls and registry footprint |
| Multi-stage build | 5 stages; prod excludes dev deps | ~100-120 MB vs ~200-250 MB |
| Build-context exclusion | `.dockerignore` (762 lines) | Documented 90-95% context reduction |
| BuildKit registry cache | `cache-from/to: type=gha,mode=max` | Avoids re-running unchanged layers |
| Pip caching | `setup-python cache: pip` + `actions/cache@v3` | Shortens dependency install |
| Superseded-run cancellation | CI `cancel-in-progress: true` | Frees runner minutes on rapid pushes |
| Path filters | `ci.yml` L3-L20 | Skips runs for unrelated changes |
| Artifact expiry | `retention-days: 30` / `90` | Bounds artifact storage growth |

#### 8.2.4.2 Cost Drivers Derived From the Repository

The following are computed from declared job timeouts, sleep durations, matrix width, and retention settings — they are worst-case envelopes, not measurements.

| Driver | Derived value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| CI runner minutes per run | ≤ 65 | 3 matrix legs × 15 + 10 + 10 |
| CD runner minutes per run | ≤ 70 | 20 + 15 + 12 + 18 + 5 |
| Full push-to-production cycle | ≤ 135 | CI + CD worst case |
| Weekly cron cost | ≈ 280 min/month | 4.3 runs × 65 min |

Two structural inefficiencies inflate those numbers:

- **Billable idle time.** `cd.yml` spends 8 minutes per production run doing nothing but waiting: `sleep 45` before staging health checks (L497), `sleep 75` before production health checks (L713), and a 360-second post-deployment monitoring loop (L830-L832, 12 checks at 30-second intervals). Retry backoff can add up to a further 4 minutes on staging (12 × 20 s) and 7.5 minutes on production (18 × 25 s). All of it is metered wall-clock runner time.
- **Duplicated artifacts.** Each matrix leg uploads `junit.xml` and `pytest_report.html` inside *both* the `coverage-reports-python-<ver>` and `test-results-python-<ver>` artifacts, so those two files are stored twice per leg — six redundant copies per CI run.

Registry storage is the driver with the worst long-run trajectory. `docker/metadata-action@v5` (`cd.yml` L176-L214) applies **seven tag rules**, two of which mint a brand-new immutable tag on every single build: a SHA tag suffixed with `{{date 'YYYYMMDD-HHmmss'}}` and a `tutorial-python-{{date 'YYYYMMDD'}}` daily tag. Each tag references a multi-architecture manifest covering `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, plus provenance and SBOM attestations. A repository-wide search confirms **no package retention, prune, or cleanup logic exists anywhere** — the only retention settings in either workflow are the five `retention-days` values applied to Actions artifacts. Registry consumption therefore grows monotonically with build count. This matters financially because <cite index="13-24,13-25">GitHub Actions artifact storage allowances are shared with GitHub Packages, so total storage across Actions artifacts and Packages cannot exceed the plan's included amount</cite>.

#### 8.2.4.3 Indicative Cost Envelope

No cost figure, budget, tag, or quota appears anywhere in the repository, and no Azure SKU, region, or App Service plan is declared — so the Azure line item **cannot be determined from source**. The list prices below are external, publicly published figures included for sizing purposes only; they are not repository facts.

| Line item | Indicative public list price | Applies when |
|---|---|---|
| Actions minutes, public repo | <cite index="13-4">Free on standard GitHub-hosted runners</cite> | Repository is public |
| Actions minutes, private repo | <cite index="14-3">2,000 Linux min/month included on the Free plan</cite>; <cite index="14-11">$0.006 per Linux 2-core minute beyond it</cite> | Repository is private |
| Actions + Packages storage | <cite index="14-3">500 MB included on Free</cite>; <cite index="12-13">$0.25 per GB per month beyond</cite> | Always |
| Azure App Service (Linux) | <cite index="6-32">Free F1 capped at 60 CPU-minutes/day with no custom domain</cite>; <cite index="6-16">Basic B1 from about $13.14/month</cite> | Per instance, per environment |

Two consequences follow for this system specifically. First, because two separate Web Apps are named (`flask-tutorial-staging` and `flask-tutorial-production`), the Azure compute line is **doubled** — a Basic-tier deployment of both environments is roughly twice the single-instance figure unless both apps share one App Service plan, which nothing in the repository specifies. Second, adding the auto-scaling that 8.2.3 shows is missing would require a higher tier: <cite index="6-8">autoscaling requires moving to the Standard tier at roughly $56.94/month per instance</cite>. Egress is a separate meter — <cite index="6-16">approximately $0.087/GB for the first 10 TB per month</cite> — though for a handler returning a few dozen bytes per request it is immaterial. If the repository is public, the entire GitHub-side cost is zero at list price, and the concurrency limit rather than the price becomes the binding constraint: <cite index="14-28">the Free plan caps concurrent standard-runner jobs at 20</cite>, comfortably above this pipeline's three-leg matrix.

#### 8.2.4.4 Available Cost-Reduction Opportunities

Each item below is a direct consequence of an observed configuration, not a generic recommendation:

| Opportunity | Current state | Expected effect |
|---|---|---|
| Narrow the CI matrix | 3 Python versions vs `requires-python >=3.12` | Removes ~2/3 of test-job minutes |
| Replace fixed sleeps with polling | 120 s of unconditional `sleep` | Cuts most of the 8 min idle |
| Deduplicate test artifacts | 2 files uploaded twice per leg | Lowers storage accrual |
| Add package retention/prune | No policy exists | Halts monotonic registry growth |

### 8.2.5 Security and Compliance Considerations

**Credential model.** Only three distinct secrets are referenced across 1,422 lines of workflow YAML:

| Secret | Consumers | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | checkout, `ghcr.io` login, `TRIVY_PASSWORD` | Auto-provisioned, run-scoped |
| `AZURE_WEBAPP_PUBLISH_PROFILE_STAGING` | staging deploy | Long-lived publish profile |
| `AZURE_WEBAPP_PUBLISH_PROFILE_PRODUCTION` | production deploy | Long-lived publish profile |

`ci.yml` references no secrets at all. Azure authentication is publish-profile based: there is no OIDC/workload-identity federation, no service principal, and no `azure/login` step anywhere. Publish profiles are long-lived credentials embedding deployment passwords, and nothing in the repository provides for their rotation — a gap that stands in tension with the rotation policy `src/backend/.env.example` L162 states for application secrets.

**Registry pull path is unconfigured.** The deploy steps supply an app name, a publish profile, and an image reference — and nothing else. No registry credential is passed to Azure, and no step makes the published package publicly readable. GHCR packages are private by default, so the platform's ability to pull the digest is not established by anything in the repository. This is precisely the outstanding "Configure container registry credentials" item in `Project Guide.md`.

**Workflow token scoping.** Neither `ci.yml` nor `cd.yml` declares a `permissions:` block at any level. The pipeline nonetheless performs two privileged operations — pushing packages to `ghcr.io` and uploading SARIF to code scanning — which require `packages: write` and `security-events: write` respectively. With no explicit block, the run inherits the repository or organisation default, which is either over-permissive (broad write scope granted to every job, including third-party actions) or too restrictive (the push and SARIF steps fail). Neither outcome is a deliberate, reviewable choice.

**Supply-chain controls present.** `provenance: true` and `sbom: true` on the build step produce attestations alongside the image; `ossf/scorecard-action@v2` runs weekly with `publish_results: true`; Trivy results and the Bandit/Safety/pip-audit SARIF outputs are uploaded to code scanning, with the container scan filed under the `container-security` category. The counterweight is `aquasecurity/trivy-action@master`: a mutable reference to third-party code executing inside a workflow that, as noted above, has unscoped token permissions.

**Transport security.** No TLS, certificate, HSTS, or HTTPS-redirect configuration exists in any infrastructure file. The staging and production URLs registered in the GitHub environments are `https://` on `azurewebsites.net`, so encryption depends entirely on platform-managed default certificates; the local Compose surface is plain HTTP on ports 3000/3001. `src/backend/README.md` L908-L930 lists "SSL/TLS Configuration: HTTPS setup with Let's Encrypt certificates" as a future consideration, confirming that none is implemented. `Project Guide.md` retains "validate HTTPS readiness for Gunicorn production" as an open human task.

**Deployment gating.** Both cloud environments are declared with GitHub `environment:` keys (`cd.yml` L444-L446, L635-L637), which is the correct attachment point for required reviewers, wait timers, and branch restrictions. Those protection rules live in GitHub repository settings rather than in version control, so their presence cannot be verified from source — the repository establishes only that the gate *exists*, not that it is *enforced*.

Cloud-layer compliance posture is covered in 8.1.1.4: no regulatory regime is declared anywhere in the repository.

### 8.2.6 External Service Dependencies

Every network dependency the build and deploy path requires, with the artifact that establishes it:

| External endpoint | Required by | Established in |
|---|---|---|
| `ghcr.io` | Image push and digest pull | `cd.yml` L79, L167-L174 |
| Docker Hub (`python:3.12-alpine`, `alpine:3.19`) | Base image pulls | `Dockerfile` L9; Compose L347 |
| PyPI | `pip install` in 3 separate stages/jobs | `Dockerfile` L88, L146; both workflows |
| Alpine package mirrors | `apk update && apk upgrade && apk add` | `Dockerfile` L24-L33 |
| GitHub API / Actions service | Runners, caches, artifacts, SARIF | Both workflows |
| Azure App Service management endpoint | Publish-profile deployment | `cd.yml` L477, L689 |
| Codecov | Coverage upload (non-blocking) | `ci.yml` L97 |
| Trivy vulnerability database | Image scanning | `cd.yml` L348-L358 |

Two properties of this dependency set are worth recording. It is entirely **egress-only** — no inbound connectivity, VPN, private endpoint, or firewall rule is required or configured. And it is **unmirrored**: every dependency is fetched live from a public source at build time with no internal proxy, mirror, or vendored fallback, so a PyPI, Docker Hub, or Alpine-mirror outage halts image production outright.


## 8.3 Containerization

Containerization **is applicable** and is the most fully developed part of this system's infrastructure. The container image is the sole delivery artifact: no wheel or sdist is published by any workflow, and both deploy steps reference a registry digest rather than source. Three artifacts define the containerization layer, all under `infrastructure/docker/`:

| Artifact | Lines | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `Dockerfile` | 291 | Five-stage image definition |
| `docker-compose.yml` | 562 | Two-environment local composition |
| `.dockerignore` | 762 | Context reduction and secret exclusion |

Section 3.6 catalogues the same three files as toolchain components; this sub-section documents them as the image supply chain. One factual correction to that section: the build defines **five** stages, not four — `base`, `dependencies`, `application`, `development`, and `production`.

### 8.3.1 Container Platform Selection

| Layer | Selection | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Runtime | Docker Engine (OCI) | `Dockerfile`; Compose `docker compose up` |
| Build engine | BuildKit | `DOCKER_BUILDKIT: 1`, `COMPOSE_DOCKER_CLI_BUILD: 1` |
| Multi-arch builder | Buildx | `docker/setup-buildx-action@v3` |
| Local composition | Compose file format 3.8 | `docker-compose.yml` L18 |

`cd.yml` L74-L89 sets both BuildKit environment flags globally, and `docker/setup-buildx-action@v3` (L157-L165) installs a builder with `driver-opts: network=host` and `platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64`, `install: true`. No alternative container runtime, builder, or image format (Podman, Buildah, Kaniko, `ko`, Jib, nerdctl) appears anywhere in the repository. The choice of Compose 3.8 as the local composition format has a consequence documented in 8.4: the `deploy:` key in that schema originates from Swarm mode, so several of its child keys are not honoured by plain `docker compose up`.

### 8.3.2 Base Image Strategy

A single upstream base serves every stage: `Dockerfile` L9 `FROM python:3.12-alpine AS base`. One additional image, `alpine:3.19`, is used by the `flask-network-setup` utility service (`docker-compose.yml` L347), which is a no-op ordering anchor rather than an application container.

The `base` stage establishes every property inherited by all four descendant stages:

| Concern | Implementation | Line |
|---|---|---|
| OS package hardening | `apk update && apk upgrade` then targeted installs | L24-L33 |
| Cache eviction | `rm -rf /var/cache/apk/* /tmp/*` in same layer | L24-L33 |
| Non-root identity | `addgroup -g 1000 python`, `adduser -u 1000` | L41-L43 |
| Privilege drop | `USER python` before any descendant stage | L59 |

Five OS packages are installed, each pinned by wildcard rather than exact version: `curl=8.*` (used by every `HEALTHCHECK`), `dumb-init=1.*` (PID-1 signal forwarding), `build-base=0.*`, `libffi-dev=3.*`, and `openssl-dev=3.*` (native-extension compilation support). Wildcard pinning intentionally accepts patch-level drift so that `apk upgrade` picks up security fixes, at the cost of build reproducibility.

The base stage also fixes the Python runtime contract via `ENV` (L46-L55): `PYTHONPATH=/usr/src/app`, `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` (unbuffered stdout so container logs stream), `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, `PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1`, `PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1`, and a production-safe default posture of `FLASK_ENV=production`, `PORT=3000`, `HOST=0.0.0.0`. The working directory is `/usr/src/app` (L37), owned by UID/GID 1000.

Two strategy limitations are worth recording. The base is **tag-pinned, not digest-pinned**, so `python:3.12-alpine` can resolve to a different image on any rebuild. And `build-base`, `libffi-dev`, and `openssl-dev` are compiler and header packages installed in the `base` stage, which means they persist into the final `production` image even though no stage compiles a native extension after dependency installation — a straightforward opportunity to shrink the runtime image and reduce its attack surface by moving those into a discardable build stage.

### 8.3.3 Build Stage Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Base["base - L9<br/>FROM python:3.12-alpine<br/>apk hardening, UID 1000, ENV baseline"]
    Deps["dependencies - L64<br/>venv at /usr/src/app/.venv<br/>pip install -r requirements.txt + verify"]
    App["application - L101<br/>COPY app.py + wsgi.py<br/>EXPOSE 3000, import smoke test, flask run"]
    Dev["development - L137<br/>+requirements-dev.txt, debugpy, watchdog<br/>COPY full src/backend + tests, EXPOSE 5678"]
    Prod["production - L184<br/>Gunicorn ENV set, chmod 444, tmp cleanup<br/>GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS, dumb-init CMD"]

    Base --> Deps
    Deps --> App
    Deps --> Dev
    App --> Prod

    CDBuild["cd.yml build-push-action<br/>target: production"] --> Prod
    ComposeDev["compose flask-tutorial-dev<br/>target: development"] --> Dev
    ComposeProd["compose flask-tutorial-prod<br/>target: production"] --> Prod
```

| Stage | Parent | Adds | Entrypoint |
|---|---|---|---|
| `base` | `python:3.12-alpine` | OS hardening, user, ENV | — |
| `dependencies` | `base` | venv, runtime deps, verification | — |
| `application` | `dependencies` | 2 runtime modules, `EXPOSE 3000` | Werkzeug `flask run` |
| `development` | `dependencies` | dev deps, debugpy, full source + tests | `debugpy` + `flask run --debug` |
| `production` | `application` | Gunicorn tuning, read-only files | `gunicorn` via `dumb-init` |

The graph shape carries real design information. `development` branches from `dependencies`, **not** from `application`, so it never inherits `EXPOSE 3000` or the application-stage import verification; it re-copies the entire `src/backend/` tree plus `tests/` (L158-L159) and additionally installs `debugpy>=1.8.0` and `watchdog>=3.0.0` (L162-L163). `production` extends `application`, so it inherits the Werkzeug-based `CMD` and then overrides it — meaning the intermediate `application` stage is a buildable, runnable image that uses the Flask development server and should never be deployed.

Each stage validates itself at build time rather than deferring failures to runtime: `dependencies` verifies `import flask` and `import gunicorn` (L88-L93); `application` runs `ls -la *.py`, `python -c "import app"`, and `python -c "import wsgi"` (L112-L116); `development` verifies `pytest`, `pytest_flask`, and `coverage` imports (L146-L155); `production` re-verifies `gunicorn` (L201-L202). This is a deliberate fail-fast strategy — and it is exactly the mechanism that surfaces the `psutil` defect described in 8.2.3, because the `application` stage's `import wsgi` executes `wsgi.py`'s import guard against a dependency set that omits `psutil`.

Per-stage runtime posture:

| Stage | Exposed ports | Health probe cadence |
|---|---|---|
| `application` | 3000 | 30 s interval, 10 s timeout, 10 s start, 3 retries |
| `development` | 5678 | 15 s interval, 5 s timeout, 5 s start, 2 retries |
| `production` | 3000 (inherited) | 30 s interval, 10 s timeout, 15 s start, 3 retries |

All three probes execute `curl -f http://localhost:3000/hello`, i.e. they exercise the business endpoint rather than the dedicated `/health` endpoint; Section 6.5 analyses the detection-window implications. The `production` stage additionally hardens the filesystem with `chmod -R 444 *.py` (L213) and evicts build residue with `rm -rf /tmp/* /var/tmp/* /root/.cache` (L206).

### 8.3.4 Image Versioning Approach

Versioning is applied entirely by the CD pipeline; the Dockerfile itself contains only static labels.

**Tag generation.** `docker/metadata-action@v5` (`cd.yml` L176-L196) declares eight tag directives, but they are event-conditional, so the effective tag set differs per trigger:

| Directive | Fires on | Mutability |
|---|---|---|
| `type=ref,event=branch,suffix=-python` | branch push | Mutable |
| `type=ref,event=pr,suffix=-python` | pull request | Mutable |
| `type=sha` + branch prefix + `YYYYMMDD-HHmmss` suffix | every build | New tag each build |
| `type=semver` × 3 (`{{version}}`, `{{major}}.{{minor}}`, `{{major}}`) | tag/release only | Mutable except full version |
| `type=raw,value=latest-python` | default branch | Mutable |
| `type=raw,value=tutorial-python-{{date 'YYYYMMDD'}}` | default branch | New tag each day |

A `workflow_run` promotion from `main` therefore produces four tags (branch, timestamped SHA, `latest-python`, dated tutorial tag); a published release adds up to three semver tags. Because the SHA directive appends a second-resolution timestamp, **every build mints a tag that no later build will ever overwrite** — combined with the absence of any prune policy (8.2.4.2), registry consumption grows without bound.

**Label metadata.** The same action attaches thirteen labels: nine `org.opencontainers.image.*` labels (title, description, vendor, version, created, revision, url, source, documentation) plus four custom labels (`tutorial.framework=flask`, `tutorial.runtime=python`, `tutorial.version=3.1.1`, `tutorial.educational=true`). These are applied at push time by `docker/build-push-action@v5`, so they land only on pipeline-built images — an image built locally through Compose carries only the Dockerfile's own static labels.

**Version identity is fragmented four ways**, and every value is independently verifiable:

| Value | Reported as | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `2.0.0` | Image `LABEL version` | `Dockerfile` L13 |
| `2.0.0` | `TUTORIAL_VERSION` env, report footer | `cd.yml` L87 |
| `3.1.1` | `org.opencontainers.image.version` | `cd.yml` L200 (see below) |
| `1.0.0` | Application/`/health` version | `pyproject.toml` |

The OCI `version` label resolves to `3.1.1` because of a defect in the version-extraction step (`cd.yml` L130-L145): it runs `grep -E "^Flask==" requirements.txt` with a fallback of `|| echo "3.1.1"`, but `requirements.txt` declares `Flask>=3.1.1` — the anchored `==` pattern never matches, so the literal fallback always wins. The image's OCI version label consequently reports the *framework* version rather than the *image* version, and does so by accident.

**Build-argument provenance is non-functional.** The Dockerfile declares **no `ARG` instructions at all**, yet three call sites pass build arguments: `cd.yml` L231-L237 supplies `FLASK_ENV`, `BUILD_DATE`, `VCS_REF`, and `VERSION`, and both Compose services supply `FLASK_ENV`, `BUILD_DATE=${BUILD_DATE:-}`, and `VCS_REF=${VCS_REF:-}`. All of them are silently discarded. Per-build provenance survives on the CD path only because `metadata-action` injects `created` and `revision` as labels independently of the build args.

**Digest pinning** is the one strong versioning guarantee in the chain: `build-push-action` exports `image_digest`, and both deploy steps consume `${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}@<digest>`, so what staging validates is bit-identical to what production receives.

### 8.3.5 Build Optimization Techniques

| Technique | Implementation | Documented effect |
|---|---|---|
| Layer-cache ordering | System packages → requirements → install → source | `Dockerfile` L225-L229 |
| Context exclusion | `.dockerignore`, 762 lines | 90-95% smaller context |
| Multi-stage pruning | Dev deps confined to `development` | ~100-120 MB vs ~200-250 MB |
| Remote layer cache | `cache-from/to: type=gha,mode=max` | Cross-run reuse in CI |
| Local warm cache | `cache_from` image tags | Compose builds |
| Cache volumes | `venv_cache_*`, `pip_cache_*` | Persist venv/pip across runs |
| Pip hygiene | `PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1`, `pip cache purge` | Smaller layers |
| Wheel-first installs | `pip install wheel>=0.42.0` before deps | Avoids source builds |

The ordering discipline is the load-bearing optimization: `requirements.txt` and `requirements-dev.txt` are copied (L71-L72) and installed (L88-L93) *before* any application source is copied (L108-L109), so an edit to `app.py` invalidates only the final small layers. `.dockerignore` reinforces this by keeping the context minimal — its own documentation (L751-L756) claims a reduction from roughly 500 MB to under 25 MB and a 70-80% build-time improvement.

`.dockerignore` is deliberately self-contained: its header (L12-L14) states that all patterns are integrated directly to eliminate circular dependencies, i.e. it does not rely on `.gitignore`. It spans more than twenty titled sections covering version control, Python artifacts, environment and secret files, IDE and test artifacts, build output, logs, platform files, infrastructure configuration (`.terraform/`, `*.tfstate*`, `k8s/`, `kubernetes/`, `.aws/`, `.gcp/`, `.azure/`), documentation, monitoring, and container-runtime scripts. It contains exactly two negation patterns — `!Dockerfile` (L415) and `!src/**/*.md` (L454) — which is how the Dockerfile survives the blanket `Dockerfile*` exclusion. Notably it does **not** exclude `requirements.txt` or `requirements-dev.txt`, which the `dependencies` stage requires, and it *does* exclude `.env*`, so `src/backend/.env.example` never enters an image; configuration arrives strictly at runtime, exactly as L119 prescribes. It also excludes `gunicorn.conf.py`, `uwsgi.ini`, and `wsgi.ini` on the stated principle that WSGI server configuration is a runtime concern — consistent with the fact that no such file exists in the repository even though `README.md` documents a `gunicorn --config gunicorn.conf.py` invocation.

Two build-optimization caveats are visible in the local path. The dev service bind-mounts `../../src/backend` over `/usr/src/app` (`docker-compose.yml` L90-L105), which masks the image's baked-in files, and its start command re-runs `pip install -r requirements-dev.txt` on every container start (L115-L127) — so the local dev loop trades image-layer caching for volume caching. Its command also activates `venv/bin/activate` by relative path while the Dockerfile creates the environment at `/usr/src/app/.venv`.

### 8.3.6 Security Scanning and Image Hardening

**Image scanning.** `aquasecurity/trivy-action@master` (`cd.yml` L348-L358) scans the *published digest* rather than a local tag, which means the artifact under test is exactly the artifact that will be deployed:

| Setting | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `image-ref` | `${REGISTRY}/${IMAGE_NAME}@<digest>` | Scans the pushed manifest |
| `format` | `sarif` | Feeds GitHub code scanning |
| `severity` | `CRITICAL,HIGH,MEDIUM,LOW` | Reports all levels |
| `exit-code` | `'0'` | Action itself never fails the job |

Because Trivy is configured never to fail, the actual gate is a downstream shell step (L360-L409) that parses the SARIF with `jq`, mapping `level == "error"` to CRITICAL, `"warning"` to HIGH, and `"note"` to MEDIUM, then:

- **Fails the job** if `CRITICAL > 0` or if Safety reported any vulnerability;
- **Warns only** if `HIGH > 5` or Bandit reported more than 3 issues;
- **Passes with `security_gate=unknown`** if the SARIF file is missing — the gate fails open.

Complementary code-level scanners run in the same job: Bandit against `src/backend/` and Safety against the installed dependency set, both invoked with `|| true` so they are non-blocking, with their JSON parsed for counts. `ci.yml` runs a third scanner set — Bandit (gated at `--severity-level medium`), Safety (`--short-report`), and `pip-audit` — plus `ossf/scorecard-action@v2`. The `Dockerfile` educational notes (L285-L291) name exactly this set as the intended posture, including "Trivy container scanning" and "SBOM generation for supply chain security tracking"; both are in fact implemented, the latter via `sbom: true` alongside `provenance: true` on the build step.

**Runtime hardening baked into the image or applied by Compose:**

| Control | Mechanism | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Non-root execution | `USER python` (UID/GID 1000) | All stages |
| Immutable app files | `chmod -R 444 *.py` | `production` stage |
| No privilege escalation | `security_opt: no-new-privileges:true` | Both Compose services |
| Read-only root filesystem | `read_only: true` + tmpfs `/tmp`, `/var/tmp` | Compose prod only |
| Minimal capabilities | `cap_drop: ALL`, `cap_add: SETGID, SETUID` | Compose prod only |

The tmpfs mounts are sized at 10 M with mode 1777 (`docker-compose.yml` L326-L328), which is what makes `read_only: true` viable for a Python process that needs scratch space. Two hardening gaps are explicit in the file itself: `security_opt` also includes `apparmor:unconfined` (L314-L316) with an inline comment acknowledging that a real production deployment would configure a proper profile; and the read-only/capability controls exist **only** in Compose, so they do not follow the image to App Service, where no equivalent constraint is configured.

### 8.3.7 Container Image Defect Register

Every item below was verified directly against the referenced lines and each materially affects the delivered image.

| # | Defect | Location |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `psutil` missing from `requirements.txt` breaks `import wsgi` build check | `wsgi.py` L34-L43 vs `Dockerfile` L88, L116 |
| 2 | `CMD gunicorn wsgi:app` — module exports `application`, not `app` | `Dockerfile` L220 |
| 3 | No `ARG` declared; 7 build-arg passes silently discarded | `Dockerfile` (none) vs `cd.yml` L231, Compose L45, L186 |
| 4 | OCI `version` label reports Flask `3.1.1` via a never-matching grep | `cd.yml` L130-L145 |
| 5 | Compiler/header packages retained in the production image | `Dockerfile` L24-L33 |
| 6 | Base image tag-pinned, not digest-pinned; no lockfile | `Dockerfile` L9; `requirements.txt` |
| 7 | Timestamped SHA tags with no prune policy | `cd.yml` L185; no cleanup anywhere |
| 8 | Trivy pinned to `@master` (mutable third-party ref) | `cd.yml` L348 |

Defects 1 and 2 are ordered: the first prevents the production image from building at all, and the second would prevent the built image from starting if the first were fixed without also correcting the callable. The Compose production command (`docker-compose.yml` L263) already uses the correct `wsgi:application`, so the local prod-simulation path masks defect 2 — a build succeeding under Compose does not imply the image's own `CMD` is sound.


## 8.4 Orchestration

**Cluster orchestration is not applicable for this system.** No container orchestrator is present, referenced, or configured anywhere in the repository. This verdict rests on exhaustive negative evidence rather than absence of documentation:

| Orchestrator | Artifacts searched | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Kubernetes | manifests, `kustomization.yaml`, `kubectl` usage | Zero matches |
| Helm | `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, templates | Zero matches |
| Docker Swarm | stack files, `docker stack`, `docker swarm` | Zero matches |
| Nomad / ECS / Fargate | job specs, task definitions | Zero matches |

The only three YAML files in the entire repository are `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.github/workflows/cd.yml`, and `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml`. The strings `kubernetes`, `k8s`, and `helm` appear solely as *exclusion patterns* in `infrastructure/docker/.dockerignore` (L392-L427) and as advisory prose in `src/backend/README.md` L908-L930, which lists "Container Orchestration: Docker and Kubernetes" among future considerations — confirming that none is implemented.

The reason orchestration is unnecessary is architectural, not incidental: the delivered system is a single stateless process serving one business endpoint. There is no second service to schedule, no datastore to co-locate, no service mesh boundary, no leader election, and no inter-service discovery requirement — Section 6.1 documents the same single-process shape. What *does* exist are two narrower forms of orchestration, both documented below:

| Layer | Mechanism | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Single-host service composition | `docker-compose.yml`, 3 services | Developer workstation |
| Managed single-app runtime | Azure App Service | Staging and production |

### 8.4.1 Single-Host Composition Topology

`infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` composes three services on one Docker host. Only two of them are application containers; the third is an ordering artefact.

| Service | Image source | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `flask-tutorial-dev` | build `target: development` | Hot-reload dev server + debugger |
| `flask-tutorial-prod` | build `target: production` | Local production simulation |
