| `flask-network-setup` | `alpine:3.19` | Echo banner, `sleep 2`, exit |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    NetSetup["flask-network-setup<br/>alpine:3.19<br/>echo then sleep 2 then exit"]
    Dev["flask-tutorial-dev<br/>host 3000 and 5678<br/>restart: unless-stopped<br/>no resource limits"]
    Prod["flask-tutorial-prod<br/>host 3001<br/>restart: always<br/>128M / 0.5 CPU"]
    Net["flask-tutorial-network<br/>bridge flask-br0<br/>172.21.0.0/16"]

    NetSetup -->|depends_on - start order only| Dev
    NetSetup -->|depends_on - start order only| Prod
    Dev --- Net
    Prod --- Net
```

Both application services declare `depends_on: [flask-network-setup]` (L166-L167, L338-L339) in the **short list form**, with no `condition: service_healthy`. That establishes start ordering only, not readiness gating — and since the dependency target is a container that prints a banner, sleeps two seconds, and exits, the ordering constraint carries no functional guarantee. The utility service is explicitly labelled `tutorial.utility=network-setup` and `tutorial.purpose=educational`; its function is pedagogical demonstration of `depends_on`.

The shared network is fully specified rather than defaulted (L368-L394): driver `bridge`, bridge device name `flask-br0`, IP masquerade and inter-container communication both enabled, host binding `0.0.0.0`, and static IPAM with subnet `172.21.0.0/16`, gateway `172.21.0.1`, and an allocation range of `172.21.240.0/20`. Five named local volumes are declared (L401-L449) — `venv_cache_dev`, `venv_cache_prod`, `pip_cache_dev`, `pip_cache_prod`, and `flask_shared_data`; the last is bound to `${PWD}/data` but is never mounted by any service and that directory does not exist.

### 8.4.2 Service Deployment Strategy

At the Compose layer, deployment is per-service and independent — the two application services can be started singly or together, and the file's header (L12-L15) documents four usage modes: start dev, start prod, run tests via `run --rm flask-tutorial-dev python -m pytest`, and start both concurrently. Running both simultaneously is possible only because the production service binds host port **3001** to container port 3000 (L230-L231), deliberately avoiding the dev service's 3000/5678 bindings.

| Concern | Development service | Production service |
|---|---|---|
| Restart directive | `restart: unless-stopped` | `restart: always` |
| Start command | `pip install` then `flask run --debug --reload` | `exec gunicorn wsgi:application` |
| Health probe start period | 10 s | 15 s |
| Interactive attachment | `tty: true`, `stdin_open: true` | Not set |

The production service's command (L255-L264) uses `exec` so Gunicorn replaces the shell as the container's main process, preserving signal delivery — and it passes `wsgi:application`, the correct callable, in contrast to the image's own `CMD` (see 8.3.7). The development command's `debugpy --wait-for-client` counterpart in the image (`Dockerfile` L179) blocks startup until a debugger attaches, which conflicts with that stage's 5-second health-probe start period.

On the cloud side there is no deployment orchestration to configure: each `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` invocation replaces the container of a single named Web App in place. No deployment slot, staging slot, or swap operation is used, so this is neither blue-green, canary, nor rolling — Section 8.5.2 documents the resulting availability characteristics.

### 8.4.3 Auto-Scaling Configuration

**No auto-scaling is configured at any layer.** There is no horizontal or vertical pod autoscaler, no KEDA, no Azure autoscale rule, and no scale-out setting in any file. `docker-compose.yml` L288 declares `replicas: 1` explicitly.

Scaling appears only twice, both times inside the educational runbook comment block, as manual commands a learner may type:

| Documented command | Location | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `up --scale flask-tutorial-dev=2` | L507 | Host port conflict on 3000/5678 |
| `up --scale flask-tutorial-prod=3` | L530 | Host port conflict on 3001 |

Both commands are unrunnable as written: each service declares a **static host-port mapping**, so the second replica cannot bind an already-claimed host port. Scaling either service would require replacing the fixed mappings with ephemeral ranges and introducing a reverse proxy — neither exists in the repository (`nginx` appears only as advisory prose in `src/backend/README.md`, and there is no Traefik or other ingress).

Vertical scaling is equally fixed. Worker count is baked into the image at `Dockerfile` L216 (`GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS` with `--workers=4`) and repeated in the Compose command (`--workers 4`), so changing concurrency requires an image rebuild or a command override. The `WORKERS` variable documented in `src/backend/.env.example` L141 is never read by `app.py` or `wsgi.py` and therefore cannot be used to tune the running service. Because the worker class is `sync`, the ceiling is a hard four concurrent requests.

### 8.4.4 Resource Allocation Policies

Resource policy exists for exactly one of the three services.

| Policy | `flask-tutorial-prod` | `flask-tutorial-dev` |
|---|---|---|
| Memory limit | 128 M | Not set |
| CPU limit | 0.5 cores | Not set |
| Memory reservation | 75 M | Not set |
| CPU reservation | 0.25 cores | Not set |

Supplementary allocation controls, all production-only:

| Control | Value | Line |
|---|---|---|
| tmpfs `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` | `rw,size=10M,mode=1777` | L326-L328 |
| Cache volumes | mounted `read_only: true` | L234-L245 |
| Root filesystem | `read_only: true` | L325 |
| Capabilities | `cap_drop: ALL` + `SETGID`, `SETUID` | L331-L335 |

Three allocation observations follow from cross-checking these values against the repository's own guidance:

1. **CPU over-subscription.** Four sync workers are allocated 0.5 CPU cores. `src/backend/.env.example` L128-L132 states that CPU-bound workloads should set workers equal to CPU cores and that single-core hosts should use one to two workers maximum — at a 0.5-core ceiling that guidance implies **one** worker, not four. The declared configuration therefore contradicts the repository's own sizing rule and guarantees worker contention under concurrent load.
2. **Reservation equals target.** The 75 M memory reservation is identical to the documented memory target (`Dockerfile` L278-L283 "Target memory usage: <75MB for production container"; `pyproject.toml` `[tool.memory-monitor] limit_mb = 75`), leaving 53 M of unmonitored headroom before the 128 M limit triggers an OOM kill. Section 6.5 records the same gap from the alerting perspective.
3. **Development is unbounded.** The dev service has no ceiling at all despite being the service that runs a reloader, a debugger, and a `pip install` at container start — it is the more resource-intensive of the two.

None of these limits apply to the cloud runtime. Compose resource policy governs the local Docker host only; on App Service, capacity is a property of the App Service plan tier, which the repository never specifies (8.1.1.2).

### 8.4.5 Schema Fidelity: Declared Versus Enforced

`docker-compose.yml` L18 declares `version: '3.8'`. In that schema the `deploy:` key originates from Swarm-mode stack deployment, and the subset of its children that takes effect depends on which runtime consumes the file. The repository documents **only** `docker-compose up` / `docker compose up` invocations — there is no `docker swarm init`, no `docker stack deploy`, and no orchestrator that performs staged service updates anywhere in the repository or its documentation.

| Declared under `deploy:` | Purpose as written | Executor present? |
|---|---|---|
| `resources.limits` / `reservations` | Cap and floor CPU/memory | Yes — applied to the container |
| `replicas: 1` | Single instance | Trivially satisfied |
| `update_config` (parallelism, delay, `failure_action: rollback`, monitor 60s) | Rolling update with automatic rollback | **No** |
| `restart_policy` (any, 5s, 3 attempts, 120s window) | Supervised restart | Overlaps `restart: always` (L252) |

Two consequences should be understood by anyone reading the file as an operational contract. First, the declared rolling-update-with-rollback behaviour has no executor in this repository's workflow; it is aspirational configuration. Second, even under a Swarm executor it would be largely vacuous, because `replicas: 1` with `parallelism: 1` means the single task is stopped before its replacement starts — there is an unavoidable availability gap, and `failure_action: rollback` can only restore the prior image after that gap. The service also declares restart behaviour twice, through the Compose-native `restart: always` and through `deploy.restart_policy`, with differing semantics; the file does not indicate which is authoritative.


## 8.5 CI/CD Pipeline

The delivery pipeline is implemented as two GitHub Actions workflows totalling 1,422 lines and eight jobs, chained by a `workflow_run` dependency:

| Workflow | Name | Jobs | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI Pipeline | 3 | Validate, scan, gate |
| `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | CD Pipeline | 5 | Build, scan, deploy, report |

`cd.yml` L13-L15 states the intended end-to-end flow: CI Pipeline success → Build and Push Image → Security Scan → Deploy Staging → Deploy Production → Monitor and Validate. Section 3.6 tabulates the same jobs from a toolchain perspective; this sub-section documents the pipeline as delivery infrastructure — triggers, gates, artifacts, promotion, rollback, and release control — and records where the implementation diverges from that stated flow.

### 8.5.1 Build Pipeline

#### 8.5.1.1 Source Control Triggers

| Workflow | Trigger | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| CI | `push` | Branches `main`, `develop`, filtered by path |
| CI | `pull_request` | Target `main`; opened, synchronize, reopened |
| CI | `schedule` | `'0 2 * * 1'` — Mondays 02:00 UTC |
| CI | `workflow_dispatch` | Manual |
| CD | `workflow_run` | Workflow "CI Pipeline", `completed`, branch `main` |
| CD | `release` | `published` |
| CD | `workflow_dispatch` | 3 inputs (see below) |

The CI path filter (`ci.yml` L3-L20) admits `src/backend/**`, `tests/**`, `requirements.txt`, `requirements-dev.txt`, `pytest.ini`, and `pyproject.toml`. Two consequences follow directly. First, `tests/**` matches nothing — the test suite lives at `src/backend/tests/`, already covered by the first pattern. Second, and materially, **changes confined to `infrastructure/**` or `.github/workflows/**` do not trigger CI**, and because CD is gated on a successful CI `workflow_run`, an infrastructure-only or pipeline-only change reaches neither validation nor staging. The Dockerfile and Compose file — the artifacts that define the deployed image — are outside the trigger surface of the pipeline that builds them.

Concurrency policy differs deliberately between the two workflows:

| Workflow | Group | `cancel-in-progress` |
|---|---|---|
| CI | `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` | `true` — supersede on rapid pushes |
| CD | `cd-${{ github.ref }}` | `false` — deployments queue |

CD's three dispatch inputs are `environment` (choice of `staging`/`production`, default `staging`), `image_tag` (string, default `latest`), and `skip_tests` (boolean, described as "Skip security scanning for emergency deployments"). `image_tag` is **never referenced anywhere else in the file** — it is inert, and the deployed image is always the digest produced by the current run. `skip_tests` is live: setting it true causes the `security_scan` job's `if` condition to evaluate false, and since `deploy_staging` declares no `if:` of its own, staging deployment proceeds with the scan skipped entirely.

#### 8.5.1.2 Build Environment Requirements

| Requirement | CI Pipeline | CD Pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| Runner | `ubuntu-latest` (3 jobs) | `ubuntu-latest` (5 jobs) |
| Python provisioning | `setup-python@v4` | `setup-python@v5` |
| Python versions | Matrix `3.12`, `3.11`, `3.10` | `3.12` only |
| Container tooling | None | BuildKit + Buildx multi-arch |

CI's workflow-level environment (`ci.yml` L28-L36) sets `FLASK_ENV=testing`, `CI=true`, `COVERAGE_THRESHOLD=100`, `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`, `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, `PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=false`, `PIP_UPGRADE_STRATEGY=eager`, and `FORCE_COLOR=1`. CD's (L74-L89) sets the registry and BuildKit flags plus `FLASK_ENV=production`, `FLASK_DEBUG=false`, `TUTORIAL_VERSION="2.0.0"`, and `EDUCATIONAL_MODE="deployment-demonstration"`.

Neither workflow declares a `permissions:` block at any level, although the pipeline pushes packages to `ghcr.io` and uploads SARIF to code scanning — see 8.2.5 for the token-scoping consequences. The three-version test matrix carries its own inconsistency: `pyproject.toml` declares `requires-python >= 3.12`, so the `3.11` and `3.10` legs test a support floor the project does not claim, while consuming two-thirds of the test job's runner minutes (8.2.4.4).

#### 8.5.1.3 Dependency Management

Three dependency manifests coexist, and different pipeline stages consume different ones:

| Manifest | Declarations | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|
| `requirements.txt` (root) | 5 runtime | Dockerfile `dependencies` stage; CD runner |
| `requirements-dev.txt` (root) | 44 dev | Dockerfile `development` stage |
| `src/backend/requirements.txt` | 42 combined | CI jobs (`working-directory: src/backend`) |

All five root runtime declarations use lower-bound `>=` constraints — `Flask>=3.1.1`, `python-dotenv>=1.0.1`, `Flask-CORS>=4.0.0`, `gunicorn>=21.2.0`, `wheel>=0.42.0`. **No lockfile of any kind exists in the repository** (no `requirements.lock`, no pip-compile output, no `Pipfile.lock`, no `poetry.lock`), so resolution is date-dependent and image builds are not byte-reproducible. `pyproject.toml` L445-L448 configures `[tool.pip-tools]` with `generate-hashes = true`, but no hashed requirements file has been generated or committed. Similarly, `[tool.setuptools_scm]` (L433-L437) is configured to write `src/_version.py`, which does not exist, and the declared `[build-system]` (setuptools + wheel + setuptools-scm) is never invoked — no workflow runs `python -m build`, confirming Section 3.6's finding that the delivered artifact is the container image rather than a Python distribution.

Caching is applied at three levels: `setup-python` with `cache: 'pip'` keyed on both root requirements files, an explicit `actions/cache@v3` on `~/.cache/pip` keyed by OS, Python version, and requirements hashes with two restore-keys, and BuildKit's `type=gha` layer cache on the CD side.

Two dependency-resolution defects are verifiable from the working directories. CI installs from `working-directory: src/backend`, where `requirements.txt` exists but **`requirements-dev.txt` does not** — the dev install therefore cannot resolve. And `flake8 . --config=.flake8` is invoked from the same directory while `.flake8` lives at the repository root, so the configuration file cannot be found; the same relative-path problem affects `bandit -r src/`, which from `src/backend` targets a non-existent `src/backend/src/`.

#### 8.5.1.4 Artifact Generation and Storage

No binary distributable is produced. The pipeline emits one deployable artifact — the container image — plus a set of report artifacts:

| Artifact | Retention | Producer |
|---|---|---|
| Container image + provenance + SBOM (`ghcr.io`) | No policy — indefinite | CD `build_and_publish` |
| `coverage-reports-python-<ver>` × 3 | 30 days | CI `test` |
| `test-results-python-<ver>` × 3 | 30 days | CI `test` |
| `security-reports` | 90 days | CI `security` |
| `python-security-scan-results` | 30 days | CD `security_scan` |
| `flask-deployment-report` | 90 days | CD `deployment_notification` |

Nine Actions artifacts are produced per full push-to-production cycle. `junit.xml` and `pytest_report.html` appear in **both** the coverage and test-results artifacts for each matrix leg, so six redundant file copies are stored per CI run. Coverage is additionally exported to Codecov (`fail_ci_if_error: false`, so upload failure is non-blocking) and SARIF is exported to GitHub code scanning. `pyproject.toml` L472-L476 declares `[tool.ci] artifact_retention_days = 30`, which matches the majority of the workflow settings but is a non-standard table that no tool reads.

The image is the only artifact with **no** expiry policy. As established in 8.2.4.2 and 8.3.4, every build mints at least one immutable timestamped tag and nothing prunes them.

#### 8.5.1.5 Quality Gates

Ten distinct checks execute across CI's three jobs. Blocking status below reflects the actual shell semantics, not the step names:

| Gate | Command | Blocking |
|---|---|---|
| Style | `flake8 . --config=.flake8 --statistics --count` | Yes |
| Tests + coverage | `pytest --cov-fail-under=100 …` | Yes |
| Static security | `bandit -r src/ --severity-level medium` | Yes |
| Dependency CVEs | `safety check --short-report` | Yes |
| Dependency audit | `pip-audit` (bare invocation) | Yes |
| Coverage re-validation | line-rate AND branch-rate ≥ 100 | Yes |
| Bandit HIGH findings | JSON parse in `quality-gate` | Yes, if report present |
| Safety vulnerabilities | JSON parse in `quality-gate` | Yes, if report present |
| Coverage publication | `codecov-action@v3` | No |
| Supply-chain posture | `ossf/scorecard-action@v2` | No |

The threshold is uncompromising: `COVERAGE_THRESHOLD=100` at workflow level, `--cov-fail-under=100` in the pytest invocation, and a second independent validation in `quality-gate` that parses `coverage.xml` and fails if **either** `line-rate` or `branch-rate` is below 100. Bandit, Safety, and pip-audit each run twice — once with `|| true` to capture machine-readable output, once bare to gate.

Three gate defects reduce the effective strength of this list:

1. **The coverage re-validation step cannot execute as written.** `ci.yml` L242-L293 heredocs a Python script to `scripts/validate_coverage.py`, but the `mkdir -p scripts` that would create the destination appears at L290 — *after* the redirect. The `scripts/` directory does not exist in the repository.
2. **The report-parsing gates fail open.** Both the Bandit HIGH-severity check and the Safety vulnerability check are wrapped in `if [ -f … ]` and merely echo a skip message when the file is absent — so a scanner that fails to produce output silently satisfies the gate.
3. **SARIF upload uses an undocumented input form.** `ci.yml` L186 passes a multi-line list of three files to `sarif_file:`, which expects a single file or a directory.

`pyproject.toml` L479-L484 declares a `[tool.quality-gates]` table stating the intended contract — `coverage_threshold = 100`, `performance_regression_threshold = 10`, `memory_limit_mb = 75`, `response_time_limit_ms = 50`, `security_scan_required = true`. Only the first and last are actually enforced by the pipeline; there is no performance-regression, memory, or response-time gate in either workflow.

### 8.5.2 Deployment Pipeline

#### 8.5.2.1 Deployment Strategy

**The deployment strategy is in-place single-instance replacement — it is neither blue-green, canary, nor rolling.** This follows from three verified facts: each environment is one Azure Web App addressed by a single `app-name`; no deployment slot or swap operation appears anywhere in `cd.yml`; and `docker-compose.yml` declares `replicas: 1`. The staged `update_config` block in Compose is Swarm schema with no executor (8.4.5).

| Property | Value | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Instances per environment | 1 | Replacement implies downtime |
| Slot / swap | None | No pre-warm, no atomic cutover |
| Traffic shifting | None | No canary or percentage rollout |
| Artifact identity | Digest-pinned | Staging and production run identical bits |

The single genuine strength is artifact identity: both deploy steps reference `${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}@${{ needs.build_and_publish.outputs.image_digest }}`, so what production receives is bit-identical to what staging validated. The environments differ only in intended configuration — staging is passed `GUNICORN_WORKERS: 2` and production `GUNICORN_WORKERS: 4` plus keepalive and max-requests values — although, as 8.1.2.2 establishes, those step-level `env:` values never reach the container.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Trig{{"Trigger: workflow_run CI success on main<br/>OR release published<br/>OR workflow_dispatch"}}
    Build["build_and_publish - 20 min cap<br/>buildx target production, 2 platforms<br/>push digest, provenance, SBOM"]
    ScanGate{{"Input skip_tests set true?"}}
    Scan["security_scan - 15 min cap<br/>Bandit, Safety, Trivy on published digest"]
    SecG{{"CRITICAL count above 0<br/>OR Safety vulnerabilities above 0?"}}
    Stg["deploy_staging - 12 min cap<br/>azure/webapps-deploy, then sleep 45"]
    StgH{{"Health check passes within<br/>12 attempts, 20 s apart?"}}
    StgS["6 staging smoke tests<br/>1 non-blocking latency warning"]
    PreG{{"Staging status success AND<br/>scan result not failed?"}}
    ProdCond{{"workflow_dispatch with<br/>environment equal to production?"}}
    Prd["deploy_production - 18 min cap<br/>same digest, then sleep 75"]
    PrdH{{"Health validation passes within<br/>18 attempts, 25 s apart?"}}
    PrdS["5 production smoke tests<br/>1 non-blocking latency warning"]
    Mon["Production monitoring<br/>12 probes across 360 s"]
    MonG{{"Failure rate above 20 percent?"}}
    Fail["Job fails<br/>NO automated rollback executed"]
    Notify["deployment_notification - 5 min cap<br/>if always: deployment-report.md, 90 d"]

    Trig --> Build
    Build --> ScanGate
    ScanGate -->|yes, scan skipped| Stg
    ScanGate -->|no| Scan
    Scan --> SecG
    SecG -->|yes| Fail
    SecG -->|no| Stg
    Stg --> StgH
    StgH -->|no| Fail
    StgH -->|yes| StgS
    StgS --> PreG
    PreG -->|no| Fail
    PreG -->|yes| ProdCond
    ProdCond -->|no| Notify
    ProdCond -->|yes| Prd
    Prd --> PrdH
    PrdH -->|no| Fail
    PrdH -->|yes| PrdS
    PrdS --> Mon
    Mon --> MonG
    MonG -->|yes, sets rollback_required| Fail
    MonG -->|no| Notify
    Fail --> Notify
```

#### 8.5.2.2 Environment Promotion Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Local["Local Compose dev<br/>flask-tutorial-dev on 3000<br/>no gate"]
    LocalProd["Local production simulation<br/>flask-tutorial-prod on 3001<br/>full container hardening"]
    PR["Pull request to main<br/>CI: 3-leg matrix, security, quality-gate"]
    Main["Branch main"]
    CIok["CI Pipeline conclusion success"]
    Staging["Environment staging - automatic<br/>flask-tutorial-staging.azurewebsites.net"]
    Dispatch["Manual workflow_dispatch<br/>environment equal to production"]
    Prod["Environment production<br/>flask-tutorial.azurewebsites.net"]
    Release["release published"]
    Dead["Unreachable path: condition requires<br/>refs/heads/main but a release ref<br/>is refs/tags"]

    Local --> LocalProd
    LocalProd --> PR
    PR --> Main
    Main --> CIok
    CIok -->|workflow_run| Staging
    Staging --> Dispatch
    Dispatch --> Prod
    Release --> Dead
```

Promotion to staging is fully automatic on any successful CI run on `main`: `deploy_staging` declares no `if:` condition, so it executes for every triggering event that reaches it. Promotion to production is guarded by the condition at `cd.yml` L631-L633:

| Branch of the production condition | Reachable? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `release` event AND `github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` | No | Release refs are `refs/tags/<tag>` |
| `workflow_dispatch` AND `inputs.environment == 'production'` | Yes | Sole viable path |

**Production is therefore reachable only through manual dispatch.** The `release: published` trigger publishes an image and deploys to staging, but can never promote to production, notwithstanding the closing comment block's claim of "Production Flask deployment with manual approval gates".

An explicit prerequisite check runs before the production deploy (`cd.yml` L652-L669) and its two arms behave asymmetrically because both read outputs that are never populated:

- `needs.deploy_staging.outputs.deployment_status != 'success'` → **exit 1**. The output is bound to `steps.deploy.outputs.status`, and `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` emits no `status` output, so this check **fails closed** and blocks production on every run.
- `needs.security_scan.outputs.scan_result == 'failed'` → exit 1. That output is bound to `steps.scan`, the Trivy action, which emits none of `result`, `critical_count`, or `high_count` — the values are produced by the later step with `id: summary`. The comparison therefore never matches and the check **fails open**.

The net effect is the opposite of the intent: the safety gate that should block on a failed security scan is inert, while the gate that should confirm a healthy staging deployment blocks unconditionally.

#### 8.5.2.3 Rollback Procedures

**No automated rollback exists.** The pipeline detects conditions that should trigger one and then does nothing about them:

| Element | State |
|---|---|
| `rollback_required` job output | Produced by `steps.monitoring` |
| Consumer of that output | None — no step or job reads it |
| Rollback step / job | Does not exist |
| Compose `failure_action: rollback` | Swarm schema, no executor (8.4.5) |

The monitoring step (`cd.yml` L825-L862) computes a rolling failure rate and, above 20%, emits `rollback_required=true` and exits 1 — failing the job and surfacing the signal in the deployment report. Nothing redeploys the previous image.

Recovery is therefore a manual procedure, and the pipeline does supply the primitives to perform it: because every deployment is digest-pinned and every build is retained in `ghcr.io` under an immutable timestamped tag, an operator can restore the previous state by dispatching a deployment against the earlier digest. Two caveats apply. The dispatch inputs offer no way to select a digest — `image_tag` is inert (8.5.1.1) — so the practical mechanism is re-running the older successful workflow rather than parameterising a new one. And no runbook for this procedure exists anywhere in the repository.

#### 8.5.2.4 Post-Deployment Validation

Validation is substantial in volume and layered in two tiers per environment.

| Phase | Staging | Production |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed warm-up | `sleep 45` | `sleep 75` |
| Health attempts | 12 × 20 s backoff, 15 s timeout | 18 × 25 s backoff, 20 s timeout |
| Worst-case duration | ≈ 7 minutes | ≈ 14 minutes |
| Smoke tests | 6 | 5 |

Staging health polling requests `/hello` and treats any success as pass; production health validation additionally requires the response body to contain `Hello world`. The smoke suites:

| # | Staging check | Blocking |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Body contains `Hello world` | Yes |
| 2 | HTTP status 200 | Yes |
| 3 | `Content-Type` contains `application/json` | Yes |
| 4 | Response time under 3.0 s | **No — warning** |
| 5 | `GET /health` returns 200 | Yes |
| 6 | `GET /nonexistent` returns 404 | Yes |

| # | Production check | Blocking |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Body contains `Hello world` | Yes |
| 2 | Mean of 10 sequential requests under 1.5 s | **No — warning** |
| 3 | 15 concurrent background requests then `wait` | **No — asserts nothing** |
| 4 | `GET /nonexistent` returns 404 | Yes |
| 5 | `GET /health` body contains `healthy` | Yes |

Two validation weaknesses are worth recording. Both latency checks are warning-only, so no performance threshold can fail a deployment — consistent with 8.5.1.5's finding that the declared `response_time_limit_ms = 50` is never enforced. And the production "load testing simulation" launches 15 concurrent requests, waits for them, and then evaluates no result at all; against a service with four sync workers, this is precisely the scenario where an assertion would be valuable. Staging test 1 declares an `EXPECTED` variable holding `{"message":"Hello world"}` but performs only a substring grep, so response-shape changes would pass.

Post-deployment monitoring then runs 12 probes at 30-second intervals over 360 seconds, computing a rolling failure rate. Section 6.5 documents the resulting detection windows and notes that the failure-rate trigger has no minimum-sample guard, so a single early failure can exceed the 20% threshold.

#### 8.5.2.5 Release Management Process

| Control | Implementation | State |
|---|---|---|
| Release trigger | `release: types: [published]` | Declared; cannot reach production |
| Semantic version tags | 3 `type=semver` rules in `metadata-action` | Fire on tag/release events |
| Approval gate | GitHub `environment:` on both deploy jobs | Rules held in GitHub settings |
| Deployment record | `deployment-report.md`, 90-day retention | Implemented |
| Change log | No `CHANGELOG.md` in repository | Absent |
| Version derivation | `[tool.setuptools_scm]` configured | Unused — no `src/_version.py` |

The `deployment_notification` job (`cd.yml` L892-L1028) runs `if: always()` and is the pipeline's release-record mechanism. It derives an overall status from the four upstream job results — SUCCESS, PARTIAL when production was skipped, WARNING when production failed, FAILED otherwise — and generates a Markdown report containing a pipeline-results table, an artifact table (image digest, Flask version, Python version, base image, WSGI server, target platforms), an environment/URL table with per-environment status indicators, a security summary, eight educational learning points, and resource links including the `ghcr.io` package page. The report is uploaded as `flask-deployment-report` with 90-day retention, giving a bounded audit trail per run.

Two release-management gaps are visible. Version identity is fragmented four ways (8.3.4), so a release tag, the image `LABEL`, the OCI `version` label, and the application's own reported version can all disagree. And the pull-request template that governs the source-control gate (`.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`) still describes the pre-migration stack, referencing Express.js v5.1.0 and Node.js v22.16.0 LTS compatibility checks — a reviewer following it would validate criteria that no longer apply to this Python codebase.

#### 8.5.2.6 Pipeline Defect Register

Consolidated list of pipeline defects verified against the referenced lines, each of which affects deployability:

| # | Defect | Location |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `target: production` build fails on missing `psutil` | `cd.yml` L215 vs `Dockerfile` L116 |
| 2 | Staging prerequisite reads an unset output — fails closed | `cd.yml` L449, L655 |
| 3 | Security prerequisite reads an unset output — fails open | `cd.yml` L278, L663 |
| 4 | Production unreachable via `release` event | `cd.yml` L631-L633 |
| 5 | `rollback_required` produced but never consumed | `cd.yml` L825-L862 |
| 6 | Deploy-step `env:` are runner vars, not app settings | `cd.yml` L481, L695 |
| 7 | App name `flask-tutorial-production` vs validated host `flask-tutorial` | `cd.yml` L637 vs L691 |
| 8 | `image_tag` dispatch input never referenced | `cd.yml` L26-L57 |
| 9 | Coverage-validation heredoc precedes `mkdir -p scripts` | `ci.yml` L248 vs L290 |
| 10 | `--config=.flake8` and `bandit -r src/` unresolvable from `src/backend` | `ci.yml` L85, L159 |
| 11 | `requirements-dev.txt` absent from `src/backend` | `ci.yml` install step |
| 12 | No `permissions:` block in either workflow | both workflows |
| 13 | `infrastructure/**` and `.github/**` outside CI path filters | `ci.yml` L3-L20 |

Defect 7 deserves specific emphasis because it makes the production path self-inconsistent even after the others are fixed: the deploy step targets the Web App named `flask-tutorial-production`, while every health check, smoke test, and monitoring probe targets `https://flask-tutorial.azurewebsites.net`. Unless a custom hostname maps one to the other, the pipeline would validate a different endpoint from the one it deployed. The staging pair, by contrast, is internally consistent — app name `flask-tutorial-staging` matches host `flask-tutorial-staging.azurewebsites.net`.


## 8.6 Infrastructure Monitoring

Section 6.5 opens with the determination that detailed monitoring architecture is not applicable to this system and documents the application-observability surface — emitters, transports, sinks, probe taxonomy, alert disposition, and the absence of metrics, tracing, and log aggregation. This sub-section covers the complementary **infrastructure** view: host and container resource observation, pipeline-side performance measurement, cost monitoring, supply-chain and security monitoring, and compliance auditing. Where 6.5 already establishes a fact, it is cited rather than restated.

The overall position is that monitoring exists as **build-time and deploy-time verification**, not as continuous runtime observation. No monitoring agent, exporter, sidecar, or collector is deployed anywhere: a repository-wide search finds no Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog, New Relic, Sentry, CloudWatch, Log Analytics, or Application Insights configuration. `src/backend/README.md` L908-L930 lists Prometheus + Grafana, Sentry, New Relic, and DataDog among future considerations, which confirms by its own framing that none is implemented.

### 8.6.1 Resource Monitoring Approach

Four mechanisms produce resource-related signal, and all four are local or build-time:

| Mechanism | Signal | Where it operates |
|---|---|---|
| Container `HEALTHCHECK` | Binary healthy/unhealthy per container | Docker/Compose runtime |
| Compose `healthcheck:` | Same, with per-service cadence | Docker/Compose runtime |
| `deploy.resources` limits/reservations | Enforcement, not observation | Compose production service |
| `docker stats` runbook commands | Live CPU/memory/IO per container | Operator-invoked |

The probe configuration is the only automated resource-health signal in the system:

| Surface | Interval / timeout | Start period / retries |
|---|---|---|
| `application` stage | 30 s / 10 s | 10 s / 3 |
| `development` stage | 15 s / 5 s | 5 s / 2 |
| `production` stage | 30 s / 10 s | 15 s / 3 |
| Compose production service | 30 s / 10 s | 15 s / 3 |

All probes execute `curl -f http://localhost:3000/hello`. Section 6.5 documents the resulting detection windows and the fact that the probes exercise the business endpoint rather than the purpose-built `/health` endpoint. Critically, these probes are consumed by the local container runtime only — nothing in the repository configures an App Service health-check path, so on the cloud surface no continuous probe exists at all after the deployment job's post-deployment monitoring window closes.

Manual resource observation is documented rather than automated. `docker-compose.yml` L510 provides `docker stats $(docker-compose ps -q)` for all services and L528 provides `docker stats flask-tutorial-prod` for the production simulation, within a runbook section titled "HEALTH MONITORING" at L487. These are operator commands, not collectors — no output is retained, thresholded, or alerted on.

Capacity signal is limited to the enforcement values themselves. The production service's 128 M / 0.5 CPU limits and 75 M / 0.25 CPU reservations (8.4.4) are the only declared capacity envelope, and `pyproject.toml` L461-L465 declares a matching test-time intent — `[tool.memory-monitor]` with `limit_mb = 75`, `growth_limit_mb = 5`, `enable_tracking = true`, and `psutil_integration = true`. That last flag is significant beyond monitoring: `psutil` is the dependency whose omission from the root `requirements.txt` breaks the production image build (8.2.3), so the repository's memory-observation capability and its build failure share a single root cause.

**No log aggregation or rotation is configured.** `docker-compose.yml` declares no `logging:` driver block for any service, so container logs fall to the platform default with no rotation policy, no size cap, and no shipping destination. Log delivery is nonetheless correctly plumbed *within* the container: `Dockerfile` L216 sets `GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS` including `--access-logfile=- --error-logfile=- --log-level=info`, directing both streams to stdout/stderr, and the base stage sets `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` so output is not withheld in a buffer. The Compose production command passes only `--log-level info` explicitly and does not unset `GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS`, so Gunicorn continues to consume those arguments from the environment and access logging to stdout is retained. The container therefore emits a well-formed stream that nothing collects.

### 8.6.2 Performance Metrics Collection

There is no metrics endpoint, no counter or histogram instrumentation, and no time-series storage. The only quantitative performance data the infrastructure produces is generated inside the deployment pipeline, at deploy time:

| Measurement | Method | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Staging response time | Single timed request | Under 3.0 s — warning only |
| Production mean latency | 10 sequential requests, `bc -l` mean | Under 1.5 s — warning only |
| Production concurrency probe | 15 background requests + `wait` | None — asserts nothing |
| Availability sample | 12 probes over 360 s | Failure rate above 20% fails the job |

Only the last of these can influence a pipeline outcome. Both latency measurements are explicitly non-blocking, so no performance regression can fail a deployment — which contradicts the intent declared in `pyproject.toml` L479-L484, where `[tool.quality-gates]` states `performance_regression_threshold = 10` and `response_time_limit_ms = 50`. Neither value is read by any tool. The documented performance characteristics in `src/backend/README.md` L952-L958 (startup under 2 s, memory under 75 MB, response under 50 ms) are therefore design targets with no production measurement behind them; Section 6.5 records the same CI-versus-production measurement split.

Two structural gaps limit what could be inferred even from the data that exists. The pipeline's samples are taken once per deployment against a just-started instance, so they characterise cold-start behaviour rather than steady state. And with `--workers=4 --worker-class=sync`, saturation behaviour is the interesting property — yet the one test that generates concurrency evaluates no result.

### 8.6.3 Cost Monitoring and Optimization

**No cost monitoring exists.** There is no budget, spending alert, cost-allocation tag, quota, or usage report configured anywhere — no Azure budget resource, no cost-management reference, and no GitHub spending-limit configuration in the repository. Because no Azure SKU or region is declared (8.1.1.2), the repository cannot even establish a baseline against which spend could be tracked.

Two cost meters grow without a governing policy:

| Meter | Growth driver | Governing policy |
|---|---|---|
| Actions artifact storage | 9 artifacts per cycle, 6 redundant copies | `retention-days` 30 / 90 |
| Registry storage | Timestamped tag per build, 2 architectures | **None** |
| Runner minutes | ≤ 135 per cycle + weekly cron | Timeouts only |
| App Service compute | 2 always-on Web Apps | None declared |

Artifact growth is at least bounded by the five `retention-days` settings. Registry growth is not: as established in 8.2.4.2 and 8.3.4, the SHA tag rule appends a second-resolution timestamp and the tutorial tag appends a date, so no later build ever overwrites an earlier tag, and no prune, cleanup, or package-retention logic exists in either workflow. Because <cite index="13-24,13-25">Actions artifact storage allowances are shared with GitHub Packages</cite>, unbounded registry growth consumes the same allowance that artifacts draw on.

The optimization levers that *are* implemented are documented in 8.2.4.1 (alpine base, multi-stage pruning, context exclusion, layer and pip caching, superseded-run cancellation, path filters, artifact expiry), and the four available reductions in 8.2.4.4. The single highest-value addition would be a package-retention policy, because it is the only meter with no bound at all.

### 8.6.4 Security Monitoring

Security monitoring is the best-developed monitoring capability in the repository, and it operates entirely on the supply chain rather than at runtime.

| Capability | Mechanism | Cadence |
|---|---|---|
| Image vulnerability scan | Trivy against the published digest | Every CD run |
| Static code analysis | Bandit, `src/backend/` | Every CI and CD run |
| Dependency advisories | Safety and pip-audit | Every CI run |
| Supply-chain posture | `ossf/scorecard-action@v2`, results published | Every CI run |

The weekly `schedule: '0 2 * * 1'` trigger is what converts these from change-triggered checks into ongoing monitoring: it re-runs the full CI suite without any code change, so newly disclosed advisories against the unpinned `>=` dependency set surface within seven days. This is the repository's only time-based security signal.

Findings are centralised rather than left in logs. Both workflows upload SARIF to GitHub code scanning — CI submits Bandit, pip-audit, and Scorecard results, and CD submits the Trivy report under the `container-security` category — giving a single queryable finding history. Retention is asymmetric and deliberate: security artifacts are kept for 90 days versus 30 for test and coverage artifacts.

Attestation-based monitoring is present via `provenance: true` and `sbom: true` on the image build, which produce a verifiable build record and component inventory alongside each published digest.

Four monitoring-relevant weaknesses in this capability are established elsewhere in this section and summarised here: the Trivy gate fails open when its SARIF output is missing (8.3.6); the security prerequisite check before production reads an unset output and therefore never blocks (8.5.2.2); `skip_tests` can bypass scanning entirely while still deploying to staging (8.5.1.1); and Trivy is pinned to `@master` (8.2.5).

**No runtime security monitoring exists.** There is no WAF, IDS/IPS, rate limiter, audit-log forwarder, or anomaly detector. Runtime security relies on preventive controls baked into the container — non-root execution, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, `no-new-privileges` — which are enforcement rather than detection, and which apply only on the Compose surface (8.3.6).

### 8.6.5 Compliance Auditing

No regulatory regime applies (8.1.1.4), so "compliance auditing" here means the evidence trail the infrastructure produces about its own changes and deployments.

| Audit artefact | Content | Retention |
|---|---|---|
| `flask-deployment-report` | Job results, digest, env URLs, security summary | 90 days |
| `security-reports` | Bandit, Safety, pip-audit, Scorecard SARIF | 90 days |
| GitHub deployment records | Per-environment deployment history | Platform-managed |
| Code scanning alert history | All SARIF submissions | Platform-managed |
| Image provenance + SBOM | Build attestation and component list | With the image |
| Git history | Every change to code and pipeline | Indefinite |

The `deployment_notification` job runs `if: always()`, so a record is produced for failed and skipped deployments as well as successful ones — which is the property that makes the trail usable as an audit source rather than a success log. Its report footer identifies the generating pipeline version, and its content includes the exact image digest deployed, giving a durable link between a release record and the immutable artifact.

Governance controls that would normally accompany such a trail are absent: `.github/` contains only `ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, and `workflows/` — there is no `CODEOWNERS` file, no `dependabot.yml` or `renovate.json`, and no `SECURITY.md` despite `pyproject.toml` L142-L148 declaring a security-policy URL. Branch protection and environment protection rules live in GitHub settings rather than in version control, so their existence cannot be verified from the repository; the `environment:` declarations on both deploy jobs establish only that an attachment point for approvals exists (8.2.5). The pull-request template that documents the review contract still validates the pre-migration Node.js/Express stack (8.5.2.5), so the human review gate is documented against the wrong technology.

### 8.6.6 Infrastructure Monitoring Gaps and Minimum Baseline

Consolidated infrastructure-monitoring gaps, each traceable to a verified absence:

| # | Gap | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | No platform health probe on App Service | No continuous availability signal in the cloud |
| 2 | No log aggregation or rotation | Container logs are unretained and uncapped |
| 3 | No resource metric collection | Memory/CPU trends invisible; 53 M headroom unwatched |
| 4 | No cost monitoring | Both storage meters grow unobserved |
| 5 | No registry retention policy | Only meter with no bound at all |
| 6 | No runtime security detection | Prevention only, no anomaly visibility |
| 7 | Performance thresholds declared but unenforced | `[tool.quality-gates]` values read by nothing |
| 8 | `rollback_required` signal has no consumer | Detection without response (8.5.2.3) |

A minimum viable baseline, ordered by cost of implementation against value, would be: configure an App Service health-check path pointed at `/health` (closes gap 1 using an endpoint that already exists); add a `logging:` driver with rotation to both Compose services and a platform log destination for the cloud surface (gap 2); add a package-retention or prune step to the CD workflow (gap 5, and the only unbounded meter); and bind the existing `rollback_required` output to a redeploy-previous-digest step, since the pipeline already retains every prior digest (gap 8). Gaps 3, 4, 6, and 7 require new components or platform resources and are correspondingly larger undertakings. Section 6.5 sets out the complementary application-observability baseline.

### 8.6.7 Maintenance and Operational Procedures

Infrastructure maintenance procedures are documented in 8.1.2.5 (cadence table, weekly cron, non-deterministic patch adoption, the embedded 110-line Compose runbook, and the two non-executable documented procedures). Two additional operational notes belong to the monitoring view:

- The runbook's six container-security verification commands (`docker-compose.yml` L451-L562) — including capability inspection via `/proc/self/status` and a write attempt against the read-only root filesystem — constitute a manual control-verification procedure, i.e. periodic assurance that the hardening in 8.3.6 is actually in force.
- `Project Guide.md` retains "set up Flask health monitoring" and "validate production WSGI endpoints" as open human tasks within the 0.5-hour Production Deployment item, confirming that monitoring configuration is understood by the project to be unfinished rather than deliberately omitted.

## 9.1 Additional Technical Information

This sub-section collects verifiable technical detail that is present in the repository but that no earlier section of this specification publishes in consolidated form. It is deliberately **additive and reference-shaped**: complete inventories, registers, and lookup catalogues rather than restated analysis. Where a topic is owned elsewhere — dependency inventories (`3.3`), toolchain configuration (`3.6`), monitoring semantics (`6.5`), infrastructure (`8.x`) — this sub-section cross-references the owning section instead of repeating it.

All figures below were measured directly against the repository checkout at branch `main`, commit `d78b068`.

Three structural observations follow. **The runtime modules declare no classes at all** — the entire application is written as module-level functions plus closures registered on the Flask app, which is why `6.x` describes components as functions rather than objects. **101 docstrings** exist across the four modules, more than one per three `def` statements. And of the 88 `def` statements in the test modules, 36 are test functions (`test_app.py` 25, `test_wsgi.py` 11), 11 are `@pytest.fixture` declarations (5 and 6 respectively), and the remainder are inline helpers; only three marker decorators are actually applied in source (`@pytest.mark.benchmark` in both modules and `@pytest.mark.parametrize` in `test_app.py`), against the 17 and 10 markers declared in the two `pytest.ini` files.

#### 9.1.1.6 Migration Provenance Comment Density

The migration mapping described in `1.1.2` is implemented as an explicit comment convention. Counting occurrences of the literal token `Replaces`:

| Module | "Replaces …" Statements |
|---|---|
| `src/backend/app.py` | 43 |
| `src/backend/wsgi.py` | 22 |
| `src/backend/tests/test_app.py` | 7 |
| `src/backend/tests/test_wsgi.py` | 7 |
| **Total** | **79** |

Sixty-five of the 79 are in the runtime modules — one provenance statement for approximately every 20 lines of runtime code. Representative anchors: `app.py` L4 (module-level, `Express.js app.js` → Flask factory), L18 (middleware stack → request lifecycle), L51 (`process.env` loading), L55 (`console.log` → `logging`), L92 (`express()` → `Flask(__name__)`), L96 (`app.set()` → config dictionary), L100 (security middleware → configuration); and `wsgi.py` L4 (`server.js` → WSGI factory integration), L15 (HTTP server lifecycle → WSGI server), L47 (`require('./app.js')` → `import`), L61 (`console.log` → enterprise logging), L73 (server instance → Flask application object).

The two modules also carry asymmetric cross-runtime vocabulary: `app.py` mentions Express on 38 lines and Node.js on 7, while `wsgi.py` mentions Node.js on 27 lines and Express on 1 — consistent with `app.py` replacing `app.js` (an Express artefact) and `wsgi.py` replacing `server.js` (a Node runtime artefact).

Two consequences are worth recording. First, the history is **machine-assembled one commit per file** rather than authored feature-by-feature, which is why it does not follow the seven-type conventional-commit scheme that `CONTRIBUTING.md` documents (see `9.2.2`). Second, **there are no git tags**, so the `[tool.setuptools_scm]` block in `pyproject.toml` — which declares `version_scheme = "python-simplified-semver"` — has no tag from which to derive a version; the static `version = "1.0.0"` in `[project]` is the only effective version source.

### 9.1.2 Consolidated Environment Variable Register

Configuration is spread across eight independent setting layers, and no single file enumerates the result. **49 distinct variable names** are set somewhere in the repository. Of those, **exactly five are read by application code**, verified by exhaustively locating every `os.getenv`/`os.environ` reference in the four Python modules.

#### 9.1.2.1 Setting Layers

| Layer | Artefact | Role |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `src/backend/.env.example` | Documented developer contract (7 active assignments) |
| 2 | `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` | Five `ENV` blocks across the `base`, `application`, `development`, and `production` stages |
| 3 | `infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml` | Per-service `environment:` maps (dev and prod) plus three build args |
| 4 | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Workflow-level `env:` block |
| 5 | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | Workflow-level `env:` block |
| 6 | `.github/workflows/cd.yml` | Step-level `env:` on the Azure deploy and Trivy steps |
| 7 | `pytest.ini`, `src/backend/pytest.ini` | `env =` blocks consumed by `pytest-env` |
| 8 | `src/backend/tests/test_wsgi.py` | Session-scoped fixture mutating `os.environ` (L98-L124) |

These five are the entire runtime configuration surface. Every other variable in the repository influences the interpreter, the installer, the WSGI server, the pipeline, or nothing at all.

| Variable | Read At | Default in Code |
|---|---|---|
| `FLASK_ENV` | `app.py` L155; `wsgi.py` L104, L462, L495 | caller-supplied in `app.py`; `'production'` in `wsgi.py` |
| `FLASK_DEBUG` | `app.py` L156 (`.lower() == 'true'`) | `'false'` |
| `SECRET_KEY` | `app.py` L161 | `'dev-key-change-in-production'` |
| `HOST` | `app.py` L721; `wsgi.py` L105, L502 | `'localhost'` / `'0.0.0.0'` / `'localhost'` |
| `PORT` | `app.py` L722; `wsgi.py` L106, L503 | `'8000'` in all three sites |

| Variable | `.env.example` | Container (`Dockerfile` / Compose) | CD Deploy Step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PORT` | `3000` (L38) | `3000` / `3000` | `8000` |
| `HOST` | `localhost` (L52) | `0.0.0.0` / `0.0.0.0` | not set |

Because `app.py` and `wsgi.py` both default `PORT` to `8000` while every container layer sets `3000` and the CD step sets `8000`, the effective port depends entirely on which layer is active — the divergence recorded in `1.3` and `2.4.1` (F-011), shown here with the value from each layer side by side.

#### 9.1.2.4 Variables Set But Never Read by Application Code

Grouped by their actual consumer. None of these reaches `app.py` or `wsgi.py`.

| Consumer | Variables |
|---|---|
| Flask / Werkzeug tooling | `FLASK_APP`, `WERKZEUG_RUN_MAIN`, `WERKZEUG_DEBUG_PIN`, `FLASK_RUN_PORT` |
| CPython interpreter | `PYTHONPATH`, `PYTHONUNBUFFERED`, `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE`, `PYTHONHASHSEED`, `PYTHON_VERSION` |
| `pip` | `PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK`, `PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR`, `PIP_UPGRADE_STRATEGY` |
| Gunicorn | `GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS`, `GUNICORN_WORKERS`, `GUNICORN_TIMEOUT`, `GUNICORN_KEEPALIVE`, `GUNICORN_MAX_REQUESTS`, `GUNICORN_MAX_REQUESTS_JITTER` |
| Nothing (declared only) | `WORKERS`, `WORKER_CONNECTIONS`, `MAX_REQUESTS`, `MAX_REQUESTS_JITTER`, `TIMEOUT`, `KEEPALIVE`, `LOG_LEVEL` |
| Test harness | `TESTING`, `WTF_CSRF_ENABLED`, `WSGI_PORT` |
| Pipeline / build | `CI`, `COVERAGE_THRESHOLD`, `FORCE_COLOR`, `DOCKER_BUILDKIT`, `COMPOSE_DOCKER_CLI_BUILD`, `REGISTRY`, `IMAGE_NAME`, `TRIVY_USERNAME`, `TRIVY_PASSWORD` |
| Metadata / labels only | `TUTORIAL_MODE`, `TUTORIAL_VERSION`, `TUTORIAL_ENVIRONMENT`, `EDUCATIONAL_MODE`, `COMPOSE_SERVICE`, `BUILD_DATE`, `VCS_REF` |

Three specific findings in this register are not recorded elsewhere:

- The **"nothing" row is the largest single group of inert configuration**. `WORKERS`, `WORKER_CONNECTIONS`, `MAX_REQUESTS`, `MAX_REQUESTS_JITTER`, `TIMEOUT`, and `KEEPALIVE` are set as `ENV` in the `production` stage (`Dockerfile` L190-L198) but Gunicorn is configured entirely through the literal `GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS` string on L216, which repeats the same numbers as command-line flags. Changing the `ENV` values therefore changes nothing. `LOG_LEVEL` is discussed in `6.5.1.3`.
- `BUILD_DATE` and `VCS_REF` are passed as Compose **build args** (L47-L48 and L188-L189) but `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` declares **no `ARG` instruction at all**, so both values are discarded at build time.
- The deploy-time variables in `cd.yml` (L482-L490 staging, L695-L706 production) are attached as **step-level `env:` on the `azure/webapps-deploy@v2` action**, not as Web App application settings; the workflow contains no `app-settings` input of any kind.

Anyone writing a log parser for this system needs only those seven plus ⚠️ and ❌.

#### 9.1.3.1 Guarded-Import Diagnostics and Exit Semantics

Both modules wrap their third-party imports in `try`/`except ImportError` blocks that print a remediation command before terminating. The three guards do **not** behave the same way, and the difference determines whether a failure is recoverable:

| Guard | Remediation Printed | Termination |
|---|---|---|
| `app.py` L38-L48 (`flask`, `flask_cors`, `dotenv`) | `pip install Flask>=3.1.1 Flask-CORS>=4.0.0 python-dotenv>=1.0.1` | `raise ImportError(...) from e` — chained re-raise |
| `wsgi.py` L35-L44 (`flask`, `dotenv`, `psutil`) | `pip install Flask>=3.1.1 python-dotenv>=1.0.1 psutil>=5.9.0` | `sys.exit(1)` |
| `wsgi.py` L46-L53 (`from app import create_app`) | "Ensure `app.py` exists in the same directory with `create_app()` function" | `sys.exit(1)` |

Each block emits four lines in a fixed order — ❌ the exception text, 🔧 an instruction, the indented `pip install` command, then 🎓 an explanatory note. The `app.py` guard preserves the exception chain and is therefore observable by a caller or test; both `wsgi.py` guards terminate the interpreter, which is why an import problem in the WSGI layer surfaces as a container that exits rather than an application that reports an error. The `psutil` line in the second guard is the remediation for the runtime-manifest gap recorded in `2.4.1` (F-010) and `3.3.2`.

Both modules configure logging with an identical single call:

```python
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                    format='%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')
```

### 9.1.5 Declarative-Only Configuration Keys

A substantial share of this repository's configuration is **documentation written in configuration syntax**: keys and tables that are syntactically valid but that no tool reads. Collecting them in one place prevents them from being mistaken for enforced settings, and it explains why several thresholds appear in the specification as "declared" rather than "enforced".

#### 9.1.5.1 Inert `pyproject.toml` Tables

`pyproject.toml` contains 28 TOML tables. Six of them are consumed by nothing in this repository:

| Table (line) | Declared Keys | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `[tool.flake8]` (L405) | `max-line-length`, `max-complexity`, `extend-ignore`, `per-file-ignores` | Self-documented as inert — the file comments say the settings "would apply if flake8 supported pyproject.toml"; the live configuration is `.flake8` |
| `[tool.pip-tools]` (L445) | `generate-hashes = true`, `upgrade = false`, `quiet = 1` | No compiled or hashed requirements file was ever committed |
| `[tool.pytest-benchmark]` (L451) | `min_time`, `max_time`, `min_rounds = 3`, `timer = "time.perf_counter"`, `disable_gc`, `histogram`, `json_output` | Not the table `pytest-benchmark` reads, and no benchmark output is archived |
| `[tool.memory-monitor]` (L461) | `limit_mb = 75`, `growth_limit_mb = 5`, `enable_tracking`, `psutil_integration` | No tool named `memory-monitor` exists in any manifest |
| `[tool.ci]` (L472) | `github_actions = true`, `artifact_retention_days = 30`, `parallel_jobs = "auto"` | Retention is actually set per upload step in the workflows |
| `[tool.quality-gates]` (L479) | `coverage_threshold = 100`, `performance_regression_threshold = 10`, `memory_limit_mb = 75`, `response_time_limit_ms = 50`, `security_scan_required = true` | Only the coverage figure is independently enforced, by `pytest` and `ci.yml` |

`[tool.pytest.ini_options]` (L156) and its nested `[tool.pytest.ini_options.benchmark]` (L224) are valid pytest configuration but are **shadowed** by the two `pytest.ini` files, which take precedence — the finding recorded in `2.4.1` (F-013). The file also closes with a "Usage" comment block (L505-L514) documenting six commands: `pip install -e .[dev]`, `pytest`, `black .`, `mypy src/`, `bandit -r src/`, and `python -m build`.

#### 9.1.5.3 Verification Method and Two Consequential Findings

The classification above was established by comparing every key against pytest's own registered ini-option table. Of the keys listed, only `junit_*`, `console_output_style`, `cache_dir`, and `doctest_optionflags` are core pytest options; `addopts`, `minversion`, and `required_plugins` are also genuine. Everything else requires either a plugin or does not exist:

- **`asyncio_mode = auto`** (`src/backend/pytest.ini` L122) requires `pytest-asyncio`, which is declared in **none** of `requirements.txt`, `requirements-dev.txt`, `src/backend/requirements.txt`, or `pyproject.toml`. This is in addition to the `pytest-timeout` and `pytest-env` gaps recorded in `3.6.9`; `timeout`/`timeout_method` appear in both ini files and `pytest-timeout` is likewise undeclared.
- **`collect_ignore` is not an ini option at all** — it is a `conftest.py` module variable — and it is written here as a multi-line Python list literal. Attempting to start pytest with either configuration file present therefore fails during configuration parsing, before any test is collected: from the repository root the error is `pytest.ini:200: unexpected line: ']'`, and from `src/backend` it is `src/backend/pytest.ini:105: unexpected line: ']'`. Both `--strict-config` settings are irrelevant because parsing never completes.

The practical reading of this sub-section is that the declared-versus-enforced distinction used throughout `2.4`, `3.6`, and `6.5` is not incidental: roughly seventy-five configuration keys in this repository are commentary, and the enforced set is limited to `addopts` coverage flags, `flake8` settings in `.flake8`, `[tool.bandit]`, `[tool.black]`, `[tool.mypy]`, `[tool.isort]`, `[tool.coverage.*]`, and the workflow-level thresholds.

### 9.1.6 Documented Command and Invocation Register

The repository documents a large number of executable command strings across `README.md`, `src/backend/README.md`, the issue templates, the Compose runbook comments, and the container assets. Individual defects are noted in `2.4`, `3.6.9`, and `6.5.4.3`; this register consolidates the **command-string level** findings, with the exact counts and the verified-correct form for each, so the fix set is enumerable.

#### 9.1.6.1 WSGI Callable Reference Divergence

`src/backend/wsgi.py` exports the callable as `application` (L531, `__all__`). Counting exact occurrences of each spelling:

| Spelling | Occurrences | Locations |
|---|---|---|
| `wsgi:app` (incorrect) | **11** | `README.md` L182, L280, L485, L488, L491, L505, L594, L601, L637, L771; `infrastructure/docker/Dockerfile` L220 |
| `wsgi:application` (correct) | **11** | `wsgi.py` L399, L400, L401, L513; `bug_report.md` L66, L413, L416, L475; `docker-compose.yml` L263; `src/backend/README.md` L190; `.env.example` L12 |

`README.md` contains **zero** correct occurrences — every Gunicorn invocation in the root README, across the local-run, Heroku, Azure, Railway/DigitalOcean, Supervisor, and debug-logging sections, names the wrong attribute. The test suite uses the dotted form `src.backend.wsgi:application` in seven places (`test_wsgi.py` L390, L481, L557, L735, L810, L886, L1157), which is correct only when the process working directory is the repository root.

#### 9.1.6.2 Command-String Correctness Register

| Command as Written | Source | Why It Fails / Verified-Correct Form |
|---|---|---|
| `gunicorn wsgi:app --bind=0.0.0.0:3000 …` | `Dockerfile` L220 (production `CMD`) | Attribute `app` does not exist; use `wsgi:application` as `docker-compose.yml` L263 already does |
| `gunicorn --config gunicorn.conf.py wsgi:app` | `README.md` L491 | Two faults: the config file does not exist and the callable name is wrong |
| `web: gunicorn wsgi:app` | `README.md` L594 (`Procfile` content) | `Procfile` and `runtime.txt` do not exist; callable name wrong |
| `command=gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:5000 wsgi:app` | `README.md` L505 (`supervisord.conf` heredoc) | `supervisord.conf` is generated by the documentation only; port 5000 matches no other layer |
| `cat > scripts/validate_coverage.py` then `python scripts/validate_coverage.py` | `ci.yml` L248, L293 | `scripts/` does not exist and is not created first; the script also reads `../coverage/coverage.xml`, a path neither `pytest.ini` produces |
| `pytest` (from the repository root or `src/backend`) | both `pytest.ini` files | Configuration parsing aborts on the `collect_ignore` list literal — see `9.1.5.3` |
| `docker-compose up --scale flask-tutorial-dev=2` | `docker-compose.yml` L507 | Both services publish fixed host ports, so no replica beyond the first can bind |
| `docker-compose up --scale flask-tutorial-prod=3` | `docker-compose.yml` L530 | Same fixed-port conflict |
| `python -m build` | `pyproject.toml` L513 usage comment | Would emit `src/_version.py` and depends on a `src/`-rooted package layout that does not match the actual `src/backend/` flat-import arrangement |
| `npm ci`, `npm test`, `npm run lint` | `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` | Wrong ecosystem entirely — no `package.json` exists; see `9.2.2` |

#### 9.1.6.3 Correct Invocations the Repository Does Publish

For completeness, the invocations that are consistent with the delivered code are: `gunicorn wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:3000 --workers 4` (`src/backend/README.md` L190); the Compose production command `exec gunicorn wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:3000 --workers 4 --timeout 30 --keepalive 2 --max-requests 1000 --max-requests-jitter 100 --preload --log-level info` (L263); the diagnostic pair `gunicorn --check-config wsgi:application` and `gunicorn wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:3000 --log-level debug` (`bug_report.md` L413, L416); the factory smoke test `python -c "from app import create_app; app = create_app()"` (`bug_report.md` L384-L396); and the four startup-banner strings that `wsgi.py` itself prints at L399-L401 and L513.


## 9.2 Project Governance, Licensing, and Provenance

The repository carries a governance and provenance layer that is substantial in its own right — 3,249 lines of licence text, contribution rules, community standards, and intake templates, plus 4,961 lines of originating brief, status record, and retained predecessor specification. Earlier sections reference these artefacts for specific facts (`1.1.3` for stakeholders, `2.4.5` for maintenance obligations, `3.6.1` for the toolchain mismatch, `6.5.3.2` for response-time and escalation targets). What follows is the **structural and legal record** of those artefacts, which no other section publishes.

### 9.2.1 Licensing and Legal Notices

MIT is asserted in four places and backed by a file in none of them.

| Declaration Site | Form of Assertion |
|---|---|
| `pyproject.toml` L43 | `license = {text = "MIT"}` — PEP 621 metadata |
| `pyproject.toml` L69 | Trove classifier `License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License` |
| `README.md` L5 | Shields.io badge `license-MIT-green`, hyperlinked to `LICENSE` |
| `README.md` L936-L957 | The full verbatim MIT permission-and-warranty text, headed **"Copyright (c) 2024 Tutorial Author"** |

The `## License` section of `README.md` (L934-L976) is the only place a complete licence grant exists. It comprises the `### MIT License` heading with the copyright line and body text, a `### License Permissions` sub-section (L958) enumerating what is permitted — commercial use, modification, distribution, private use — the limitations (no liability, no warranty) and the single condition that the licence and copyright notice be included, and finally a `### License File` sub-section (L973) whose entire content is the sentence at L975 directing the reader to a `LICENSE` file "for complete license text and terms".

#### 9.2.1.1 Licensing Gaps and Inconsistencies

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| No `LICENSE` file exists | The 29 tracked files contain no `LICENSE`, `LICENSE.txt`, `LICENSE.md`, or `COPYING`; the badge target and the L975 link are both dead |
| Copyright holder is not the declared author | `README.md` L938 names "Tutorial Author"; `pyproject.toml` L45-L48 names "Flask Migration Tutorial Team <tutorial@example.com>" as both author and maintainer |
| Only one copyright notice in the repository | `README.md` L938 is the sole `Copyright` line; `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`, and `src/backend/README.md` carry none, and no source file carries a header notice |
| Advertised security-policy path is unbacked | `pyproject.toml` L148 publishes a `Security Policy` URL; no `SECURITY.md` exists anywhere |
| `Typing :: Typed` is claimed without a marker | `pyproject.toml` L79 declares the classifier; no `py.typed` file exists, so the claim is not machine-discoverable |
| Maturity claim exceeds recorded completeness | `pyproject.toml` L64 declares `Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable` while `blitzy/documentation/Project Guide.md` records 15 of 100 estimated hours outstanding |
| `.dockerignore` excludes licence files | L440-L441 list `LICENSE` and `LICENSE.txt` as build-context exclusions, so even if added they would not enter the image |

The `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` attribution block asserts (L340) that the code of conduct "is compatible with the MIT license of the … tutorial project", and the badge at `CONTRIBUTING.md` L6 renders the code-of-conduct link with the label `code%20of%20conduct-MIT` — conflating the conduct document with the software licence.

#### 9.2.1.2 Declared Project Metadata and URLs

The remaining PEP 621 metadata that constitutes the project's public identity:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `name` / `version` | `flask-migration-tutorial` / `1.0.0` (static, L40-L41) |
| `readme` / `requires-python` | `README.md` / `>=3.12` (L42, L81) |
| `keywords` (9) | flask, python, tutorial, migration, nodejs, web-framework, hello-world, pytest, enterprise (L50-L60) |
| `classifiers` (19) | Includes `Framework :: Flask`, `Intended Audience :: Developers` and `:: Education`, `Topic :: Education`, `Topic :: Internet :: WWW/HTTP :: WSGI :: Application`, and Python `:: 3.12` and `:: 3.13` (L62-L80) |

The six `[project.urls]` entries (L142-L148) all resolve under `github.com/flask-migration-tutorial/flask-hello-world`: `Homepage`, `Documentation` (a Read the Docs address), `Repository`, `Bug Tracker`, `CI/CD Pipeline`, and `Security Policy`. No `[project.scripts]` or `[project.entry-points]` table is declared, so the distribution would install no console entry point. The classifiers advertise Python 3.13 support although `.github/workflows/ci.yml` tests 3.12, 3.11, and 3.10.

### 9.2.2 Contribution Governance and Review Standards

`CONTRIBUTING.md` is the second-largest file in the repository (1,891 lines, 63,174 bytes) and the most structurally elaborate: 31 second-level headings, 105 third-level, 72 fourth-level, 10 tables, 118 fenced code blocks, and 64 checkboxes. Its title is `# Contributing to Node.js Hello World Tutorial` and it carries four badges (Node.js v22.16.0 LTS, Express.js v5.1.0, Contributions Welcome, Code of Conduct). The toolchain mismatch this creates for a contributor is analysed in `3.6.1`; the content model is documented here.

#### 9.2.2.1 Document Structure

| Thematic Group | Sections | Lines |
|---|---|---|
| Orientation | Guidelines for Educational Contributions; Table of Contents; Contribution Overview | L8, L25, L39 |
| Environment and standards | Development Setup; Code Standards; Testing Guidelines | L84, L286, L509 |
| Pull-request lifecycle | Pull Request Process; Summary; Educational Alignment; Technical Implementation; Testing and Quality Assurance; Quality Assurance Checklist; CI/CD Integration; Review Feedback Template | L808 – L1053 |
| Documentation and accessibility | Documentation Standards; Learning Objectives Supported; Accessibility Guidelines | L1120, L1314, L1338 |
| Issue intake and escalation | Issue Reporting; Educational Enhancement Proposal; Documentation Enhancement; Issue Escalation Guidelines | L1361 – L1480 |
| Security | Security Guidelines; Security Vulnerability Report Template; Security Education Goals | L1503, L1512, L1624 |
| Recognition and progression | Recognition Program; Contributors; Community Support Awards; Monthly Contributor Recognition; Contributor Nomination; Learning Achievement Recognition; Path to Maintainership | L1696 – L1861 |

#### 9.2.2.2 Branch, Commit, and Workflow Conventions

The prescribed workflow (L814-L838) is a five-step fork-and-branch model: synchronise `main` with the upstream remote; create a descriptively named branch; commit with a subject line plus a bulleted body; push the branch to the fork; open the pull request through the GitHub interface.

| Convention | Prescribed Form |
|---|---|
| Branch prefixes | `feature/`, `fix/`, `docs/`, `test/` — worked examples `feature/add-health-check-endpoint`, `fix/resolve-port-binding-error`, `docs/improve-setup-instructions`, `test/add-performance-testing` (L821-L824) |
| Commit subject | `Type(scope): Brief description`, optionally followed by a detailed explanation, an educational-impact note, and breaking changes (L897-L902) |
| Commit types (7) | `Add`, `Fix`, `Update`, `Docs`, `Test`, `Refactor`, `Security` — each documented with a description and two examples (L895-L910) |

The delivered git history does not follow this convention: 72 of the 81 commits carry the subject form `File: <path>` (see `9.1.1.7`), so the documented scheme has never been exercised in this repository.

#### 9.2.2.3 Review Weighting Model

`CONTRIBUTING.md` L1037-L1040 assigns explicit numeric weights to four review dimensions — the only weighted review rubric in the repository:

| Criterion | Weight | Reviewer Question Set (as written) |
|---|---|---|
| Educational Value | 40 % | Does this improve concept understanding? Are the framework patterns clear? Is educational progression maintained? |
| Technical Quality | 30 % | Runtime best practices, framework patterns, error handling, performance targets |
| Testing Completeness | 20 % | Test-framework patterns, HTTP assertion library usage, 95 % coverage, edge cases |
| Documentation Quality | 10 % | Educational comments, updated documentation, clear examples, accessibility |

Two properties of this rubric are worth recording. It is **weighted toward pedagogy rather than correctness** — educational value alone outweighs technical quality — which is coherent with the project's stated purpose but means a functionally correct change with low explanatory value scores poorly. And its Testing Completeness row still names the Node-era test stack and a 95 % coverage figure, which the pipeline's hard 100 % gate supersedes.

#### 9.2.2.4 Contributor Progression

`Path to Maintainership` (L1861-L1886) is the only role-progression definition in the repository. Core Contributor status requires six or more months of consistent quality contributions, twenty or more merged pull requests with educational value, active code-review participation with constructive feedback, community mentoring experience, technical expertise in the (Node-era) stack, and educational leadership. The section then lists five maintainer responsibilities — code-quality oversight, community leadership, educational vision, mentor development, and technical architecture — and five benefits, including repository merge permissions and input on framework updates. Because no `CODEOWNERS` file exists (`9.1.4.2`), these roles have no mechanical enforcement in the repository.

### 9.2.3 Community Standards and Code of Conduct

`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` (359 lines) is an adaptation of the **Contributor Covenant version 2.1** (attributed at L334, with the canonical URL), extended with sections specific to an educational project. It contains 11 second-level headings, 15 third-level, 31 fourth-level, and — unusually for this repository — no tables, no code fences, and no checkboxes.

Its heading chain declares the pre-migration identity explicitly: `# Code of Conduct` (L1) → `## Node.js Tutorial Application Community Standards` (L2) → a subtitle at L4. The scope line (L6) covers the GitHub repository, issues, pull requests, discussions, and related communications; the educational-context line (L8) names Node.js v22.16.0 LTS and Express.js v5.1.0 as the subject matter.

| Section | Line | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Our Pledge | L12 | Harassment-free participation pledge plus three educational commitments |

| Enforcement Responsibilities | L68 | Leader obligations |

| Enforcement | L104 | Reporting Violations (L106), Investigation Process (L119), Enforcement Guidelines (L135) |
| Educational Environment Guidelines | L167 | Supporting Learners, Skill Level Inclusivity, Accessibility and Inclusion |
